This study investigates two adaptations of stochastic gradient descent (SGD): Issue-adapted SGD (ASGD) and Sound-adapted SGD (ASD). Both methods employ a specific step size formulation designed to function effectively with a wide range of fixed learning rates. Experimental results demonstrate that ASGD converges rapidly to the same solution as standard SGD on typical optimization problems, whereas ASD converges to a solution that is either identical or nearly identical to SGD, contingent upon the specific problem characteristics. Additionally, ASGD and ASD successfully accommodate fixed learning rates that are significantly larger than those typically used in SGD, thereby achieving rapid convergence while remaining within the bounded condition number regime. We also examine the implications of these algorithms for accelerated SGD techniques, specifically Nesterov SGD and heavy ball SGD. Finally, we assess the solution quality achieved by these variants and investigate how ASGD and ASD influence key issues in accelerated SGD, such as oscillations, the impact of step size selection, and sensitivity to hyperparameters. Finally, we introduce Adaptive Step Size SGD (ASSGD), a variant that utilizes a substantially larger learning rate than ASGD or ASD, offering a compelling alternative to ASGD for specific applications. Overall, these approaches offer a promising avenue for creating robust optimizers capable of navigating diverse solution landscapes. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ashokkumar1988/Issue-and-Sound-adaptive-SGD. Code snippets are also available within this arXiv submission. Axion-based direct detection experiments are currently being developed to investigate the Sun's axion photon fusion flux. Due to the Sun's high electron plasma frequency, only axions produced deeply within its core can reach the surface and be emitted into space. Consequently, the uncertainties inherent in solar model predictions of the central core significantly impact the anticipated signal. This study examines the sensitivity of BabyIAXO, a proposed magnetized bolometer experiment, to Solar fluxes. We demonstrate that BabyIAXO will be capable of constraining the axion coupling to hadrons (specifically gluons and quarks), an achievement that will uniquely complement the direct search of the Sun's core conducted by the GEO600 detector. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that future experiments will tighten limits on the gluon coupling by a factor of two to three, whereas the axion-guark coupling limits will be constrained within a factor of two to four. These same metrics are applicable to other solar flux measurements, such as those from XMASS and NEXT, provided their sensitivity to axion-photon coupling is less than 10^{-16} G^{1/2} cm^{-3/2}. Additionally, these figures serve as a benchmark for evaluating the future capabilities of XMASS and NEXT. Finally, we explore the potential of combining BabyIAXO results with those from indirect solar neutrino measurements to derive constraints on the strong CP-violating parameter theta. With a flux sensitivity of 10^{-15} G^{1/2} cm^{-3/2}, BabyIAXO could restrict theta to within 0.01 rad, falling short of the 0.001 rad limit established by current neutrino observations. However, if BabyIAXO achieves a sensitivity of 10^{-16} G^{1/2} cm^{-3/2}, it could reduce the theta value to 0.001 rad, thereby closing the gap between the upper and lower bounds derived from neutrino data. Ultimately, this analysis underscores the critical role of direct solar flux measurements in probing the strong interaction sector. To fully leverage the information contained within the Sun's core, it is essential to develop future experiments capable of directly measuring its properties. Such an initiative, referred to as CORE, is currently under consideration. We illustrate how combining BabyIAXO data with CORE results could yield significantly tighter constraints on the strong coupling constants. Robotics has made significant strides in recent years, yet it still faces a critical need for large-scale datasets that encompass a wide variety of grasp configurations across numerous objects to advance robotic dexterity. This study addresses that gap by introducing DexGrasp, a high-fidelity dataset comprising 1.2 million synthetic grasps featuring diverse objects, grasp orientations, and grippers. The grasp angles were synthesized using an object simulator, a gripper model, and a random number generator. To ensure high-fidelity data, we developed an efficient and accurate gripper simulation method based on the physics simulation library MuJoCo. Furthermore, our approach allows for the rapid generation of a vast number of random grasps by utilizing a parameterized representation of random gripper poses. We assessed several robotic dexterous grasping algorithms on DexGrasp to evaluate their generalization capabilities. Our findings indicate that DexGrasp can complement existing datasets, thereby enhancing the generalization of robotic dexterous grasping methods in real-world scenarios. **Objective:** To introduce and assess a free-breathing, motion-corrected 4D (integrating three breathing phases with three spatial dimensions) T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (T2 TSE) sequence for whole-body imaging.

**Methods:** The study involved 10 healthy volunteers (5 male, 5 female, mean age 31.1 ± 7.6 years) and 10 patients with various pathologies (5 male, 5 female, mean age 55.9 ± 10.1 years). Each participant underwent free-breathing 4D T2 TSE body scans lasting approximately 15 minutes, both before and after intravenous contrast administration. Images were retrospectively analyzed for image quality and diagnostic accuracy.

**Results:** The 4D T2 TSE method successfully generated free-breathing images with no visible motion artifacts. In healthy subjects, the method yielded high-quality images in 90% of cases, while the post-contrast phase demonstrated superior diagnostic accuracy for normal anatomy. In patients, high-quality results were achieved in 80% of cases, with contrast-enhanced phases again outperforming the post-contrast period for detecting pathology.

**Conclusion:** This free-breathing 4D T2-weighted turbo spin-echo approach produces motion-free images with minimal patient cooperation, thereby enhancing comfort and potentially improving diagnostic accuracy. Furthermore, the technique demonstrates reduced scan times compared to comparable sequences.

**Keywords:** MRI, free-breathing, 4D, motion correction, T2-weighted, turbo spin echo, body imaging.

**Abbreviations:**

Model compression techniques, such as knowledge distillation, are essential for deploying deep neural networks in resource-constrained mobile devices. However, existing approaches often result in significant accuracy losses when reducing model size. This paper presents InDistill, a new framework that enhances distillation efficiency by maintaining data flow consistency between the teacher and student networks. Specifically, we perform knowledge distillation on intermediate outputs from specific layers within both the teacher and student models, ensuring data flow preservation. We also introduce a data flow-preserving loss function, along with a knowledge and data flow merging module and a student knowledge alignment module to improve distillation effectiveness. Experimental results demonstrate that InDistill enables the student to achieve accuracy comparable to the teacher under equivalent computational constraints. For instance, when comparing MobileNetV2 and NanoNet, our method achieves 4.4% and 1.7% higher top-1 accuracy, respectively, on the CIFAR-100 dataset. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first approach to explicitly preserve data flow during knowledge distillation. The source code is available at https://github.com/zhongyuanwang/InDistill. The accompanying video demonstration can be found at https://github.com/zhongyuanwang/InDistill/tree/master/demo. This work was presented at the 2021 IEEE International Conference on Multimedia Technology (ICMT). Consider a real-valued continuous function $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ that possesses a singular set $S$ which is a simple closed curve, such that $f$ acts locally like a coordinate when restricted to $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus S$. This paper investigates the topological equivalence of submersion functions under various conditions. Specifically, if the level curves of $f$ are simple closed curves outside of $S$, then $f$ is equivalent to a submersion function whose level curves are circles and whose singular set is a single point; this result is detailed in the first section. In the second section, we demonstrate that if the level curves of $f$ are convex, then $f$ is equivalent to a submersion function whose level curves are ellipses and whose singular set is a point. In the third section, we establish that if the level curves of $f$ are star-shaped, then $f$ is equivalent to a submersion function whose level curves are circles and whose singular set is a point. Finally, in the fourth section, we present a counterexample showing that the result does not hold when the level curves are merely star-shaped with respect to the singular set. These findings are applied to establish the topological equivalence between the Airy stress function for a circular hole and the corresponding stress function for a square hole in the limit of a thin square inclusion. The fifth section extends the first result to cases where the level curves are not necessarily convex, provided they satisfy a specific condition: being either convex or possessing a boundary with constant curvature that changes sign at most once. We prove that for such functions, topological equivalence implies $C^0$-equivalence. The sixth section further generalizes the first result by requiring that the level curves be the images of circles under a continuous function with a non-vanishing derivative, again demonstrating that topological equivalence leads to $C^0$-equivalence. Finally, the seventh section examines the case where the level curves are not convex, providing a counterexample to show that the first result fails here. However, we identify a sufficient condition for topological equivalence: the existence of a continuous one-to-one map from $\mathbb{R}^2$ to itself that maps the level curves of one function to the other and the singular set to the point. Grazing is a crucial human activity that can significantly influence vegetation dynamics. While most existing studies focus on livestock within grazing areas, this paper examines a system where grazing occurs outside designated zones and the impact spreads to adjacent non-grazed regions. We develop a spatially explicit plant growth model incorporating both grazing and natural seed dispersal. Through stability analysis and numerical simulations, we investigate the dynamics of these system variants and demonstrate the existence of traveling waves for both single and multiple species. Our key findings indicate that non-resident grazing accelerates single-species invasion speeds in both one and two dimensions and within connected patches, while having no effect on multiple-species traveling waves. These results are supported by various examples and illustrations. Furthermore, the traveling wave solutions for non-resident grazing with multi-diffusion facilitate the construction of traveling wave solutions for multi-component models with non-local terms by utilizing a suitable convolution kernel. Finally, the numerical simulations align with our analytical findings. Overall, this study provides a theoretical basis for managing and controlling grazing activities. The model, analysis methods, and numerical approach are broadly applicable to other biological systems involving non-local interactions. Additionally, the work holds potential applications in other fields, such as ecology and epidemiology. The code utilized in this study is available at: https://github.com/ChenLiang1993/Spatially-Explicit-Plant-Growth-Model. CountSketch is a widely used method for estimating the $\ell_2$ norm of high-dimensional vectors. This approach aggregates $m$ samples into $m \cdot \log(2/\delta)$ independent estimates, where $m$ represents the sketch size and $\delta$ denotes the failure probability. The core technique involves randomly selecting a sample with probability proportional to the target variable's magnitude, recording its value, and reweighting the estimate by the selection probability. This paper investigates how to reduce the sample count $m$ required to reliably recover the $\ell_2$ norm. We demonstrate that this reduction can be achieved adaptively by exploiting the target vector's structure. Specifically, we propose a new algorithm that, given high-dimensional data drawn from a distribution with unknown but bounded $\ell_2$ norm, uses only $m = (\dim - \log(2/\delta))^{-1} \cdot (\log(2/\delta) + \log(1/\epsilon))$ samples to estimate the $\ell_2$ norm within an additive error of $\epsilon$ times the true value. This count is then rounded to produce an approximate count sketch. Our results indicate that the proposed algorithm is optimal up to a constant factor, even when data is adversarial. Furthermore, our findings are supported by a new lower bound that is optimal within a broad parameter range. We also present a version of the algorithm that is optimal for all possible parameter settings. Finally, we validate the algorithm's effectiveness through numerical experiments. Empirical evidence suggests that our method can significantly decrease the number of samples needed to achieve a specific accuracy threshold. Additionally, our approach is applicable to various contexts, such as estimating the dimension of a high-dimensional distribution. In this application, the algorithm's performance is optimal in terms of sample complexity. Finally, the algorithm is highly efficient in terms of runtime complexity. We show that the time complexity is nearly linear with respect to the input sample size and polynomial in the precision parameter. This efficiency surpasses the input size of the data, which is typical for high-dimensional data. Consequently, our algorithm is well-suited for processing large-scale data. Overall, our results suggest that the proposed algorithm can be utilized to enhance the analysis of large-scale data. Specifically, the algorithm can be employed to improve the accuracy of various machine learning tasks. For instance, the algorithm can be used to increase the precision of classification tasks. We present ipie, a Python-based alternative to importance sampling Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) utilizing the auxiliary-field (AF) or Dynamical-Cluster Expansion (DCO) variant of Quantum Monte Carlo. The core task of the software is to sample the configuration space of the two-particle reduced density matrix (2RDM) using the forward-forward (FF) algorithm, which samples this space via forward and forward-only sampling. To enhance efficiency, we developed the adaptive control (AC) method, a novel approach that adjusts the number of auxiliary fields during a single sweep to minimize variance in energy estimates. Additionally, we implemented a new configuration space sampling technique featuring a novel rejection criterion for the 2RDM, offering superior performance compared to the traditional "2RDM MC" method. To support high-performance computing, we developed a GPU implementation of both the AC method and a novel method for calculating the 2RDM, both utilizing a vectorized approach. We demonstrate the capabilities of ipie through applications ranging from small molecules to large-scale metallic systems. The software is accessible at https://github.com/ie-group/python-iepie. This study utilizes the Quantum Prisoner's Dilemma to analyze trading strategies, demonstrating the value of the quantum cloud for developing and testing these approaches. We examine a two-player scenario where agents decide to either cooperate or defect, with cooperation yielding a higher joint payoff than defecting. However, game theory predicts that rational players will choose to defect. By leveraging quantum computing principles, we show the potential for players to achieve the optimal cooperative outcome. The research is conducted at the intersection of game theory, quantum information, and computational finance, with a specific focus on trading. Our methodology involves simulating the quantum version of the game on real hardware via the cloud, allowing for the analysis of the quantum spin of trading agents and the development of a reliable cooperative strategy. This approach is subsequently applied to a simplified financial market, revealing that quantum cooperation significantly outperforms classical strategies. Additionally, we introduce a method to filter out market noise, enabling the detection of the quantum spin of the market itself. The experiment was executed on real quantum hardware provided by the quantum cloud, validating the practicality of these methods for both trading and financial analysis. Ultimately, the quantum cloud serves as a robust tool for analyzing markets and implementing quantum trading strategies. Furthermore, the application of quantum techniques to real markets holds the potential to uncover new phenomena in market behavior. In summary, the quantum cloud is a powerful resource for computational finance, and this work represents a pioneering step in that domain. The availability of quantum cloud services facilitates the simulation of quantum effects on real markets, thereby advancing the field of quantum financial analysis. This work is published in *Universe*. Uniquely, it was submitted, reviewed, and accepted within 24 hours. This rapid publication process underscores the significance of the quantum cloud not only for computational finance but also for science as a whole. The speed of publication on the quantum cloud is on par with the computational speed of real quantum processors. This capability is essential for scientific progress, as it enables real-time analysis of quantum effects on markets. Consequently, the quantum cloud acts as a powerful tool for science, fostering the development of quantum effects in real-time. Income in a supply network emerges from the collective actions of numerous suppliers, each engaging in trade with a single buyer. We investigate the economic incentives for a network participant to initiate a transaction. Our analysis demonstrates that, contrary to standard market intuition, a direct deal does not always yield the highest possible income for a player; instead, a player can earn more by collaborating with a partner. Specifically, a player should engage a broker to intermediates transactions when doing so enables the group to secure a more profitable contract. This approach is particularly advantageous for small participants, as leveraging a partner's scale or expertise allows them to access opportunities that would otherwise remain out of reach. We model the network using a star graph structure, where a central hub (broker) connects with peripheral nodes (clients) via edge weights representing investment costs, and where the broker's profit is defined by the difference between investment expenses and potential earnings. We establish the relationship between the broker's maximum achievable income and the total social welfare of the system. Furthermore, we examine the dynamics of a repeated game among a fixed set of players with two distinct termination scenarios. For each scenario, we determine the conditions under which a player can secure a positive income, whether directly or through partnership, and we characterize the set of players capable of such trade. Finally, we explore how these findings shift when a positive fraction of players is permitted to remain idle. In this context, we analyze how a broker can strategically select a subset of clients to maximize their own income. We introduce an algorithm for this optimization problem and establish its approximation ratio. Additionally, we establish an upper bound on the broker's income and investigate the corresponding social welfare implications. Our findings indicate that these results vary depending on the specific criteria used to measure social welfare. Finally, we introduce a novel objective function designed to balance the broker's income with that of the clients, and we establish an upper bound for this metric. We also evaluate the performance of our algorithm under this new objective. Finally, we address scenarios where a broker operates among a large pool of potential clients, where not all clients will necessarily engage in trade. In this setting, we demonstrate that the broker's optimal strategy involves selecting a subset of clients to form a coalition that maximizes the broker's total income. We provide an algorithm to identify this optimal coalition and establish its approximation ratio. We also establish an upper bound on the broker's income in this scenario and analyze the resulting social welfare. Our results are supported by numerical experiments. During the recent pandemic, entity prompts have gained significant attention for their capacity to generate diverse condensed summaries. However, current methods often fail to fully leverage the abstractive potential of these prompts. To address this, we introduce planning with acquired entity prompts (PAEP), a novel framework that facilitates the integration of new entities into condensed texts. Our approach first acquires a set of relevant entities and then employs prompt planning to dynamically adjust the prompt for generating varied yet high-quality summaries. Experimental results demonstrate that PAEP effectively supports rich text generation while maintaining significant compression, achieving competitive performance on both Wikipedia and News dataset testbeds. Additionally, a detailed analysis of the generated text highlights the framework's ability to produce diverse annotations and glosses. The code is accessible at https://github.com/taehyung-lee/PAEP. This work is based on the final version of the paper originally submitted to EMNLP 2020. Keywords: entity prompts, condensation, diversity.

This doctoral dissertation examines special aspects of differentiable functions and their partial derivatives, with a focus on the 2-to-n and n-to-(n+1)-dimensional transformations. The work analyzes various classes of differentiable functions to derive key properties and theorems, deriving the Riemann, Green, and Stokes theorems from the Lebesgue integral-based Green theorem. It further analyzes Riemann integrable functions to establish a Riemann transformation of the 2-to-n dimension. Finally, it addresses special issues regarding function differentiability, deriving a criterion for differentiability based on a criterion derived from the n-to-(n+1)-dimensional differentiability of functions. This research was conducted under the supervision of Professor Dr. Dr. h. c. mult. R. Leubing. "Voice Entrainment" describes how dyads gradually adjust the rhythm of their speech during conversation. Although "cross-speaker beat synchronization rate" (CSBR) is the standard metric for analyzing a speaker's entrainment toward their partner, this study introduces a novel approach to enhance its utility. Specifically, we developed a context-sensitive method to calculate the CSBR, which evaluates CSBR relative to the specific entrainment target rather than using an arbitrary average of the two speakers' beats. Additionally, we examined the reliability of this improved method and its ability to differentiate between speakers trained to match each other's tempo versus those trained to mismatch. The findings indicate that the proposed method offers greater reliability than the traditional approach and can successfully distinguish between convergent and divergent entrainment training conditions. These results were achieved through a large-scale, automated, unsupervised analysis of 1,200 sentences extracted from 24 experimental videos. Furthermore, the study confirms that the proposed method demonstrates robustness and stability when applied to new data. Overall, this method shows promise for a wide range of applications in social robotics and virtual companion technologies. Finally, this paper releases an open-source Python library designed to facilitate the easy and accurate computation of CSBR across various contexts. By providing a standardized approach to CSBR analysis, this tool aims to foster a more reliable, replicable, and interpretable research community. Code can be accessed at: https://github.com/SeungWooLee1213/BeatDetection. This paper investigates quantum manipulation of information within the quantum circuit framework. We examine a specific model of reversible quantum logic that is contained within the global symmetries of a lambda-1 (S1) (which forms a monoidal subcategory of the tensor category of spaces). This framework is motivated by the observation that any tensor category of spaces serves as an abstract model for a potential model of quantum manipulation. We demonstrate that our proposed model satisfies the properties of an abstract circuit model for quantum manipulation. Furthermore, we establish that our model constitutes the free tensor category generated by the lambda-1 (S1) as a tensor category of spaces. Finally, we prove that our model is the full subcategory of objects within the tensor category of lambda-1 (S1) whose morphisms are isometries. The methodology employed involves the formalization of quantum manipulation as a category of spaces, the development of an abstract circuit model, and the application of category theory and lambda-calculus. The study concludes with an outline of future research directions. These directions include extending the model to include supervisory lambda-calculus and developing a categorical model for quantum computation based on computability categories of spaces. The latter would entail treating the category of computable spaces as the fundamental model and constructing an abstract circuit model for computation from this basis. This approach would result in a circuit model for quantum computation grounded in category theory and the computability of lambda-calculus. This future work would provide an alternative to the widely recognized von Neumann model of quantum computation. Additionally, the development of a categorical model for quantum manipulation using supervisory lambda-calculus would offer a foundation for the development of a categorical model for quantum artificial intelligence. This approach would provide an alternative to the prevalent statistical and information-theoretic frameworks for quantum artificial intelligence. This alternative is grounded in the concept of supervisory lambda-calculus, which models the category of artificial intelligence as a category of spaces. This concept draws upon the computational theory of artificial intelligence, which defines intelligence as the ability to learn. Consequently, this work serves as a precursor to the development of quantum artificial intelligence. This contribution is based on the author's doctoral thesis, which explores the mathematical foundations of quantum artificial intelligence. The formalization of quantum artificial intelligence is achieved through the application of category theory to abstract computational theory. This approach provides a foundation for future research into quantum artificial intelligence. This study addresses a semicoercive Stokes variational inequality arising in glaciology, focusing on the finite element estimation of inf-sup stable nonconforming C0 VEM and FEM approximations. We develop and analyze nonstandard techniques within a novel framework that avoids the need for pulling back approximation spaces to infinitesimal scales or employing regular extensions. Instead, we employ a separation argument that partitions the error into components handled via distinct estimation methods. Consequently, we establish a stable a posteriori error estimator, whose reliability and efficiency are guaranteed by the established error estimates. Numerical experiments confirm the reliability of this estimator. Additionally, we propose a strategy for selecting a suitable approximation space that is at least as stable as existing alternatives. Finally, we detail the implementation of a C0 VEM within the deal.II software package and validate our theoretical findings through numerical tests. Specifically, for a simplified one-dimensional problem with known exact solutions, we compare the performance of VEM and FEM, demonstrating that VEM offers a viable alternative to FEM. A comprehensive implementation is available at: https://gitlab.com/Deal.II/finite-element-methods-for-ice-sliding. This includes a variational inequality class featuring an efficient energy-norm based a posteriori error estimator, which provides upper and lower bounds for the error. The bounds are nearly tight, as indicated by the small gap between them. A corresponding finite element function class is also provided. All results are accessible via the deal.II website: https://www.dealii.org/current/doxygen/variational_inequalities/. We conclude that the inf-sup stability of VEM is robust, and a rigorous error analysis is feasible. Furthermore, the energy estimates derived here offer a viable alternative to those in [10]. Finally, a posteriori error estimates can be computed with minimal additional effort.

We present the DUVET project, an HST/STIS investigation into how galactic outflows regulate star formation. By analyzing the 1500-1700 A rest-frame UV spectrum of a nearby, starbursting disk galaxy (z=0.044), we identified a strong absorption feature attributed to the Lyman limit edge of an outflowing gas cloud. This absorption exhibits spatial variation across the galaxy, revealing that the outflow intersects the interstellar medium in a patchy manner. Our findings indicate that outflowing gas can effectively suppress star formation in specific regions, thereby altering the galaxy's co-evolution with its central supermassive black hole. These results offer a novel perspective on the mechanisms driving galactic evolution. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Lyman edge absorption is detectable in star-forming galaxies at low redshifts, a capability that will be leveraged by upcoming JWST/UVIS observations of high-redshift galaxies. This approach will enable researchers to map the three-dimensional structure of outflowing gas and clarify its role in galaxy evolution. The data utilized in this study can be obtained by contacting the corresponding author. This study analyzes the impact of the equation of state (EoS) on triangular flow ($v_3$) within Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at 20 GeV/nucleon using the AMPT model. We examined four EoS configurations derived from different hadron resonance gas (HRG) formulations: HRG1 (no Pauli blocking), HRG2 (Pauli blocking), HRG3 (four-velocity EoS), and an ideal EoS. Results indicate that the non-monotonic behavior of $v_3$ relative to $p_T$ observed in AMPT is EoS-independent. However, the $v_3$ yield is significantly enhanced when Pauli blocking is applied to leptons in lepton-hadron EoS. Furthermore, we compared these findings with an EoS constructed from the QCD phase diagram (QMD) to explore how the QCD phase transition influences $v_3$. Our analysis reveals that the QMD, which incorporates the strong first-order quark-hadron phase transition, produces a $v_3$ signal approximately 2.5 times larger than that of the standard HRG3 model. Finally, we discuss the sensitivity of $v_3$ to the EoS and its potential utility in mapping the QCD phase diagram. These conclusions are supported by comparisons with experimental data. Future research will address the fine structure of the EoS near the phase transition. This paper introduces a new approach for simultaneously and robustly estimating a robot's structure and motion from a single 2D image. While the structure estimation is inherently ill-conditioned and the overall problem suffers from local minima, our method robustly calculates the most probable solution by leveraging two novel and straightforward concepts. First, we develop and apply a new, fast, and reliable initial value estimator that effectively manages outliers and provides a reliable starting point near the global optimum. Second, our robustness is enhanced by a new, fast, and reliable gradient search algorithm designed to avoid local minima. We rigorously validate the efficacy and speed of our robust estimator through extensive experiments on real-world data. The entire pipeline runs in under 100ms on a standard CPU, making it suitable for real-time deployment. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/10000ten/SimultaneousRoboticStructure. This work is partially funded by the Samsung Advanced Institute of Technology (SAIT). Recent research indicates that pre-training semantic segmentation models on monocular depth estimation tasks yields better performance than standard classification benchmarks. However, the superior performance of deep networks in depth assessment compared to classification remains unexplained. This study investigates the underlying reasons by analyzing network characteristics across various tasks. We observe that when adapted for semantic segmentation, networks pre-trained on depth assessment exhibit smoother class transitions and higher accuracy in ambiguous regions than those pre-trained on classification. To explain this, we examine the relationship between the loss functions of the respective tasks and their impact on network behavior. Furthermore, we propose a novel loss function for depth assessment that balances its effects on smooth transitions and boundary precision. Experiments using this new loss function for network pre-training confirm its effectiveness, demonstrating that it explicitly optimizes semantic segmentation performance. Additionally, we find that the influence of a task's loss function on network behavior is more pronounced in deeper architectures than in very deep ones. These insights offer a clearer understanding of the connections between deep learning tasks and their associated losses, which can guide future research in self-supervised learning. To facilitate this, we provide an extended version of our code for reproducibility. Finally, we explore the connection between the proposed loss function and the number of training samples, discovering that it is more effective with smaller datasets but less so with larger ones. This finding is validated through an experiment comparing pre-training on the SUN RGBD dataset versus a combination of SUN RGBD and KITTI datasets. Our analysis reveals that the root cause lies in the distribution differences between these two depth estimation tasks. Let $B$ denote the open unit ball in $\mathbb{C}^n$, and let $H(B)$ represent the collection of holomorphic functions defined on $B$. Consider a function $f = f_2 \circ h_2 \circ \cdots \circ h_1$, where each $h_j$ is a holomorphic mapping from $B$ to itself and $f_0 = f$. Assume that $f$ is normalized such that $D f(0) = I$, where $I$ is the identity matrix. We establish that:

$$\|f - I\| \leq \frac{2(n+1)^2}{n} \left[1 - \frac{1}{\|D f(1)\|}\right], \quad n \geq 1.$$

Furthermore, both the derived inequality and several related results are generalized to arbitrary order. Specifically, we investigate starlike log-harmonic mappings and derive an enhanced Bohr radius result for this category. Additionally, we examine the relationship between the distance to convexity and the Bohr radius.

Kendall's tau serves as a nonparametric metric for correlation. We establish novel finite-sample convergence rates for empirical estimates of Kendall's tau, demonstrating that a simple nearest-neighbor-based correction achieves post-processing shifts in both $L_1$ and $L_\infty$ distances. This correction facilitates novel hypothesis testing procedures for Kendall's tau under weak dependence assumptions, including block bootstrap and graph-based plug-in bootstrap methods. Simulations indicate that our margin-based tests possess superior power compared to existing alternatives when samples are dependent. Furthermore, we effectuate a conceptual comparison of the pros and cons of empirical estimates versus modern proxy-based approximations of Kendall's tau. Finally, we apply our bootstrap inference framework to a time series of US housing prices to evaluate the statistical significance of the dependence between housing prices and local unemployment rates. Our bootstrap tests reveal a significant correlation between the two variables at monthly and quarterly intervals, whereas empirical estimates fail to demonstrate significance. These findings underscore the statistical value of post-processing adjustments to empirical estimates under weak dependence conditions. Overall, our methodology enables fair and precise comparisons of Kendall's tau across varying sample sizes, approximation techniques, and convergence rates. To our knowledge, this represents the first development of inference procedures for Kendall's tau that achieve convergence rates comparable to those of other empirical risk estimators. Additionally, our tests are computationally efficient, scalable, and applicable to a broad range of scenarios. To our knowledge, these tests also exhibit greater statistical power than competitor methods. We have open-sourced all proofs, experimental code, and implementation to facilitate replication and extension. To the best of our knowledge, these results represent the first convergence rate analysis for Kendall's tau, bootstrap inference, post-processing techniques, and proxy-based approximations. Consequently, this work may enable further research on inference procedures for other non-differentiable, non-convex, and discontinuous population risk functionals. Our convergence rate analysis may also be of interest to the broader machine learning community. Specifically, our finite-sample convergence rates imply minimax rates of the order $O(n^{-2/3})$ for empirical estimates of Kendall's tau, which align with known optimal rates for a broad class of non-smooth risk functionals. This suggests that inference post-processing via nearest-neighbor corrections may offer advantages for other nonsmooth, non-convex risks. Our work may also benefit the optimization community by providing insights into the landscape of Kendall's tau, such as the local geometry around the optimum, the count of critical points, and the number of local minima.

The fusion of Internet of Things (IoT) and vehicular networks has driven significant research into self-driving cars, which rely on the exchange of data between vehicles and the cloud. However, this communication introduces privacy risks, as malicious actors may exploit data to compromise vehicle security. To address this, we propose a unified, privacy-preserving edge intelligence framework that leverages the IoT-vehicular network synergy. This framework integrates two critical privacy mechanisms: data anonymization and data sharing secrecy. We detail two practical protocols that implement these techniques, demonstrating their ability to safeguard vehicle data during transmission to the cloud and analysis by the edge cloud. Furthermore, we validate the framework's feasibility and security through real-world experiments using a vehicular dataset. Our results show that the proposed protocols are effective in protecting vehicular data privacy while enabling intelligent decision-making via edge analytics. Additionally, we evaluate the framework's performance in four real-world applications, confirming its suitability for deployment in urban environments. Finally, we discuss potential threats and provide recommendations for enhancing the framework's security. Overall, this work is expected to inspire further research into privacy-preserving edge intelligence for vehicular networks. This study integrates Allée effects into a Holling–Tanner predator–prey model, acknowledging that the presence of a population does not guarantee its persistence. The proposed framework utilizes Sigmoid functional responses to capture the dynamics of a prey species that fails to survive when an Allée threshold is unmet, specifically when population density is too low to sustain essential activities. We analyze three scenarios based on this sigmoid response: one where only the prey exhibits Allée effects and two where both species do. Our investigation examines the conditions under which prey survives or goes extinct at the boundary, as well as the criteria for the simultaneous survival of both prey and predator in the interior. Furthermore, we identify and establish the existence of a stable limit cycle through a specific bifurcation. Finally, we address the conditions that allow for the invasion of the system by either the predator or prey. While our findings are grounded in a theoretical framework, they also hold significant implications for real-world applications. To demonstrate the model's efficacy, we apply it to a case study involving a real-world scenario where the prey population is at risk of extinction due to Allée effects. This highlights the necessity of maintaining a critical population threshold to ensure the species' survival. The associated data can be accessed at [1]. This study introduces a novel strategy for terminating the aspect pivot simplex algorithm within linear programming. A key termination condition is identified as the emergence of an open cycle involving a specific subset of basis variables, which signals that the algorithm is set to execute an infinite number of pivots. The analysis provided in this paper aims to demonstrate the termination of the algorithm under this condition. The core argument relies on constructing a convex combination of the objective function and a specific linear combination of constraints, ensuring that the objective function value either increases or remains identical for every potential pivot. Furthermore, this paper establishes a necessary condition indicating that the limit of the linear variable sequence generated by the algorithm must be finite. To achieve this, the concept of "potential" is defined and utilized to construct the aforementioned linear function, which is proven to be finite at the limit. This approach marks a significant advancement over the methodology presented in our prior work, which failed to guarantee the termination of the algorithm. Additionally, it is argued that the objective function value strictly increases with each pivot, thereby preventing cycle formation during the algorithm's execution. Consequently, this research successfully overcomes a critical limitation of our previous study. Finally, under the assumption that the open cycle condition occurs, a new procedure is developed to identify a finite limit for the algorithm's linear variable sequence. This procedure involves solving a specific linear programming problem to derive the finite limit value. Through this method, it is demonstrated that the algorithm pivots finitely and converges to a finite value at the limit. This work investigates how off-shell effects impact the extraction of the top quark pole mass from ttj data. To address this, we employ a reweighting technique that incorporates off-shell and decay contributions, utilizing Monte-Carlo events generated with the POWIGG (on-shell) and LeptoTop (off-shell) generators. We analyze a simplified, model-independent experimental dataset. Our results indicate that while the distribution of extracted pole masses is largely model-independent regarding the theoretical generator, it is significantly influenced by off-shell effects. Specifically, if data are fitted with an on-shell top sample, the resulting pole mass distribution is smeared out, leading to a substantial underestimation of the off-shell contribution. Conversely, fitting with an off-shell sample allows for the recovery of these effects. Furthermore, we observe that the distribution of extracted masses is notably asymmetric when using an off-shell sample. This study serves as a proof-of-principle, demonstrating that accurately describing off-shell effects is essential for a precise measurement of the top quark mass. Future research will utilize a more realistic data set and incorporate additional background subtraction. Additionally, we will evaluate various experimental and theoretical systematic uncertainties, which are expected to be a major source of uncertainty in the pole mass extraction. In conclusion, this work provides a proof-of-principle for measuring the top quark mass while accounting for off-shell effects. Future efforts will focus on applying these methods to real ATLAS and CMS data. This approach represents a crucial step toward achieving a high-precision measurement of the top quark mass. We anticipate that the techniques developed here will be essential for the upcoming World Average of Top Quark Masses. The emergence of deep learning has enabled the creation of highly realistic face and speech synthetic media, posing a significant risk to society. To mitigate this, researchers have developed various countermeasures designed to detect these fakes. A key challenge lies in the disparity between the high cost and difficulty of collecting real data for fake faces and voices, and the scarcity of such data hinders the development of effective countermeasures. Consequently, there is growing interest in zero-shot detection methods, which utilize vision transformers (ViT) to identify synthetic content without task-specific training. This study aims to assess the efficiency of ViTs by comparing them against patch-free variants like convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and vision transformers without self-attention (ViT-SA). Our findings indicate that a simple CNN outperforms both the ViT-based approach and the standard ViT, suggesting that current state-of-the-art countermeasures relying on pre-trained ViTs may be unnecessarily expensive. This conclusion is supported by a novel and effective countermeasure based on simple CNNs that achieves top-tier performance in face and video deepfake detection. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that these countermeasures are equally effective for audio and speech synthesis, achieving state-of-the-art performance in zero-shot audio deepfake detection. Finally, we introduce new datasets for lipreading and speech recognition to aid in the detection of synthetic media. Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) models for self-driving vehicles (SDVs) have recently demonstrated significant potential in enabling autonomous capabilities. However, these models frequently struggle to generalize across different environments, particularly when transferring from simulation to real-world conditions. This challenge, known as the Sim2Real gap, often results in degraded performance in practical deployments. To address this, we introduce a novel approach utilizing multiple domain randomization techniques to enhance DRL model performance for self-driving applications. Our method incorporates two key strategies: first, a deep feature alignment technique designed to reduce the discrepancy between simulated and real datasets; and second, a reward shaping mechanism that incorporates real-world data to provide more accurate feedback during training. We validated our model across three datasets: nuScenes, KITTI, and a real-world dataset collected from our own fleet of self-driving cars. Our results indicate that these proposed methods effectively mitigate the Sim2Real gap, resulting in improved performance across all three datasets. Additionally, we conducted ablation studies to analyze the specific contributions of each component and performed further experiments to evaluate robustness and scalability. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChengyuanLi1999/MDR. By offering a straightforward and effective solution to a persistent challenge, our work provides a valuable resource for the autonomous driving community. We hope this contribution fosters collaboration and accelerates progress toward safe and reliable SDV systems. Asynchronous parallel evolutionary algorithms enable the generation of multiple generations within a single iteration, facilitating the parallelization of objective function evaluations. This feature enhances computational efficiency, particularly for complex problems where the generational interval significantly exceeds the time required to evaluate individual solutions. However, this environment introduces evaluation time bias, a factor that hinders traditional synchronous parent selection mechanisms. Specifically, asynchronous parallel multi-objective evolutionary algorithms suffer from evaluation time bias because fitness assessments occur at irregular intervals, causing early evaluations to disproportionately influence later decisions. Conversely, late evaluations allow for more accurate assessments influenced by accumulated genetic diversity. Consequently, there is a pressing need for effective parent selection strategies capable of mitigating evaluation time bias without incurring performance penalties. This study addresses this challenge by introducing a novel parent selection mechanism designed to counteract evaluation time bias. The proposed approach is integrated into the ZMOEA-D framework, which serves as a tool for developing multi-objective evolutionary algorithms for asynchronous parallel execution. By combining this with adaptive parent selection, the resulting AFZMOEA-D algorithm achieves superior solution quality compared to existing methods, effectively eliminating the performance loss typically caused by evaluation time bias. Extensive experiments were conducted to validate the efficacy of the proposed asynchronous multi-objective evolutionary algorithm. The source code for this framework is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1993/ZMOEA-D. Additionally, the experimental code and datasets are available at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1993/Parallel_Eval_MOEAD. The ongoing rise in planet counts detected via microlensing has paralleled a growing appreciation of the diverse planetary systems these methods uncover. This approach is uniquely capable of identifying systems far from their host stars, revealing planets with low masses and high albedos that are inaccessible to other techniques. This study reports the discovery and validation of a new planet within the microlensing event OGLE-2017-BLG-1434, achieved by combining adaptive-optics imaging from the Keck Observatory with follow-up photometry and modeling. The planet, OGLE-2017-BLG-1434b, is located at approximately 2.8 AU from its 0.62 solar mass host star. With a mass of 2.7 Earth masses and an equilibrium temperature of 240 K, it is the coldest planet confirmed through microlensing to date. Its properties align with those of other cold super-Earths found by this method, and it likely formed beyond the snow line via core accretion or gravitational instability. This verification enriches the population of cold, high-albedo planets identified by microlensing, further demonstrating the method's distinct ability to explore regions of parameter space that remain unreachable by alternative detection techniques. The system is predicted to remain gravitationally bound for several billion years, making it a prime candidate for future investigations into the prevalence of icy worlds and the potential for life. This work illustrates the growing synergy between adaptive optics and planet-finding strategies, offering a promising pathway to enhance microlensing detection capabilities. Additionally, we introduce a novel technique for measuring host star masses by comparing adaptive-optics imaging with light curve modeling, a method that may be applicable to other microlensing events. This study utilizes neutron depolarization as a novel technique to investigate magnetic phase transitions in CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ (with x = 0.1 and 0.2). These compounds, which contain both 4$f$ electrons from Cerium and $l$-$f$ hybridization, exhibit a variety of complex phases, including Kondo lattice behavior, heavy fermion characteristics, and valence fluctuations. Our results show that the depolarization rate ($1/\tau_{dep}$) rises with temperature, reaching its maximum at the magnetic phase transition point. This depolarization signal originates from the gradient of the local magnetic field produced by Ce$^{3+}$ ions. The temperature dependence of $1/\tau_{dep}$ aligns with the local magnetic moment gradient, which is influenced by the local Ce$^{3+}$ concentration, its magnetic moment magnitude, and the spatial distribution of these moments. Furthermore, depolarization analysis reveals that Ce$^{3+}$ magnetic moments solidify into a long-range ordered state at 1.5 K for x = 0.2. This finding indicates a first-order phase transition, a conclusion supported by specific heat and resistivity data. The observed depolarization signal provides the first evidence of ferromagnetic order in CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ compounds. Finally, the temperature evolution of $1/\tau_{dep}$ is modeled using the Kondo model, which accounts for the valence fluctuation of Ce ions. These findings offer new insights into the complex electronic and magnetic properties of CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$. Overall, depolarization analysis emerges as a valuable method for studying magnetic phase transitions in materials with local magnetic moments. Future research will extend this approach to other materials to detect phase transitions, such as spin glasses, utilizing advanced neutron imaging methods. This depolarization technique offers a unique means to study the local origin of magnetic phases in these systems. We conducted a 21-cm continuum survey of the high-mass star-forming region G176.51+00.20 using the Green Bank Telescope, identifying 13 compact continuum sources with flux densities ranging from 0.04 to 0.70 mJy. Subsequent Very Large Array observations revealed narrow absorption features in the neutral hydrogen (HI) 21 cm line spectrum for six of these sources, with absorption depths varying from 0.001 to 0.11. These HI self-absorbed structures exhibit a wide range of absorption depths (10⁻⁴ to 10⁻²) and velocity widths (10 to 30 km s⁻¹), and are situated approximately 10 kpc away. Their physical sizes span 1.5 to 10 parsecs, with HI masses between 10³ and 10⁵ solar masses, and HI surface densities fall within the 10–100 g cm⁻² range. These characteristics suggest they are cold, dense molecular clouds currently in the process of forming. We propose that the HI self-absorption arises from neutral gas located in front of or within the infrared-bright compact sources, which emit 21 cm radiation via thermalized blackbody radiation. This study represents the first detection of HI narrow-line self-absorption toward the G176.51+00.20 region, and the identified structures are likely in the early stages of star formation. Furthermore, these findings may aid in understanding the initial phases of high-mass star formation. Finally, the presence of these structures could help explain the observed HI mass deficit in high-mass star-forming regions. We have developed a wordless proof by demonstration of Sylvester's Three-Triangles Theorem within the context of the triangular lattice. This approach extends naturally to Slater's Generalization. The demonstration utilizes the Euclidean algorithm to generate the lattice and employs color changes to visually illustrate the theorem's statement. Furthermore, three-dimensional versions can be demonstrated in the simple cubic and face-centered cubic lattices. In these 3D demonstrations, the number of octahedra is shown to be at most 12, consistent with a three-dimensional analogue of Slater's Generalization. These demonstrations align with the educational philosophy of making mathematics accessible. We contend that this method fosters an appreciation for the beauty of mathematical proofs and encourages mathematical thinking. Additionally, we believe this approach fosters an openness toward mathematics that is often missing from traditional classroom settings. Finally, we outline several directions for future research. This paper is the result of a collaboration between a mathematician and an artist. We contend that working together enhances our individual strengths and that such collaboration is essential for advancing mathematics education. We conclude with several remarks regarding mathematics and art. Supporting material is available at www.demonstrationswithoutwords.com. We report a serendipitous discovery of the RXCJ0232.2-4420 cluster during a search for substructure in the X-ray emission from the main cluster. This cluster is a bright, low-redshift (z=0.41) system that also hosts a central galaxy with a significantly higher redshift of z=0.45. Our analysis of X-ray data reveals that RXCJ0232.2-4420 exhibits a complex morphology indicative of an ongoing merger. The X-ray emission is characterized by two distinct lobes, with the southeastern lobe being more intense and containing a prominent X-ray source. We identified a 1.2 sigma peak in X-ray surface brightness at the cluster's core, accompanied by a significant (4.8 sigma) peak in the X-ray spectrum. The spectrum is well-fit by a thermal bremsstrahlung model with a temperature of 6.7 keV, which is approximately 1.5 times hotter than the average temperature derived from XMM-Newton data. Furthermore, the morphology of the X-ray emission aligns with the distribution of the cluster's stellar members. We propose that the X-ray source originates from an active galactic nucleus (AGN) within a member galaxy. The stellar distribution displays a clear elongation along a northwest-southeast axis, mirroring the cluster's overall morphology. Additionally, we examined the stellar velocity dispersion profile, which reveals a peak at the cluster center, and investigated the radial velocity distribution, which shows a secondary peak corresponding to the central galaxy's higher redshift. We conclude that RXCJ0232.2-4420 is a massive cluster with a total mass of 1.4x10^14 solar masses, and the elongation in both the stellar distribution and velocity dispersion suggests a past merger along a northwest-southeast axis. We also identified a possible substructure feature in the radial velocity distribution, which may indicate a past merger along a southeast-northwest axis. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for understanding galaxy cluster mergers. Driven by the intriguing dynamics of language emergence, we introduce a straightforward yet potent framework for studying diachronic linguistic stability. In this model, a network of communities, each assigned a unique name, exchanges members over time. Interacting individuals attempt to replicate the linguistic habits of their peers, evolving the language through communication. Our primary focus is on the stability of the emergent categorization language within the social network's categorization scheme. We demonstrate that, contrary to common assumptions, stability does not necessarily arise in this system; however, the migration mechanism can foster a society with a strong desire for linguistic consistency. This propensity is measured by the ratio of consistent messages in their dialogue language. We validate this mechanism using both simplified and intricate societies. The migration process is driven by the desire to join populous communities, quantified by their average agent count. We show that an appropriate selection of migration and dialogue frequencies, combined with a suitable agent desire for community joining, can yield stable, linguistically consistent communities across a broad spectrum of initial conditions. These findings are supported by extensive numerical simulations and validated through an intricate analytical analysis. The resulting stability is evaluated via both an emergent order parameter and an information-theoretic measure. Furthermore, the information-theoretic approach provides a clear explanation of the mechanisms driving both linguistic emergence and stability. These insights are expected to offer valuable guidance for designing future societal systems. Additionally, the proposed analysis methodology is applicable to a wide range of models. Finally, we extend this analysis to a more generalized scenario where communities are defined by arbitrary labels rather than a categorical scheme. This analysis reveals the specific conditions under which the mechanism operates and identifies the most suitable migration and dialogue frequencies for achieving stability. Crucially, this analysis remains applicable to any modeling framework, even those that do not exhibit the mechanism itself. Notably, the analysis successfully identifies why an existing stable society, where migration and dialogue frequencies are fixed, has not collapsed. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) are widely used to solve partial differential equations, yet they frequently exhibit spectral bias, preferring to learn lower-frequency components before addressing higher ones. This paper demonstrates that incorporating a momentum term into the adversative training loop of PINNs can significantly mitigate this spectral bias. Our findings show that adding momentum not only accelerates training but also enhances the PINN's ability to capture high-frequency features. We validate these results on both synthetic datasets and a real-world scenario: estimating wind speed from pressure readings. Ultimately, we present a momentum-based PINN variant that reduces the number of training iterations by one order of magnitude compared to standard PINNs. The implementation is available at https://github.com/andreasmeyer12/PINNs-with-momentum. Furthermore, we show that this approach can be extended to other physics-informed generalized neural network frameworks.

We investigate the stability characteristics of a water wave system featuring linked waves and locally disturbed exponential Kelvin-Voigt attenuation to model energy dissipation. This scenario necessitates the utilization of weakly nonhomogeneous coordinates. The primary focus is on identifying instability mechanisms, which arise from the interaction between the nonhomogeneity-induced Coriolis-like force and the dissipation. By analyzing the boundary between stable and unstable regimes, we demonstrate that these mechanisms violate the second law of thermodynamics on an open system level, although the local entropy production density remains non-negative. Furthermore, the characteristics of these mechanisms are shown to be analogous to those of dissipative coherent structures observed in nonhomogeneous fluids without linked waves, such as shear-driven or Rayleigh-Bénard convection. Finally, we examine the potential implications of these mechanisms for oceanic boundary layers and discuss their relevance to dissipative phenomena in non-Oceanic contexts. This study serves as a preliminary analysis of linked-wave systems with exponential attenuation, laying the groundwork for a future comprehensive linear stability theory. This theory will address the full problem, which involves the local variation of the attenuation coefficient's argument within a finite region, thereby eliminating the use of weakly nonhomogeneous coordinates. That comprehensive theory will serve as the foundation for analyzing dissipative dissipative coherent structures in systems with linked waves. The resulting insights will enable the development of dissipative coherent structures in systems with linked waves to be modeled using the same framework currently applied to non-Oceanic contexts. This will facilitate the investigation of these structures in a broader range of physical systems. Additionally, the associated energy transfer mechanisms can be investigated using the same methodologies. This work will provide a basis for understanding the energetics of non-Oceanic systems with exponential attenuation and for developing numerical models of systems with linked waves. This research will also contribute to the development of attenuation models for systems featuring dissipative coherent structures. Finally, the findings will contribute to a more accurate representation of attenuation mechanisms in numerical models of systems with linked waves. This approach will enhance the reliability of numerical simulations and support the interpretation of observational data in systems where exponential attenuation occurs. Overall, this work will provide a more complete understanding of the physics of systems with linked waves, thereby contributing to the broader field of fluid dynamics. This contribution will help address some of the remaining challenges in our understanding of fluid dynamics. Specifically, this work will contribute to a more complete picture of the energy transfer mechanisms in systems with linked waves. This insight will aid in the development of more accurate models of energy transfer in these systems.

This study addresses two key challenges in reinforcement learning (RL): the need for human-interpretable policies and the difficulty of balancing exploration and exploitation. In many scenarios, the action space is organized hierarchically, where actions at one level depend on those of another. However, existing approaches that leverage this hierarchy to facilitate learning and generate explainable policies often fail to produce actions that are simultaneously optimal and coherent across levels. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a method that trains neural networks to select hierarchical actions while ensuring coherence and human interpretability through inductive logic programming. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves superior performance compared to prior hierarchical RL methods designed for human-interpretable policies. Furthermore, we show that hierarchical RL policies derived from our method exhibit higher quality and greater human interpretability. Finally, in contrast to model-free RL techniques, our formulation allows for more informed exploration by providing access to the environment model. We introduce a novel method for investigating spin-dependent nuclear targets by utilizing the internal structure of $^6$Li. This approach leverages the non-negligent spin of both protons and neutrons, as well as the significant spatial separation between the target and the single neutron. We establish a relationship connecting the spin-dependent $^6$Li form factors to those of the proton and neutron, demonstrating that spin-dependent signals can be enhanced by an order of magnitude compared to standard nuclear targets like $^{12}$C or $^{16}$O. Furthermore, we show that form factors derived from $^6$Li nucleon data can effectively constrain form factors from traditional targets such as $^{129}$I, $^{83}$As, $^{89}$Y, and $^{197}$Au. These findings indicate that future experiments employing $^6$Li could achieve sensitivity comparable to or surpassing current limits, potentially establishing $^6$Li as an optimal target for constraining spin-dependent dark matter interactions. This research was conducted using the OpenDark matter Framework (ODF), an open-source toolkit designed for dark matter research. The framework is publicly accessible at https://github.com/OpenDarkmatter/ODF. Our analysis utilized nuclear form factors sourced from the JeonLab group, available at https://www.physik.uni-jena.de/~jeonlab. Blind image restoration (BUR) is a challenging task that seeks to recover high-quality images from low-quality inputs without knowledge of the specific degradation parameters. This paper introduces a novel approach to BUR by leveraging the underlying generative process of image data, which is modeled as a mixture of kernels. The degradation parameters are estimated by maximizing the likelihood of the observed images under this model. To enhance computational efficiency, a parameterization based on the singular value decomposition (SVD) of the degradation matrix is utilized, and an efficient optimization algorithm is proposed. Experimental results on standard benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms several state-of-the-art approaches in restoring images from severe under-sampling. Furthermore, the method is applied to reconstruct dynamic scenes from sequences of highly blurred images, yielding promising outcomes. Additionally, the method is employed for super-resolution (non-blind restoration), achieving performance that compares favorably with existing techniques on standard benchmark datasets. Finally, the method is extended to 3D volume restoration for medical imaging, yielding encouraging results. To facilitate future research, the method has been implemented in C++ and made available on GitHub. The source code, along with benchmark datasets and results, can be accessed at: https://github.com/SebastianSchaefer/BlindImageRestoration. Sebastian's contact email is sebastian.schaefer@tum.de. We gratefully acknowledge his contribution to this method. We believe the method's strong performance across various applications will be valuable to the research community. Nonuniform associative algebras constitute a broad category of nonassociative algebras introduced recently, characterized by the presence of multiple bilinear products derived from the antilinear map $x\mapsto \bar{x}$. This paper establishes the applicability of associative Yang-Baxter equations involving anti-linear involution within the context of nonuniform associative algebras. Furthermore, we present a constructive method for generating solutions to the associative Yang-Baxter equations based on nonuniform associative algebras. Specifically, for any two spaces $V$ and $W$ equipped with two compatible nonuniform associative products $\cdot$ and $\odot$, and provided $f:V\rightarrow W$ is a two-sided morphism between these structures, the map $id\oplus f:V\oplus W\rightarrow V\oplus W$ defined by $id\oplus f:(v,w)\mapsto (v,f(w))$ yields an associative Yang-Baxter solution. Additionally, we demonstrate that the associated $R$-matrix $(id\oplus f)\cdot p_{id\oplus f}$ is both nondegenerate and regular, where $p_{id\oplus f}$ denotes the permutation operator. Finally, we propose a method for constructing nonuniform associative algebras from uniform ones; in this context, we identify a class of $R$-matrix solutions to the associative Yang-Baxter equation originating from UASAs and construct new solutions via linear involutions. As an illustration, we apply this approach to various instances involving the space $Cl_{1,1}$, derived from the uniform associative algebra $Cl_{2}$ via involution, and present the resulting $R$-matrices. Notably, some of these $R$-matrices satisfy both the Knizhnik-Zamolodchikov and associative Yang-Baxter equations. This outcome is significant because it demonstrates that the existence of a regular solution to the associative Yang-Baxter equation does not inherently preclude it from being also a Knizhnik-Zamolodchikov solution. Consequently, this finding refutes a conjecture by Zhang and Zhang. To achieve this, we constructed a two-dimensional space $V$ featuring a nonuniform associative product and a bilinear solution to the associative Yang-Baxter equation that is also a Knizhnik-Zamolodchikov solution, which was subsequently extended to $Cl_{1,1}\otimes\cdots\otimes Cl_{1,1}$. This work addresses the formal validation of software systems specified in natural language. We present a framework for validating programs annotated with Hoare logic formulas written in natural language. By leveraging recent advances in extracting logical forms from text, our approach enables the formal verification of requirements directly embedded within system specifications. To develop and assess this method, we created a dataset consisting of Hoare triples in both natural language and $\lambda$-PM$^*$ notation (a variant of Maltman's notation designed for machine checking). We constructed this dataset from open-source software repositories and collaborated with domain experts to manually annotate the data. Using this resource, we implemented a prototype system featuring two methods for checking extracted logical forms: a straightforward but conservative strategy and a more sophisticated, yet potentially unsound, technique called Constraint Satisfaction. Finally, we present a method for automatically generating sound and complete checkers for logical forms, which significantly reduces the computational resources required by current approaches. This research forms the foundation for developing software validation tools that assist software engineers in verifying their software against formally analyzed requirements. Software tools and additional details are publicly accessible at: https://github.com/alexei-maltsev/natural-hoare. The source code is also available at: https://github.com/alexei-maltsev/hoare-requirements. Canopus is a Byzantine fault-tolerant (BFT) replica state machine (RSM) designed for sharded systems that process high-throughput, low-latency requests. It features a streamlined protocol that minimizes network communication, reduces disk operations, and mitigates lock contention. However, Canopus's original design assumes all replica failures are instantaneous, a limitation that can lead to system halts when non-instantaneous failures occur. This paper introduces RCanopus, an enhanced version of Canopus that maintains safety despite non-instantaneous replica failures and behaviors from some nodes that violate common BFT assumptions. Compared to other existing solutions, RCanopus offers superior request processing performance. We validate these claims through extensive simulations that model various failure scenarios. Additionally, we identify novel optimization opportunities that further boost RCanopus's resilience and efficiency. We also evaluate the impact of different failure models, such as network partitions, on Canopus's performance, revealing that accounting for failure overheads is essential for accurate evaluation. Our experimental results demonstrate that, in most cases, RCanopus outperforms other BFT RSM systems for sharded architectures. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to propose specific optimizations for Canopus. We have open-sourced RCanopus on GitHub. Given its superior resilience and performance, RCanopus is well-suited for production deployment. Furthermore, the proposed improvements can be applied to other systems derived from Canopus to enhance their fault tolerance and efficiency. Finally, the methodologies used to analyze Canopus's failure behaviors can be leveraged by the broader BFT community to better understand failure characteristics and their effects on system performance. Our source code is available at: https://github.com/ai4bft/RCanopus. Canopus's code is hosted at: https://github.com/ai4bft/Canopus. Recent experiments have indicated that cholesterol's influence on the bending modulus of lipid membranes is more intricate and significant than previously assumed. This study investigates the relationship between the bending modulus and cholesterol concentration using a coarse-grained model. We observe a maximum in the bending modulus at low cholesterol levels, aligning with prior research. Our simulations reveal that cholesterol enhances membrane rigidity by reducing the average area per headgroup and increasing interfacial tension, with the modulus scaling linearly with interfacial tension. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the previously proposed scaling law, which relates membrane rigidity to the fractional area occupied by cholesterol, is only valid for very low cholesterol concentrations. Additionally, we find that the bending modulus is highly sensitive to simulation parameters, such as the spring constant applied to the initial constraint between head and tail groups. Finally, we show that cholesterol can increase membrane rigidity through two distinct mechanisms, resulting in non-monotonic behavior. These findings suggest that the interplay between different mechanisms could explain the conflicting experimental reports found in existing literature. This work underscores the necessity of conducting precise, quantitative measurements of the bending modulus across a broad range of cholesterol concentrations to fully elucidate cholesterol's impact on lipid membrane properties. This can be achieved by employing techniques capable of isolating the effects of cholesterol on both lipid packing and interfacial tension. We conclude that our theoretical framework can facilitate the design of appropriate experiments to clarify the relationship between cholesterol and membrane bending rigidity. Finally, our results indicate that cholesterol-induced changes in rigidity are more pronounced in membranes with pre-existing disorder, implying that cholesterol has a greater impact on disordered membranes. This aligns with experimental evidence showing that cholesterol preferentially partitions into liquid-disordered domains. These findings may help explain the non-monotonic dependence of membrane protein binding on cholesterol concentration. Specifically, since membrane proteins typically favor interfaces between ordered and disordered regions, an increase in cholesterol could either raise or lower the bending modulus, thereby either promoting or inhibiting line tension-driven binding. This underscores the critical role of the lipid bending modulus in regulating membrane protein binding. To fully understand cholesterol's effects on membrane properties, it is essential to experimentally determine the concentration dependence of the bending modulus in both liquid-disordered and liquid-ordered phases. We propose that this can be accomplished by utilizing nanodiscs, which allow for the independent control of lipid composition and cholesterol concentration. We have also conducted preliminary simulations on nanodiscs to support this conclusion. This conclusion is consistent with our earlier findings regarding the effects of membrane curvature on lipid binding
