This study presents a catalog of the most energetic cosmic rays recorded during the first year of Phase I at the Pierre Auger Observatory, spanning energies from 50 to 90 EeV. The dataset includes 1,124 events, with the ten most energetic identified as AE070725, AE080504, AE080916, AE081204, AE090104, AE090304, AE090504, AE090704, AE090904, and AE091004. For the five highest-energy events, the analysis provides reconstructed energies, arrival directions, and shower sizes. Additionally, we compare the observed flux against predictions derived from several nucleon composition models. Our results indicate that the flux of the five most energetic events aligns well with a proton composition model. However, this proton-based model fails to reproduce the flux of the remaining 1,119 events, suggesting that the five most energetic events likely possess a heavy nucleus composition. Furthermore, the data show no evidence of a suppression in the high-energy flux. Finally, the observed flux is compared with the AE070725 prediction, confirming no significant deviation. These findings are consistent with both proton and heavy nucleus compositions. To further constrain the nature of the most energetic events, we have conducted an analysis of the AE070725 shower using AugerString data, which will be presented in a future publication. Based on this analysis, we conclude that the AE070725 event cannot be definitively assigned a proton composition. Consequently, the high-energy events cannot be considered a new class of ultra-high-energy particles; rather, they represent the most extreme manifestation of the same particle population that generates the AE070725 prediction. The inability of the high-energy flux to match the AE070725 prediction implies that the source of the highest-energy events differs from the source of the highest-energy neutrinos. This conclusion is supported by the lack of observed neutrino events in IceCube during Phase I. The temporal and spatial distribution of the highest-energy events is also examined. Finally, the study addresses the question of whether the highest-energy events are correlated with nearby active galactic nuclei (AGNs). Deep object detectors are widely used across numerous computer vision applications; however, their black-box nature prevents users from accurately gauging response reliability. This paper introduces BayesOD, the first adaptation of Bayesian inference to a state-of-the-art deep object detector. By employing a novel strategy, we successfully mitigate the excessive computational costs typically associated with Bayesian methods. Our experiments demonstrate that, despite requiring more training time, BayesOD achieves detection accuracy comparable to non-bayesian detectors while providing a robust uncertainty metric for evaluating detection quality. Furthermore, our results indicate that specific components within BayesOD maintain robustness even when trained on limited datasets. Finally, we observe that integrating BayesOD with a non-bayesian detector can enhance overall performance. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/andreypavlov/BayesOD. A video demonstration of BayesOD is available at https://youtu.be/4222222222. Our implementation scores 45.4 on the benchmark task of quantifying detection uncertainty. Additionally, we explore how to leverage this uncertainty to improve object classification performance. Our approach yields a 2.5% improvement over baseline methods on the ImageNet dataset. Video demonstrations are available at https://youtu.be/_EXAMPLE_VIDEO_1 and https://youtu.be/_EXAMPLE_VIDEO_2. Our implementation scores 74.2 on the benchmark task of image classification.

This study tackles short-term traffic prediction for traffic streams by initially identifying segments with similar speed patterns. Specifically, we introduce a new metric called the "clustering rate," which quantifies the degree of moving pattern similarity within a traffic stream. This rate serves as the input for a denoising autoencoder, which subsequently estimates the degree of pattern similarity for unseen data to guide segment classification. To forecast traffic volume, we employ recurrent neural networks trained to predict speed for each segment. We evaluated the model's performance using data from San Francisco, Los Angeles, and New York City. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach effectively predicts traffic volume during both free-flow and congested conditions. Furthermore, we provide evidence that the proposed clustering rate acts as a robust indicator of moving pattern similarity across all tested cities. Finally, we show that the accuracy of our model surpasses that of a baseline model which utilizes existing clustering techniques to identify segments with similar speed patterns. A major category of consistency proofs within mathematical logic involves applying semantic syntactic methods to establish consistency for specific formal systems. In this context, the semantic component comprises consistency arguments based on the model-theoretic properties of these systems, while the formally syntactic part involves the construction of new classes and rewriting rules alongside the demonstration of their term-completeness. This paper presents a method for proving the term-completeness of such constructed classes across a broad spectrum of general algebraic varieties. To achieve this, we utilize concepts from free algebraic lattices and their relational analogues, known as free relation algebras. We introduce and examine the concept of quasi-term equivalence, which extends the standard notion of term equivalence, and leverage this to demonstrate the aforementioned results. Consequently, our primary contribution is a novel approach to proving term-completeness that holds significant generality. As an application of these findings, we provide a straightforward proof for the term-completeness of the class governing the consistency of first-order logic, as previously established by Hájek and Subrahmoniam. Furthermore, we extend this result to several other logical systems, including those related to probabilistic and non-monotonic reasoning. We also address applications in model theory by presenting a novel application of semantic syntactic methods to the Lindström conjecture. Specifically, we explore the term completeness of classes associated with abstract model theoretic properties, such as elementary classes and Lindström characterized classes. Our approach offers a unified framework for analyzing term completeness across diverse varieties of abstract classes. Additionally, we develop a theory of quasi-term equivalence applicable to various algebraic problems, demonstrating that this framework often simplifies the analysis of term equivalence in general algebraic varieties. Finally, we illustrate applications in universal algebra by proving the term-completeness of varieties defined by quasi-identities, a result that had previously been established only under the stronger condition of conjunction. These findings represent a significant generalization of our primary contributions. Collectively, this work demonstrates that semantic syntactic methods, which are fundamental to numerous consistency demonstrations in mathematical logic, also hold substantial utility in other areas, such as universal algebra. This underscores the necessity for further research into the properties and applications of such methods. To facilitate these applications, we have also developed a specialized computer algebra system. The methodologies and results discussed herein are detailed in the author's doctoral thesis, which also elaborates on the concept of quasi-term equivalence. This study introduces a novel end-to-end deep learning framework designed to partition the human hippocampus for individuals with epilepsy and Alzheimer's disease. We developed multiple convolutional neural networks to estimate the boundaries of hippocampal subregions, specifically the head, body, and tail. The proposed network architecture is lightweight, featuring the *multi-attentional block (MAB)* as its core component. This block integrates spatial, channel, and hippocampus-specific attention layers to effectively extract features and enhance the network's capacity to capture fine details. Furthermore, the framework supports both supervised and unsupervised training methods. Experimental results indicate that the proposed network achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of accuracy, computational efficiency, and generalization capabilities. Additionally, our results demonstrate a strong correlation between the proposed method's performance and hippocampus morphology characteristics associated with epilepsy and Alzheimer's disease. This synergy suggests that the framework holds significant potential for assisting clinicians in investigating these neurological conditions. A recent study by Li et al. (arXiv:2101.01002) introduced a classical pigeonhole phenomenon, suggesting a strong bond between quantum and classical physics. However, this interpretation overlooks non-classical aspects of both the phenomenon and the underlying computation. This comment presents an alternative classical explanation rooted in linear algebra, which contradicts the claims made by Li et al. regarding transversal modes. Specifically, we demonstrate that this phenomenon is not exclusively quantum but can also occur in classical settings, thereby challenging the notion of a deep connection between the two regimes. Consequently, this work underscores the necessity for greater clarity and precision when labeling classical computations as exhibiting quantum phenomena. Ultimately, this alternative interpretation diminishes the significance of the research by Li et al. and refutes the validity of conclusions drawn by Cao et al. (arXiv:2101.05002) concerning retarding and anti-retarding phenomena. Both of these studies rely on the pigeonhole phenomenon as a core component of their findings. Additionally, we introduce a novel classical analogue that produces the quantum effect, further supporting the existence of this phenomenon in classical physics. Finally, we suggest a potential source of confusion that may have led to the initial proposal of the classical pigeonhole phenomenon. Our work aims to foster a more rigorous and responsible discourse regarding the attribution of quantum phenomena to classical systems. By promoting greater clarity and precision in labeling, we hope to enhance the integrity and credibility of scientific research. Ultimately, this effort seeks to strengthen the credibility of the scientific community and ensure that claims of quantum phenomena in classical settings are made with due care and precision. In conclusion, this line of research serves as a valuable exercise in teaching the importance of rigor and responsibility in scientific inquiry. This study utilizes a Monte Carlo code to simulate the production of CRAND particles with charge $Z=-1$ and energy levels of 100, 200, and 300 MeV/nucleon as they interact with nitrogen and oxygen nuclei within the Low Earth Orbit (LEO) region. The simulation results indicate that the mean path length of these CRAND particles in the LEO is approximately 100 meters. These findings suggest that CRAND particles could serve as a potential candidate for Low Earth Orbit navigation and communication systems. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that a $Z=-1$ beam can be generated by irradiating a hydrogen-rich target with protons. Additionally, these particles are expected to cause radiation damage to Low Earth Orbit satellites, posing a risk to astronauts during space missions. Consequently, there is an urgent need to develop shielding materials capable of protecting against this damage. The study concludes that shielding composed of aluminum, copper, or lead is highly effective at mitigating CRAND radiation. Additionally, the concept of a space elevator is proposed as a viable solution for shielding Low Earth Orbit against CRAND radiation. Finally, the paper recommends that future research prioritize the development of CRAND-based navigation and communication technologies, shielding materials, and communication protocols. Specifically, it suggests that government agencies and research institutions in China, such as the China Academy of Space Technology (CST) and the China Manned Space Engineering Office (CMSE), should allocate funding to support these initiatives. The author also recommends that the United States Space Force, NASA, and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) conduct similar investigations. Ultimately, international collaboration is deemed essential to advance the development of CRAND technology. To facilitate this, the paper introduces a new concept known as the "CRAND Space Station," which is expected to significantly impact future space exploration and utilization. The author has submitted a patent application for this CRAND Space Station concept. The paper also references existing patents related to CRAND technology, including those filed in 2018 and 2019, and highlights the necessity of establishing a global patent pool for CRAND to support its widespread development. The author invites researchers and government agencies worldwide to collaborate on advancing CRAND technology. The paper also addresses the challenges of CRAND radiation, including its effects on astronauts, satellites, and space debris, and discusses the associated risks. Finally, the study explores potential applications of CRAND technology in LEO navigation and communication, emphasizing the critical role of international cooperation

The swift emergence of Deep Graph Neural Networks (DGNNs) has garnered substantial scholarly interest, driven by their capacity to address complex predictive issues within high-dimensional time-series data. However, existing research often overlooks critical architectural design principles, including network depth, information flow, and topology representation. This paper proposes a global pyramid-like shrinkage framework to guide network depth design and introduces a novel local topology link reconfiguration method to optimize sequence information flow. By integrating these strategies, we establish a unified framework for DGNNs. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art models, thereby offering valuable insights and a foundational blueprint for future DGNNs research and development. Recent years have seen significant growth in research on privacy-preserving matrix completion, a task that involves inferring missing values in a matrix based on observed entries and the assumption that the matrix has a low-rank structure. This work presents a method for performing matrix completion on tabular data while safeguarding individual privacy through differential privacy. This approach is particularly vital for table data, as such datasets are prone to inference attacks where an adversary exploits the high likelihood of certain value combinations. To balance privacy and utility, we adopt a privacy-utility optimization framework and introduce an efficient, differentially private algorithm for low-rank matrix fulfillment. Our proposed method, DP-LRMCF, is based on the robust statistics technique developed by Huber. We validate the effectiveness of our approach using both synthetic and real-world datasets. Our method is differentially private and incorporates noise via the Gaussian mechanism. We demonstrate that, in terms of utility, our approach outperforms existing methods, including those that do not offer differential privacy. Furthermore, we show that our method is robust to perturbations caused by noise addition, thereby maintaining high utility even under differential privacy constraints. Finally, we illustrate that DP-LRMCF is effective in mitigating the risk of inference attacks on tabular data. To facilitate reproducibility, we have released the source code and preprocessed datasets as a public Jupyter notebook. Our findings indicate that DP-LRMCF is a promising method for achieving privacy and privacy, effectively reducing the likelihood of inference attacks on tabular data. We anticipate that this method will be a valuable tool for future research in privacy-preserving matrix completion. The "crisis of opacity" represents a significant challenge in both cosmology and astrophysics, stemming from the conflict between the observed optical depth of the interstellar medium (ISM) and the theoretical predictions of Galactic star formation rates. This discrepancy drives two primary lines of inquiry: the first seeks to resolve the optical depth crisis by either reducing dust production or opacity, while the second seeks to explain the high optical depth through a distinct physical mechanism. In this study, we introduce a model that unifies the extinction, polarization, and emission properties of polarized dust grains in the low-density phases of the ISM, thereby advancing the solution to the opacity crisis. Our approach relies on a parameterized grain size distribution and a set of free parameters that define the relative abundance of grain species. We develop a polarized Rayleigh-Gans scattering matrix to calculate extinction curves, polarization, and scattered light emission, with results compared against observational data. Our findings indicate that a single dust component is insufficient to replicate the observed trends; instead, a mixture of silicates, amorphous carbon, and PAHs is required. Specifically, we identify a population of large, highly polarizable grains with a maximum size of approximately 0.5 microns that are prevalent in the ISM's diffuse phases. This research is conducted as a collaborative effort between the Astrophysics Division of the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy and the Department of Physics at the University of Oxford. The polarization component of our work is led by J.G., while the emission and extinction aspects are led by M.S. We have provided a user-friendly, open-source implementation of the model at https://astrodustpah.org, which includes a comprehensive set of extinction curves, scattering matrices, and polarization data. Additionally, we provide a collection of models that fit the observed Galactic dust polarization data. Our results suggest that the "crisis of opacity" is not a binary issue but rather a continuum of solutions, where the relative contributions of dust properties vary across different regions of the ISM. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the astrophysical origins of large, polarized grains remain an unresolved question. Finally, we show that the high optical depth of the ISM can be reconciled with star formation rates if large grains are preferentially formed in dense clouds or destroyed in the diffuse ISM. Our work offers a comprehensive framework to unify previously disparate research areas, including extinction, polarization, and recombination, into a single, cohesive model. This model provides a pathway to unify the solutions to the "crisis

We report the detection of a substantial gas disk surrounding the young, low-mass pre-main-sequence star CIDA 1, which has a mass of approximately 0.008 solar masses. This disk exhibits a large scale height and a temperature gradient that aligns with predictions from photoevaporation models. By integrating CO emission data with a radiative transfer model, we derived the disk's physical properties, including a total mass of 0.02 solar masses and a scale height of 1.1 AU at 1.0 AU radius. The disk's inner region is likely truncated by a massive planet with a mass exceeding 10 Jupiter masses, as evidenced by a pronounced drop in surface density at 1.0 AU. The system's photoevaporation rate is estimated at 10^-8 solar masses per year, indicating that CIDA 1 is losing its disk mass at a rate comparable to other young, low-mass stars. The presence of a massive planet within this disk supports the view that massive planets can form around very low-mass stars via disk accretion. Additionally, the high mass-loss rate suggests that massive planets may be more readily formed around low-mass stars than around solar-mass stars. The analysis of CO emission from this disk will be the subject of a future paper. This study is based on observations from the ALMA and VLA facilities. [abridged]

This study examines the mathematical properties of the game "Lights Out" played on a two-dimensional $m \times n$ grid. Under specific conditions, the count of winning configurations—where all lights are initially off and a solution exists—exhibits both oscillatory and exponential behaviors as functions of $m$ and $n$. We define and analyze several "extreme" variants, including the maximum-number game, which demands the fewest possible moves to extinguish all lights, and the maximum-clicks dilemma, a version where an adversary sets the number of moves, and the player wins if they can complete the task in fewer clicks. Furthermore, we explore a variant featuring a fixed number of winning clicks, offering a systematic approach to solving such puzzles. Our methodology relies on the fundamental theory of the game, combined with linear algebra, matrix theory, graph theory, and number theory. We establish lower and upper bounds for both the maximum and dilemma scenarios, demonstrating that our findings for square grids align with existing literature. Additionally, we offer a closed-form solution (modulo 2) for triangular grids and extend our results to both even and odd rhombus-shaped grids. This work aims to foster interest in the field of puzzle mathematics. Our approach leverages modern computational tools, enabling the rapid generation of data and its subsequent analysis to formulate conjectures regarding other puzzle types. We conclude by outlining several open problems. This paper serves as a tutorial on the fundamental theorems governing this classic game. For readers with a background in mathematics, we have endeavored to provide detailed explanations of our arguments. We hope this research inspires further investigation into the fascinating world of mathematical puzzles. We welcome any questions, corrections, or suggestions from the readership. For correspondence, please contact Dr. Mohamed A. Al-Shaikhli at Dr.Mohamed.A.Shahin@SQU.edu.om. Additionally, we offer tutorials, including PowerPoint presentations and Python code, to assist in replicating our results. These resources can be accessed via email at Dr.Mohamed.A.Shahin@SQU.edu.om. We extend our gratitude to all who have contributed to this endeavor. Mohamed A. Al-Shaikhli, Shamseldin A. El-Morshedy, and Tamer A. El-Said.

This study introduces a new variational image reconstruction algorithm designed to reduce noise in single-exposure images. The proposed reconstruction technique is integrated into the backward step of an existing active contour model. Numerical experiments conducted on both synthetic data and actual x-ray and optical images demonstrate that the proposed approach effectively eliminates noise while preserving image edges and structural details. These numerical findings confirm the method's success in noisy environments. Although this numerical integration is not guaranteed to yield a global minimizer for the segmentation problem, it serves as a valuable starting point for one. Specifically, an approximate local minimizer is generated by applying the method to an initial pair consisting of a reconstructed image and a straight line separating the background from the object. Subsequently, this pair is used as the initial input for a segmentation scheme based on the Mumford–Sharp model. The approach is highly versatile and can be adapted to various standard imaging techniques, including optical, x-ray, magnetic resonance, and ultrasound. Furthermore, it is applicable to several widely used balance models, such as Mumford–Sharp, Chan–Vese, and Mumford–Peyre. The segmentation scheme is implemented using an alternating minimization strategy that iteratively solves the Mumford–Sharp reconstruction problem and minimizes the Mumford–Sharp energy. To address the nonconvexity inherent in the segmentation process, the algorithm is solved multiple times with different initializations. Finally, the proposed scheme is extended to handle cases involving a known background. Numerical results indicate that the approach is highly effective at preserving image edges and details while eliminating noise. The entire algorithm is implemented in MATLAB. Future research will explore convergence analysis, the development of more efficient solvers, and the application of the scheme to time-dependent image data. Additionally, the method will be tested on real-world images to assess its performance in removing noise from single-exposure captures. Finally, the scheme will be evaluated across diverse imaging modalities, such as x-ray, magnetic resonance, optical, and ultrasound. Keywords: image reconstruction, image segmentation, active contours, Mumford–Sharp, alternating minimization, convergence analysis.

Abstract interpretation operates within the framework of Semicontinuous Positively Ordered Algebras (POAs). This category includes all complete lattices, such as power sets of any set and lattice domains representing computational states with infinite precision. A POA is defined as semicontinuous when its supremum-preserving endomorphisms constitute a complete lattice ordered by the pointwise order. The operational model of abstract interpretation consists of four components: an abstract domain (a POA $D$), a Galois connection linking $D$ to concrete domains, a Galois invariant $D'$ representing program semantics, and a theory $T$ defined on the domain. This theory comprises two operators: $F$, which represents the semantics of program constructs, and $G$, which performs abstractions of programs. The operator $F$ is typically sup-morphisms from $D'$ to itself, while $F$ and $G$ together form a continuous adjunction between the powers of $D$ and $G$ to $D'$. Within this framework, the "rising phase" involves computing the least fixed point of the function $G \circ F$ for a specific input, whereas the "falling phase" involves calculating $(G \circ F)^\omega$, the limit of the rising phase. This paper introduces a new approach to abstract interpretation by decomposing the rising and falling phases into independent mechanisms. We demonstrate that the falling phase can be viewed as the limit of a chain of post-fixed points of $G \circ F$, characterized by a specific algebraic property termed "compactness." Utilizing this property, we show that the falling phase corresponds to the unique fixed point of $G \circ F$ that is both supremum-preserving and continuous. Furthermore, we illustrate that this perspective enables the development of novel techniques for the falling phase, such as approximations and sound upper bounds. These advancements are validated through a case study on loop invariant generation. The proposed solution offers a generic framework for computing tight abstract fixed points, applicable to any abstract domain, input set, or program construct. Additionally, it supports various strategies for calculating these fixed points, including abstraction before or after iteration, sound over-approximation, and heuristic methods. This flexibility allows for the easy integration of new techniques into existing frameworks. Finally, experimental results confirm the practicality of our solution. All code is accessible at: https://github.com/raphael-poux/decoupling-rising-and-falling-phases-in-abstr-interpret

Topological materials have attracted significant attention due to their unique physical characteristics, including topologically protected states and robustness. However, a primary limitation of oxide ceramics is their susceptibility to external factors, such as illumination, which restricts the design of practical devices. This study demonstrates that the topological phase of oxide ceramics can be effectively managed through the application of surface electric fields, enabling the creation of topological phonons. By applying an external electric field to the surface of BaTiO$_3$ ceramics, we successfully induced a transition from surface to topological phonon states. Furthermore, the resulting topological phonons exhibit protection guaranteed by time-reversal symmetry and leverage quantum geometric properties to enhance pyroelectric responses. These findings pave the way for developing next-generation optoelectronic devices that integrate strain engineering, topological physics, and quantum mechanics. Additionally, this work offers a pathway to manipulate surface states in oxide ceramics using external electric fields and holds promise for discovering new topological phonon systems. Finally, the topological phonons identified here may contribute to solving the longstanding "majorana paradox" in phononics.

Outlier detection is a critical task within data mining and machine learning. This paper introduces a novel outlier score estimation approach leveraging proximity graphs, with its efficiency relying on a strategic selection of an optimal induced subspace. We demonstrate the role of metric dimensionality reduction (MDR) in rapid and precise BIRCH-based outlier detection for high-dimensional metric spaces, such as images and spectra. Our method's accuracy depends on choosing a subspace that strikes a favorable balance between dimensionality and the Euclidean structure inherent to the original metric space. Specifically, we prove that for any given metric space, there exists a specific dimensionality where our algorithm achieves the most accurate score estimation. To address this, we developed and validated a new metric-based criterion for identifying this optimal subspace. Furthermore, we show that our approach can be integrated with machine learning to significantly enhance classification performance. Experimental results indicate that our method identifies the best subspace at least ten times faster than state-of-the-art techniques, while maintaining comparable or superior accuracy in outlier score estimation. Additionally, our method reduces classification training time by up to 99% and lowers prediction error by as much as 15% compared to existing state-of-the-art subspaces. Finally, we provide a theoretical analysis of the algorithm's computational complexity. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first complexity analysis of MDR for outlier detection in metric spaces. The source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/fernandoalvarado2000/BIRCH-OD. This work is based on the following publications: F. A. Rodriguez, J. A. G. Sanz, and A. M. Rodriguez, J. A. G. Sanz, and A. M. Martinez, "Subspace-based outlier detection using a proximity graph," in *2021 IEEE International Conference on Data Mining (ICDM)*, 2021, pp. 107–116. The excitation dynamics and electromagnetic emissions from an atom positioned near a slender conducting mirror are investigated. Determining the mirror's response requires solving the three-dimensional Poisson equation for a geometry lacking translational symmetry, a challenge addressed using finite element methods. Furthermore, the derived force is compared against an analytical thin-sheet approximation valid under specific conditions. The study's primary finding is the emergence of novel phenomena when the atomic transition wavelength is comparable to the mirror's width. In these scenarios, energy exchange between the atom and the mirror is substantially altered, leading to either significant suppression or enhancement of excitation probabilities relative to those observed with a thick mirror. Additionally, analysis of optical emissions reveals that the spectrum and total power are markedly dependent on the mirror's width, with the system capable of operating as a tunable single-mode optical source. These results suggest broad applications, including force sensing, the manipulation of atomic lifetimes, and controlled photon emission. Ultimately, this work establishes a computational framework capable of modeling cavity quantum electrodynamics problems involving slit-like cavities of arbitrary shape. By enabling the study of quantum emitters within such cavities, it facilitates investigations into quantum phenomena and their associated technological applications. The accompanying software is publicly accessible. This study addresses node classification on unlabelled graph datasets where community structures are provided, aiming for fair labels while leveraging the graph's connectivity. We introduce a new framework designed to minimize both discriminatory bias and the loss of connectivity information. Our approach employs a novel objective function that integrates community structures and connectivity through an undifferentiated aggregation mechanism, subsequently optimizing node labels to achieve fair results. We demonstrate that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches regarding fairness metrics and connectivity preservation, particularly in scenarios involving highly disparate graph structures. Furthermore, we apply this model to a real-world case study focused on fair node labeling within a COVID-19 dataset. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance of node classification on an unlabelled COVID-19 dataset, and our approach has never before been evaluated in this context. Additionally, we present the first comprehensive empirical analysis of node classification fairness across various real-world COVID-19 datasets. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/DeepMind/graph_fairness. This work was conducted by researchers at DeepMind.

An analytical investigation of the reversible Michaelis-Menten enzyme reaction is conducted within the framework of general nonlinear kinetic equations. This study examines the reaction under conditions of arbitrary substrate and product concentrations, as well as the simultaneous presence of free enzyme and enzyme-substrate or enzyme-product complexes. The proposed methodology enables the modeling of reversible reactions for scenarios involving only substrate-enzyme complexes, complex equilibrium, and reversible inhibition. By utilizing a kinetic energy functional, the reaction's trajectory is determined, and its asymptotic behavior is analyzed. The main challenge lies in the nonlinearity of the reaction's right-hand side; however, the iterative method introduced in this work allows for the construction of the reaction's stationary state. This approach is applicable to systems of ordinary differential equations featuring the specific structure required to address the kinetic problem. The proposed iterative scheme is demonstrated to converge both globally and at a geometric rate. Additionally, the study establishes the convergence of the iterative process, the stability of the reaction's stationary state, and the rate at which the system approaches this state. Finally, the relevance of this method to reversible reaction systems involving enzyme-product complexes is illustrated through a specific example. This demonstration includes the construction of the first four approximations of the reaction's stationary state and an analysis of the convergence rate for this particular instance. All results are derived based on the kinetic equation of a reversible enzyme reaction involving only enzyme-product complexes. Furthermore, the paper addresses several open problems and proposes several conjectures. Finally, computer simulations of the iterative process for both the Michaelis-Menten and Lineweaver-Bauck equations are presented. These simulations examine the impact of substrate, product, and enzyme concentrations on the reaction's asymptotic behavior and the convergence rate of the iterative process toward the stationary state. Key parameters of the Michaelis-Menten and Lineweaver-Bauck equations are determined through computer simulations of the reaction. Additionally, the influence of enzyme concentration on the rate of approximation of the stationary state is analyzed. All conclusions are supported by computer simulations. Notably, the Michaelis-Menten and Lineweaver-Bauck equations are proven to be the first and second approximations of the reaction's stationary state, respectively. The paper concludes with several open problems and conjectures. Finally, the iterative method is shown to be applicable to systems of ordinary differential equations that arise in the study of the kinetics of reversible enzyme reactions involving only enzyme-product complexes. This method is also applicable to the kinetic equation of the reversible Michaelis-Menten enzyme reaction when enzyme-product complexes are present. However, it

This study examines the potential for detecting supersymmetry (SUSY) and substructures of SUSY models within proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The analysis focuses on final states characterized by high-transverse-momentum (pT) jets, missing energy from neutral weakly interacting particles, and no significant hadronic transverse activity. Two distinct scenarios are investigated: a "natural" SUSY model prioritizing large gluino masses and light electroweakino masses, alongside a "divided" SUSY model featuring heavy electroweakino masses. The investigation incorporates various intermediate mass spectrum configurations for both light and heavy SUSY particles. The necessary luminosity for achieving 5$\sigma$ discovery significance at the LHC varies depending on the specific SUSY mass spectrum. Furthermore, the analysis addresses the impact of the high-luminosity upgrade on discovery potential and evaluates the feasibility of such discoveries in proton-lead collisions at the future Large Hadron Collider. A key challenge in these searches is the substantial irreducible background from the Standard Model, primarily originating from top quark pair production. Consequently, the study places significant emphasis on reducing theoretical uncertainties associated with this process. Additionally, the analysis explores the detectability of these signatures in final states with pT > 1 TeV and assesses the discovery potential of the proposed channels at the HL-LHC. Finally, the work provides an overview of the discovery potential for these signatures in the future FCC-hh and HE-LHC colliders. This report is based on the findings of the Phenomenal Higgs and Beyond the Standard Model (PhenBSM) working group of the European Strategy for Particle Physics. The group's activities include conducting phenomenological studies of the LHC, HL-LHC, and future proton-proton colliders, as well as analyzing the discovery potential of the Higgs boson and beyond-Standard-Model physics. Furthermore, the working group is responsible for conducting phenomenological studies for the European Future Colliders (FCC) and the High Energy Large Hadron Collider (HE-LHC). The outcomes of these studies will be presented at the European Strategy for Particle Physics (ESPP) plenary meeting in Lausanne, Switzerland, in September 2021. The proceedings will also be shared with the US Strategy for Particle Physics (USP) and the US Future Circular Collider (FCC) meetings. We propose a diagnostic based on the options-implied volatility term structure to identify significant deviations from constant diffusion models within non-negative asset classes, such as financial bubbles. By framing the valuation of non-negative assets under these models as a first-exit problem with random termination times, we derive a differential equation for the diagonal of the transition density. This equation involves random constants representing the mean return over the expected period, incorporating both deterministic and stochastic components. Consequently, returns are modeled as the sum of a deterministic drift and a stochastic process. The volatility gap between this model and a constant-diffusion framework depends on the diagonal of the transition density and its curvature. We demonstrate that standard bubble indicators can be reformulated using this approach and extend the framework to financial bubbles characterized by stochastic mean returns and random maturity dates. Finally, we apply the methodology to examine the 2015–2016 Japanese bubble. This methodology offers a more general framework for bubble detection, integrating both deterministic and stochastic elements. It facilitates the distinction between assets with predictable periods and those possessing only a distribution of potential termination times. Furthermore, it enables the measurement of the deviation of an asset's return from its expected value and assesses the stability of this deviation. Empirical results indicate that this methodology can detect and characterize financial bubbles. Additionally, we discuss how this approach can be extended to differentiate between assets with constant, increasing, or decreasing expected returns. This paper extends the authors' prior research published in *Chaos* (Vol. 28, No. 10, 2018). For this extension, we utilize a broader class of models that encompass both random and non-random maturity dates, thereby enabling the comparison of bubbles across different assets. Specifically, we analyze the Japanese bubble of 2015–2016 and compare it with bubbles observed in 2007 and 2009. The comparison of bubbles across various assets is detailed in our work published in *Chaos* (Vol. 28, No. 10, 2018). Additionally, the return decomposition is further explored in our study published in *Chaos* (Vol. 29, No. 1, 2019). This methodology was initially developed to analyze the Japanese bubble during the 2015–2016 period. We have also applied it to compare bubbles in the Japanese and US markets from 2007 to 2016. We investigate quantum states of a driven harmonic oscillator that are not in equilibrium by employing the difference equation method. By expanding the integrand in a Taylor series, we transform the quantum mechanical problem into classical integrations. Specifically, we calculate the $Q$-function at each time step using Simpson's rule within a Monte Carlo framework, and we also determine the reduced Wigner function through this method. Our results demonstrate that the system transitions into a driven harmonic oscillator state, which can be verified by observing the expectation value of the position operator. Additionally, the trajectories for the $Q$ and Wigner functions show perfect agreement with the difference equation method. Finally, the driven conditions are confirmed by examining the expectation values of the annihilation and creation operators. This approach offers an efficient alternative to the difference equation method, as it provides complete quantum states in the form of quasiprobability distributions. Furthermore, the path integral technique, grounded in the idea of equivalent classical systems, enables the investigation of quantum effects in driven harmonic oscillators without solving the corresponding classical equations of motion. Recent research indicates that product reviews contain rich sentiment information. This study introduces a new model, the Sentiment-sensitive Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN), designed for review-based product recommendation. The framework is composed of two submodules: the Sentiment-sensitive Semantic Extraction Network (SSEN) and the Sentiment-sensitive Interactive Fusion Network (SIF). To effectively capture both semantic and sentiment features, SSEN integrates sentiment polarity and sentiment terms. Meanwhile, SIF combines sentiment polarity and term similarity to enhance the fusion of feature representations. Experimental results demonstrate that SIFN significantly outperforms baseline models. Furthermore, an ablation study confirms that the proposed improvements positively impact the suggestion of recommended products. Finally, case studies illustrate the model's superior performance and high interpretability. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/zhongyuan1992/SIFN.

Data sparsity and the absence of high-quality lexical resources pose significant hurdles in modeling lexical substitutions for Arabic-English code-switched text. This study investigates enhancing data augmentation during cross-lingual lexical substitution. We introduce a data augmentation approach utilizing weak supervision through dictionary lookups, which enables the generation of new training samples from existing ones. This method leverages the versatility of code-switched Arabic, producing diverse training data without requiring additional annotations. Furthermore, we examine the impact of generated samples on model performance through experiments on text classification and machine translation tasks. Results indicate that our approach effectively improves model performance on both code-switched and non-code-switched datasets. Finally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the generated samples. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan12345/Data-Augmentation-For-Arabic-English-Code-Switching. We demonstrate that no precompact subgroup of the diffeomorphism group of a compact hyperbolic surface $S$, equipped with the Roelcke uniform structure, admits a left-invariant probability measure. A connectable brane refers to a fixed point brane that remains static under conformal invariance, specifically representing a point at infinity in the deformed theory. Our analysis demonstrates that such branes exist exclusively in generalized $\lambda$-deformations constructed from a specific subset of simple, simply connected Lie groups within the $G$ family. Furthermore, although these branes appear at a single point at infinity in the unfolded theory, they form a finite region in the folded theory whenever a simple, compact subgroup exists in $H$. This research expands upon our earlier findings regarding 1/4 BPS strings in 6D supergravity, which we previously showed correspond to a connectable brane in the generalized $\lambda$-deformation of $E_6/(-128)$, where $(-128)$ denotes a 128-dimensional lattice polytope. These results suggest the existence of additional dual Chern-Simons matter theories, where the matter content is determined by the root polytope of $G$ and the shape of the fundamental polytope of $Sp(2)$ or $S(2)$. We introduce a new family of continuous variable splines defined on hex meshes, termed "tet splines." In trivariate space, these splines are constructed by joining "tetrahedrons" along the faces of the original mesh. Our technique leverages the specific topology of hex meshes, enabling the creation of continuous functions on arbitrary grids that are significantly harder to compute than those achievable through tesselations. We outline the underlying theory, provide an algorithm to generate these "fake tets," and demonstrate an interactive hex mesh model featuring up to 58 tets per hexahedron. Our findings open new avenues for research into continuous functions on hex meshes. The source code and interactive results are accessible at https://github.com/brunag/tetsinhex. Furthermore, tet splines are integrated into OpenSubdiv, the industry-standard tessellation framework utilized by major graphics software like Maya and Blender. This inclusion allows for the rapid experimentation and deployment of our methodology. Our work holds significant potential for advancing research on continuous functions over hex meshes. Specifically, we address and resolve several longstanding challenges in this domain, including: (i) the design of continuous subdivision schemes for hex meshes; (ii) the development of continuous variable splines on this grid type; and (iii) the creation of subdivision-based remeshing techniques that maintain continuity. Our approach meets and exceeds multiple criteria established by existing solutions. Additionally, the computational cost of our method is comparable to, or lower than, that of comparable approaches. Relation extraction focuses on identifying entity pairs within textual data and mapping them to specific relations. This task is vital for building knowledge graphs and generating knowledge-based question-answer systems. Although recent advancements in deep learning have enhanced performance, the field still faces significant hurdles. To address the scarcity of labeled data, we introduce a novel approach that leverages knowledge graph link prediction to improve relation extraction. By integrating semantic information from the knowledge graph, our method enables relation classification to make more informed predictions. Experimental results demonstrate that this framework outperforms state-of-the-art techniques on two public datasets. The human visual ventral temporal cortex (VTC) contains specialized regions for recognizing animacy categories, such as faces, scenes, and bodies. While numerous models have been proposed to explain how these regions differentiate between them, their predictive capabilities remain unverified. This study evaluates multiple analytical and computational approaches that characterize distinct representations for animacy categories and tests their effectiveness in predicting neural activity. We found that the most robust prediction arises from a low-dimensional structure defined by the relative ordering of categories across VTC neurons. This result holds true across diverse datasets, including those comprising hundreds of categories and thousands of images, and remains consistent across different individuals. We developed several computational models to capture this structure, with the best performance achieved by a category-based model that utilizes the relative ranking of categories within individual neurons. Our findings suggest that the fundamental mechanism for animacy selectivity in the human VTC is the ability of neurons to rank visual categories consistently. This low-dimensional, locally ordered structure likely supports the development of category-selective regions and enables the differentiation of hundreds of distinct animacy categories. The code and data utilized in this study are accessible at https://github.com/alexmaheswaran/animacy_ranking. Supplementary data is available at https://osf.io/49523/. We tested various analytical and computational methods to explain how these regions differentiate between animacy categories like faces, bodies, plants, landscapes, and crowds. Our results indicate that the most robust prediction comes from a low-dimensional structure defined by the relative ordering of these categories among neurons. This finding was replicated across diverse datasets containing hundreds of categories and thousands of images, as well as across different individuals. We developed several computational models to capture this structure, with the best performance achieved by a category-based model that leverages the relative ranking of categories within individual neurons. This suggests that the core principle of animacy selectivity in the human VTC is the consistent ranking of visual categories by neurons, a locally defined ordering that serves as the essence of the animacy structure in the human VTC. This low-dimensional, locally defined ordering provides a parsimonious explanation for the differentiation of hundreds of distinct animacy categories and offers a novel perspective on the organization of categorization regions in the human VTC. This study introduces a new, robust framework for developing arrangement-preserving filters (APFs) designed for convolving two-dimensional and three-dimensional finite element meshes with data. The proposed APF formulation relies on solving a convex optimization problem, specifically minimizing a low-pass cost function subject to a set of constraints. These constraints ensure the preservation of mesh arrangements, maintain the original data topology, and define an admissible range for interpolated values at unmeasured locations. To enhance computational efficiency, the method employs a closed-form solution for the optimal low-pass data. Furthermore, the proposed APF is evaluated against conventional interpolation techniques, including linear, cubic, and thin-plate spline interpolation, as well as against covariance-based Gaussian smoothing. The assessment utilizes a synthetic data generator, which is anticipated to be released as an open-source tool. Results from both numerical experiments and a case study indicate that the proposed APF outperforms traditional interpolation methods in terms of smoothing capability while superiorly retaining key geometric features. Additionally, the APF demonstrates effectiveness in removing data outliers. A critical component of this approach is its efficient algorithm for calculating influence functions, which quantifies the impact of measured data points on unknown data points. This study also presents a novel technique for estimating the optimal filter bandwidth by analyzing data outliers. Finally, the developed APF algorithms are implemented as a user-friendly feature within the open-source software FEToolbox. Type-C quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in black hole X-ray transients have historically been observed exclusively during the hard-intermediate state, a regime characterized by a radio-loud transition and the emergence of low-frequency quasi-periodic oscillations (LFQPOs) in radio frequencies. This study investigates the evolution of LFQPOs in the black hole X-ray binary MAXI J1535-571, focusing on the transition from the hard-intermediate to the soft state. Data were collected using the Insight-HXMT observatory, which offers a broad energy range and high time resolution. We identified a type-C LFQPO with a frequency of 0.7 Hz, exhibiting a consistent fractional amplitude of approximately 10% across both hard and soft spectral states. As the system evolves toward the soft state, the spectral energy distribution shifts, and the power spectrum transitions from a single-peak to a double-peak configuration. These findings suggest that type-C QPOs are not confined to the hard-intermediate state and may serve as a critical indicator of the radio-loud transition in black hole X-ray binaries. Furthermore, our results support the frequency mapping model, which links the evolution of LFQQPOs to the movement of the accretion disc and inner jet base. Additionally, we propose that the inner accretion flow, likely a thin accretion disc, is the probable origin of the type-C LFQPO. Finally, we demonstrate that the type-C LFQPO frequency in MAXI J1535-571 aligns with the Keplerian frequency at approximately 100 gravitational radii, a distance that correlates with the radio-loud transition. These conclusions are consistent with those of a prior study by the same group, which employed NuSTAR and RXTE data. Collectively, our results indicate that type-C QPOs may act as a marker for the radio-loud transition in black hole X-ray binaries. Additionally, the detection of type-C QPOs in the soft state suggests that the soft X-ray state of MAXI J1535-571 may be a transient feature. These insights may aid in understanding the nature of the radio-loud transition and the origin of LFQPOs. However, further investigation is required to confirm the link between type-C QPOs and the radio-loud transition. This paper introduces a new approach to transfer learning for the empirical discovery of social intrinsic motivation. Empirical discovery involves the automatic generation of goals and intrinsic rewards, which are essential for achieving transferable intrinsic motivation. Our proposed method, named TIEmp (Transfer of Interdependent Empowerment), functions by identifying the correlation between the partner agent's past actions and future behaviors, empowering the partner's state based on this correlation, and subsequently rewarding the subject agent if its current action aligns with the predicted future behavior. TIEmp demonstrates significant transfer across domains, learning a substantial portion of skills from a single source domain without reliance on human guidance. These discovered skills include caring for the partner, such as pushing it in a pusher domain or feeding it in a feeding domain, as well as playing with the partner, like tag or chase games. Furthermore, the application of TIEmp within population-based training has resulted in the emergence of complex joint behaviors, such as joint empathy, coordination, and role reversal. In summary, our research advances the fields of social intrinsic motivation, task specification, and intrinsic motivation discovery by offering a novel, non-human-in-the-loop technique for empirically discovering social intrinsic motivation that achieves significant transfer between domains. Empirical code and videos are available at https://github.com/andrew-lee-kaist/emp_discovery. Video demonstrations can be found at https://youtu.be/4221141114I. Spectroscopy is a fundamental technique in chemistry and physics, enabling the analysis of chemical structures and reactions. By measuring light absorption across various wavelengths, spectrosopic data reveals the unique molecular fingerprints of substances. Traditionally, interpreting this complex signal requires a reference to a substance, often needing physical access to it. However, in many scenarios, direct access is impossible, and a prior sample is unavailable for initial data identification. While computational chemistry methods can simulate these fingerprints, generating a single shot identification model for any substance anywhere remains challenging. In contrast, our physics-informed contrastive learning approach effectively identifies any substance from just one spectral image. By simulating the interaction between light and molecules, we generate synthetic spectra and successfully map real spectral images to the corresponding simulated substances. This study demonstrates our method's ability to accurately identify diverse substances, including organic and inorganic acids, inorganic salts, and alkaloids. Furthermore, we apply this technique to analyze the chemical composition of archaeological artifacts, such as seals and beads. Ultimately, our findings indicate that our model can reliably identify substances even without a real physical reference. This represents a significant advancement in computational chemistry, offering a new tool for chemical analysis that reduces reliance on physical references. Additionally, it enables the simultaneous identification of multiple substances, thereby enhancing the efficiency of chemical analysis workflows. Finally, this approach holds potential for identifying unknown substances in various applications, such as drug discovery and environmental monitoring. We introduce a new end-to-end method for keypoint-based image matching that operates without predefined image features. Our approach, named LoFTR (Local-Freeze Global Attention), utilizes a global descriptor bank integrated with local feature modules to identify and match images based on their local attributes. By employing a detector-free strategy, we allow the global descriptor bank to implicitly identify high-relevant areas through high-confidence descriptor pairs, thereby eliminating the need for separate interest point detectors and reducing reliance on precise keypoint localization. Furthermore, we have developed a novel synthetic dataset, ArgLine, specifically designed to train keypoint-based matching models effectively in the absence of keypoint annotations. This model is lightweight, completing an inference on a single NVIDIA TitanX GPU in approximately 0.3 seconds. Algorithms used to infer vector magnetic field data from the Sun's photosphere, such as those employed by the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) on the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO), rely on physical models of the observed formation height. These models can be sensitive to biases in their inputs, leading to spurious patterns in the resulting magnetic field maps. Such artifacts may be misinterpreted as genuine large-scale magnetic field structures, thereby skewing scientific conclusions. This study examines the bias sensitivity of HMI's Inferred (Inferno) product, which reconstructs 3D magnetic fields from 2D line-of-sight brightness and intensity gradients. Inferno's formation height is derived from a statistical analysis of HMI's continuum intensity images. We demonstrate that systematic variations in the inferred 3D magnetic field magnitude exist across the HMI imaging field of view (FOV), driven by the Inferno's formation height model. These variations are most pronounced near the FOV's edges, where the formation height model is most inaccurate. Consequently, the magnetic field magnitude is overestimated in the central FOV and underestimated at the periphery. To mitigate this, we propose a new method for self-consistently estimating formation height from SDO/AIA images across all available EUV wavelengths. This approach utilizes a machine learning technique to identify the EUV wavelength that most closely approximates the traditional Galloway et al. (1981) formation height. We apply this method to Inferno and show that it significantly reduces the bias-sensitive pattern observed in the magnetic field magnitude. This research offers a pathway for self-consistent formation height estimation, which can be applied to future 3D magnetic field inference products. By addressing this specific bias, such products will enable more accurate and robust scientific analysis. Additionally, we provide open-source Python code for performing Inferno with self-consistent formation heights, which can be utilized by the community. This code is available at https://github.com/psf1069/Inferno-formation-height-estimation. We conclude that this technique is applicable to other 3D magnetic field inference products, including the Multi-chromospheric (Inferno-MCM) product, to enhance the accuracy of 3D magnetic field estimates. Furthermore, we outline the necessary steps to integrate this method into the public Inferno and Inferno-MCM products. The rise of smart grid technologies has enabled utilities to regulate real-time energy consumption, allowing them to influence when consumers draw power and thereby mitigate the environmental and financial costs associated with peak demand. This study introduces an independent demand-side control approach for consumers, utilizing a collective game theoretical framework to enhance the method's performance. The proposed system, which incorporates an energy usage planner and real-time load controller, enables participants to achieve the highest possible quality of service by jointly optimizing the utility function's parameters. These two key parameters are the weighting factor for the cost function and the maximum allowable deviation from the scheduled load. Furthermore, an analysis is provided to determine an optimal value for this deviation. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the collective game approach significantly outperforms an uncoordinated control strategy. Specifically, it achieves a 40% reduction in financial cost, a 20% improvement in utility function value, and a 30% reduction in the optimal cost function value compared to uncoordinated control. Additionally, the proposed control scheme achieves a 43% reduction in optimal scheduled load, final cost, optimal cost function value, and optimal generation power relative to an uncontrolled scenario. Finally, the proposed collective game is proven to be a potential game, ensuring the existence of a pure Nash equilibrium. Consequently, an iterative best-response algorithm is suggested to facilitate the attainment of the Nash equilibrium. In this control framework, consumers can achieve their optimal objectives without requiring communication with the utility company. Instead, they only need to exchange information with other participating consumers. By implementing this collective control method, consumers can achieve a 40% reduction in the cost function value, representing a substantial financial benefit. This work thus offers a promising pathway for consumers to manage their energy usage effectively. A primary advantage of this approach is that it allows consumers to achieve their goals without relying on the utility company, thereby promoting a more democratic smart grid environment. Additionally, the proposed collective control strategy can be extended to incorporate the utility company's control signals, enabling consumers to further optimize their cost and energy savings. Finally, the control method can be easily adapted to address other objectives, such as reducing the carbon footprint or enhancing the reliability of the power grid. However, it is important to note that the reliability analysis is beyond the scope of this paper. To address this, a separate paper has been submitted to detail the reliability analysis of the proposed control method. Leveraging the fact that the convergence is uniform and bounded by the second largest eigenvalue of a specific self-adjoint operator family dependent on the measure, we reduce the problem to analyzing a trigonometric sum. This analysis utilizes a notable identity that expresses the sum as a linear combination of trigonometric terms weighted by the first few Stirling numbers of the second kind. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the supremum of the absolute value of the characteristic trigonometric sum, linking it to the maximum value of a particular polynomial with real coefficients, and we compute the asymptotic behavior of this supremum. Finally, we present a significant extension of von Neumann's theorem that relaxes the initial assumptions. Stars with masses below 0.8 solar masses follow an evolutionary path where they shed their outer envelopes before becoming white dwarfs. This transition typically occurs when stars reach old ages and low metallicities. By analyzing the BP/RP spectra of 22 such stars from the Gaia Data Release 3, we identified key spectral features useful for detecting these specific spectral types. We developed a neural network capable of distinguishing these low-metallicity, evolved stars from younger or metal-rich counterparts. Our results show that, using a 10% misclassification rate, the flux from BP/RP spectra allows us to accurately identify these stars. This approach is particularly valuable for designing follow-up observations of similar objects within the Gaia survey volume. Our findings indicate that approximately 1000 of these stars are present in the Gaia Early Third Data Validation (EDRV) catalog. Furthermore, we demonstrated that the BP/RP data can be utilized to identify a population of metal-poor stars with [Fe/H] below -1.5. Leveraging the BP/RP data, we propose that this population could be selected using a cut of [Fe/H] < -1.5 and A(V-I) > 1.5 mag. This selection method offers a more than tenfold increase in the number of stars compared to the equivalent count selected solely through photometry. We anticipate that this technique will facilitate the discovery of rare, extremely metal-poor stars in the future. Additionally, we have made our code and the BP/RP sample available to the public. We conclude that Gaia BP/RP spectra serve as a valuable tool for identifying this specific stellar population. Our findings suggest that these stars are more common than previously believed, and they may play a significant role in the chemical evolution of the Galaxy. We recommend that astronomers prioritize these stars for follow-up observations to investigate their unique properties. We also note that these stars may provide insights into the early stages of galaxy formation and evolution. Finally, we propose that these stars could be used to test various astrophysical models and theories. We conclude that the BP/RP data will be instrumental in identifying and studying these stars in the future. Furthermore, we suggest that the BP/RP data will contribute to a better understanding of the chemical evolution of the Galaxy. We also note that these stars may provide a link between the early universe and the present day. Finally, we propose that the BP/RP data will help us understand the role of low-metallicity stars in the chemical evolution of the Galaxy

Global fire intensity is a critical component of wildfire severity, yet it has received limited attention. This study introduces a novel, straightforward approach to assess and predict worldwide fire season intensity. We compile a new dataset of yearly fire intensity records, measured in total radiative power, spanning from 2003 to 2018 across 115 countries. This dataset is constructed using Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) active fire detection records and the EARTHDATA geospatial database. Our analysis reveals that fire season intensity scales with the heterogeneity of historical climate change. We further demonstrate that fire intensity can be forecasted using a model that incorporates both historical climate change heterogeneity and the heterogeneity of the previous season's fire intensity. These findings underscore the significant role of climate change in determining global fire intensity and offer valuable insights for regional fire risk assessment. The dataset is accessible via the Mendeley Data repository at https://doi.org/10.17613/12470017. Additionally, the supporting code can be found at https://github.com/zhijianwang1989/FireIntensity. To effectively compare morphological complexity across languages, a set of reliable, formally defined complexity metrics is necessary. This study investigates the relationship between a proposed corpus-based complexity indicator, denoted as M, and nine other established metrics, analyzing how this indicator aligns with the volume of morphological data within a corpus. The analysis reveals a strong positive correlation between M and data size, demonstrating a clear linear relationship. Consequently, this research confirms that a consistent pattern of variation exists among both the corpus-based indicator M and the other eight existing metrics. These findings suggest that the proposed indicator M serves as a reliable measure of lexical morphological complexity in spoken and written languages. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that a corpus size of 1,000 words is sufficient for calculating M with a high degree of accuracy. Finally, the paper explores the implications of these results for the design of morphological richness measures intended for typological applications. A dataset comprising lexically tagged corporors from 111 languages is made available for research use. All analyses were conducted using an open-source Python package named morplexity, which is also provided for further application. The underlying data for this study can be accessed via Zenodo. This work builds upon the methodology introduced in J. Moralex, 2020, which proposed a formal definition for a corpus-based complexity indicator. By offering an alternative, computationally efficient definition for M, this paper facilitates the large-scale analysis of complexity metrics across a vast number of languages. Additionally, the study addresses the challenge of identifying a single, reliable indicator for typological research and underscores the critical need for validating such indicators against diverse methodological approaches. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of these findings for typological research. To facilitate replication, a dataset containing gold-standard annotations for 111 languages is provided. This resource enables researchers to evaluate the reliability of M across a variety of typological scenarios. The code used for analysis is available on GitHub. These contributions support the broader goal of advancing typological research through rigorous validation and reproducibility. By facilitating a large-scale analysis of morphological complexity across numerous languages, this work provides a foundation for comparative studies and promotes a deeper understanding of how complexity varies across different language families. The availability of this analysis code allows other researchers to replicate the findings and extend the work in their own studies. This support is essential for driving future research in the field of typology. We investigate magnification effects caused by substructure within galaxy clusters, utilizing both N-body simulations and analytic calculations. Our analysis focuses on the impact of small-scale substructure on image magnification in strongly lensed systems, with particular attention to the ratio between the observed Einstein ring radius and its value in the absence of such substructure. We examine subhalo abundance predictions derived from both cold dark matter (CDM) and self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) models. Under the assumption of CDM, we demonstrate that the average magnification factor for small circular sources remains nearly independent of the subhalo concentration parameter. Conversely, we find that the subhalo fraction in SIDM halos is approximately 2.5 times lower than in CDM halos, a reduction that remains consistent across different scattering cross-sections. This outcome contrasts with the widely held expectation that SIDM leads to a lower subhalo fraction but results in deeper subhalo potentials, thereby producing comparable tidal effects on host halos as those in a collisionless scenario. Furthermore, we demonstrate that subhalos in SIDM halos possess lower internal mass concentrations, which diminishes their gravitational influence on lensed sources. Finally, we show that the probability distribution of the magnification ratio is asymmetric and skewed toward higher values in the presence of subhalos. We conclude that the likelihood of observing a magnification ratio exceeding 2 is roughly 10% in a CDM universe, but drops to approximately 1% in an SIDM universe. These findings offer a potential observational method to distinguish between these two primary dark matter candidates. Additionally, our results suggest that current observations of magnification ratios in galaxy clusters do not definitively favor either cosmological model. However, we note that the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) possesses the sensitivity to detect substructures in galaxy clusters that could resolve this distinction. We illustrate this by presenting a simulation of a galaxy cluster within the Atacama Large Millimeter Array Cosmology Legacy Survey (ALMAGS) survey area, showing that substructure can enhance magnification by up to an order of magnitude. This capability may enable future observations to differentiate between the standard $\Lambda$CDM model and the self-interacting dark matter alternative. Finally, we demonstrate that the Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA) can detect substructures in galaxy clusters that significantly affect magnification. We conclude that ALMA will play a crucial role in clarifying the nature of dark matter.

Large-scale deep neural networks are essential for numerous real-world applications, particularly those involving private data like speech and vision, where the high network size impedes deployment. While moving data to the model is a standard strategy, moving the model to the data is often more practical, especially for edge computing environments. This paper introduces a novel model compression technique that facilitates distributed training and inference by deploying smaller models close to the data. Our approach relies on distilling knowledge from a large global model into these local smaller models based on partial observations of the same data. Unlike traditional methods that require joint model access or significant storage, our method enables smaller models to capture comparable recognition and speech quality using only a subset of the full model's knowledge. This is achieved through a specific pairwise interaction between the querying large model and the serving small model. Furthermore, our approach eliminates the need for complex synchronization mechanisms typically found in knowledge distillation, allowing small models to be trained in a batch mode that ignores the large model. We demonstrate the method's efficacy with a new dataset containing over 100 hours of speech from 1,000 speakers. Results indicate that a small model containing 1/16th of the large model's parameters can match its performance through pairwise learning, whereas standard distillation causes a substantial drop in performance. Additionally, when applied to visual data, the method enables a 3-layer model to achieve the accuracy of much larger models. Finally, the computational efficiency of our approach allows it to serve as a speech front-end in real-time applications. Extensive evaluations on speech and vision datasets confirm that small models can effectively retain partial knowledge of the global model to deliver high-quality service. The efficacy of this strategy is further demonstrated by its application to emerging personalized AI applications. This paper introduces M-ar-K-Rapid Independent Component Analysis (M-K-R-ICA), a novel framework designed to separate mixed signals originating from independent sources. The mixing process is modeled as a combination of a known matrix and an unknown matrix with unknown parameters. This approach is particularly valuable for separating signals from sources with known characteristics, such as audio files or music, from unknown sources, or for isolating known signals from those with unknown parameters, including power line carrier signals in the presence of noise. We provide theoretical justification and derive the objective function for M-K-R-ICA. Furthermore, we establish the necessary and sufficient conditions under which the true independent component matrix can be recovered using M-K-R-ICA, ensuring the method avoids local optima. Finally, simulations are conducted to validate the theoretical findings and assess the method's performance. The results demonstrate that, given a sufficient number of observed signals, M-K-R-ICA can successfully separate mixed inputs into their original independent components. The method is implemented in Python and made available at: https://github.com/abrar1234567/M-K-R-ICA. Future research will explore the application of M-K-R-ICA to real-world data. Additionally, the method is being translated into various other languages to enhance its accessibility and utility for a broader global audience. Finally, we welcome contributions from researchers and individuals with proficiency in any language to assist in this translation effort.
