Initial resources serve as fundamental quantum phenomena from which other resources are derived; they are invariant under local operations and classical communication (LOCC) and possess state-independent maximum asymptotic convertibility to other resources under LOCC. This study establishes an initial law regarding quantum resources. We define the resource ratio between two resources $R_1$ and $R_2$ as the state-independent limit of the conversion rate between $R_1$ and $R_2$ achievable via LOCC. The ratio theorem demonstrates that the resource ratio between any two pure states remains constant regardless of the specific initial resource theory. Furthermore, it is proven that the asymptotic conversion rate between any two pure states achievable within a general resource theory is determined by the resource ratio of those two states. Consequently, it follows that any initial resource is state monotonic within a general quantum resource theory. Leveraging these findings, we derive the capacity of any resource theory to distill a specific type of quantum resource from a classical ensemble of states. Additionally, the analysis yields new insights into resource equivalence and the construction of resource graphs. Finally, the universal nature of initial resources and the established theorems are validated through quantum coherence and entanglement as initial resources in various quantum scenarios. These results offer a novel perspective on initial quantum resources and their applications in quantum information processing. Moreover, the paper introduces a new framework for initial quantum resource theories, which may hold significant interest for future research. Specifically, this new framework enables the characterization of initial quantum resources using a distance metric between quantum states. This approach not only facilitates the calculation of initial resource measures but also facilitates the construction of initial resource theories for various quantum resources. This framework is particularly valuable for resource theories involving multiple subsystems. Additionally, the study examines initial quantum resources within the context of post-hoc quantum resource theories. This examination reveals that initial resources in post-hoc quantum resource theories are not necessarily state monotonic, thereby highlighting the distinct characteristics of initial quantum resources across different theoretical frameworks. The paper concludes by exploring the relationship between initial quantum resources and resource monotones. Specifically, it is demonstrated that initial resources can be constructed from resource monotones, with their effectiveness illustrated through the relative entropy of coherence. The exploration of initial quantum resources in this study may provide a new perspective on quantum resource theory and offer new avenues for future research. Furthermore, the results can be extended to initial resources for quantum channels. The characterization of initial quantum channel resources will be the subject of future work. Overall, this work provides a new perspective on quantum resource theory

We introduce a technique for evaluating data consistency with a model defined by exponential moments. This approach involves formulating and solving a non-linear semi-infinite programming problem to determine the maximum deviation a function can deviate from the model while remaining consistent with the data. Although conceived for eugenetics, the method is broadly applicable. Its utility extends to verifying assumptions in statistical testing, such as those used in the Kolmogorov-Mirsky goodness-of-fit test. Additionally, it aids in understanding the interpretation and limits of inverse problems, such as reconstructing a probability density from its cumulative distribution. We apply the method to a simplified problem in astrophysics and discuss a variant that addresses the maximum deviation between two functions integrating to one, subject to a fixed set of exponential moments. This variant is particularly useful for analyzing data sets like the solar metallicity debate. Finally, we highlight several open questions arising from this methodology. Key words: extremum problems, exponential moments, exponential families, exponential sums, non-linear optimization, inverting the cumulative distribution function, statistical testing, statistical testing, astrophysics.

This work addresses inference challenges within non-stationary time sequences characterized by heavy tails and time-dependent autocorrelation. To address these issues, the study introduces a new class of non-stable, non-stationary multivariate time sequences, for which it develops estimators, obtains asymptotic results, and establishes the asymptotic non-consistency of conventional approaches. Furthermore, simulation studies are conducted to validate the reliability of these findings. The framework is motivated by economic time series that exhibit persistent fluctuations around zero due to policy interventions, such as central bank actions following the 2008 financial crisis. As an illustrative application, the paper proposes a testing procedure to non-rigorously detect non-stationarity and compares it against standard methods. Additionally, high-frequency financial data is analyzed under the alternative hypothesis of stationarity. This empirical analysis demonstrates that tests designed for stable, stationary series may yield misleading conclusions when applied to heavy-tailed, non-stationary multivariate time series. The proposed testing framework offers a significant advantage by remaining robust to violations of both independence and stability assumptions. Finally, the study examines the asymptotic behavior of the test when applied to stationary and stable data, as well as heavy-tailed and non-stationary data, to ensure a comprehensive understanding of the method's properties. Overall, the findings indicate that the proposed framework facilitates reliable inference in persistent heavy-tailed economic and financial time series, even in the presence of non-stationarity induced by economic shocks. Notably, the analysis suggests that the impact of non-stationarity diminishes as the sampling frequency increases. These results are supported by the observation that the number of observations within a single transaction period (e.g., 15 minutes) is sufficiently large to ensure asymptotic validity. Consequently, the proposed framework is well-suited for high-frequency data inference, including intraday and high-frequency event studies. This study examines the distributed $r$-dominating set problem, which involves identifying a $r$-dominating set of minimal cardinality. We focus specifically on graphs characterized by a low vertex degree $\Delta$ and a high girth $g$. By integrating two graph-theoretic techniques—local greedy strategies and tree-width decomposition—we formulate two distinct algorithms for distributed $r$-domination. The first approach is a time-efficient $r$-dominating set algorithm that remains effective within a limited number of rounds. The second is an asymptotically optimal degree algorithm, which leverages the first algorithm's output to refine the initial solution into a more optimal one utilizing a reduced number of rounds. Collectively, these two algorithms address the distributed $r$-dominating set problem. Experimental results indicate that the theoretical predictions of both algorithms are valid and demonstrate that our proposed algorithms outperform existing ones. Finally, we analyze the time complexity of our algorithms in relation to the distance $r$. In recent years, neural visualization has increasingly adopted deep learning techniques, with this research often falling into two distinct categories: either employing deep learning to learn representations for classical methods or utilizing neural radiance fields to model 3D scenes. However, these existing approaches fail to meet the specific requirements of neural visualization, particularly the need for bright field rendering. Bright field rendering is essential for visualization because the rendering equation—which renders the integral of incoming radiance over the entire hemisphere—cannot be directly applied to neural radiance fields, which are defined by a neural network predicting radiance and density at 3D points. While a recent paper addressed this by deriving a bright field rendering method, the complexity of the resulting algorithm makes it difficult to implement and integrate into deep learning models. To address this, we introduce a method that enables bright field rendering in neural visualization. Our approach involves learning the transmission function of neural radiation media to calculate the transmission depth, a process that can be combined with neural radiance fields to render new views. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method for neural visualization through several examples. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/1229chen/bright-field-neural-visualization. Furthermore, we plan to release a open-source framework for neural visualization that supports both bright and dark field rendering, with contributions from the community welcome. Specifically, we invite collaborators to enable various existing techniques for neural visualization, such as color harmony, semantic understanding, and anomaly detection, to be applied within neural visualization. Colour-kinematics duality has recently been extended to integrable systems, where it manifests as a transformation mapping solutions of the flatness condition into a pair of local Poisson bi-flat commutative algebras. Solar jets originate from magnetic reconnection events occurring above active regions, where heated plasma is expelled into the corona and along open magnetic loops. This study presents LOFAR observations of a jet-driven piston surge occurring in the low corona. The surge, detected on May 12, 2018, above a jet's footpoint near active region CSHAR 2991, was observed simultaneously by LOFAR and the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA). LOFAR's sensitivity to non-thermal emission allowed for the detection of jets and surge fronts that are typically invisible to optically sensitive instruments like AIA. Our analysis reveals that the surge front moves at approximately 100 km s$^{-1}$, while the jet exhibits a significantly higher average speed of 300 km s$^{-1}$. Furthermore, LOFAR's ability to image low coronal plasma and jets at a specific frequency of 1.4 GHz suggests a plasma temperature of roughly 1 MK. These findings suggest that jets and surge fronts are driven by reconnection outflows, with the surge's dynamics influenced by the underlying jet. This research underscores the value of LOFAR for studying low-coronal dynamics and its capacity to detect low-frequency non-thermal emission from jets and surge fronts. Future observations of similar events will enhance our understanding of the coupling between jets and surge fronts and their associated energy release. Temporally ordered data is vital for describing dynamic processes in life science, yet the complexity of these sequences often hinders their analysis. Reinforcement learning focuses on agents operating within partially observable environments, where they must manage incomplete information regarding their state and the mechanisms governing their interactions. In many practical scenarios, computational constraints prevent agents from maintaining a full model of their prior beliefs. This study demonstrates that recurrent neural networks can effectively learn in such settings without explicitly representing their posterior beliefs. Consequently, this finding suggests that recurrent neural networks may serve as a universal computational substrate capable of supporting partially observable decision-making.

In video-based action detection, the challenge of distinguishing between foreground actions and background confounders remains significant. Although context is vital for human perception, it is frequently overlooked. This paper addresses that gap by introducing a novel approach that integrates both semantic and structural context. We model the relationship between the actor and the background using a graph, where the action subject is represented as a central node connected to central-confounder edges, while peripheral confounders are connected via peripheral-central edges. To effectively leverage both semantic and relational context, we propose a model that combines central-confounder information with back-to-back confounder data. Furthermore, we employ a graph convolutional network to fuse confounder features, allowing the action region to be inferred from the central confounder node. Experimental results on the KITTI dataset validate the efficacy of our model in action detection. Additionally, visual comparisons with other confounder-aware methods demonstrate the superior performance of our approach on visually similar objects and confounders. To further evaluate the model, we conducted a user study, which revealed insights into the types of confounders that are most critical for human perception. This study addresses the challenge of training deep learning models for privacy-sensitive data stored in distributed devices by introducing a new framework called Differentially Private Recommunication (DP-REC). Our approach integrates two core strategies: first, we employ differentially private (DP) recommunication in every training round to substantially lower noise injection while keeping privacy leakage within minimal, acceptable limits; second, we design a novel communication-efficient DP-REC module that merges DP-REC with quantization, ensuring the method remains both privacy-preserving and communication-efficient. We rigorously validate the efficacy of DP-REC across three representative datasets on four diverse mobile devices. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that DP-REC not only boosts model accuracy but also reduces differentially private learning noise by nearly 50% compared to existing state-of-the-art communication-efficient techniques. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the method's privacy leakage and computational complexity. We introduce the outcomes of an far-ultraviolet (FUV) survey conducted with the International Ultraviolet Explorer (IUE) across the Taurus, Perseus, and Auriga regions, with a specific focus on young stellar objects (YSOs). Our analysis examined 108 FUV images capturing 69 YSOs, revealing that 59 of these objects exhibit detectable FUV emission. We have established a comprehensive FUV spectral energy distribution (FSD) for the Taurus YSO IC 348, alongside newly acquired FUV data for the Taurus cluster IC 486, the Auriga cluster IC 50, and the Perseus cluster NGC 1333. Additionally, we present FUV observations for 13 previously unimaged YSOs, including the Class I object L1448 IRS 1, and discuss the implications of these findings. We observed that FUV emission is predominantly detected in T Tauri stars and protostars, with the majority of sources showing significant emission originating from their circumstellar disks. Furthermore, we identified two possible FUV-emitting protostars. This study represents the first survey of FUV emission from YSOs in the Taurus, Perseus, and Auriga regions, providing the first FUV data for L1448 IRS 1 and the first FSD for IC 348. We introduce a new two-player extensive-form game featuring a sequence of stages with incomplete information at each point. The game begins with nature randomly assigning one of several types to Player 1, a scenario only Player 2 observes. First, Player 2 chooses between a cheap talk phase and a contest. If the cheap talk phase is selected, Player 2 reveals part of the private type information to Player 1, who then selects between a second round of cheap talk followed by a contest, or immediate entry. Finally, both players compete using effort levels to maximize the probability of winning. We demonstrate that, regardless of the specific assumptions, the game possesses a unique subgame perfect equilibrium. A key insight is that the effort exerted in the first cheap talk phase is typically higher than in the second. Furthermore, we find that the design of the contest significantly influences Player 2's initial choice of cheap talk phases, whereas Player 1's entry decisions are largely unaffected by the type sequence revealed during the first phase. These findings highlight the complex interactions between pre-play information disclosure and subsequent strategic efforts. Additionally, we explore the potential for extending this framework to settings with multiple players. **Keywords:** Extensive form game, Insufficient information, Subgame Perfect Equilibrium, Effort, Information Disclosure, Multiple Players **JEL Classification:** C73, D822. In an instance of size $k$ with $c$-bit counters, the queries supported by ELMF are limited to those with at least $k^2/c$ estimated insertions. The authors demonstrate that ELMF offers improvements over both traditional filters and existing ZFPF variants. Specifically, the new information theoretic lower bound for filters without false positives is shown to be tight for ELMF. Additionally, the paper presents a method for generating false positive free collections. By applying this construction to ELMF, a superior filter class is obtained, where all operations remain free of false positives. The performance of the proposed filters is evaluated through numerical experiments. These results indicate that the superior performance of ELMF over other filters is achieved when the number of elements is at least the square of the filter size, provided the counter size is adequate. This study theoretically examines spinor atom-molecule transformation driven by laser-induced three-body recombination across different spin-components. The analysis covers both two- and three-channel systems, incorporating interactions among atoms, molecules, and atom pairs. Results indicate that, provided the coupling between the atom and molecule spin-components is negligible, the system achieves complete atom-molecule conversion when the laser is tuned to the threshold of the three-body recombination process. Furthermore, by adjusting the laser frequency, one can control the population distribution across multiple spin-states of the resulting molecules. These findings may prove valuable for generating spin-squeezed spin-cat states in spinor Bose-Einstein condensates. Additionally, the proposed method offers a mechanism for converting the kinetic energy of a moving molecule into optical energy via the laser. In practical applications, the model's validity is supported by the use of off-resonant laser frequencies and the selection of alkali atoms with specific electronic configurations. Finally, numerical simulations of the spin-dependent model demonstrate the generation of atom-molecule entanglement. These outcomes are anticipated to be observable in current cold-atom experiments. Machine learning is rapidly expanding, driven by the growing availability of data and the computational power needed to analyze it. Although quantum computing has long been envisioned as a means to accelerate these tasks, this work presents a practical, non-variational quantum unmonitored and instructed learning algorithm implemented on superconducting processors. By developing a quantum version of the Hebb rule, we demonstrate an implementation utilizing few-qubit circuits that are feasible for current hardware. Our approach offers a fundamental shift from the recent focus on variational methods, marking the first experimental evidence of quantum processors functioning as effective learning devices. We conclude that these devices are now capable of executing quantum machine learning, paving the way for the creation of hybrid classical and quantum systems designed for data analysis. Furthermore, the presented algorithm serves as a critical step toward larger-scale implementations on systems with greater connectivity and qubit counts. With further development, these systems could deliver the exponential speedups anticipated from quantum machine learning. Additionally, we anticipate that the experimental framework established in this work will facilitate the creation of new research fields, including quantum hardware benchmarks and performance evaluations. This is achieved by providing a comprehensive, open-source, step-by-step implementation of the algorithm across various quantum processors, complete with detailed circuit descriptions and data analysis tools. We believe that making these tools publicly available will enable the broader community to explore the advantages of quantum machine learning. All necessary code and data are available at https://github.com/QuantumMachineLearning. Finally, we demonstrate the implementation of quantum instructed learning, offering another step toward larger-scale applications. We conclude by outlining potential future research directions. This study measures the differential cross-sections for this process as a function of the invariant mass of the lepton pairs, specifically for electron and muon final states. Furthermore, this analysis represents the first instance of combining lepton-only and lepton-plus-jet $W$ mass measurements to achieve the highest precision to date. Telepresence robots (TPRs) serve as effective solutions for remote scenario monitoring and support. To achieve this, we conducted a comprehensive user study involving 20 participants across 120 sessions, where TPR users navigated and observed a room using a specific robot while communicating via audio. Our image quality assessment utilized a modified version of the MOS-Image-Task (MOSIT) method, originally designed for foveated imaging, adapting it to account for both pan and zoom movements. Additionally, we introduced a new approach to assess user satisfaction with motion control. Our results reveal that both image quality and motion control significantly influence overall user satisfaction, with the latter being particularly critical for users managing TPRs. Ultimately, we conclude that the TPR use case necessitates a joint evaluation of both imaging and motion control to achieve satisfactory user experience outcomes. To facilitate this, we have made our experimental results and the questionnaires used in the study publicly available for replication purposes. Hierarchical linear models are linear regression approaches incorporating random effects, typically arranged in a hierarchy. The term "hierarchical" arises because inferences are drawn at multiple levels or orders; for instance, in a clinical trial involving patients across various centers, the first order corresponds to the patient level while the second corresponds to the center level. Bayesian methods constitute the third order, representing a distinct philosophical framework for analysis. This paper aims to demystify these models for researchers and clinicians who may lack expertise in advanced statistics. We demonstrate the utility of hierarchical linear models using a nested design through a straightforward example. Furthermore, Bayesian hierarchical linear models offer computational advantages when employing Markov Chain Monte Carlo techniques to estimate posterior distributions and perform inference. The demonstration utilizes the R programming language along with its dedicated packages.

Mafia, or Werewolf, is a widely enjoyed social game that has inspired numerous algorithmic algorithmic models and computational simulations. This study introduces a novel, first-time mathematical algorithmic description of the game. We present two distinct algorithmic formulations of Mafia and analyze their algorithmic complexities. Our development process involved creating a new numerical model to examine the Mafia's dynamics. This straightforward numerical framework relies on a single parameter: the ratio of civilians to traitors at the start of a round. We demonstrate that this single parameter dictates the complexity of every Mafia variant. Specifically, when this parameter exceeds 2, the mafia team possesses a computational advantage, enabling them to complete their agenda more quickly than the blue team. Conversely, if the parameter falls below 2, the mafia team holds no such advantage. Furthermore, our findings indicate that a mafia team can never achieve a strict advantage over the blue team. Finally, we illustrate that the mafia team's advantage can be quantified by the probability that the game concludes with the complete elimination of the blue team. Our analysis reveals that this probability increases as the initial population of both the mafia and spy populations rises relative to the civilian population. Additionally, we observe that this probability is influenced by the specific roles of the mafia members. Finally, we show that this probability can be determined by identifying the shortest sequence of moves in the game's directed graph representation that leads to a terminal state where only the spy remains. The mass and structure of the early solar system are fundamentally shaped by the accretion of its primary planets, which occurs through the capture of gas and solids from the surrounding protoplanetary disk. This process is governed by the planet-disk interaction, where the migration of protoplanets and the evolution of the disk itself are critical. In this study, we introduce a new model that tracks the evolution of a massive disk and the growth of multiple planets simultaneously. Our model incorporates the migration of massive planets ($M_p \geq 0.3$~M$_{\rm J}$), where migration velocity depends on the local disk's surface density and temperature. We assume that the radial direction of migration is determined by the balance between accretion and evaporation of planetary mass. The model's output includes the final planet masses and the resulting disk structure. Our results indicate that a significant positive or negative migration phase can substantially alter a planet's ultimate mass. Furthermore, the migration phase where a planet simultaneously gains both gas and solid mass from the disk is a key determinant of its final size. We also observe that a single migration phase often fails to explain the formation of a massive planet, suggesting that multi-stage migration is likely. Additionally, we demonstrate that a single disk model cannot account for the properties of both Jupiter and Saturn. Finally, our findings suggest that this new model could serve as a valuable tool for interpreting the observed properties of exoplanets. Specifically, the system HD 151310, which hosts two massive planets in a 3:2 orbital resonance, may have formed via a different mechanism than standard theories predict. We propose that these planets could have evolved concurrently from an initial hot Jupiter state. This study represents a significant step toward a new generation of global models capable of predicting the final planetary systems. Such models will be essential for understanding the solar system's formation and for interpreting observations of young stellar systems and exoplanets. This work is dedicated to the memory of Dr. Toshiro Nakagawa, a pioneer in planet-disk interaction research. This study introduces a novel fuzzy clustering technique designed for high-dimensional data, termed the entropy-driven variable feature weighted fuzzy k-means (Enfwk-m). In many real-world datasets, specific data points within certain dimensions are more critical than others. To address this, we developed an Enfwk-m method capable of dynamically assigning weights to features, thereby enhancing clustering performance in high-dimensional spaces. Drawing from the principle that the total entropy of independent events equals the sum of their individual entropies, we utilize total entropy to determine each dimension's weight. Extensive experiments were conducted to evaluate the method's efficacy across various dimensions using diverse datasets. The findings indicate that, compared to state-of-of-the-art fuzzy clustering approaches, Enfwk-m achieves superior accuracy in clustering high-dimensional data. Furthermore, an analysis of the algorithm's computational complexity reveals that its time complexity is linear relative to the number of data points. Finally, the method's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application in classifying Alzheimer's disease. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/zhonghaochen/Enfwk-m. Future research will focus on addressing the cold-start problem, which occurs when there is insufficient information to assign weights to dimensions in newly introduced datasets. The category learning problem is a fundamental aspect of human cognition, involving the discernment of distinct object categories and their shared attributes. This study investigates the dynamics of learning categorical structures through a lens that integrates cognitive and statistical principles. We demonstrate that existing Mean-Field Variational Bayes (MFVB) algorithms, which model category selection as an expert system, frequently encounter a deadlock phenomenon. Specifically, when prior beliefs suggest a high number of categories, MFVB can erroneously converge to a local minimum corresponding to very low cluster counts. The critical failure point is that once MFVB selects an expert to categorize a new item, it becomes practically impossible for subsequent items to influence the estimate of the total number of categories. To address this, we introduce a novel algorithm that avoids the associated technical challenges, ensuring it is both reliable and efficient. Furthermore, we present a new Bayesian model that unifies previous approaches, offering a more parsimonious and interpretable framework. This enhanced model not only eliminates the deadlock issue but also yields more accurate results. Finally, we validate the proposed algorithms using a new dataset comprising human perceptions of vegetables. Our model selection criteria indicate that the new Bayesian MFVB outperforms the original formulation. Additionally, we show that the updated model can be efficiently approximated using the popular EM algorithm. We conclude that the proposed algorithms are robust, reliable, and effective for modeling categorical expertise. The code is accessible at https://github.com/akimk/MFVB.2.0. Our findings are published in *Psychometrika* (2021). These forms generalize both Schur nilpotency and the kernels associated with Jacobian maps. The results provide an elementary demonstration of the local equivalence between Schur nilpotency and the vanishing of Brill-Noether determinants, as well as the primary result of Gieseker theory regarding the Jacobian. The work also yields contributions to algebraic geometry, matrix theory, and combinatorial matrix theory, including contributions to the theory of matrix pencils, graph invariants, and polynomial optimization. A key application involves the complete characterization of the critical locus of the period map for double covers of curves, which yields several novel combinatorial results. This study examines the UVIT ultraviolet data of the globular cluster NGC 4147, located in the Virgo cluster, to investigate the evolution of hot stars. The UVIT images were captured on UT-2014/08/18, utilizing the U-band (2500–3200 Å) and W1-band (2200–3200 Å) filters. Transferability is a vital capability for deep learning, underpinning numerous applications like transfer learning and knowledge transfer. This study re-examines two core agreements regarding transferability: (1) the transferability of deep learning to other tasks, and (2) the transferability between distinct architectures. To address the first claim, a cross-architecture transfer learning transferability task was introduced to explore the transferability of trained models across different tasks. For the second claim, a cross-task, cross-architecture transfer learning transferability task was proposed. Additionally, the generalizability of two transferability tasks was evaluated by employing three distinct deep learning backbones. Finally, two novel metrics for assessing transferability were developed. Empirical results indicate that trained deep learning models exhibit transferability across tasks and architectures, with Wide Residual Networks (WRN) demonstrating superior transferability compared to other architectures. Furthermore, Depthwise Residual Networks (DRN) achieved the highest score for transferability across both tasks and architectures. Finally, ResNet was found to possess the greatest stability among the evaluated models. The experimental outcomes validate the proposed tasks and metrics, offering a more comprehensive and accurate approach to evaluating transferability in deep learning. Furthermore, this work provides a deeper understanding of deep learning transferability, potentially aiding in the selection of models for transfer learning scenarios. The Standard Perturbation Model (SPM) within a closed-loop feedback system serves as a widely accepted method for analyzing and predicting the precision of open-loop components in the time domain. For unamplified links, the SPM equation can be formulated as a function of the component's group delay and bandwidth. This study presents a precision analysis of the SPM for unamplified links, expressing group delay and the SPM equation in a coherently normalized time system. The analysis examines the error between the actual open-loop feedback signal and the theoretical SPM prediction across three scenarios: noise-limited, component-limited, and mixed limitations. Results indicate that for noise-limited analysis, the error is minimal when sampling at or above the Nyquist rate. However, in component-limited analysis, a significant discrepancy exists between the SPM prediction and the real feedback signal; this gap narrows as sampling rate increases. Consequently, a higher sampling rate is essential for accurate analysis in component-limited conditions. Additionally, the group delay in the SPM equation for unamplified links is shown to be contingent upon the specific analysis being conducted. Finally, an example is provided to demonstrate how to determine the necessary sampling rate for a given feedback link. This work aims to guide engineers in selecting an appropriate sampling rate for precision analysis in their designs. Furthermore, the proposed methodology can be extended to analyze the precision of amplified links. Future research will explore the SPM for open-loop links in the frequency domain, the model for nonlinear components, and the development of a general SPM-based design tool. This approach will also address the challenge of characterizing unamplified links in the time domain, where measuring group delay is difficult. The suggested methodology will be presented at the 2021 IEEE International Microwave Theory and Techniques Conference (MITT). Let $G$ denote an infinite Bohr-locally finite abelian group such that its Bohr topology $\mathcal{B}$ renders $(G, +, \mathcal{B})$ a first-countable topological group. We demonstrate that for any subset $A \subseteq G$ and summands $G_1, \ldots, G_{\ell} \subseteq G$ satisfying $A + G_2 + \cdots + G_{\ell} = G$, the set $A$ possesses a finite Bohr neighborhood $U$ if, for every sequence of nonempty bounded sets $S_i \subseteq G_i$ ($1 \leq i \leq \ell$), there exists an element $x \in U$ satisfying
$$x + \sum_{i=1}^{\ell} \sigma_i(S_i) \subseteq A$$
for all sign choices $\sigma_i : \{0,1\} \to \{\pm 1\}$. This finding offers a positive resolution to an inquiry raised by P. P. Pálfy. Furthermore, this result is instrumental in characterizing the Bohr structure of sumsets $A + B$ within infinite summands of $G$, where $A$ and $B$ are symmetric subsets of $G$ with a nonempty sum. Specifically, it establishes the inclusion
$$\mathcal{B}(A + B) \supseteq \mathcal{B}(A) \otimes \mathcal{B}(B),$$
where $\mathcal{B}(A)$ and $\mathcal{B}(B)$ represent the finest Bohr topologies on $A$ and $B$, respectively, and $\mathcal{B}(A) \otimes \mathcal{B}(B)$ denotes the corresponding product topology. This inequality generally fails in the category of all topological spaces. Additionally, we present a ZFC construction of a counterexample to a conjecture by P. P. Pálfy and an independent proof of a theorem by J. H. Smith and A. S. Tetali. Finally, we investigate the conditions under which the inclusion becomes equality, a question that remains unresolved even in the context of finite groups. The primary techniques employed involve the theory of central sets and a novel variant of the van der Waerden's theorem applicable to infinite Bohr-topological groups. Spin-orbit interaction (SOI) is a critical element in spintronics, a field that leverages this phenomenon to manipulate electron spin for data processing. While SOI is inherently weak in light-element systems, enhancing it could significantly advance spin-based technologies. This study demonstrates a substantial improvement in SOI within a correlated metal by employing the dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) framework. Specifically, electron-electron correlations amplify the system's magnetic moment and magnetic anisotropy. These findings indicate that correlated metals are promising candidates for developing efficient spintronic devices. The research utilizes the strongly correlated Kondo-Heusler alloy Gd$_{50}$Pt$_{49}$Ni$_{1}$, which exhibits a substantial increase in total magnetic moment and magnetic anisotropy when analyzed via DMFT. The magnetic anisotropy energy (MAE) for the systems with the [001] easy axis is $-1.1$ meV (DMFT) versus $-0.2$ meV (DFT), representing a five-fold enhancement. Furthermore, the spin-orbit torque (SOT) is also predicted to rise significantly under the DMFT approach. These results highlight the critical role of electron correlations in boosting SOI, thereby paving the way for the creation of high-efficiency spintronic devices based on correlated metals. Additionally, the study underscores the necessity of using DMFT to accurately investigate spin-orbit phenomena in this class of materials. Finally, the proposed method offers a viable pathway for achieving improved spin efficiency through the design of new materials. The theoretical analysis was conducted using the COMADRE DMFT code, a newly released open-source platform for strongly correlated systems. COMADRE integrates density functional theory (DFT) with dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) and supports various extensions, including the GW approximation, self-energy corrections for spin fluctuations, and the dynamical cluster approximation (DCA). This comprehensive code is now accessible through the Comadre website. Future work will explore the effects of electron correlations on spin-orbit phenomena in other materials, such as topological insulators and strongly correlated oxides. We present a four-dimensional, asymptotically de Sitter spacetime containing a shadow. The matter responsible for generating this geometry is termed shadow substance and possesses negative energy density alongside a negative pressure that exceeds the magnitude of the energy density. At a specific scale, the equation of state of this substance approaches that of a conformal field theory, resulting in a name derived from this property: metastable conformal shadow substance. This substance exhibits a nonzero entropy, indicating it is not purely conformal; consequently, its stress-energy tensor is traceless but not conformally invariant. We demonstrate that the shadow is metastable to perturbations with wavelengths longer than the horizon scale. Although the shadow itself is not extremal, extremal surfaces within this spacetime exhibit negative matter on them. Furthermore, we establish that the spacetime adheres to both the weak and strong energy conditions. Finally, we calculate the entanglement entropy of an extremal surface and the thermal entropy of a black hole within this spacetime. In the limit of large mass, the extremal entropy scales as $M^{2/3}$, whereas the black hole entropy scales as $M^2$. These two entropies become equal at a specific mass scale, which serves as another characteristic scale of the shadow. This equality can be interpreted as another indication of the shadow's connection to the conformal group. Additionally, this matching of entropy values supports the recent conjecture regarding extremal black holes in de Sitter space. At the mass scale where the entropies align, the shadow's temperature approaches zero. We also examine an information paradox associated with the shadow and argue that it can be resolved. The shadow's geometry features a horizon with a radius comparable to that of an extremal black hole in de Sitter space. This extremal black hole is characterized by a matter stress-energy tensor that is both traceless and conformally invariant. We argue that the shadow's geometry may also be viewed as the black hole limit of a D1-D5 system. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the shadow arises as the extremal limit of a D1-D5-charged black hole in four-dimensional anti-de Sitter space. Finally, we outline a potential relationship between the shadow and the Kerr/de Sitter spacetime. This relationship may offer an explanation for the recent observational evidence suggesting that the angular momentum of real de Sitter black holes is significantly smaller than the cube of their mass. Deep learning has achieved significant breakthroughs in medical image analysis, leading to a surge in clinical adoption of AI-driven diagnostic tools. However, a persistent challenge remains the discrepancy between high performance on training data and a decline in accuracy when deployed in real-world clinical settings. This study introduces a framework to evaluate the predictive uncertainty of deep learning models facing distribution shifts during training or deployment. Specifically, we utilize conformity scores and their corresponding prediction intervals to measure performance, offering a more granular assessment than traditional metrics like accuracy or F1 scores. These scores effectively capture the impact of distribution shifts and serve as calibration indicators for AI tools already in clinical use. In a proof-of-concept application, we analyzed a deep learning model designed for predicting hospital length of stay in intensive care units, demonstrating how distribution shifts influence both predictive uncertainty and overall model performance. Our findings indicate that distribution shift significantly affects deep learning models, resulting in miscalibrated prediction intervals that either overestimate or underestimate confidence. Consequently, we conclude that incorporating predictive uncertainty into AI medical tools is essential for enhancing their real-world applicability and reliability. We contend that this proposed framework will serve as a valuable metric for quantifying the performance of AI medical instruments when distribution shifts occur. To facilitate broader adoption, we have made the code and data for this work publicly available. Simulating the three-dimensional conformations of DNA is challenging due to its inherent flexibility. We introduce a straightforward yet effective technique to bias DNA toward extended states by applying an off-axis force to the terminal base pairs. This approach, termed Stiff Base Biasing (SBB), maintains the first and last base pairs fixed in space while allowing the DNA backbone greater freedom to explore conformational space. SBB accurately reproduces the equilibrium probability distribution of extension, end-to-end orientation, twist, and bend. Furthermore, the method facilitates the sampling of DNA states with significantly higher stiffness than what is achievable through standard Brownian dynamics. SBB achieves these results in just a few nanoseconds, offering a valuable alternative for studying DNA's mechanical and three-dimensional properties. Additionally, we analyze how various sequence-dependent factors influence SBB sampling efficiency and find that forces of approximately 10 pN are sufficient to generate samples closely matching those from unbiased simulations, with only a minor sequence dependence observed. Consequently, SBB can be readily applied to any DNA sequence without requiring custom modifications. This technique is readily accessible via a new release of the OpenMM molecular dynamics simulation package, which includes a simple plugin that automatically applies the specified force to any DNA simulation. The dielectric properties of cementitious materials have been extensively investigated to determine water content via dielectric sensors. However, a complete physical description of cement paste's dielectric behavior remains absent from current literature. This study employs electrical measurements on micro-structured model systems to identify the primary mechanisms governing the dielectric response of cementitious materials. By utilizing an experimental setup capable of measuring low-frequency dielectric properties, we analyzed heterogeneous systems comprising calcium hydroxate and calcium silicate hydrate, which serve as simplified representations of real cementitious materials. Our results indicate that a physical description relying solely on the classical Maxwell-Wagner-Sillars (MWS) model is insufficient for cementitious materials. Instead, we demonstrate that the dielectric response is primarily driven by the geometry of the dielectric inclusions rather than the chemical composition of the pore fluid. Furthermore, the electrical behavior of these materials is better described by a modified microstructural model that accounts for the dielectric fluid's dipolar polarization. Consequently, this research suggests that traditional dielectric water content measurements may be inaccurate in cementitious materials, as they depend on the assumption of classical MWS behavior. These findings are particularly significant for applications such as concrete structures exposed to seawater, where pore fluid composition differs from freshwater. Additionally, the methodology employed can be applied to other porous media, such as soil, to investigate the interaction between pore fluid characteristics and the dielectric response of the host material. Ultimately, this work aims to advance the understanding of the dielectric response in cementitious materials, thereby facilitating more accurate and reliable water content measurements. Finally, the approach utilized offers a pathway for developing new technologies, including dielectric sensors designed to monitor the aging of concrete structures. This could enable the detection of critical events, such as the carbonation of concrete, which significantly alters the dielectric response of the material. Ultimately, this could lead to the development of novel concrete monitoring systems. Additionally, a concrete monitoring system could be engineered to detect the presence of chloride ions in the concrete. Since the concentration of calcium hydroxide in concrete is significantly higher than that of chlorides, the pore fluid in concrete structures is expected to be saturated with calcium hydroxide. Therefore, future concrete monitoring technologies should focus on detecting the presence of sodium chloride in the pore fluid. This can be achieved by measuring the dielectric response of calcium hydroxide-saturated cement paste and observing changes when the pore fluid is altered. The findings presented in this study support the development of new dielectric sensors specifically designed to monitor the durability of concrete

The Lyman-$\alpha$ forest serves as a valuable probe for studying matter distribution, cosmology, and the evolution of dark matter halos. We demonstrate that a minimal, one-dimensional model of baryon and dark matter correlations can yield precise estimates for the Hubble parameter and the effective baryon density. By utilizing observed correlations between Lyman-$\alpha$ absorbers and galaxies, we constrain these cosmological parameters. Our results indicate that the combination of baryon and dark matter density ratio is $\Omega_b/\Omega_c = 0.051 \pm 0.001$, and the redshift of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest at the $1\sigma$ level is $z = 2.335 \pm 0.011$. Additionally, we observe that the model's predictions align with COBE-normalized primordial power spectra, the baryon density derived from Big Bang nucleosynthesis, and X-ray observations of galaxy clusters. We conclude that this new method for measuring cosmological parameters is robust and that the model successfully captures the essential physics of the system. Furthermore, we suggest that this approach can be applied to other absorber systems, such as the green valley and quiescent galaxies, to provide independent cosmological inferences. This study establishes a foundation for future research into cosmological parameters and the evolution of dark matter halos using the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest. Our findings suggest that the effective density of halos hosting galaxies at this epoch is $\Omega_h(z=2.335) = 0.14 \pm 0.01$. We also note that the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest probes a volume of approximately $V \simeq 1.5 \times 10^5 h^{-3} Mpc^3$, which is comparable to the volume of a single $z \sim 0.5$ BOSS galaxy survey field. This implies that the statistical uncertainties in the measurements presented here are comparable to those of the BOSS galaxy survey. Finally, we discuss the potential for enhancing these measurements by utilizing the upcoming 3D spectroscopy capabilities of the WEAVE instrument. We anticipate that the WEAVE survey will enable the measurement of cosmological parameters with a precision of roughly $1\%$ using a sample of approximately $10^5$ Lyman-$\alpha$ absorbers and $10^6$ galaxies. This experiment marks a significant advancement toward realizing non-dissipative emittance amplification for particle accelerators. The longitudinal charge transfer was managed by adjusting the initial separation between the two linear charges. To achieve transverse emittance transfer, we set the initial relative angle between the two rings to a non-zero value. By the end of the experimental sequence, the target oscillator possessed both the transverse emittance and total energy of the source oscillator, while the source retained half of the initial total energy. Furthermore, we achieved near-perfect transverse emittance transfer when the initial relative angle was approximately 1 rad. Human trajectory prediction is a critical research area with extensive applications in various domains, including wayfinding, autonomous driving, and crowd management. However, predicting the future paths of mobile agents remains difficult due to the complexity of human behavior, particularly the influence of dynamic social cues and constraints. This study introduces an enhanced Sequential Conditional Variational Autoencoder (SCVAE) that incorporates a novel Sliding Sequential CVAE (SSCAE) network. This network predicts a series of candidate trajectories by iteratively forecasting multiple future states and sequentially eliminating early candidates. Crucially, each prediction step accounts for social influences and constraints, allowing the model to adapt to changing social cues. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms other state-of-the-art methods in predicting high-quality trajectories. This study introduces two distinct metrics for information-theoretic complexity within the weight space of a Boltzmann machine. The initial approach employs the mutual information (MI) between weights, tailored for sparse representations, while the second utilizes the total correlation (TC) of features generated by visible units. These methods offer an alternative to standard metrics, such as the trace of the Hessian, by functioning as linear predictors of a novel complexity measure derived from the trace of a specific tensor related to the manifold of sufficient representations in weight space. Notably, these identified tensors—whether projected into weight space or conditioned on data within the space of sufficient sufficient representations—serve as promising candidates for developing integrated metrics that can determine equilibrium states across diverse models, such as those found in deep learning. Finally, we demonstrate that for a restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) trained on the MNIST dataset, the proposed metrics yield distinct outcomes, thereby challenging the conventional perspective that an RBM learns a product distribution over its local units. Specifically, mutual information reveals a non-trivial structure among the weights connecting hidden and visible units, while total correlation indicates dependencies among the units representing the visemes of the MNIST digits. These findings align with previous research suggesting that an RBM trained on the MNIST dataset encodes the manifold of visemes in its hidden units. This leads to an alternative inference technique that surpasses traditional techniques, such as contrastive divergence, in predicting the manifold of visemes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this alternative technique surpasses a recently introduced method that utilizes the score function gradient in a neural tangent kernel (NTK) to identify the trace of the Hessian as a measure of complexity. Finally, we observe that the proposed complexity metrics can serve as regularizers in neural network training, where they have been shown to enhance generalization performance. This paper is an extended version that includes experimental results from additional training runs compared to our arXiv version [1]. Our code is accessible at [2]. This paper introduces a new research and development direction focused on integrating human-salm interactions through hand gestures. It outlines the initial findings from this endeavor, beginning with the initial phase of research that sees humans driving swarms of legged robots to navigate complex environments. To facilitate interaction between humans and these robot swarms, this study first tackles the challenge of recognizing the trajectories of hand sequences. This is accomplished by applying transfer learning and transferable data augmentation techniques to a deep neural network, utilizing a large-scale, high-quality human-sarm hand trajectory dataset. Second, the paper addresses another critical issue: enabling a human-sarm team to collaborate effectively by allowing each robot to independently recognize hand trajectories. This is resolved by employing a distributed deep neural network that leverages transfer learning. Finally, the paper presents two promising applications for this technology: (i) a simulation environment for conducting experiments with human-sarm interaction, and (ii) a real-world use case for human-sarm team cooperation within a warehouse setting. The proposed technology is expected to significantly enhance human-sarm collaboration, and we anticipate that these findings will inspire further research into human-sarm interaction. Additionally, we believe this technology will play a vital role in advancing the field of human-robot collaboration. This study addresses the challenge of classifying morphological blood cells, a critical component in diagnosing various conditions. We introduce and evaluate multiple techniques for combining neural network models to enhance both average and per-class accuracy. Our approach involves training several neural network architectures—such as CNNs, ResNets, and DenseNets—on datasets containing images of white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets. We experiment with and compare different model-merging strategies, specifically ensemble methods and knowledge distillation. Our findings indicate that the average performance of these merging approaches is consistent across different underlying models, suggesting that morphological blood cell categorization may be inherently simple and that current state-of-the-art models are potentially over-parameterized for this task. Furthermore, we benchmark current state-of-the-art models against our implementations and explore parameter-efficient knowledge distillation techniques to improve red blood cell, white blood cell, and platelet categorization. Finally, we analyze the impact of data splitting strategies on per-class accuracy and discuss potential avenues for future research. This study demonstrates that ground states can be efficiently obtained by applying a counterdiabatic (CD) protocol to a phase-separation model, which mimics the initial stage of dynamics for a system with a known excited state. This approach offers an alternative to the commonly used CD protocol for SWAP-driven ground-state assembly. We derive a analytical CD field for the phase-separation model that ensures an exact reproduction of the SWAP-driven evolution. For finite systems, we show that the CD field remains effective even when a two-site repulsive CD model is applied. Additionally, we find that a three-site CD field composed of a two-site repulsive component and a ferromagnetic component can achieve an accurate approximation of the SWAP evolution. These findings are supported by numerical simulations. Our results indicate that phase-separation models exhibit significantly lower requirements for CD field strength compared to SWAP models, suggesting that CD steering of phase-separation models is a viable strategy for achieving ground states. Furthermore, this study provides a valuable reference for understanding the characteristics of CD fields in many-body systems. Finally, we propose an experimental scheme utilizing a Bose-Hubbard model to demonstrate the counterdiabatic driving of phase-separation models. The results of this scheme are also consistent with numerical simulations. We conclude that the proposed approach is highly effective for achieving phase-separated states and offers an alternative to the traditional SWAP-driven ground-state assembly method. This makes it a promising experimental scheme for investigating the CD protocol and its associated field characteristics. Additionally, the proposed scheme is expected to serve as a platform for studying the counterdiabatic driving of other types of states. We anticipate that these insights will contribute to advancing the field of accelerated quantum dynamics. Finally, we note that our conclusions are also applicable to the Fermi-Hubbard model. We believe that the proposed approach can provide a new perspective for ground-state assembly in the context of cold-atom experiments. In this work, we have demonstrated the counterdiabatic driving of the Bose-Hubbard model; extending this approach to the Fermi-Hubbard model is expected to yield valuable insights into the characteristics of CD fields in the context of fermionic systems. We anticipate that these findings will contribute to a deeper understanding of the counterdiabatic protocol and its field characteristics for ground-state assembly in the context of cold-atom experiments. We hope that our conclusions will provide a new perspective for advancing the field of accelerated quantum dynamics. Finally, we note that our conclusions are also applicable to the Fermi-Hubbard model.

High-velocity desaturation (HVS) is a tone-mapping technique that leverages human perception, which is more tolerant of color temperature shifts than shifts in hue. This method calculates the perceived hue temperature for every pixel, then selectively desaturates or "cooks" those with an insufficient temperature to achieve an artistic effect. The source code is available at https://github.com/alextorrens/hvst. The following sections detail the method, present experimental results, and discuss its application within creative workflows. Additionally, an open-source implementation is provided, which includes a parameter for adjusting the cooking speed. This paper introduces a novel exponential Taylor series representation for arbitrary functions of one or more variables. The first three sections develop mathematical concepts relevant to information theory, specifically addressing probability distributions and entropy. Section five extends the exponential Taylor expansion to functions involving one or more vectors. Section six applies these theories to non-equilibrium statistical physics, deriving both the Boltzmann and Gibbs distribution laws. Subsequently, an application in machine learning demonstrates the relevance of the exponential Taylor series within the context of artificial neural networks. Finally, Section 9 outlines potential applications for quantum computing. A key advantage of this novel approach is its capacity to handle complex functions of one or more vectors, a capability that proves essential for the exponential solution of non-equilibrium problems in statistical physics. This solution yields a general distribution law applicable to systems of any dimensionality, comprising an infinite series of probability distributions for individual quantum states. Each term in this series corresponds to an information-theoretic quantity, such as the mean value of quantum information. Collectively, these form a new law of non-equilibrium statistical physics, serving as a generalization of the H-theorem. This generalized law describes the evolution of probability distributions over time in non-equilibrium states, characterized by the gradual reduction of information content. Furthermore, this generalized law is applicable to open quantum systems, where it serves as a generalization of the Lindblad equation for the density matrix. The density matrix of an open system is determined by the superposition of two components: one representing the non-equilibrium probability distribution and the other describing the entanglement between the open system and its environment. The $n$ value is determined by the number of interactions between the open system and its environment. We present a novel approach to the uniformization problem for cat($k$) branched surfaces, as introduced by J. Scott and C. Thomas. Our methodology is rooted in a recent advancement by J. Scott regarding the harmonic properties of Scott extensions. Specifically, we demonstrate that the harmonic property of a Scott extension is contingent upon the conformal uniformization of the compact polyhedral surface formed by folding the original surface along the core curves of the surface's graph components. This finding establishes a recursive framework that enables the resolution of the general uniformization problem. Furthermore, we offer a comprehensive characterization of the uniformization characteristics for Scott extensions of cat($-\infty$) surfaces and present an algorithm designed to generate minimal immersions of uniformized surfaces into hyperbolic 3-space. Additionally, we address the uniformization of cat($k$) surfaces through the utilization of Scott extensions derived from optimal cut systems. Finally, we outline the application of our algorithm to a specific example introduced by J. Scott. This application involves constructing a minimal immersion of a uniformized cat($-2$) surface resulting from the Scott extension via an optimal cut system identified through computational techniques. The algorithm is implemented in C++ using the HyperTools library. Finally, we propose an algorithm for Scott extensions based on our primary algorithm and provide a corresponding implementation using HyperTools. This implementation provides a minimal immersion into hyperbolic 3-space for a cat($-2$) surface derived from the connected sum of two linked trefoils, achieved through an optimal cut system found via computational methods. This specific implementation is available as a standalone program within HyperTools. The algorithm is also applicable to cat($k$) surfaces; however, while the theory for cat($-2$) surfaces is robust, it becomes less developed for higher cat($k$) surfaces. In such cases, the harmonic property may fail to be necessary, and an alternative minimization algorithm is required. We intend to address these issues in future research. While standard translation tools like rdfloader and rdftranslate generally ignore shape expressions and validate them separately, rdftranslate specifically validates only constant expressions. To ensure consistency and enable comparison, we introduce a novel validation process for karmas that incorporates both data from relational source tables and instance graphs, supporting constant, functional, and class expressions. This process has been experimentally evaluated on the DBLP knowledge base, which contains 1.1 million classes and 4.5 million tuples across 12 tables. Shape-constrained regression, characterized by its nonparametric nature, robustness, and capacity to infer bivariate boundaries, has emerged as a significant alternative to parametric methods. The Nedler Polyhedral Convex Regression (NED) algorithm, introduced in 2012, is a leading efficient solver for convex regression problems. This work introduces pyStoNED, a Python library that adapts the NED algorithm to a Python environment. Built on the native StoNED C++ framework, pyStoNED utilizes the CGAL geometry library to manage complex geometric computations. To enhance performance, the development team employed vectorization and parallelization. Furthermore, to ensure the software remains accessible to a broader audience, the library includes a comprehensive tutorial with sample data and code. This paper outlines the design and development of pyStoNED, details the algorithmic enhancements, and demonstrates the library's capabilities through various examples. Additionally, performance evaluations are provided to illustrate the efficiency of the implemented algorithms. The pyStoNED library is available at https://pypi.org/project/pyStoNED/. Keywords: convex regression, convex optimization, convex hull, convex hull algorithm, convex hull solver, convex hull library, Python, C++, CGAL, parallelization, vectorization, optimization, regression, boundary estimation, shape-constrained regression.

This study investigates the production of top quark pairs accompanied by a neutral Higgs boson ($t \bar t \phi$) at the LHC, focusing on decay channels involving a pair of bottom quarks ($b \bar b$) and a flavor-neutral vector boson ($\phi = H$ or $Z$). We demonstrate that standard searches for the Higgs boson in association with top quarks may overlook the process if the two bottom quarks decay into jets that fall within the exclusivity requirements of the primary search channels. Consequently, we propose a novel search strategy for the $b \bar b \phi$ final state, utilizing $Z$ boson tagging to suppress the dominant Standard Model $t \bar t$ background. Our analysis covers both the on-shell production of a Standard Model Higgs boson and an off-shell scenario for a heavier Higgs variant. We find that, given sufficient integrated luminosity, this dedicated search for the heaviest Higgs boson possible at the LHC could achieve approximately 50% of the sensitivity expected from the more direct $t \bar t H$ search that does not rely on the $b \bar b$ channel. This finding is particularly relevant for the future high-luminosity phase of the LHC. Furthermore, we observe that the $Z$ boson acts as an effective Higgs tagger, suggesting that the $b \bar b Z$ channel could serve as a sensitive probe for beyond-Standard-Model physics involving heavy scalar particles. Specifically, we examine the potential for discovering a second Higgs boson with a mass up to 1 TeV, which could be a component of extended Higgs sectors in supersymmetric theories. Such a heavy scalar might couple to the top quark at the few-percent level, a coupling strength that is currently inaccessible through conventional Higgs searches. This capability is especially pertinent for the upcoming Phase-II of the LHC. Finally, we address the issue of irreducible background from purely QCD $t \bar t$ production, which can mimic the signal when top quarks decay semileptonically. We show that this background can be significantly reduced by imposing a lower cut on the invariant mass of the $t \bar t$ system, thereby enhancing the signal-to-background ratio. Our findings indicate that this approach offers a promising avenue for exploring Higgs couplings to third-generation fermions at the LHC. Few-shot image analysis from pretrained text-based models represents both a practical necessity and a promising avenue for future unsupervised machine intelligence. While existing few-shot methods have made progress, they still depend on handcrafted features and representations. We contend that unsupervised image analysis from pretrained language models should instead leverage data and representations already embedded within those models. We introduce LPM-SEEDS, which performs unsupervised template selection from pretrained language models to generate discriminative templates that facilitate few-shot image analysis without extracting visual features. Our results demonstrate that LPM-SEEDS surpasses state-of-the-art few-shot learning techniques for object recognition and achieves state-of-the-art performance in few-shot anomaly detection and scene attribute recognition. Furthermore, we reveal that the syntactic and semantic knowledge within transformer language models can be effectively harnessed for few-shot image analysis through carefully selected templates. Code and data are accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhatt/SEEDS.

This study demonstrates that building a speech recognition system for German is feasible and can be achieved with high accuracy by utilizing a comprehensive dataset of freely accessible audio files paired with corresponding transcripts. Additionally, we offer a step-by-step guide on how to replicate our results. Our aim is for this paper to serve as an entry point for researchers interested in developing speech recognition systems for under-resourced languages. Specifically, German researchers can use this as a starting point to create systems with performance comparable to commercial solutions. Consequently, this enables German researchers to concentrate on specific enhancements tailored to their target language. For other languages, we show that it remains possible to construct functional speech recognition systems using only publicly available data. This approach allows researchers to focus on targeted improvements to boost performance. Ultimately, our goal is to provide other languages with access to German-level performance, thereby providing a solid foundation for further research. We demonstrate that significant progress can be made by analyzing common errors and implementing targeted improvements to enhance accuracy. Our developed system achieves a Word Error Rate (WER) of 7.71 on the test set of the GW2 German speech recognition benchmark, compared to the top system's WER of 7.40. To address the remaining errors, we analyzed the most frequent incorrect word substitutions. This analysis revealed that the largest source of errors stems from German's complex morphology. We then developed rules to model these errors and incorporated them into the language model, which reduced the overall Word Error Rate by 0.4. Furthermore, we explored the use of external knowledge sources, such as the German Wikipedia, which yielded a WER improvement of 0.1. We also tested a data augmentation technique by artificially increasing the training data size by up to 100 times. This resulted in a WER improvement of 0.1 for the smallest expansion and 0.3 for the largest. Finally, we demonstrated that combining all proposed methods yields a cumulative WER improvement of 0.9. Our final system achieves a WER of 6.5 on the GW2 German benchmark test set, compared to the best system's WER of 4.9. We conclude that all proposed techniques can be applied to low-resource languages to significantly enhance performance. Additionally, we emphasize that open-source projects should be shared to foster a community that can contribute to developing speech recognition systems for languages lacking sufficient training data. We report the findings of a study on 12 Be-type stars within the 30 Doradus region, selected from a sample of 32 O-type stars with known radial velocities. This selection prioritized early O stars exhibiting strong hydrogen absorption and prominent He I 5876 Å lines. We present new spectra for eight of these targets, while five were previously analyzed. By fitting observed spectral lines with synthetic spectra generated via the SYNTHE program, we determined physical parameters. Our analysis indicates that most of the Be-type stars in 30 Doradus possess initial masses exceeding 10 solar masses. Additionally, we identified four stars exhibiting signs of significant mass loss, with rates reaching up to 10^-6 solar masses per year. Our investigation further reveals that three of the five 30 Doradus Be stars with known companions are likely interacting binary systems. Finally, we discuss the nature of these 30 Doradus Be-type stars. (Astronomy Letters, Vol. 47, No. 10, 2021)

This study investigates the application of data augmentation in text standardization, specifically within intractable historical languages. We present a novel, automated method for creating synthetic inverse standardization models, which are subsequently utilized to enhance these new inverse models for precise one-to-one text mapping. Experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our data augmentation strategy surpasses inverse standardization. Furthermore, we show that even a minimal amount of real data is sufficient to train a DeeperBigU model that performs as well as a standard one-to-many model on the TATB Hebrew test set. This research is part of our broader initiative to develop a general framework for learning inverse standardizers across various intractable languages, with a primary focus on Yiddish. We provide open-source code and data to facilitate future investigations. Finally, we outline our methodology for generating synthetic data and report outcomes on the Hebrew track of the inaugural Inverse Text Standardization shared task, demonstrating that our synthetic data yields a model performing comparably to one-to-many models on the test set. The shared task's second track, dedicated to Yiddish text standardization, is also detailed. While our synthetic data does not outperform one-to-many models on the TATB Hebrew development set, it successfully trains a state-of-the-art inverse standardizer for Yiddish. The results indicate that our synthetic data approach is a viable method for generating training data for inverse standardization tasks. Tangent kernel methods have proven effective in various machine learning domains, offering a principled mathematical basis for transferring prior knowledge from auxiliary tasks. Typically, transfer learning relies on a core assumption of exchangeability, where related tasks are expected to share similar parameters. This study introduces NFT-K, a tangent kernel method that accommodates non-exchangeable task configurations by applying specific transformations to tasks based on their relatedness. NFT-K provides a unified framework capable of handling diverse non-exchangeability scenarios, such as those involving non-independent features, non-stationary distributions, and task permutations. Comprehensive experiments across various benchmark datasets confirm the method's efficacy. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/DeepTalent/NFT-K. This study demonstrates how correlations in non-Hermitian systems reduce the winding number topology of the single-particle system, which is characterized by point gaps. We analyze a non-Hermitian generalized Hubbard model featuring nonreciprocal hopping. By applying the Bogoliubov transformation, we derive the many-body band structure and show that a phase transition from visible to invisible topological rings occurs due to the emergence of an exceptional tensor. Furthermore, we prove that the system's phase diagram, defined by the threshold for this topology reduction, can be controlled by adjusting the nonreciprocity strength. Finally, we outline how to design non-Hermitian platforms that exhibit this topology reduction, with potential experimental realization on graphs using ultracold atoms. This research offers a new perspective on the topology of non-Hermitian many-body systems. Experimental setups to observe these phenomena can be achieved on photonic, photonic crystal, and photonic crystal fiber platforms, as well as using graphs with ultracold atoms. This study investigates the potential of embedding social characteristics, specifically gender and age, into synthetic speech. By utilizing a social age discriminator and a gender discriminator, we enhance the quality of text-to-speech (TTS) outputs generated by the foundational model, FastSpeech2. Our findings indicate that the integrated system maintains the original speaker attributes while effectively integrating them with discriminator-guided enhancements. We evaluate the social attributes of the unenhanced and enhanced speech using the voice paradigm (formant-based voice quality) and the avatars' perceived similarity. The similarity scores were assessed through an online survey involving 25 participants. Results demonstrate that the system is capable of generating synthetic speech with enhanced social traits. Furthermore, we observed that the synthetic voice quality (SVQ) of the enhanced speech is perceptually similar to that of the avatar, though not statistically significant. Finally, we analyzed the correlations among the levels of enhancement in social attributes between the avatars, participants, and the models. Our analysis reveals that the forms of social attributes in the enhanced speech are more closely correlated with the avatars' levels than with the participants'. These insights deepen our understanding of the relationship between synthetic speech and human perception, offering valuable guidance for the development of social TTS applications. Ultimately, this research establishes a foundation for the future development of social TTS. Additionally, we provide open-source code and datasets to support further exploration of social TTS. This study investigates the relationship between residual entropy and viscosity by analyzing 150 molecular fluids spanning diverse temperature and pressure conditions, alongside 50 spherical Lennard-Jones (LJ) and hard-sphere (HS) model systems. The analysis of molecular fluids reveals a linear correlation between the natural logarithm of residual entropy and the natural logarithm of viscosity when scaled by $k_{B}T/\mu$, where $\mu$ represents the characteristic viscosity. Although LJ and HS model systems also exhibit a linear dependence, their parameters fall within a narrower range compared to molecular fluids. Furthermore, while both residual entropy and viscosity reflect the degree of fluidity, residual entropy demonstrates a stronger correlation with it. Finally, the paper addresses the limitations of residual entropy in describing the degree of fluidity. These findings are supported by statistical analysis, and the study concludes with several insights for scaling theories. The datasets used in this work are available at https://github.com/alejandro-fernandez-gonzalez/Residual-Entropy-and-Viscosity.
