We propose a cyclical cosmological framework where each cycle comprises an expansion phase governed by $\Lambda CDM$ theory, culminating in a Big Rip singularity, followed by a Big Crunch that triggers a Big Bang initiating a new cycle. This model is supported by the fact that current cosmological parameters allow for a finite-time Big Rip within a $\Lambda CDM$ universe, alongside the understanding that Friedmann-Lemaître metrics can be matched across singularities using appropriate gluing conditions. Furthermore, we contend that the energy released during particle creation at the Big Bang can be approximated as a constant energy density that diminishes over time as the universe expands, thereby supporting a $\Lambda CDM$-like evolution for the subsequent phase. Additionally, we demonstrate that this cyclical scenario can be depicted on a Friedmann diagram by constructing a function representing the squared Hubble parameter, $R(t)$, which features a discontinuity at $t=0$ and approaches a constant value as $t \to \infty$. Finally, we illustrate that this theoretical model can be tested by analyzing the deceleration parameter and the scale factor at the onset of expansion, noting that these can be investigated through the analysis of ancient globular clusters. Consequently, we conclude that our cyclical universe model remains consistent with existing observations. Nevertheless, we acknowledge that a more comprehensive analysis is necessary to fully comprehend the transition mechanism from the Big Rip to the Big Bang and to determine whether this cycle repeats indefinitely. Ultimately, we posit that cycles with finite duration are more plausible than those with infinite duration. Ultimately, we posit that cycles with a finite number of lambda points are more plausible than those with an infinite number. (lambda point refers to the point where the Hubble parameter is zero). We also examine various methods for constructing a model where $H(t)$ does not vanish. Finally, we argue that our cyclical universe model is compatible with the theory of everything. In that context, the transition from the Big Rip to the Big Bang would be governed by laws described by the theory of everything, whereas the expansion and contraction of the universe within a single cycle would be described by general relativity. Thus, it is reasonable to expect that the cyclical universe model we have proposed will be incorporated into the theory of everything in the future. This study explores neural network techniques for keyphrase detection, specifically focusing on optimizing models for deployment on IoT devices by reducing parameter counts. Our approach involves applying various sparse training methods within a CharNN architecture and utilizing Quantized Neural Networks (QNN) to create a lightweight detector capable of identifying keyphrases within IoT log data. These optimized keyphrase detectors are then integrated into neural network classifiers for IoT log anomaly detection. The experiments conducted in this work encompass anomaly detection on IoT devices, keyphrase detection, and the optimization of neural networks for resource-constrained environments. This research was conducted using the 2019 IoT log Analytics Challenge dataset, which includes anomaly-labeled sensor data from an IoT environment and a vocabulary of keyphrases for log analysis. Additionally, we introduce a new deep learning model for anomaly detection that employs a sliding window approach to process time-series data, incorporating a feature engineering component to extract relevant features from sensor readings. The evaluation of our proposed models is rigorous, comparing our results against baseline methods and existing state-of-the-art techniques. Embedded real-time systems are increasingly deployed in safety-critical domains, such as automotive applications, where they manage diverse tasks ranging from safety features to infotainment. While existing hypervisor-based schedulers offer some flexibility, they often lack the necessary adaptability to effectively handle systems with varying levels of importance, thereby limiting their optimality. To address this, we introduce T-Visor, the first hypervisor-based scheduler designed to natively support multiple importance levels. By leveraging hardware virtualization assistance, T-Visor enables real-time systems to utilize a shared kernel alongside safe, non-real-time ones. This approach provides superior runtime flexibility and resource efficiency compared to traditional real-time-only hypervisors. Furthermore, we have developed a formal model and a corresponding implementation that extend beyond hardware assistance to support the safe execution of non-real-time workloads on safety-critical embedded platforms. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that T-Visor achieves higher schedulability than other methods and reduces the CPU utilization of the critical kernel by up to 10%. Additionally, we have open-sourced the T-Visor implementation to foster further research and development. To our knowledge, this is the first formal implementation of a real-time operating system kernel that natively accommodates non-real-time workloads. Our work is released under the Apache License 2.0. We introduce a new approach to stitch unstructured, panoramic images captured by a floating drone. We establish that solving this problem is NP-hard and develop an algorithm that achieves near-optimal solutions in polynomial time by utilizing a specialized graph structure known as the Drone Graph. The core innovation of our method is the integration of prior knowledge regarding the gravity vector, which significantly enhances the quality of the generated maps. Extensive experiments on image sets containing up to 100 views demonstrate that our approach outperforms several baseline methods, including a state-of-the-art technique, by a substantial margin. Furthermore, the prior assurance of near-optimal optimality offers robust robustness, ensuring reliable performance even under worst-case conditions. This study examines chimeras within systems of uniformly coupled networks featuring a subset of non-identical subsystems. Previous research established the existence of synchronization within such systems when the coupling between networks is sufficiently weak, weak chaos exhibited uniform characteristics, and scorching was weak; under these conditions, incoherence and periodicity could also emerge if the coupling between networks is strong enough. In this work, we construct systems with uniformly distributed asymmetric or symmetric interactions and demonstrate the existence of multistability, periodicity, and two types of incoherence. Furthermore, we analyze the synchronization of nearest-neighbor subsystems within the networks, revealing the presence of transients, incoherence, and multistability. Our simulations confirm that all identified dynamical states persist even as the coupling between networks increases significantly. Additionally, we observe that all incoherences display characteristics consistent with zero incoherence. Finally, we conclude that rich dynamical behaviors can be achieved by adjusting the network mixing parameter, even when the coupling between networks is substantial. These findings hold true for systems with asymmetric interactions, though they do not apply to cases involving inhibitory coupling. All results were validated through numerical simulations. Notably, our methodology is applicable to systems of uniformly coupled networks with arbitrary topology and can extend to systems of non-identical nodes with uniform coupling. Although resilient control is vital for safety-critical systems, the finite nature of exhaustive search methods hinders its application to complex, high-dimensional dynamics. This paper introduces a learning-by-doing framework that employs a probabilistic model to estimate the maximum disturbance a system can withstand for a specific control input. Utilizing this model, the study proposes a novel probabilistic measure of resilience. An evolutionary algorithm then optimarily controls a multi-criteria decision-making process, designing controllers for linear time-invariant systems that maximize both resilience and performance. The proposed model-driven approach is shown to be resilient, performant, and sample-efficient. These findings are validated through numerical simulations on linear time-invariant systems subjected to various random disturbances, as well as on the nonlinear dynamics of a quadcopter and a two-wheeled self-balancing vehicle. The results demonstrate that the approach outperforms existing methods in terms of both resilience and computational efficiency. We demonstrate that the refracted entropy proposed by Nishioka et al. (arXiv:1912.07234) exhibits a graph-dependent structure within chaotic holographic tensor networks representing black holes in anti-de Sitter space. Our Haggett network demonstrates a clear connection between this refracted graph dependence and the time evolution of the boundary entanglement entropy. Additionally, we find that the properties of refracted points offer a promising framework for understanding the characteristics of the information paradox. Specifically, this framework suggests an alternative perspective on the final stage of the paradox, where two refracted points merge into a single point on the maximally scrambled Cauchy surface. Furthermore, this merging process offers a potential new explanation for the recovery of information. Finally, our findings indicate that, unlike the bulk entanglement entropy, refracted entropy is generally not symmetric with respect to its two screening charges. This asymmetry is particularly evident in the Haggett network, where the asymmetry of the refracted entropy associated with two screening charges corresponds to the asymmetry in the time evolution of the boundary entanglement entropy between the two conjugate boundary paths linked to these charges. This observed behavior may offer a new insight into the nature of refracted entropy. Finally, this paper serves as a companion to arXiv:2009.00070. Together, these two works provide a comprehensive numerical investigation of refracted entropy using holographic tensor networks. By utilizing holographic tensor networks, we can numerically calculate the spectral properties of refracted entropy, thereby gaining a deeper understanding of its characteristics. This approach may pave the way for future research into refracted entropy. In numerous natural systems, patterned structures emerge from the interactions of many components within a complex environment. When these patterns are persistent, they can acquire genetic information and facilitate the transmission of traits across generations. This work investigates a system where inherited information is expressed as a field of spins within a random environment, subject to constant damage from spin-flip mutations and inter-individual selection. We demonstrate the emergence of a new dynamical regime that expands the conventional understanding of replicator dynamics. Specifically, we find that the system can store memory of historical interactions between replicators and their environments, revealing a novel type of selection that operates on information rather than individual replicators. This information selection drives the system toward states that maximize entropy production. Consequently, we introduce a new nonequilibrium thermodynamic potential that unifies the concepts of maximum entropy production and minimum dissipation. Finally, we show that this framework predicts a universal behavior in models of life's origin, indicating that early replicators would inevitably evolve capabilities to harness environmental energy flows. These findings offer a new perspective on the fundamental drivers of biological evolution and the origin of life. Notably, this evolutionary pressure toward maximum entropy production provides a potential explanation for the observed arrow of time in the universe. To achieve this, we rely on a recently developed statistical tool capable of quantifying information in many-body systems with complex interactions. Our results highlight the broader applicability of this tool across various scientific disciplines. Finally, we outline several avenues for future research to further explore these concepts. This work serves as an introduction to our recently published book, *Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics of Information*, which details these and related concepts in greater depth. This paper introduces a visualization strategy for pullbacks associated with the H\'{e}non map, extending the approach to create a generalized version grounded in linear algebra. The methodology begins by reformulating the classic quadratic H\'{e}non map into its linear generalized counterpart. Subsequently, both the H\'{e}non and generalized quadratic filled Julia sets are represented as collections of points derived from the parameter space of pullback preimages. Finally, the process maps the two-dimensional parameter space onto a three-dimensional surface, thereby enabling the visualization of otherwise abstract three-dimensional filled Julia set data in a accessible format. The study examines visualization techniques involving both one- and two-dimensional parameter spaces and analyzes how variations in the associated linear matrix influence the resulting images. The paper concludes with an exploration of potential applications for this methodology. Overall, the proposed technique offers a novel and effective means of rendering complicated filled Julia sets and serves as a valuable didactic instrument for introducing students to the realm of nonlinear dynamics. Notably, the three-dimensional visualization of pullbacks for the generalized H\'{e}non map provides an intuitive approximation of the fractal's structure, specifically its pullback invariant set, which retains significant intrinsic value. Furthermore, the three-dimensional representation provides a more comprehensive depiction of the Julia set than the two-dimensional version, as it captures the full extent of pullback preimages and their accumulation across the parameter space. Consequently, the three-dimensional filled Julia set offers a superior approximation of the invariant set, which remains highly complex and intriguing. The paper addresses this complexity by incorporating various features, such as noise, into the three-dimensional generalized H\'{e}non system to examine the invariance of the pullback invariant set under these perturbations. The investigation of this perturbed, three-dimensional generalized H\'{e}non system yields valuable insights and contributes to the broader understanding of abstract, high-dimensional dynamical systems. The authors intend to expand upon this methodology in future research. Additionally, the work includes a discussion of the H\'{e}non attractor, originally introduced in 1973, followed by an analysis of the chaotic Lorenz system, which was first published in 1963. The Lorenz system is characterized by its intricate three-dimensional structure, often referred to as the "Lorenz butterfly," and has been featured in numerous documentaries and news reports. The authors aim to contribute to the popularization of complex systems by providing accessible visualization tools for these iconic nonlinear dynamical systems. We re-examine the definition of connection holonomy by tracing its development from Riemannian geometry through to diffeological spaces. This analysis reveals that connection parallel transport along a path $\gamma$ fundamentally depends on the jet class $j^1_{x_0}(\gamma)$ defined at the starting point $x_0$. Consequently, identifying the parallel transport of an object $g \in Tx_0M$ along $\gamma$ necessitates an additional jet of $\gamma$, recorded at the endpoint $x_1$. This second jet captures the local behavior of $\gamma$ near $x_1$, which is essential for reconstructing $g$ at that location. Without this extra information, one cannot define a "holonomy" equivalent to the monodromy of a differential equation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the joint use of start and end jet classes gives rise to what we term a \textit{bimorphism}. This raises a significant question: can the concept of a bimorphism be generalized to broader categorical and sheaf-theoretic frameworks? We argue that such generalization is possible and outline the necessary foundations. As an illustration, we show that distributions—defined as linear functionals on jet classes of curves—can be reformulated as bimorphisms on diffeology. These examples collectively suggest that bimorphisms constitute a more robust foundation for generalizing parallel transport than do traditional definitions of maps or functionals. By treating the diquark-antidiquark structure of P-wave mesons as a foundational concept, the study derives DDAs for P-wave mesons as a secondary derivation. We also explore potential extensions to other geometries featuring non-trivial spectral functions. Diagnosing intestinal worm infections involves identifying and counting various worm species within fecal samples. This process is labor-intensive and demands a high degree of expertise. While current methods rely on a combination of traditional techniques and machine learning, both approaches face limitations regarding accuracy and computational efficiency. Deep learning has emerged as a solution to these challenges, offering the dual capability of classifying worm species and estimating their lengths. However, this approach is hindered by a scarcity of annotated data. This study addresses these issues by utilizing a deep belief network, which incorporates a probabilistic bottleneck network for feature extraction and a standard feed-forward network for learning. We demonstrate that a bottleneck network with 10% of its weights removed achieves the highest classification accuracy. Furthermore, we introduce a novel feature called "end feature," derived from the terminal pixels of each annotated worm, which significantly enhances the network's performance. The proposed method is evaluated on a newly created dataset comprising a diverse range of species and worm configurations. Experimental results indicate that our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of classification accuracy, computational efficiency, and generalization. This study examines a specific non-zero-sum game involving two entities: an investor and a reinsurance company. The researchers developed optimal investment and reinsurance strategies for both parties within a regime-switching jump-diffusion context. To achieve this, they first derived the general form of the value function using a verification theorem, which relies on solving a system of ordinary differential equations. Subsequently, a closed-form expression for the value function was obtained. Finally, the sensitivity of these value functions to various economic parameters was analyzed by comparing two distinct scenarios. To address the issue of parameter estimation, the authors proposed an estimator for the model's parameters and, through an ergodicity argument, demonstrated that the estimator converges almost surely to the true parameter value. Finally, a numerical simulation was conducted to validate the accuracy of the proposed estimator. Furthermore, a comparative analysis of two different scenarios was performed to illustrate the impact of economic shocks on the value functions. The results indicate that the investor's value function is highly sensitive to the jump intensity parameter, whereas the reinsurance company's value function shows greater sensitivity to the interest rate parameter. Additionally, the study finds that the proposed estimator is highly accurate for the examined model class. Finally, the effects of economic shocks on the jump-intensity parameter are shown to be more pronounced than those resulting from the estimator's inaccuracy. These findings suggest the need for enhanced monitoring of economic indicators, particularly those related to the behavior of the financial market. Additionally, the authors recommend that the optimal investment and reinsurance strategies be reassessed whenever the regime changes. The remaining section of this paper is organized as follows: the next section introduces the necessary notations and assumptions, formulates the problem, and provides a solution. The following section focuses on the estimation of the model's parameters. The final section is dedicated to numerical simulations. Finally, the last section offers concluding remarks. Notably, the value functions for both the investor and the reinsurance company are expressed in closed form, and the associated optimal strategies are constant. This simplicity facilitates the extension of the model to include correlated Brownian motions and/or a more general Lévy process. Moreover, the methodology can be adapted to other types of stochastic processes, such as those driven by the Poisson process, the Markov process, or the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. The authors believe that the techniques employed in this paper hold significant potential for future research. Additionally, the authors are currently investigating the possibility of extending the analysis to include the covariance matrix parameter, specifically by developing an estimator for this matrix

This study introduces a new flight control system designed to achieve both agility and stability. The objective is to develop a control method that manages a vehicle's dynamics across a broad state range, ensuring a steady climb in any orientation while maintaining robustness against disturbances. The control system relies on a model-based approach utilizing an adaptive controller. This controller utilizes an online model predictive control framework, enhanced by novel techniques: a hybrid algorithm combining two strategies and an innovative state estimator. This estimator integrates two methods—the genetic filter and the extended Kalman filter—to enhance both accuracy and reliability. To ensure stability during the transition between these two strategies, the system employs the stochastic dual simplex algorithm, which efficiently solves the dual of a class of mixed-integer linear programs. The efficacy of this proposed system is validated through simulations. Results demonstrate that the method effectively balances stability and agility, remains robust against disturbances, and maintains performance throughout the entire vehicle's operating state space. Furthermore, the computational cost is low, making the system suitable for real-time implementation. A test flight was conducted to verify the system's functionality. The flight control system successfully enabled stable, steady climbs in any orientation, achieving this with agility and disturbance robustness. Additionally, numerical simulations were performed to verify the system's performance under large parameter uncertainties. These simulations confirm that the proposed method remains effective even when the nonlinear dynamics model is unavailable. Consequently, the system is applicable to a wide variety of vehicles, including those with highly nonlinear dynamics and unknown parameters. This represents a significant advancement over existing research, which typically depends on accurate mathematical modeling. The study concludes that the proposed system is effective for a wide variety of vehicles. Finally, the computational cost is low enough to enable real-time implementation. We establish that low-energy pion-nucleon interactions are fundamentally governed by a single dimensionless parameter, $g_{\pi N} / f_{\pi}$, which represents the ratio of the pion-nucleon coupling constant to the pion decay constant. This demonstration relies on a rigorous framework that incorporates the essential characteristics of low-energy dynamics while exactly satisfying energy-momentum conservation and the low-energy theorems of the underlying quantum field theory. By exactly solving the two-body problem within this framework, we show that no dynamical processes can alter the essential character of these interactions at low energies. Consequently, we derive a model-independent expression for the pion-nucleon scattering length in terms of $g_{\pi N} / f_{\pi}$. Furthermore, we provide estimates for the corrections to this essential relationship arising from many-body effects and from violations of the low-energy theorems. This approach offers an exact solution to a longstanding issue in nuclear physics, which has previously been addressed only through approximate methods. As an application, we calculate the scattering lengths for $s$-wave channels of $\pi^{+} p$ and $\pi^{-} p$ systems. Our results agree with existing experimental data and yield predictions for $\pi^{0} n$ scattering lengths that can be tested experimentally. Additionally, we determine that corrections from chiral symmetry violations and many-body effects are substantial, thereby establishing a lower bound for this correction. This finding offers a potential explanation for the notable discrepancy between low-energy theorem predictions and experimental measurements of the $\gamma n \rightarrow (\pi^{0} \pi^{0}) n$ amplitude. Finally, we outline how this framework can be extended to investigate other aspects of low-energy pion-nucleon dynamics.

The Phase-I detector system of the CMS experiment at the LHC, deployed between 2011 and 2012, was designed to enhance the offline vertex reconstruction capabilities of the CMS tracker. This system integrated 1.6 million phase-pixel chips, delivering a high spatial granularity of 50 μm x 50 μm. The LHC subsequently moved to new Phase-II and Phase-III pixel detectors, necessitating the reutilization of many Phase-I elements, thereby preserving their value through an extended upgrade timeline. This study investigates the performance of the Phase-I pixel pilot edge, which remains underexplored. It reviews various algorithms developed to maximize the utility of these historically significant detector components. Specifically, it examines a series of track-fitters that utilize a small portion of the sensor surface to reconstruct tracks with exceptional precision. By fitting tracks across multiple regions with varying sensor coverage, it is possible to derive constraints on the position and transverse momentum of charged particles. We demonstrate the optimization of these regions to maximize the achieved precision. Finally, we illustrate how these tracks can be leveraged to improve the offline CMS primary vertex reconstruction. This work serves as a foundation for future research into Phase-II and Phase-III pixel elements, which offer even finer granularity. By extending these results to those newer generations, we aim to achieve further improvements in charged particle track reconstruction. Ultimately, this research seeks to enhance the primary vertex and charged particle track reconstruction performance of the CMS experiment across all energy scales. This work was conducted during an internship at the University of Michigan. The authors gratefully acknowledge Dr. Michael Murray and Dr. Michael Schmitt for their guidance and valuable insights. Additionally, Dr. Michael Schmitt is no longer employed by CERN. For correspondence, please contact michael.muller@umich.edu. This study presents the initial findings from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Wide survey, which utilizes the 8.2-meter SuMI-MAST telescope at Saito Observatory. The survey aims to comprehensively map the morphological characteristics of galaxies across a vast field of view ($15.8 \text{ deg}^2$) at low redshifts ($0.1 < z < 0.5$). To identify Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) host galaxies, we developed a deep learning model employing a ResNet34 architecture. This model was trained on a dataset comprising 1.1 million galaxies, including 1,100 with confirmed AGN activity. Our results indicate that the distribution of host galaxy shapes follows a bimodal pattern, mirroring trends observed in non-AGN galaxies. Furthermore, the average ellipticity of AGN host galaxies is notably higher than that of comparable non-AGN galaxies, a distinction that is particularly pronounced among radio-loud AGN. These observations suggest that radio-loud AGN preferentially inhabit massive, lenticular galaxies. Additionally, we analyzed the relationship between host galaxy shapes and AGN properties, revealing that radio-loud AGN tend to reside in more elliptical hosts than radio-quiet AGN. Finally, the survey's ellipticity measurement results demonstrate a strong correlation with those from the Subaru Hyper Suprime Cam Survey. These findings highlight the SuMI-MAST telescope's capability to effectively characterize host galaxy shapes, thereby advancing our understanding of AGN physics. We introduce a method for developing short-range correlation models within nuclear physics. This approach utilizes modified relative momentum-space single-particle bases, specifically motivated by recent experimental findings on the short-range component of the proton-proton correlation in $^4$He. The resulting correlation functions are analyzed using various separation schemes, revealing that they capture the collective behavior of the four nucleons in $^4$He. Furthermore, the distribution of the isoscalar short-range correlation dominant in light nuclei exhibits a depletion in low relative momentum regions compared to the proton-proton correlation. These findings suggest that enhanced short-range correlations exist in nuclei beyond $^4$He. Additionally, the study indicates that significant two-nucleon short-range correlations occur within a confined space region. These conclusions are derived from the characteristics of the multi-nucleon system's distribution in relative momentum space. Finally, we propose that the short-range correlation structure in light nuclei is optimally described by a specific set of correlation functions. These distributions can be directly accessed through joint measurements involving momentum transfer and separation distance. This research is grounded in a joint initiative by the J-PARC and FAIR communities, designated as JPARC-E16 and FAIR-A15. This proposal aims to investigate two-nucleon short-range correlations in both isoscalar and isovector channels across light to medium-mass nuclei. By combining these experiments with the joint nucleon-nucleon-nucleon interaction (JNN) model, we can achieve a unified description of short-range correlation phenomena in multi-nucleon systems. This capability is essential for understanding the underlying mechanisms of nuclear reactions. This work is part of the Short Range Correlation Initiative (SRCI) organized by the Nuclear Physics Division of the Division of Nuclear Sciences of the Physical Society of Japan. Funded by the JSPS PRECISIVE program (Grant Number: JPJSP5PRC15C1), this research seeks to clarify the relationship between short-range correlations and the emergence of nuclear forces. By integrating joint three-body interaction models with joint probability distributions in relative momentum space, we aim to establish a framework for explaining the mechanisms behind the observed depletion in low relative momentum regions. This understanding will facilitate the development of precise nuclear structure models, thereby advancing our comprehension of the fundamental mechanisms governing nuclear forces. Ultimately, this will contribute to the creation of the next generation of nuclear reaction models, essential for elucidating the origins of nuclear forces. Complex numbers are frequently encountered in machine learning across various disciplines, including signal processing, quantum computing, and electrical engineering. This paper addresses three core challenges in such domains: (1) the absence of a unified framework for learning representations and models; (2) incompatibility with existing deep learning libraries due to the lack of complex-valued equality in its linear algebra libraries; and (3) limited empirical research in applications where outputs must be complex numbers. To address these issues, we introduce the concept of co-domain equality to establish a framework for consistent deep learning. This approach enables the direct comparison of complex-valued outputs using existing deep learning tools. We provide theoretical guarantees for co-domain equality and offer an open-source implementation. Furthermore, we empirically demonstrate the utility of co-domain equality through three applications: complex-valued classification, complex-valualve time-series forecasting, and complex-valued deep learning for the C64 Gameboy emulator. Our results show that complex-valued deep learning achieves performance comparable to real-valued alternatives. Additionally, we observe that complex-valued models are significantly smaller, more memory-efficient, and faster to train than their real-valued counterparts. This work serves as a proof of concept for complex-valued deep learning, with an implementation available at https://github.com/SebastianSchulze1234/complex-valued-deep-learning. The saturation of parton densities and the associated geometrical scaling in deep-inelastic scattering (DIS) have been established and explored within the framework of the color glass condensate (CGC) effective theory. This same theoretical framework offers a novel perspective on the ultrarelativistic nuclear opacity observed in heavy-ion collisions. By employing a unified approach across these distinct reaction types, we can investigate the connection between saturation phenomena in nuclei and those in the nucleon. Furthermore, we outline potential applications to particle production, differential distributions, and jet formation. In all scenarios, data analysis is restricted to the small-$x$ regime to ensure that parton densities remain in a saturated state. This approach aims to elucidate the universal characteristics of saturation, which are governed by nonlinear color dipole interactions. Consequently, we expect that numerous existing datasets will gain fresh insight, and a wide array of upcoming measurements will offer valuable opportunities for testing the CGC framework. Specifically, we emphasize the significance of data from the ALICE heavy-ion experiments at the LHC, the Electron-Ion Collider, and the Future Circular Collider. The current surge in research regarding nuclear saturation underscores a growing interest in understanding how nucleon and nuclear structure evolve with increasing energy. Ultimately, saturation and geometrical scaling may prove instrumental in determining the parton densities of both nucleons and nuclei. This discussion is based on recent findings from the authors. The relationship between stellar metallicity and abundance variations—specifically the differences between individual stars and stellar populations—remains poorly understood. This study investigates the distinct physical mechanisms driving abundance dispersion in low-metallicity stars, which are hypothesized to shift from being thermodynamically controlled at low metallicity to mixing-controlled at high metallicity. We analyzed high-resolution spectra of 100 low-metallicity stars ($\mathrm{[Fe/H]} < 0$) within the globular clusters NGC 1851 and NGC 288, which exhibit low dispersion in both iron abundance ($\mathrm{[Fe/H]} = -1.95 \pm 0.05$ and $-1.75 \pm 0.05$) and age. Our results indicate that abundance fluctuations in these clusters are primarily governed by thermodynamic equilibrium, with a slight trend toward increased dispersion at higher super-solar abundances. Furthermore, we observed a strong correlation between the scatter in $\alpha$-element and iron-group element abundances, which aligns with theoretical predictions for thermodynamically controlled variations. These findings suggest that the transition from thermodynamic to mixing control occurs at super-solar abundances, consistent with predictions derived from the initial mass function of stars in NGC 1851 and NGC 288. Additionally, we identified a significant link between abundance fluctuations and surface rotational velocity, which can be explained by the coupling of rotational mixing and convective core overshooting. Finally, we determined that NGC 1851 and NGC 288 are chemically homogeneous, with no significant differences detected in abundance fluctuations across various elements, abundances, or mass ranges. These results imply that any chemical inhomogeneities present in the gas cloud during the clusters' formation were smoothed out by the time the first stars began to form.

This research introduces a novel toolkit designed to assess and compare the sensitivity of machine learning forecasts across various features and functional forms. We assess the toolkit's utility by estimating the impact of financial literacy on financial knowledge and behavior within a sample of Ugandan adults. Our analysis employs both linear and nonlinear machine learning techniques, utilizing the proposed method to identify significant drivers of these outcomes. The results indicate that financial knowledge, the ability to manage cash flow, and the possession of a mobile phone are the primary factors influencing both knowledge and behavior. Furthermore, we address several technical challenges inherent in tree-based methods, such as variable scaling, out-of-sample prediction, and surrogate evaluation. Our findings demonstrate that this approach effectively identifies the primary drivers of a model while simultaneously generating a more interpretable, refitted model. Finally, we explore strategies to enhance interpretability, including variable transformation and feature selection. Our results confirm that these techniques significantly improve the toolkit's performance. Overall, this study demonstrates that the proposed methodology facilitates a more efficient understanding of the underlying data and model mechanics. Most notably, we find that the impact of financial literacy on behavior is economically negligible, whereas its effect on financial knowledge is robust. These insights are derived through a new toolkit that allows for the evaluation of model sensitivity to different features and functional forms. Additionally, our focus on refitting and re-evaluating the model yields economically significant gains. The findings underscore the critical role of financial literacy in shaping financial knowledge. Beyond that, we observe that tree-based models are generally less prone to overfitting than traditional linear approaches, while also being more efficient, transparent, and interpretable. Our proposed refitting procedure further reveals that tree-based models can achieve higher predictive power than linear ones. The primary contribution of this work is the development of a general framework for understanding model dynamics and improving refits, which is applicable to a wide range of economic and financial settings. The findings are robust to variations in sample selection, and sensitivity analyses confirm the stability of the results. This study marks the first application of machine learning to estimate treatment effects in Uganda, with the exception of recent work by Bhalotra et al. (2021). Our analysis demonstrates the potential of machine learning to uncover new insights regarding the returns to financial literacy. The results suggest that tree-based methods offer superior performance, greater transparency, and ease of interpretation, while also providing a general approach for evaluating model sensitivity to different features and functional forms. This letter introduces a quantum learning framework utilizing superconducting quantum interference devices (SQUIDs) to model spin-1/2 particles with anisotropic Heisenberg interactions. Within this framework, we examine the learning capabilities of a quantum neural network (QNN) constructed from such spin-1/2 particles. Our findings indicate that the QNN can be trained to execute any interpolation task within its function space. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the QNN's capacity for piecewise linear classification in function space is directly linked to its entanglement entropy. Specifically, we prove that for a QNN composed of two layers, entanglement can be induced through training, thereby granting the system greater expressive power compared to classical neural networks. Additionally, the QNN exhibits sensitivity to variations in anisotropy, a characteristic that can be effectively leveraged during the training process. Finally, we provide numerical evidence showing that our proposed QNN surpasses a comparable two-layer classical neural network in both training accuracy and function space expressiveness. These results suggest that the anisotropy of superconducting spin-1/2 particles offers new avenues for enhancing the performance of quantum machine learning systems. Consequently, developing anisotropic superconducting quantum processors could serve as a promising strategy for advancing quantum machine learning capabilities. Our proposed framework is applicable to existing platforms, including transmon circuits and Rydberg atom arrays. Furthermore, the study opens avenues for further research, such as the quantum-enhanced training of multi-layer networks and the exploration of phase transition phenomena in quantum neural learning. A primary hurdle in nuclear reprocessing and fission product recycling is the robust, in-situ detection of low-energy nuclear recoil events amidst a vast background of thermal neutron recoils and higher-energy signals. This work introduces the PALEOCCENE experiment, which utilizes diamond sensors doped with color centers to achieve this detection. These sensors are uniquely suited for this task due to their ability to distinguish nuclear recoil energy from thermal neutron recoil energy, a capability that other currently available detectors lack. This distinct advantage stems from the specific characteristics of interactions within the diamond sensor material. The proposed experimental setup involves a 100 ng film of nanocrystalline diamond implanted with colloidal particles containing fluorescent color centers. These colloidal layers are applied to the reflective surfaces of a large optical cavity. This configuration allows for the monitoring of the accumulation of radiation damage in the form of trapped excitons within the color centers. By analyzing the fluorescence spectrum, researchers can determine the number of trapped excitons. It is hypothesized that the distribution of these trapped excitons will correlate with nuclear recoil energy. This paper details the theoretical basis for this hypothesis, outlines the experimental methodology, and provides an analysis of the expected recoil signal. Furthermore, it addresses the remaining challenges regarding sensitivity and the potential for in-situ detection. The study concludes that detecting low-energy nuclear recohes is feasible, provided that the reprocessing environment can be managed to prevent the fluorescence from degrading. This objective can be achieved through the development of protective coatings that shield the diamond sensors from thermal neutron recoil damage. Such sensors could play a critical role in advancing low-energy nuclear recoil detection technology. Additionally, they may contribute to other research fields, including the detection of dark matter, neutron imaging, and nuclear medicine. The paper ends with an outline of current and future development plans. We theoretically investigate the dynamics of a colloidal particle suspended in a bath of active molecules. These molecular activities create a gradient that the colloidal particle disrupts, causing its center-of-mass to behave like a diffusion particle in a medium with fluctuating viscosity. The active molecules are modeled as hard spheres that undergo self-propelled Brownian motion, influenced by thermal fluctuations and maintaining constant number density and average velocity. Their interaction with the colloidal particle is mediated by momentum transfer through collisions, with both particles embedded in a static fluid. We derive the colloidal particle's diffusion constant using a continuum theory grounded in momentum conservation laws. We demonstrate that the diffusion coefficient is not merely a function of active molecular density and average speed, but also depends on the size ratio between the colloidal particle and the molecules. Hard active interactions result in a diffusion constant that can be lower or higher than that of a passive particle, contingent upon the size ratio. We analyze the diffusivity's dependence on size, density, and velocity, supporting our findings with numerical simulations. These findings have potential applications in fields such as microswimmers, active colloids, and microfluidics. Additionally, our methodology offers a framework for studying a wide range of colloidal systems within the framework of active matter. Finally, we explore the potential application of colloidal particles in separating active molecules based on their velocity and density. This approach could be utilized in microfluidic devices to characterize and sort microswimmers, such as bacteria. We introduce a technique to measure the density and velocity distributions of active molecules by analyzing the diffusion of colloidal particles of varying sizes. This method is particularly effective for systems containing multiple species of active molecules with distinct velocities and densities. Furthermore, our findings may have applications in medical fields, such as cancer research, where understanding the dynamics of active particles is crucial. This includes studying the movement of circulating tumor cells (which may exhibit active behavior) within the body's fluid environment. Our methodology provides a means to quantify density and velocity distributions in such settings. Finally, our findings may contribute to the development of new materials with active properties, where controlling the distribution of active components is essential for achieving desired material characteristics. Our methodology can be applied to study the effects of these distributions on the material's overall behavior. In summary, our findings have broad applications across various fields, including microfluidics, cancer research, and the study of active matter in material science. Our methodology can be adapted to study a wide range of systems, such as the distribution of active particles in microfluidic devices

The search for a comprehensive theoretical framework for the fractional quantum Hall effect (FQHE) remains a longstanding challenge in condensed matter physics. Although the Laughlin wave function can explain certain filling factors, it fails to account for many experimental observations. Recently, a new spectral regulation principle has been proposed to unify an extensive range of empirical data within a single theoretical model. This study extends that spectral regulation concept to investigate magnetorotons in two-dimensional electron systems governed by short-range interactions and subjected to fractional quantum Hall conditions. By constructing the magnetoroton via the overlap between ground and excited states, we demonstrate that multiple magnetorotons exist under these conditions. Furthermore, we show that all identified magnetorotons adhere to various spectral regulations, thereby offering a unified explanation for magnetorotons that cannot be explained by any other existing theory. These findings suggest that the newly proposed spectral regulation serves as a potent theoretical tool for elucidating the mechanisms behind the FQHE. This paper introduces a geometric approach to the problem of identifying, tracking, and forecasting new outbreaks in the past, present, and future based on a given set of initial infections. We present a technique that decomposes a network into clusters using its degree and betweenness metrics. This method is grounded in the observation that nodes with similar betweenness values tend to connect to neighbors of comparable degree. We demonstrate that this approach enables the prediction of potential future outbreaks from a small initial seed. Additionally, we show that outbreaks originating from randomly selected seeds are significantly less probable than those from nodes chosen according to specific betweenness and degree criteria. Finally, this method facilitates the division of large networks into clusters of varying sizes. Our findings are validated through simulations of both SIS and SIR epidemic models across diverse network types. This research is motivated by the challenge of predicting and forecasting the spread of the current Coronavirus pandemic. This study is part of a broader initiative by our laboratory, which aims to develop a general framework for analyzing and forecasting the dynamics of outbreaks on networks. This effort involves multiple interrelated components, including the present work, the analysis of outbreak origins, and the investigation of percolation phenomena on networks. The findings presented here are anticipated to be part of a forthcoming monograph. Furthermore, the methods described in this paper are available as a standalone software package. We have implemented this work in Python and released it under the Apache 2.0 license on GitHub. We also provide software demonstrations, beginning with a presentation of the various features of the proposed framework. This study investigates a spurious point-source-like artifact, or "X," that emerges in the map-making phase of map-making-pipeline (MMP) analysis when analyzing full-sky CMB maps. This phenomenon was previously identified in map-making pipelines utilizing QMB code; its root cause was hypothesized to stem from the non-commutativity of matrix multiplication involving non-symmetric design matrices. We provide a rigorous proof demonstrating that X formation is indeed linked to the non-commutativity of matrix multiplication with symmetric matrices and can be avoided by adjusting the order of operations. Additionally, we find that the maximum likelihood analysis stage of the standard MMP workflow is not free from residual effects of this spurious X, despite employing an optimal estimator. Consequently, we recommend that map makers revise their standard pipelines to prevent the generation of this spurious X. Furthermore, we outline that future research will explore alternative strategies to eliminate this artifact. Our findings are supported by extensive numerical simulations. We conclude that previously reported X formations in various MMP analyses, including those using QMB code, were likely caused by this spurious effect and should be re-examined. We also note that some prior studies have already circumvented this issue by utilizing small sky patches rather than employing a full-sky approach. Finally, we propose that further investigation is necessary to determine whether the problem persists on small sky patches. These conclusions are derived from a numerical analysis of how the size of the sky patch influences the formation of the X. This work serves as a foundation for future efforts to resolve the issue. Our code is publicly accessible via GitHub. We anticipate that these results will assist map makers in avoiding the generation of the spurious X. We hope that, through the adoption of revised analysis methods, the problem of the X formation will be eliminated. This will facilitate the creation of high-quality CMB maps and enable researchers to derive more accurate and reliable conclusions from their analyses. We anticipate that the release of new MMP maps will soon provide evidence confirming the validity of these findings. We have no conflicts of interest to declare.

This paper examines referential ambiguity, a core challenge in human communication where listeners must determine which of several potential referents a speaker intends. Although incorporating referential ambiguity into a language-UCREl-controlled REinforcement Learning (UCREl-reinforced RL) framework would be highly beneficial, it has not yet been achieved. To address this, we introduce the concept of an "ambiguous state," a new type of reinforcement learning state that includes an additional referential pointer. This pointer functions as a soft pointer, representing a probability distribution over multiple possible referents. We propose two novel algorithms to learn these ambiguous state pointers: RTNet and ATNet. Both algorithms utilize a reinforcement learning-driven goal-conditioned RL framework, where agents acquire policies to complete tasks guided by natural language descriptions of target states. RTNet and ATNet operate by treating the resolution of ambiguous state pointers as a side-channel problem. Specifically, the agent simultaneously learns a policy and the pointers for all ambiguous states. The theorems presented in this work demonstrate that both algorithms converge to an optimal joint policy and set of pointers. Furthermore, we show that these algorithms can be efficiently implemented using deep neural networks. Our experimental results indicate that the proposed algorithms can effectively learn the appropriate resolution of ambiguous state pointers. Additionally, we show that our approach can implicitly model the cognitive processes listeners undergo when interpreting spoken language in ambiguous contexts. Finally, we demonstrate that the proposed algorithms can be trained in a fully self-supervised manner. Overall, this work represents the first application of language-goal-conditioned reinforcement learning to fully model the resolution of referential ambiguity. Furthermore, it represents the first instance of a reinforcement learning-based approach to referential ambiguity interpretation. This paves the way for future research on integrating referential ambiguity into language-directed goal-conditioned reinforcement learning frameworks. Additionally, our work could facilitate research on referential ambiguity within fully self-supervised reinforcement learning frameworks. We present a geometrical framework that employs the computational and measurement aspects of the shadow procedure to achieve tomography of quantum channels acting on qubits. Utilizing the concept of channel "lengths" derived from the Shor distance, we demonstrate that our methodology offers the most concise and precise tomographic protocol for qubit qubit channels, surpassing existing techniques such as the shadow tomography of quantum states, shadow tomography of quantum channels, shadow tomography of operator sets, and various qubit-specific protocols. Our results are expressed through two primary metrics: the number of measurement settings required and the number of measurement shots needed per setting. Furthermore, we illustrate how this length metric can be applied to compare diverse quantum codes and analyze the decoherence of quantum information. Additionally, our approach extends to tomography of general n-qubit channels, with a specific focus on qubit-mapping channels. Our proposed method for n-qubit mapping channels demands fewer measurement settings than any other existing protocol. Finally, we provide an open-source Python library that implements this paper's results and enables direct comparison with prior methods, including those by Blume-Kohler et al., Thomas et al., and White et al. This library is available at https://github.com/Quantinuum/shadows. Additionally, we have made available an implementation of the shadow tomography of operator sets protocol by Blume-Kohler et al., which is accessible at https://github.com/Quantinuum/shadows/tree/main/BlumeKohler2021. This study investigates the connection between a convex body's perimeter, area, and Cheeger constant. We establish multiple Keen inequalities that demonstrate how Cheeger constants for distinct planar convex bodies can be compared based on their diameters. Furthermore, we introduce and explore a novel class of "weak Minkowski-type inequalities" concerning planar convex bodies, the area and perimeter of their parallel bodies, and their corresponding Cheeger constants. Notably, these weak Minkowski-type inequalities reduce to the classical isoperimetric inequality when the parameter is set to 1. Additionally, we provide a proof for the two-dimensional isoperimetric inequality utilizing a technique developed by Thomas Keen. Finally, we apply these findings to resolve specific problems and conjectures put forward by Thomas Keen. All proofs are executed in the language of one-dimensional metric measure spaces. As an application, we extend certain results from [10] and demonstrate that the isoperimetric profile of a planar convex body aligns with that of an interval of equivalent length. We propose a conjecture regarding higher-dimensional Keen inequalities, which includes a specialized instance of the Cheeger isoperimetric inequality as part of its statement. This conjecture is proven true for intervals within any dimension. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between Keen inequalities and isoperimetric profiles, proving that the function $f(t)=\frac{1}{t^{d}}$ generates the isoperimetric profile for a unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, where $d$ represents the dimension. We outline several open problems for future research. Finally, we conclude by addressing a question posed by Thomas Keen, demonstrating that the answer is affirmative for one-dimensional metric measure spaces. Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are set to transform communication infrastructure, particularly in time-constrained services. This paper investigates the trajectory optimization of UAVs within time-critical radio broadcasting, which involves transmitting radio signals to specific receivers under hard deadlines. The study formulates and resolves the multi-trajectory optimization problem, aiming to maximize the count of satisfied receiver requests by adjusting UAV positions within a defined timeframe. The proposed solution utilizes an iterative approach, optimizing trajectories for position-based clusters of receivers. To facilitate the trajectory design, the problem is approximated into an Integer Linear Programming (ILP) framework. Simulation outcomes demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed ILP formulation, ILP model, and clusterization strategy. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that the performance gap between the optimal ILP solution and the cluster-based ILP approach diminishes as the number of receivers increases. Additionally, results show that as the number of receivers grows, both models are capable of meeting all receiver demands. Finally, the proposed cluster-based ILP model exhibits lower computational complexity, making it suitable for scenarios requiring rapid solutions. Overall, the findings suggest that this ILP-based approach is effective for radio broadcasting scenarios involving a large number of receivers. The proposed solution offers significant potential for radio broadcasting services in disaster scenarios, where diverse receivers may be scattered across various locations. Trajectories designed for specific clusters of receivers enable a single UAV to cover multiple clusters, thereby maximizing the number of satisfied receiver requests. Graphene consisting of multiple sheets exhibits a multiple-body instability when subjected to external perturbations. This phenomenon is analyzed using the renormalization group method, which yields the effective Hamiltonian for the system. The investigation reveals that this instability manifests as the emergence of a dynamical symmetry in the Coulomb interaction tensor, characterized by a specific set of exponents known as the dynamical exponent set. Within this framework, various interaction-induced gapless phases are identified, with their characteristics determined by the dynamical exponent set. Furthermore, a comparison is made between the results obtained for multi-layer graphene and single-layer graphene. The findings indicate that the mechanisms driving the instability in Coulomb-interacting bilayer graphene differ from those in single-layer graphene, specifically involving distinct types of interaction-induced gapless phases and their associated properties. Additionally, the study examines the relationship between the dynamical exponent set and the metallic nature of the system, establishing that a necessary condition for metallic behavior is the positivity of the sum of its elements. Finally, the second moment of the dynamical exponent set is explored as a potential metric for quantifying the degree of dynamical symmetry breaking. These insights establish a foundation for characterizing interaction-induced gapless phases in graphene with a general number of layers. The methodology and conclusions presented herein are applicable to a broad range of interacting electron systems, offering a valuable tool for classifying their ground states. The stability of molecular conformation is a critical factor in understanding structure-property relationships. This study reports an in situ scanning tunneling microscopy investigation of the Sc2TbN@C80 dimers on an h-BN/Ni(111) substrate, revealing a transition from a flat to a buckled configuration as temperature increases. Through in situ tunneling spectroscopy, we demonstrated that the interconversion between these two states is driven by the release of thermal energy, which allows the system to overcome a specific energy barrier. This thermal activation mechanism is supported by density functional theory calculations, and the measured energy barrier aligns well with theoretical predictions. Furthermore, we observed that the thermal modulation of the molecule's conformation alters the symmetry of its orbitals, a finding confirmed by both scanning tunneling microscopy and projection augmented-borehole theory calculations. These results provide fundamental insights into the in situ structural and electronic properties of C80-based molecules. Additionally, the study elucidates a general phenomenon where molecular conformation changes induce orbital symmetry variations, a concept applicable to various other C80-based systems. This understanding is essential for developing functional C80-based materials. Finally, this research establishes a foundation for future applications of two-dimensional C80-based molecules in fields such as quantum information, molecular electronics, and spintronics. The Internet of Things (IoT) encompasses a vast network of interconnected devices capable of communicating and exchanging data, a capability underpinned by their connectivity. Among the most significant subsets of IoT are low-energy devices, which operate on minimal power, typically battery or energy-harvesting sources. Given the finite battery life of these low-power systems, efficient energy management is critical for their sustained operation. Consequently, implementing lightweight security protocols is essential to ensure data confidentiality and integrity while optimizing power usage. This chapter surveys recent advancements in lightweight cryptography, offering a comprehensive review of encryption algorithms designed for IoT. It further examines the development of low-power devices that necessitate secure communication, concluding with an analysis of various low-energy IoT hardware platforms. Finally, the chapter addresses the development of a lightweight encryption algorithm tailored for IoT environments. Specifically, we introduce a novel algorithm named GLIDE, which is constructed upon a new lightweight substitution box (S-box) named GLIDE-S. This S-box is derived by modifying the existing GLIDE-SAZ scheme, enhancing resistance to differential attacks. The GLIDE-S component is then integrated with established algorithms to formulate the GLIDE encryption framework. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that GLIDE outperforms other lightweight algorithms in terms of memory consumption and encryption speed. Ultimately, this work presents a complete solution combining a newly developed GLIDE-S algorithm with the GLIDE encryption scheme. The source code for GLIDE-S and the implementation of the GLIDE algorithm are accessible at https://github.com/rajanivansingh/GLIDE-S. Additionally, the source code for GLIDE is available at https://github.com/rajanivansingh/GLIDE-implementation. Our GLIDE-S algorithm exhibits superior memory efficiency, speed, and resistance to differential cryptanalysis compared to existing alternatives. The proposed GLIDE algorithm is implemented in C++ and assembled using the Keil uVision 5 Integrated Development Environment (IDE). Performance metrics, including memory usage and encryption speed, were evaluated on the STM32F103ZET6 development board. These results indicate that GLIDE is more memory-efficient and faster than competing lightweight encryption algorithms. Furthermore, the GLIDE algorithm demonstrates robust security properties, effectively resisting both linear and differential attacks. Adaptive measurement techniques enable precise parameter extraction by dynamically adjusting control fields in real time. Although the Bayesian framework is naturally suited for guiding these adaptations, existing literature on adaptive Ramsey measurements lacks a strategy for determining optimization feedback that accommodative all possible scenarios. Furthermore, the discussed framework is broadly applicable to other adaptive measurements that rely on trial-and-error optimization. We introduce a novel centrality measure grounded in the comparison of actual geodesic distances within a network against the straight-line distances defined by an ambient Euclidean space, utilizing the concept of triangle inequality surplus. This metric, termed Gromov centrality, offers a resolution to the challenge of assigning centrality scores to networks with cyclic structures. By focusing on the triangle inequality surplus associated with triples involving a specific node, Gromov centrality offers both a qualitative and a mathematical description, providing an intuitive framework for developing new centrality metrics. In this approach, nodes are evaluated based on their capacity to form long-range shortcuts across the network. Empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness of this metric in identifying key nodes within various network models, including Erdős-Rényi and small-world networks, as well as real-world datasets such as the fruit fly and Arabidopsis networks. Furthermore, we illustrate the metric's utility in a randomized setting through a probabilistic analysis of its performance. Additionally, we propose two variants of Gromov centrality, one of which serves as a graph-theoretic analogue. Finally, we provide a comprehensive benchmark of the metric's behavior under both random and small-world network models. Notably, the analysis reveals that Gromov centrality exhibits the opposite trend compared to degree centrality when identifying the most central nodes in small-world networks. This article introduces the first of three proposed papers detailing an alternative theory of gravity. We propose a new framework built upon a novel application of Newtonian theory, grounded exclusively in a Euclidean reference frame characterized by global rotational symmetry. This fundamental frame is established on a specific moment within a global timeline, which lacks any preferred direction. The temporal evolution of this frame is determined through a step-by-step process, where each step corresponds to an infinitesimal increase in the step number. This number serves as an absolute reference for time across the entire universe. Building upon this structure, we develop an azimuthally symmetrical theory of gravity. This approach yields new equations for calculating gravitational acceleration and the potential associated with a point mass. Consequently, it enables the prediction of the motion of a test particle under the influence of a point mass's gravity. These predictions can be applied directly to celestial bodies, provided their motion aligns with the azimuthal symmetry of the established frame. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that this framework successfully reproduces established experimental results from both Newtonian theory and Special Relativity. Additionally, the Azimuthally Symmetrical Theory offers a method for predicting gravitational acceleration that can operate independently of Special or General Relativity. Such predictions could be validated against existing experimental data, including those from the LIGO observatory. Ultimately, this paper aims to stimulate further discussion and collaboration regarding this alternative gravitational theory, with the potential to generate exciting new research opportunities. The proposed theory is detailed in this initial paper, while its experimental verification will be the focus of the subsequent paper in the series. Second, the reference frame described herein remains valid under conditions where relativistic effects are negligible. This process is applicable to any particle or body, including those exhibiting relativistic motion. Furthermore, we define the concept of a simultaneously structured basis for a collection of matrix pencils and analyze how this property is affected by equivalence between two sets of these pencils. We develop a formalism for T-duality within supergeometry by applying supergroup versions of classfield theory and Langlands duality. This approach yields explicit descriptions of dual twisted tori as quotients of the 'dual' torus regarding their Lie algebras. Additionally, we successfully handle complex and split forms of twisted tori, offering a clear explanation for the rank drop observed in the dual of the Ising-Kazama model. Several examples are provided to illustrate the diversity and richness of these dual twisted tori. Finally, we demonstrate that our method aligns with topological T-duality for R4 twisted tori, specifically in the context of superstring theory. One such example, the four-dimensional super-Weierstrass model, corresponds to a recently discovered T-dual of the K3 superstring. Furthermore, our results offer an explicit construction for a double field theory-consistent toric supergravity on a twisted torus. This finding extends previous work by incorporating a complex structure on the Lie algebra of the twisted torus, which was previously absent. Our work thus provides a comprehensive description of all super-T duality manifolds based on twisted tori with a Lie algebra dimension of 4. Additionally, our findings elucidate the relationship between T duality and super-Lie algebras, revealing that most super-Lie algebras associated with twisted tori are not isomorphic to the direct sum of their bosonic and fermionic subalgebras. Finally, we highlight a novel feature of super-T duality: the existence of discrete parameters in the isomorphism classes of twisted tori that have no counterpart in standard T duality. These parameters correspond to super-Weil vectors in the twisted torus' super-Weil realization, a concept that appears to be new in the literature. This phenomenon is particularly significant for the super-Weierstrass model, where the super-Weil realization of the twisted torus exhibits a nontrivial line bundle. Consequently, this leads to a T duality circle with a nontrivial line bundle, a feature that would be impossible in standard T duality. This outcome is consistent with recent findings regarding T duality circles in toric supergravity models. In 2011, Demaine et al. demonstrated that any n-node graph with an outerplanar minor can be embedded into a treewidth-3 planar graph such that all short edges remain short; however, they noted that an explicit bound for "short" was unavailable. This paper presents an algorithm achieving the opposite of their result: for any integer k, we construct an embedding of a general n-node graph with an outerplanar minor into a metric space with a treewidth-O(k log n) representation, ensuring that edges of length l remain of length l, with the count of edges exceeding length l bounded by O(n log n / l). This approach is adapted to handle weighted graphs and graphs with forbidden minors other than K_{5}, specifically including series-parallel graphs and those excluding an n-node minor. Furthermore, we show that these embeddings can be made additive, meaning edge lengths may be distorted by at most an additive error of 1. We also provide a negative embedding theorem for outerplanar graphs, proving that no family of representations exists where every outerplanar n-node graph with an m-edge subgraph can be embedded isometrically using only those edges. Finally, we conjecture that the logarithmic factors in our main theorems are unnecessary. These findings have significant implications for routing and network design, as they enable the study of minimum-cost embedding problems with quasi-linear running times. Additionally, we propose a conjecture regarding additive embeddings, suggesting that the logarithmic factors in the results of Demaine et al. can be eliminated. We present the most general findings to date regarding the long-term dynamics of smooth, strongly monotonic discrete-time systems defined on compact manifolds. Specifically, we demonstrate that every non-wandering orbit is stable and that all omega-limit sets consist solely of fixed points or stable periodic orbits. These findings represent a substantial extension and simplification of prior research focused on specific dynamic behaviors. Furthermore, we establish that the system possesses a global attractor where the only non-wandering orbits are stable; this result holds significant utility for classifying the global dynamics of such systems and finding applications in solving nonlinear equations. The framework encompasses notable cases, including smooth strongly convex functions and maps exhibiting the one-sided ball property found in optimization and machine learning. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive characterization of the non-wandering set and construct a chain decomposition that fully describes the system's dynamics. Finally, we explore applications to the classification of global behavior in discrete-time dynamical systems and address a specific class of nonlinear equations. This work is a collaborative effort by researchers from various disciplines, offering a unified foundation for mathematical analysis, engineering applications, and machine learning. Engineering contexts are detailed in a companion paper. We have also prepared an extensive tutorial for mathematical applications, which is scheduled for release in the near future. Our motivation stems from the critical need to understand the global behavior of discrete-time dynamical systems, arising from their extensive application across numerous fields. This understanding is essential for developing reliable numerical algorithms with guaranteed convergence to stable fixed points or their approximations. Such guarantees are particularly vital for solving highly nonlinear problems, including those found in machine learning, where the underlying optimization landscapes are often complex and challenging. This research was conducted by a multidisciplinary team of mathematicians, engineers, and machine learning experts, with applications to machine learning detailed in a companion paper. To support the broad audience we aim to reach, we have developed an accompanying video and website. Given the diverse interests of our readership, we have also prepared an extensive tutorial on applications in mathematics and engineering, which will be released soon alongside this work. The concept of discrete-time dynamical systems originated in the 1950s within control theory and has since become fundamental across many scientific disciplines. The variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) serves as a key method for obtaining ground-state energies of quantum many-body systems using near-term noisy quantum hardware. However, its primary reliance on repeated measurements to estimate energy expectation values can be time-consuming. This study introduces a qubit-excitation-driven adaptive VQE that leverages quantum feedback to accelerate convergence during vqe calculations. The algorithm dynamically adjusts circuit parameters through an adaptive process, prioritizing excitation operators with the largest variance in their estimated coefficients. When applied to specific problems, this approach demonstrates rapid convergence to a more accurate ground state utilizing fewer measurement shots. Additionally, it exhibits superior noise resilience compared to the standard vqe, maintaining convergence even under extreme noise conditions. These findings suggest that the method is well-suited for deployment on current noisy quantum devices. Furthermore, the potential of qubit-excitation-driven VQE is illustrated through an application to a small molecular energy problem. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/quantumlib/. Keywords: quantum chemistry, quantum algorithms, quantum excitation operators, quantum feedback. Representational learning focuses on transforming input data into internal representations that are informative, task-relevant, and robust. While generative models can support this process, they frequently fail to achieve task-robust representations because their training depends on random perturbation patterns that conflict with the dynamics of the corruptions they are trained to reverse. This discrepancy creates a fundamental tension between generative and discriminative objectives, which often leads to suboptimal outcomes. To address this, we introduce a novel hybrid approach that leverages the task-supportive capabilities of generative models. Unlike traditional methods, our approach utilizes the trained model to perturb representations with a fixed pattern rather than relying on stochastic data splits. By applying a linear shift to these preprocessed representations, we can recover the original values without needing to learn the reverse process. This technique yields superior results compared to both standard generative and contrastive methods on both empirical and synthetic datasets. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the improvement stems from two factors: first, a change in optimization landscape that reduces the influence of local minima, and second, the utilization of the full information content within representations. This framework is broadly applicable to various generative models, including noise-conditional, contrastive, and diffusion variants. Our code is available at https://github.com/DeepMind/prod. Finally, our findings have significant implications for biological neuroscience, where neurons appear optimized to extract task-relevant information from highly perturbed sensory inputs. This suggests that the trade-off between robustness and accuracy is not an inherent limitation of neural network architectures but can be resolved through appropriate training strategies. We demonstrate that this conclusion holds for a wide range of neural network models. Our source code can be found at https://github.com/DeepMind/prod.
