This study examines the dynamical characteristics of the Iochroma group, a collection of asteroids located near the 3/1 mean motion resonance with Jupiter. We present an analysis of their orbital element distributions, focusing on the resonance parameters of individual asteroids. Our results indicate that the group's orbital elements are not uniformly distributed; instead, they cluster around specific values, revealing substructures that appear to be shaped by the mass of the dominant asteroid, Iochroma. Additionally, we investigate the group's configuration in phase space. By integrating asteroid mass into our dynamical model, we simulate the resonance behavior of Iochroma and compare the outcomes with the observed data. Our findings suggest that the group was captured by the 3/1 mean motion resonance approximately 4 billion years ago, with the disturbances currently observed being primarily driven by the mass of asteroid Iochroma. Furthermore, we explore the potential influence of the Kuiper Belt Object 1998 KF27 on the group, noting that while it may have played a role in their dynamical evolution, it is unlikely to be the main perturber. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of these results for understanding asteroid group formation and evolution. Overall, this work underscores the significance of incorporating asteroid mass into dynamical models when analyzing the behavior of asteroid groups within the solar system. The data and code utilized in this study can be accessed at https://github.com/Sebastian-Beck/3_1-resonance-Asteroids. We establish that the complex projective space functor admits a strong deformation to a projective line functor, which follows from the fact that any representation can be deformation-retracted onto a maximal torus. Additionally, we provide the formula for the complex circle-equivariant K-theory of $CP(V)$, noting that its formal dual serves as the universal $\sigma$-difference cycle. Finally, we derive the formula for the formal deformation of the complex circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology of $CP(V)$ using the representation $V$ and the universal $\sigma$-difference cycle. To achieve this, we introduce the concept of a "rational elliptic cohomology theory," which extends complex oriented elliptic cohomology to any $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra. We demonstrate that a rational elliptic cohomology theory $E$ admits a formal deformation to the rationally completed equivariant K-theory theory $K_G^*[G]$, where $G$ is a complex Lie group. This result serves as the primary instrument for calculating the deformed elliptic cohomology of $CP(V)$. Furthermore, we establish that any equivariant $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra scheme admits a strong deformation to the equivariant affine space of a complex Lie group $G$ with dimension equal to that of the original scheme. Leveraging this, we calculate the equivariant cohomology of $CP(V)$ in any $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra theory. Machine learning has emerged as a highly effective machine-accessible language for modeling the dynamics of physical systems. Nevertheless, current methods often overlook the underlying structure of these systems, such as the conservation laws that emerge from symmetries. This manuscript demonstrates that conservation laws can be derived from the topological structure of data via algebraic topological methods. We introduce a framework for representing data through simplicial sets and define a procedure to identify conservation laws within this representation. Our approach is validated through a standard machine learning regression task involving both synthetic and experimental data. Furthermore, we outline strategies for extending this methodology to broader contexts, suggesting that algebraic topology can serve as a foundational language for machine learning applications in physics. Our research is available at github.com/beyerscher/algebraic-topology-ml. ArXiv link: 2105.04604v1.

This study investigates $CP$-even $J/\psi$ angular distributions for the processes $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi+\eta_c$ and $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi+\chi_{cJ}$ at $\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{3})$. Within the nonrelativistic QCD (NRQCD) factorization framework, we compute the coefficients of the $1-\lambda_{\parallel} - \lambda_{\perp}\cos\theta - \lambda_{\perp}\cos(2\theta)$ angular distribution at next-to-leading order (NLO) in the power expansion, specifically for $10.58 \leq \sqrt{s} \leq 10.62$ GeV. Our findings indicate that the $\cos(2\theta)$ term is suppressed due to the cancellation of the corresponding coefficient, $\lambda_{\perp}$, between the $\eta_c$ and $\chi_{cJ}$ contributions. Additionally, we examine the impact of higher-order corrections on the total cross sections and the $\lambda_{\parallel}$ coefficient, demonstrating that NLO QCD corrections enhance the $J/\psi+\eta_c$ production by approximately 15%. Finally, we compare our predictions with existing experimental data. Based on these results, we conclude that the $\eta_c$ polarization is longitudinal, with $|P_{\eta_c}| \lesssim 0.15$ at $\sqrt{s} = 10.58$ GeV and $|P_{\eta_c}| \lesssim 0.20$ at $\sqrt{s} = 10.62$ GeV. Furthermore, we determine that the ratio of the polarization parameters, $P_{\eta_c}/P_{J/\psi}$, is positive and satisfies $0.01 \lesssim P_{\eta_c}/P_{J/\psi} \lesssim 0.20$ at $\sqrt{s} = 10.6$ GeV. These outcomes offer valuable insights for future experimental investigations. Notably, the observation of the $\cos(2\theta)$ term in $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi+\eta_c$ at the Belle II collider would definitively rule out the NRQCD prediction. Although the secure messaging application Signal employs numerous security mechanisms, it recently introduced a 6-to-20 character PIN as an additional barrier to unauthorized access. This study examines how non-expert, enthusiastic users perceive and understand this PIN, exploring their reasoning through the lenses of security theory and cognitive psychology. The findings reveal that users hold diverse and often flawed beliefs regarding the PIN's security, frequently overlooking specific features such as the strength of uppercase letters. These insights into user cognition have significant implications for both Signal developers and the broader information security community when designing and evaluating security protocols and user education programs. This research is grounded in a survey of 100 Signal enthusiasts, with all participants being active users or those possessing extensive experience with the app. While the sample is not representative of the general population, the depth of their engagement suggests a richer understanding of Signal's security architecture compared to typical users. Consequently, their responses likely reflect a wide spectrum of common opinions, offering valuable context for the development of security features across various applications. The study identifies several key misconceptions, including concerns over memorability, confusion regarding the PIN versus a password, and incorrect assumptions about the meaning of character counts. These concepts are analyzed through the frameworks of perceived usability, perceived security, and cognition. Finally, the paper concludes with recommendations for future work aimed at enhancing both the perceived and actual security and usability of the PIN. This research aligns with the 2nd Call for Papers titled "2022: Security and Privacy Education for Everyone: From IT Professionals to General Public and K-12." This paper is scheduled for presentation at the following conference: Security and Privacy Education for IT Professionals (SPEIT 2022). More information is available at: https://www.speit.org/2022/. The work is grounded in the following survey: https://forms.gle/6555555555555555.

This study introduces an algorithm capable of accurately integrating any function defined over the unit sphere, provided its solar visibility from the sphere's center can be determined. The method's precision is governed by the number of evaluation points an underlying solar Gaussian quadrature scheme generates for that specific sphere. Consequently, spatial regions not illuminated by the sun during a specific integration time are effectively excluded from the algorithm's precise calculation. This approach is particularly well-suited for computing total energy content in planetary or satellite systems, as energy is contingent upon solar orientation. By leveraging pre-existing solar quadrature sets and visibility calculations, the method avoids the need for complex function interpolation. We demonstrate the algorithm's efficacy by precisely and efficiently calculating the total energy of a function across a tetrahedron, a sphere, and a torus. These cases are significant because they represent common boundaries in planetary and space physics models, such as the magnetopause, bow shock, and terminator. For the tetrahedron, the results are benchmarked against both a brute-force method and a prior algorithm, showing that our solution achieves greater accuracy at lower computational costs. For the sphere and torus, we compare our method's accuracy against brute-force outcomes. Furthermore, the technique is broadly applicable to any object where a quadrature scheme exists; for instance, a quadrature scheme for a function on a general ellipsoid can be derived by applying an affine transformation to the spherical quadrature scheme. This capability facilitates precise energy calculations for ellipsoids, which are frequently encountered in various physical models. Finally, we outline several applications, including the precise computation of total energy for a magnetopause, bow shock, and terminator, as well as total energy for a planetary atmosphere and a satellite's power system. These applications are currently under active development. Overall, the proposed algorithm offers a precise and efficient solution for total energy calculations involving solar-weighted functions on diverse shapes. Future enhancements to quadrature schemes and the shapes they support will further improve the algorithm's accuracy and efficiency. The primary objective of this study is to introduce the structure of the generalized Gauss-Newton (gGN) matrix, also known as the diminished, to enable curvature information to be utilized within machine learning frameworks. The gGN matrix represents the most comprehensive expression of curvature, as it fully incorporates the Hessian of the forward operator. This allows for the integration of backward (data) information with the forward (model) description in curvature-based approaches. We demonstrate that established methods, including those based on the Hessian, can be derived from the gGN matrix by applying specific linear transformations to its primary components. Furthermore, we propose a novel application of this matrix within the Hessian-Limited Memory BFGS (LM-BFGS) context. By approximating the inverse of the gGN matrix, we achieve the ability to employ both forward and backward information in curvature-driven learning. Additionally, we introduce a curvature matrix with a reduced structure designed for use with model curvature information. This approach enhances computational efficiency by utilizing model curvature information derived from the Hessian of the forward operator, which may be partially or entirely available. We demonstrate that various existing Hessian-based methods can be recovered using these reduced structures. Finally, we evaluate the proposed methods against standard state-of-the-art Hessian-based techniques on various tomographic and x-ray CT imaging tasks. Our results indicate that the methods grounded in the generalized Gauss-Newton matrix achieve superior performance compared to existing Hessian-based approaches. This study examines how grammatical gender influences word representations in neural language models using English, which is predominantly a gender-transparent language. By employing a cross-conditional conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN) to enforce gender consistency across a dictionary while allowing semantic variability, we observe that the model induces significant shifts in the majority of lexical items. The exceptions are nouns that are either inherently gendered or denote male or female animals. We attribute this finding to human annotators utilizing gendered language as a heuristic to enhance the efficiency of lexical acquisition. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this heuristic is sufficiently effective to enable a transformer model trained on English to learn gender-marked morphologies for a German-like language. This research offers new insights into psycholinguistic theories regarding how humans acquire gender assignment and reveals a functional advantage of grammatical gender in language learning. Additionally, this work holds significant implications for the field of multilingual neural machine translation, which often struggles to accurately transfer gender features. Finally, we provide a Python implementation of the proposed cGAN model. The source code and pre-trained models are accessible at: https://github.com/ashwinbhat/ConditionalGAN. This research was supported by a Google Ph.D. Fellowship. The first author's primary focus is on multilingual neural machine translation, while the second author is primarily interested in natural language generation. Both authors utilize grammar as a lens to explore how computational language models can elucidate the cognitive processes of human language acquisition. We aim to explore these and related questions through a collaboration between a psycholinguist and a computational linguist. This paper serves as a foundational step toward that partnership. We establish conditions on a locally finite field ensuring that specific families of higher-dimensional arithmetic groups, defined over their corresponding finite fields, possess desirable rigidity and finiteness characteristics, such as finiteness signatures, torsion cogrowth, and Laplacian spectral growth. Our analysis reveals that these findings are intrinsically linked to a finiteness condition on the associated Lang parameters. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this condition holds for numerous interesting cases by applying a newly developed charm theorem for reductive groups, which was recently proven by Helminck and the second author. Additionally, we explore an application of our results to the study of monodromy groups arising from p-adic Galois representations attached to Calabi-Yau varieties. In this context, we propose a finiteness condition on Lang parameters that encapsulates the conjecture asserting that Calabi-Yau varieties exhibit finite charm. Finally, we construct examples of reductive groups and reductive pairs that are neither charming nor rigid, thereby highlighting the sharpness of our results. Our approach to proving both the charm theorem and the characterization of reductive groups and pairs relies on the theory of root data. To facilitate this, we introduce a combinatorial framework for examining root data, which we believe will be valuable in broader contexts. We also suggest a conjecture regarding the charm and rigidity of reductive groups and pairs that is grounded in this combinatorial perspective. Through careful examination, we demonstrate that this conjecture accurately characterizes all reductive groups and pairs with finite charm and/or rigidity. We conclude by investigating the relationship between charm and rigidity within the context of reductive groups and pairs. Our investigation yields a new conjecture concerning the charm and rigidity of reductive groups, which we verify for all known reductive groups of rank less than or equal to 4. We also provide a complete characterization of charm and rigidity for reductive groups of rank 5, and for those with rank greater than 5, we prove that they are charming and rigid if and only if they are simply connected and split. Our methods for proving these results also depend on the charm theorem and the combinatorial perspective regarding root data. We further present a conjecture concerning the charm and rigidity of reductive groups, derived from the charm and rigidity of reductive pairs with simply connected semisimple components, which we show is sharp. Object pose estimation is a critical research area that facilitates a wide range of applications, including robotic manipulation and autonomous driving. While most existing methods rely on extensive annotated training data, we introduce a zero-shot class-level approach that requires only a single class description, such as a template image, video, or a set of exemplars. Drawing inspiration from recent class-agnostic instance pose estimation techniques, our framework is built upon a robust and versatile two-stage network architecture, making it compatible with various underlying detectors and pose estimation models. Furthermore, our two-stage design allows for independent optimization of each component, enhancing flexibility and performance. Extensive evaluations on multiple datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed framework. On the challenging NYUv2 dataset, our two versions of the proposed method achieve state-of-the-art zero-shot class-level object pose estimation without employing any complex training strategies. Additionally, our approach outperforms existing methods in few-shot and unsupervised scenarios, validating the strength of our framework across diverse settings. The code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/ChenYixuan0712/ZeroShotPose}. Accurate short-term traffic forecasting is essential for traffic management, planning, and control. However, current deep learning approaches struggle to simultaneously achieve high prediction accuracy and low inference time when handling the high dimensionality and sparsity characteristic of real-world traffic data. To address this, we introduce a system designed to predict traffic flow across the entire road network. This system utilizes a graph convolutional network to perform feature extraction on the traffic state, significantly reducing the input dimension for the subsequent deep learning forecast system. Experimental results indicate that, given sufficient historical data, this system achieves prediction accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art direct forecasting methods. Furthermore, for nodes with extreme traffic conditions, the system produces more accurate predictions than existing methods. Finally, by predicting flow for a subset of nodes rather than the full network, the system achieves an inference time approximately 100 times faster than previous approaches. These findings highlight the critical importance of balancing prediction accuracy with computational efficiency in traffic forecasting. We also present a graph-based interventional model utilizing VACA for variational inference, demonstrating superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods on synthetic tabular data regarding counterfactual prediction accuracy. Real-time analysis of the sky has emerged as a promising field within radio astronomy. The Irish LOFAR station, being the most recent real-time surveying radio telescope, has integrated a new real-time backend known as REALTA. This system processes data from 16 dual-polarization dipoles within a compact package. This work details the initial results from the REALTA real-time transient surveying service, which monitors the sky and alerts users when new transients appear. We have identified several new transients, including Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs), which will be analyzed using LOFAR high-resolution imaging. Additionally, we have observed new bursts from Sgr A*, the Crab Nebula, and Cygnus X-1, as well as new outbursts from known radio stars. The system also detected a new radio source in the constellation Auriga, which was subsequently tracked and confirmed as a new blazar. Furthermore, REALTA's real-time spectral monitoring has enabled the study of new radio bursts from Jupiter and the Sun. Driven by the twin objectives of intelligent design and superior functionality, metaphotonics has emerged as a promising methodology for crafting superior optical components and systems. This approach integrates the concepts of metaphotonic band gaps and topology into the broader fields of photonics and optoelectronics. This review examines recent advancements in metaphotonics, offering a perspective on the current state of the field and its future trajectory. It begins by outlining fundamental concepts and theoretical frameworks for metaphotonics, followed by an analysis of recent progress in metaphotonics devices and systems, an evaluation of existing challenges, and a proposal for future research directions. Specifically, the report addresses intelligent design, in-situ tuning, the interplay between metaphotonic band gaps and topology, the one-photon-energy regime, and the convergence of metaphotonics with quantum physics. Ultimately, we contend that metaphotonics holds the potential to revolutionize the fields of sensing, communication, and quantum information processing. Furthermore, we argue that machine learning and artificial intelligence are indispensable for designing practical metaphotonics systems, capable of overcoming the inherent challenges posed by the weak light-matter interaction in these structures. By synthesizing these two disciplines, we anticipate a significant leap forward in the development of superior optoelectronic technologies. This study examines a frequency-regulation model incorporating elastic demand to determine its linear stability region within parameter space. By integrating these findings with results from prior research on parallel-compensation and vertical-damping models, we establish a framework for analyzing key electrical network parameters. Specifically, we address the network size required to achieve positive frequency regulation—a condition that is impossible in small networks but achievable in sufficiently large ones. Furthermore, we assess how effective frequency regulation, both locally and globally, is in mitigating voltage instability. Our study also explores the network size needed to ensure that linearly stable network states remain close to their equilibrium points in network space. Finally, based on our linear stability analysis, we identify the set of symmetric parameter profiles in the complex plane that enable symmetric linear stability regions in the positive half-space of parameter space. These profiles include those associated with constant network parameters, constant admittances, and constant impedances, with the latter two being particularly effective at dampening voltage fluctuations. Additionally, the model demonstrates that the network size required for linear stability is substantially smaller than that needed for global stability. Finally, we examine how the network size necessary for linear stability varies as parameters approach the boundaries of the parameter space, thereby influencing the size of the linear stability region. In this final investigation, we observe that the network size required for linear stability is highly sensitive to parameters in the vicinity of the boundary, yet this sensitivity diminishes as parameters move further from the boundary into the parameter space. Consequently, the network size needed for linear stability is significantly smaller than that required for global stability, as established in our earlier examination of how specific models achieve global stability. This conclusion is supported by numerical simulations. Overall, the network size required to achieve frequency regulation as described in this paper is notably smaller than that needed for successful frequency regulation to stabilize voltage behavior. This implies that while large networks are essential for achieving frequency regulation that stabilizes voltage, they are not strictly necessary for achieving the same outcome. In this sense, frequency regulation can be realized in smaller networks, thereby enhancing the overall efficiency of the power system. Finally, our findings regarding the relationship between network size and stability align with established results in the literature. Specifically, the need for a large network to achieve frequency regulation is consistent with the observation that large networks exhibit natural oscillatory behavior, whereas small networks tend to converge to a steady state. Additionally, our results corroborate the understanding that frequency regulation is essential for stabilizing voltage in large networks, while sufficiently damped load dynamics can stabilize voltage in small networks. Cyber-physical networks are characterized by the intricate interconnections of diverse, heterogeneous network technologies. As these networks grow in size and intricacy, they increasingly incorporate intelligent devices and technologies, such as software-defined networking and the Internet of Things. This complexity introduces significant challenges regarding network management, control, and security. Consequently, there is a pressing need for innovative approaches to enhance the robustness and resilience of cyber-physical networks. This thesis explores the application of machine learning and data analytics to the management and control of these systems. Specifically, it develops machine learning-based data analytics methods to optimize network resource allocation and facilitate real-time decision-making. Furthermore, these analytics techniques are utilized to strengthen the robustness of cyber-physical networks against both natural and malicious threats. The research also investigates data privacy within these environments, aiming to create secure and efficient resource allocation strategies. Additionally, the thesis addresses the challenges posed by the interconnection of multiple cyber-physical networks, utilizing machine learning-based data analytics to achieve near-optimal performance in multi-network resource allocation. Finally, the thesis explores the integration of data analytics with Software-Defined Networking, leveraging SDN's centralized control and flexible resource management capabilities to deliver real-time, data-driven solutions for cyber-physical network enhancement. This work offers a novel methodology for improving cyber-physical networks through machine learning and data analytics. Numerical simulations and experimental evaluations demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approaches, outperforming existing methods and benchmarks. Ultimately, this research provides a new pathway for the future improvement of cyber-physical networks. Keywords: Cyber-physical networks, multi-network, machine learning, data analytics, SDN.

This study introduces MAPPIES, an extension of the prior Monte-Carlo code MAPPIES I, specifically designed to model the ultraviolet (UV) and soft X-ray excesses observed in blazar spectra. While the previous work detailed the code's functionality, this paper applies those capabilities to interpret the radiation from two specific blazars, 3C 273 and M87* (observed by the Event Horizon Telescope). We employ MAPPIES to simulate emission arising from electrons that have been inverse Compton scattered by an external photon field, alongside standard synchrotron and Compton scattering processes. The results indicate that these externally Comptonized (EC) electrons generate distinct spectral features: a UV excess when scattering low-energy photons and a soft X-ray excess (SXR) when scattering higher-energy photons. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a single population of EC-scattering electrons can simultaneously produce both the UV and SXR surpluses. Finally, we explore how variations in the characteristics of the external photon field can account for the diverse spectral signatures seen in these sources. These findings suggest that astrophysical mechanisms capable of generating external photon fields with the requisite properties may be essential for a comprehensive understanding of the UV and SXR surpluses found in blazar spectra. Additionally, we outline the potential for MAPPIES to assist in analyzing recent black hole imaging data from the Event Horizon Telescope. Ultimately, this work establishes a foundation for future investigations into the origins of the UV and SXR surpluses in active galactic nuclei spectra. The MAPPIES code is publicly accessible at http://www.astro.ubc.ca/~kristian/Mappies.html. A general theoretical framework for analytically extending observations onto a complex surface into the surrounding volume is developed, focusing on the extension along the normal direction. A key result expresses the extended field through a Taylor series based on the normal curvature of the observation surface. For the physically significant scenario involving harmonic functions, the series simplifies to an exponential form, characterized by the norm of the gradient of the observed data on the surface and subsequently linked to data covariance. This development introduces a novel concept of local uncertainty for the extended field, defined by the variation in the exponential term and interpreted as normal depth uncertainty. The proposed solution is evaluated using synthetic data, demonstrating its effectiveness over both flat and curved reference surfaces. Finally, the method is applied to a real-world dataset consisting of 12,000 points distributed across a mountainous region. In this case, the analysis confirms that the uncertainty of the extended field increases consistently with the distance separating the observation and extension surfaces. Furthermore, a spatial uncertainty metric is calculated for mountainous zones, aiding in the identification of areas suitable for modeling. This approach is particularly valuable for geostatistical methods, where it can serve to detect regions where spatial interpolation yields reliable results. The paper concludes by outlining the method's limitations and suggesting potential avenues for future research. We introduce a framework for digitally assessing symmetric pure states by digitally modeling their associated Bochner polynomial (BP). In this approach, real parameters are approximated by a finite set of discrete values, with digital operations substituting arithmetic operations within a bounded relative error. Consequently, the relative error of a digital operation corresponds to the maximum error of a finite approximation, while the relative error of a digital operation's output is represented by the error of its infinite equivalent. The precision of these approximations is contingent upon the available memory capacity. We establish the conditions under which a symmetric pure state can be effectively and efficiently digitized, specifically regarding the conditions allowing the representation of a one-qubit state via a two-level subspace. Furthermore, we demonstrate that any symmetric pure state can be converted into a two-level symmetric pure state through a symmetric generalized Pauli rotation around an axis aligned with the Sx, Sy, or Sx components. Finally, utilizing the properties of digital representations, we derive methods for digitally determining the eigenvalues and eigenstates of the associated SU(2) generators. As an application, we show that the Rabi frequency can be calculated from the Rabi model's symmetric pure state using a specific recursive formula derived from the associated two-level symmetric pure state. Furthermore, the initial condition for a Schrödinger equation can be determined from its solution at any given time by employing the corresponding two-level subspace and a symmetric generalized Pauli rotation. Finally, we illustrate that the proposed method for digitizing symmetric pure states is both effective and efficient. Our findings indicate that the efficiency of this method depends on the available memory, which is defined as the minimum number of discrete values required to represent the BP. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first work to address the problem of digitizing symmetric pure states. Additionally, the theoretical and experimental results presented in this study are expected to contribute to the development of new methods for quantum information processing. **Keywords:** symmetric pure state, symmetric generalized Pauli rotation, Rabi model, Schrodinger equation, eigenvalues, eigenstates, error, efficiency, effectiveness, memory. **AMS Subject Classification:** 81Q30, 81Q35, 81Q99, 94A12, 94A17. **MSC Subject:** 81Q30, 81Q35, 81Q99, 94A12, 94A17. **DOI:** 10.1

Baryon generation through the quantized fragmentation of a helical QCD filament is investigated by modeling the filament as an extended object featuring a quantized core. Fragmentation, driven by a quasi-helicoidal expansion, is simulated using a tension that depends on the radius. The simulation results indicate that the transverse size of the final baryon increases with higher tension values. Furthermore, the scenario successfully accounts for the experimentally observed suppression of baryon production relative to meson production. Additionally, the created baryon exhibits significant dependence on the fragmentation geometry, with its momentum aligning with the helicity of the filament. These findings suggest that the fragmentation process may be responsible for the experimentally observed baryon chemistries. Consequently, this study provides the first numerical evidence supporting the three-dimensional filament model and establishes a foundation for future research into baryon formation. New avenues for investigating filament properties are also proposed. This work was conducted in collaboration with R. L. Jaffe, A. Kovner, and J. Thacker. J. A. Solar oscillations are influenced by various phenomena, including large-scale flows, granulation, and magnetic structures. This study examines the impact of magnetic structures on global helioseismic travel-time measurements used to detect solar north-south flows. We developed a theoretical model to estimate the contribution of movements around active regions to travel-time perturbations. Our results indicate that these perturbations are substantial, reaching approximately 10 m/s at the solar surface. Furthermore, we demonstrate that active regions can generate a net signal resembling a solar north-south flow. Consequently, it is crucial to quantify the influence of active regions when interpreting global helioseismic travel-time data. We conclude that to accurately interpret global travel times, one must either correct the data for active region effects or employ a physical model capable of accounting for them. Additionally, we illustrate how uncorrected global travel times can be utilized to estimate the surface solar north-south flow. Finally, we discuss how this estimated flow can inform the construction of a solar rotation model that includes a north-south component. This approach offers a potential solution to the long-standing "bipolar paradox," which questions the existence of the observed solar north-south flow. To validate this interpretation, we will apply the proposed method to historical sunspot records and corresponding global travel-time measurements. This analysis aims to establish a reliable empirical relationship between sunspot activity and the observed solar north-south flow. Ultimately, this could provide a robust empirical basis for the complex physical models required to explain the solar global north-south flow. The analysis is currently in progress. The primary outcome of this work is a more comprehensive understanding of the physical mechanisms driving the solar global north-south flow. Additionally, the research has yielded a new theoretical framework for interpreting global helioseismic travel-time measurements in the presence of active regions. Finally, the study has established a new method for deriving the solar global north-south flow from global travel-time measurements corrected for active region contributions. By applying this method to historical data, we aim to generate a new, empirically validated time series of the solar global north-south flow. This will serve as a valuable reference for physical models attempting to explain the origin of the solar global north-south flow. In summary, this work represents a significant step toward a more complete understanding of the physical processes governing the solar global north-south flow. This study presents and evaluates the measurement error and coverage results of five estimation techniques—direct, raking, Bayesian kernel average, Bayesian minimum mean square error, and predictive mean estimation—alongside two integrated approaches (Bayesian and deep learning) utilizing spatio-temporal models. These methods were employed to generate monthly estimates of maternal, neonatal, and child mortality rates for Ethiopia's 520 zones between 2016 and 2019. The analysis leveraged 2016 census data, including population counts, sex ratios, urbanization levels, and education statistics, alongside 2016–2019 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) data. The datasets were fused via a Bayesian framework, with deep learning serving as an alternative to traditional spatio-temporal models. The resulting small-area estimates were subsequently compared against direct, raking, and Bayesian kernel smoothing techniques. Findings indicate that direct estimation suffered from high coverage errors (exceeding 100%) and was ineffective for small zones. Raking produced biased results, while Bayesian kernel smoothing demonstrated poor coverage in certain zones. In contrast, both the Bayesian and deep learning methods yielded low, comparable coverage errors. However, the deep learning approach provided superior coverage for zones lacking survey representation, making it the most suitable method for Ethiopia's context. Coverage errors ranged from 17% to 70%, while the mean absolute percentage error for the integrated methods was 1.7%. The research concludes that integrating survey and small-area data through a Bayesian framework or deep learning offers a promising strategy for small-area estimation in low- and middle-income countries. Additionally, the study provides open-source code for the analyzed methods, which can be accessed via a GitHub repository. Keywords: Small-area estimation, Maternal mortality, Child mortality, Low and middle income countries, Bayesian estimation, Deep learning.

In prior work [1], we demonstrated that after $N$ repetitions of the quantum version of "How much is a million?" [2], the probability $p_N$ of a player winning exceeds that of a classical player by an amount $\delta p_N \sim 0.003/N$. This quantum advantage stems from providing players with quantum copies of the input state, enabling the use of quantum cloning strategies. Building on this, we propose a new gambling game with continuous variables that offers an analogous quantum reward. In this framework, players receive a continuous-variable quantum state $\rho_x$ where the x-coordinate is encrypted using a one-time pad based on a random key $k$. The goal is to determine the key $k$. The game is played repeatedly with different inputs, and the players' measurements provide an a-priori probability $p_k$ for each potential key. The quantum advantage arises because, for continuous variables, optimal cloning is possible, allowing players to extract all relevant information from $\rho_x$. Consequently, the sum of the classical errors $\Delta_{cl}$ is greater than the sum of quantum errors $\Delta_{Q}$ by a factor of $N$, i.e., $\Delta_{cl} - \Delta_{Q} \sim 0.003 N$. Furthermore, while classical players can only determine the probability $p_k$, quantum players can implement a strategy that allows them to identify the key $k$ with certainty. This result indicates that quantum cloning is essential for achieving optimal performance in continuous-variable gambling games. Finally, the game's connection to the "Quantum Reverse Data Processing Inequality" [3] is explored. By providing explicit examples, we demonstrate that the inequality can be saturated in the quantum domain. This is achieved by selecting a probability distribution $p_k$ and a quantum cloning channel that maps the input state to an optimal cloned state $\rho_x'$ where $x = k \oplus k'$. In this scenario, the output probability distribution $p'_k$ becomes a delta function centered at $k$, thereby saturating the inequality. We also examine the effects of noise on the gambling advantage. For the discrete case, we show that as long as the noise remains below the threshold of a depolarizing channel, the quantum advantage is maintained. In the continuous variable domain, we analyze the impact of loss and find that the quantum advantage persists as long as the loss rate does not exceed the entanglement distillation threshold of the continuous variable state used in the game.

The rare flavor-changing neutral current transition $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ has been investigated using LHCb data collected at a hadronic center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 7$ TeV. An upper limit on the branching ratio of $\mathbf{B(\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-) < 5.2 \times 10^{-9}}$ was established within the combined mass window of $0.1 < q^2 < 0.99$ GeV$^2$. This result is consistent with Standard Model predictions and aligns with the previously reported constraint derived from the rare hyperon decay $\Lambda \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$. Furthermore, the study examines the sensitivity of the LHCb experiment to New Physics through this channel. Any observed signal would provide a stringent test of the Standard Model and could potentially uncover new physics effects in flavor-changing neutral current processes. Additionally, the analysis explores the sensitivity of this mode to New Physics within the context of an effective weak Hamiltonian. Finally, the work investigates potential new physics contributions to this rare process via a flavor-changing $Z'$ boson and in a model incorporating $\mu$-$\tau$ nonuniversality. These scenarios are benchmarked against LHCb bounds on other rare hyperon decays, including $\Lambda \to p e^+ e^-$, $\Lambda \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$, and $\Sigma^- \to n \mu^+ \mu^-$. Notably, these new physics models are capable of simultaneously explaining the recently observed anomalies in $R_{K^{(*)}}$ and $a_{\mu}$. This demonstrates that the LHCb bound on $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ will play a crucial role in testing New Physics scenarios that have recently been proposed to account for the observed anomalies in $R_{K^{(*)}}$ and the muon magnetic anomaly. Finally, the LHCb bound on $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ is compared with the expected sensitivity of the LHCb experiment in the near future and with the anticipated bounds from the Belle II experiment. The future LHCb and Belle II experiments are expected to provide stringent tests of New Physics in flavor-changing neutral current processes, specifically $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$,

We present findings from a novel simulation tracking the evolution of a pre-stellar core from its initial state to the formation of a protostar accompanied by a rotating protoplanetary disk. These initial conditions were derived from observations of real cores within the Taurus star-forming region. Our results indicate that the initial cloud collapse yields a final configuration featuring a central protostar, a circumstellar disk, and a large mass reservoir in the outer disk region. The simulation successfully reproduces key observed characteristics of real disks, including their mass, size, and temperature profiles. Furthermore, the model can account for a specific population of disks that are notably massive and large. This significant outer mass reservoir represents a critical opportunity for planet formation. Additionally, we demonstrate that disk mass and radius are strongly correlated with the initial mass of the pre-stellar core, whereas there is no such correlation observed for disk size or temperature. Our initial analysis of this simulation suggests that a substantial fraction of the mass originally present in the pre-stellar core may be retained within the disk. This implies that disks can achieve masses far exceeding typical values, potentially reaching up to 100 Jupiter masses. Such massive disks could explain the existence of very massive planets and brown dwarfs, as well as the recently identified substellar companions orbiting at large distances from their host stars. Finally, our initial examination of the simulated system indicates that planet formation may have commenced at very early stages. This conclusion is supported by the presence of a significant mass of gas in the inner disk region, which could have condensed into a central object, and by the detection of a shock wave originating from the inner disk and propagating outward. These initial observations suggest that the system may have already begun forming a central object within its disk. Overall, our results indicate that the initial mass of a pre-stellar core is a primary factor in determining the final mass of the circumstellar disk. Consequently, this initial cloud mass serves as a key predictor for the potential of a star to host a massive disk capable of forming massive planets or even brown dwarfs. This model provides a robust explanation for the presence of massive disks in star-forming regions and offers a viable mechanism for the creation of massive planets and brown dwarfs. By establishing a link between the initial cloud mass and the properties of the resulting disk, this framework offers a novel perspective on the relationship between the mass of a pre-stellar core and the mass of its associated disk. Atmospheric correction is a critical component of remote sensing, yet its accuracy relies heavily on the precision of the atmospheric models employed. This study presents a comprehensive at-sensor validation of three prominent models: MODTRAN, 6S, and 6SV. We conducted at-sensor observations of atmospheric variability using the Visible and Infrared Satellite Sensor (VISSR) aboard the NOAA-15 satellite, covering the 0.5 to 5.0 $\mu$m range. Our results indicate that MODTRAN and 6S yield consistent outcomes, demonstrating a strong correlation with at-sensor data. Conversely, significant discrepancies were found in the 6SV model, which appears to be influenced by the spectral response function (RSF) of the VISSR sensor. Furthermore, the at-sensor validation of MODTRAN and 6S reveals a strong correlation between modeled and observed at-sensor data. Finally, we examine the impacts of key atmospheric parameters on these models. Overall, this validation study provides a robust foundation for the subsequent analysis of atmospheric parameters. Additionally, we outline a future approach for MODTRAN that incorporates an RSF convolution process to enhance the accuracy of at-sensor simulations. These methods are also applicable to other at-sensor observations. Finally, we discuss the necessity of conducting at-sensor validations using multiple sensors with varying RSFs to further refine these models. This research is particularly relevant for 6SV, as it addresses the previously identified divergence between 6SV and MODTRAN outputs. This study addresses the challenge of modeling temporal series across multiple time periods within a multi-period framework. The objective is to generate predictions for each period using data from the current period and previous ones. To achieve this, the research introduces a novel Bayesian formulation of a multi-period time series model, integrating a dynamic model with a Gaussian process to estimate temporal series for various periods. This approach enables the prediction of the current period based on historical data. To manage the resulting high-dimensional parameter space and avoid overfitting, an sparsity-inducing prior is applied to the Bayesian variational inference process. The efficacy of the proposed method is validated through numerical experiments, with a specific focus on predicting daily, weekly, and monthly temperatures. The results demonstrate that the method outperforms existing approaches in terms of prediction accuracy. Furthermore, the paper provides a comprehensive review of temporal series modeling, and the code is made available on GitHub. By Gwanghyun Lee, Seungryul Kim, and Donghoon Lee.

Federated learning (FL) represents a distributed approach to training machine learning models, where the training dataset is partitioned across multiple clients, and the model is subsequently refined through the aggregation of individual client updates. Despite the privacy and security advantages of FL, the emergence of differential privacy (DP) within this framework has raised significant concerns regarding model utility. This study examines the impact of various noise injection techniques employed in DP-FL, demonstrating how varying client participation rates and data sample sizes influence the trade-off between privacy and performance. Our findings indicate that smaller client groups yield results more comparable to central server training, whereas larger groups produce models with performance more akin to a global server. Furthermore, we validate the efficacy of DP-FL across a diverse range of real-world datasets. Finally, by applying DP-FL to multi-task learning scenarios, we illustrate that this method can simultaneously enhance both privacy and model performance. This paper offers the most comprehensive analysis to date on how differential privacy influences the efficacy of federated learning systems. We demonstrate that successful $b-\tau$ unification can be achieved through an inverse seesaw mechanism involving three right-handed neutrinos, three singlet superfields, and a specific charge assignment. Additionally, we investigate the $X$ gauge boson as a viable dark matter candidate, showing that it can account for the dark matter within this framework. Finally, we project that upcoming collider experiments will be able to probe the parameter space of $X$ gauge boson dark matter up to a mass of approximately 2.5 TeV. Our analysis indicates that the $X$ gauge boson dark matter can comprise at most 10% of the total dark matter content, with the remainder attributed to a stable right-handed sneutrino. This paper introduces a new disruption-aware unsupervised learning approach to optimize throughput in wireless networks assisted by intelligent reflecting surface (IRS). We develop a general throughputs-oriented wireless charged network (WTWCN) model that incorporates disruption, network topology, and IRS deployment. Based on this WTWCN framework, we propose a novel unsupervised learning technique named Clustering and Rate Adaptation (CARA). We provide a detailed description of the CARA method and prove the convergence of its underlying iterative process. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed CARA scheme achieves significant throughput improvements compared to existing approaches in the network. Furthermore, we analyze the CARA scheme's performance characteristics, revealing its ability to enhance throughput substantially, particularly in large-scale networks. Additionally, we evaluate the CARA scheme's robustness against disruption probability, showing that it maintains high throughput even under severe disruption conditions. Finally, the CARA scheme is shown to be computationally efficient, making it well-suited for practical implementation. Overall, the CARA scheme represents a promising solution for future wireless charged networks. Additionally, the paper provides a comprehensive review of recent research on IRS-assisted wireless charging networks. Finally, the work aims to inspire further investigation into disruption-aware unsupervised learning for optimizing the throughput of generic WTWCNs. Keywords: Intelligent reflecting surface (IRS), wireless charged network, disruption, Clustering and Rate Adaptation (CARA), unsupervised learning. Throughput optimization.

We introduce a new learning-based control framework designed for systems with limited data, particularly when only partial state information is available. This approach utilizes data from an unlearned system that shares similarities with the target system through the learning process. By integrating model predictive control (MPC) with reinforcement learning (RL), our method employs an MPC controller to regulate the learning system while an RL agent concurrently refines its policy. Crucially, the MPC optimization problem incorporates an explicit penalty term that integrates information from the secondary learning system, enabling the primary system to replicate the secondary system's behavior despite missing state variables. We demonstrate this proposed Data-driven control with Limited information and Side information (DLS) approach on two case studies: a quadrotor lacking depth camera data and a quadrotor-swimmer hybrid system. Simulation results indicate that the proposed method achieves superior performance compared to standard MPC and model-based RL techniques. Furthermore, this method holds significant potential for performance enhancement in various other applications. Extending recent research on learning control for under-actuated systems, we show that the DLS method can achieve high-performance control using substantially less data than traditional approaches. This is particularly advantageous for expensive-to-operate systems, such as quadrotors or quadrotor-robot configurations, where data collection is costly. Additionally, we highlight that the DLS approach offers a more data-efficient alternative for model-free control in complex systems, such as quadrotor-swimmer setups. This conclusion is supported by experiments conducted on a real-world system featuring a quadrotor and a soft robot fish. We present and experimentally validate a dual-field quantum key distribution (QKD) scheme that eliminates the need for phase stabilization during key generation. By employing continuous-wave light sources, this approach compels users to actively maintain only the average power and frequency, greatly simplifying system operations. We implemented a 100-metre dual-field QKD setup utilizing a modified BB84 protocol, transmitting one signal field through an optical fiber and another through an adjustable attenuator. Under ambient conditions, the system achieved a raw key rate of 1.2 kbps at distances up to 100 m, with a secret key rate of 1.0 kbps at 200 m. We analyzed the impact of various attack methods, demonstrating resistance to phase attacks within 100 m and without phase stabilization beyond that range. This research paves the way for cost-effective, secure short-range wireless communication. Furthermore, we outline the essential requirements for adapting dual-field QKD to optical communication, specifically for enabling secure data transmission in low-earth orbit between satellites. Additionally, we discuss how recent advancements in quantum repeaters could facilitate wider coverage. Most current lexicon-based object detection methods depend on a predefined lexicon, restricting their application to scenarios where class labels are fixed and known in advance. In contrast, we tackle open lexicon object detection, aiming to identify classes using an open-ended lexicon that can introduce new class names during training. Our method significantly enhances the robustness of vision-langauge models in real-world zero-shot detection tasks, such as identifying drug molecules in microscopy images or recognizing various types of asteroids in telescope captures. We analyzed the distribution of ionized, atomic, and photodissociation region (PDR) gases surrounding the S1 cluster in the Rho Ophiuchus star-forming region, which contains approximately 1000 stars with a total luminosity of about $10^4 L_{\odot}$. This paper offers a comprehensive survey of recent research utilizing transformers within computer vision, serving as an extensive resource for current developments and trends in the field. It outlines key concepts and core components relevant to transformer-based vision applications, while also addressing data requirements and evaluation metrics. Furthermore, the study identifies significant challenges and future directions, with a particular emphasis on 3D vision. Finally, it provides a resource list and code repositories to facilitate quick access to prominent vision frameworks and datasets. Given the vast and rapidly expanding landscape of transformer-based vision research, the authors aim to contribute to the community by delivering a thorough and well-organized review. Additionally, the paper is available as an accessible document at the following link: https://transformers-insight.github.io/. Keywords: Survey, Review, Deep Learning, Computer Vision, Transformer.

This paper introduces a new class of factor models featuring time-varying factor loadings to forecast mortality rates. While loadings are unobserved, their time-varying nature is driven by a low-dimensional dynamic process. The study applies this framework exclusively to male death rates, as historical data indicates a stronger link between male mortality and the business cycle compared to females. Empirical results demonstrate that this proposed model outperforms the standard Li model and the factor-based model by Crawford and Skoog (2013) in predicting short-term mortality. Furthermore, a simulation study confirms that the potential gains from time-varying factor loadings remain consistent even in shorter datasets. These methodological advancements are essential for enhancing mortality prediction, particularly when data is limited. Additionally, the paper provides a comprehensive guide for implementing the Li model with time-varying factor loadings using R. Finally, we outline several promising avenues for future research.

To streamline the time-consuming neural architecture search (NAS) process, researchers have explored sharing knowledge across multiple architectures to design a final, high-performance model. This shared knowledge encompasses the architecture search space, optimization method, and often a shared optimization state. While this approach reduces the computational burden, it introduces the challenge of interference, where one architecture may negatively impact the learning of another. We present empirical evidence of this interference within a specific NAS framework: Evolutionary Architecture Search (EAS). Our analysis demonstrates that interference is highly dependent on the search space and can be significantly mitigated by utilizing non-overlapping search spaces. We conducted an empirical study to validate this solution, confirming that it effectively reduces interference without compromising performance. Furthermore, we examined an application of this strategy for multi-task learning, showing that it achieves the same performance while substantially lowering training costs. This article introduces the theft package, which enables users to inspect various characteristics of a time series, such as periodicity, seasonality, and trends. It also provides utilities for visualizing, comparing, and simulating these series. While primarily designed for univariate and real-valued discrete-time data, the package is extensible to other data types. We outline the package's architecture and core capabilities, with a strong emphasis on integration with the R timeseries4vis extension packages (specifically within the t4v namespace). This approach facilitates enhanced visualization features, including interactive and animated time series visualizations. The proposed methodology complements existing techniques; while methods like those in the stisim and stisimr packages focus on generating synthetic series from statistical distributions, theft offers an examination focused on descriptive statistics. Furthermore, unlike the method comparison tool in the methodComparison package, theft provides a framework for both visual and programmatic (via reports) analysis. The article demonstrates these features through applications to both synthetic and real-world datasets. Ultimately, theft serves as a valuable resource for exploratory data analysis, feature selection, and understanding the properties of time series data. In an open, time-reversal invariant scattering system, energy absorption reaches a maximum when at least one initial channel is fully populated and all other channels are empty. This study examines how energy absorption varies across all possible superpositions of incoming channels by utilizing scattering matrix sum rules. For the first time, we present a comprehensive set of findings that connect the energy dependence of absorption to that of reflection. Furthermore, in the regime of near-maximal absorption, these sum rules can be expressed through integrals of universal functions dependent solely on the phase matrix of the S matrix. These functions exhibit distinct behaviors for low and high energies, offering new perspectives on the quantum chaos of absorbing open systems. Finally, in the mean-field context, these results are compared against classical trajectories. In this classical limit, all sum rules are satisfied, yielding simple expressions for absorption that depend only on reflection. Specifically, at high energies, absorption is governed by the transmission coefficient, which is determined by the phase of the classical trajectory. These findings are supported by numerical calculations. These results may find applications in analyzing energy absorption in absorbing chaotic billiards, as well as in nuclear and astrophysical reactions. Additionally, they provide a foundation for future investigations into energy-dependent measures of scattering matrix complexity. In the realm of quantum information, this includes the analysis of initial state sensitivity to noise in absorbing open systems. Finally, these findings contribute to the broader field of sum rules in open quantum systems. This contribution is particularly relevant for investigating non-Hermitian random matrix ensembles, where sum rules are derived by extending the standard GOE sum rules to include absorption. The validity of these extended sum rules is confirmed by comparing numerical findings with those derived from random scattering trajectories. These extended sum rules are also applicable to quantum systems with absorption. Finally, numerical results demonstrate that absorption is maximized when all incoming channels are equally populated, contrary to the equipartition theorem observed in elastic scattering. We present a comprehensive framework for marketing new lottery games, where potential buyers must decide whether to purchase a ticket and, if so, which one. The Lottery Commission aims to sell a specific volume of tickets while avoiding an excessive number of major jackpot winners. We model the anticipated worth of a new lottery game by integrating the assessments of existing games, where each is characterized by a set of parameters derived from the frequency of major and minor prize wins. Consequently, the decision to buy a new ticket is contingent upon the specific ticket details, the purchase volume, and the outcomes of previous draws. Our proposed framework is applied to the Canadian Lotto 6/49, demonstrating that the optimal purchase volume significantly impacts the winning distribution. Furthermore, our analysis of the post-purchase draw reveals that the new winning distribution is often more favorable than before, leading to the counterintuitive finding that new tickets can enhance a lottery's appeal. Finally, we examine the validity of the commonly held belief that "numbers are due" to win.

The decision to invest in a lottery ticket is a daily choice faced by millions, yet the value of that investment remains ambiguous. This determination depends on individual risk tolerance, the allure of a jackpot, and the value of entertainment. While the probability of winning a jackpot is extremely low, the anticipation of a win is more valuable. This insight has led to the creation of new "value-added" lotteries that allow players to influence the draw to increase the likelihood of winning. This decision-making process relies on the perceived value of the new lottery ticket. However, the true value of a lottery ticket remains a subject of debate.

The objective of this study is to develop a framework for valuing new lottery tickets. To achieve this, we analyze the characteristics of new tickets and the preferences of buyers. We demonstrate that the anticipation of winning is influenced by the characteristics of existing lottery tickets. To capture player preferences, we introduce a new parameter called the "expected worth" of a lottery ticket. This metric is defined as the sum of the expected monetary value and the expected entertainment value. We show that the value of a new lottery ticket is a function of these intrinsic and extrinsic factors.

We have determined the unusual scaling dimension for the $\phi^Q$ operator within the $O(N)$ symmetric model up to order $1/L^4$, utilizing the expansion in inverse even powers of $L = \sqrt{Q(N-2)}$. This expansion approach is detailed for the first time in the context of the $\epsilon$ expansion. Using this refined unusual dimension, we reevaluated the transition from the unusual fixed point governed by the $\phi^4$ operator to the standard Wilson-Fisher fixed point in the $O(N)$ model, as well as in the $O(4l-2)$ symmetric model for $l=1, 2, 3$, which describes the large-$l$ limit of the $4l+1$ dimensional Wilson-Fisher critical point. Furthermore, we examined the validity of the expansion method in the odd-$N$ Heisenberg model and the nonlinear $\sigma$ model. Our findings indicate that the calculated unusual dimension aligns well with results derived from the method of successive approximations and the functional renormalization group. Additionally, the derived dependence of the transition from the unusual fixed point to the Wilson-Fisher fixed point on $Q$, $N$, and $l$ appears consistent with the anticipated smooth transition of the nonlinear $\sigma$ model's critical point from the Wilson-Fisher fixed point to the unusual fixed point characterized by the $\phi^4$ operator. Finally, our analysis confirms that the transition point between these two phases in the nonlinear $\sigma$ model corresponds to $Q=1$. Specifically, the $Q=1$ nonlinear $\sigma$ model exhibits a continuous spectrum of excitations and a critical point that coincides with the Wilson-Fisher fixed point in the three-dimensional $O(2)$ symmetric model. This conclusion is also supported by the observation that the unusual fixed point in the $O(2)$ Wilson-Fisher critical point becomes unstable in the $Q$ direction. Consequently, the $Q=1$ nonlinear $\sigma$ model lacks a distinct fixed point in the renormalization group flow, aside from the Wilson-Fisher fixed point. In this scenario, the critical point is identified as the Wilson-Fisher fixed point, and the critical exponents are derived from the eigenvalues of the linearized renormalization group equations at that point. Notably, the expansion in inverse powers of $Q$ proves to be more effective for the $O(2)$ nonlinear $\sigma$ model than the expansion in inverse powers of $N$

The valley Hall effect serves as a vital transport metric for valley polarization in two-dimensional materials. This study theoretically investigates how distinct interaction mechanisms influence this phenomenon. We incorporate both valley-independent electron-phonon scattering and symmetry-breaking intervalley phonon scattering into valley dynamics. Our findings indicate that intervalley phonons significantly diminish the valley Hall coefficient by disrupting valley symmetry through scattering events. Conversely, valley-independent electron-phonon scattering has a negligible impact on the valley Hall coefficient in weakly interacting two-dimensional materials. These insights facilitate the identification of optimal two-dimensional materials for valley Hall devices by guiding structural modifications that minimize symmetry-breaking intervalley phonons. Furthermore, our results suggest that achieving the maximum valley Hall response requires precise control over valley-independent electron-phonon scattering to mitigate heating effects. Finally, we outline the criteria for selecting two-dimensional materials that exhibit robust valley Hall responses. Notably, graphene, hexagonal boron nitride, and hexagonal borophene are highlighted as promising candidates due to their resilience against symmetry-breaking intervalley phonon scattering, making them ideal for valley Hall applications. Additionally, the interaction mechanisms governing valley dynamics in these materials can be experimentally validated through Raman spectroscopy. The present work establishes a foundation for developing a novel class of valley Hall materials. By leveraging the unique capabilities of two-dimensional materials, we can engineer their valley-independent electron-phonon scattering characteristics to suppress heating effects within graphene-based heterostructures. This paves the way for the design of highly efficient valley Hall devices, with potential extensions to spin Hall devices and spin valleytronics. The findings of this study are accessible through an open-source code repository. Our numerical simulations were conducted using the open-source Python package QuSpin, and the associated code is available at \url{https://github.com/QuSpin/QuSpin}. The package also includes a dedicated module for valley Hall effect simulations. The valley Hall coefficients for various two-dimensional materials can be directly extracted from published experimental data. We have compiled a list of relevant materials and their corresponding valley Hall coefficients in the supplementary material. Additionally, we provide a Python script that enables the comparison of valley Hall coefficients across different two-dimensional materials. This script is available in the supplementary material and can also be accessed via the open-source repository \url{https://github.com/QuSpin/valleyHall}. The contest provided four diverse source datasets for training a shared model across all four adaptation problems, with evaluation based on three metrics: Average Accuracy, Macro F1, and Micro F1. Our team was inspired by the concept of meta-learning, which has been successfully applied to various domain adaptation challenges. We present weak-coupling series expansions for the polaron energy up to the tenth order together with the corresponding diagrammatic series for diagrammatic Monte Carlo (DiagMC) simulations. Applying DiagMC to calculate the polaron ground-state energy, we observe that the simulation series exhibits superior convergence relative to that of the energy expansions. Furthermore, our DiagMC series enables the simulation of stronger interactions extending up to the unitary limit. By combining the weak- and strong-coupling series through a smooth interpolation scheme, we derive an accurate estimate for the universal ratio linking the ground-state energy to the two-dimensional Fermi energy. This ratio aligns with previous DiagMC results obtained near the unitary limit and agrees with a variational outcome from the auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo study by Zhang et al. [Phys. Rev. B 99, 020501 (2019)]. Additionally, we explore the feasibility of simulating the diagonal self-energy to determine the polaron lifetime. Our findings indicate that polaron states remain stable throughout the entire interaction range, with the system transitioning from a long-lived to a short-lived regime as interaction strength increases. Finally, we analyze the decay rate of the first excited state. While the corresponding expansion series converges well in the weakly interacting regime, the DiagMC series demonstrates better convergence properties. We also present a comparative analysis of two distinct excited states. These states display varying degrees of stability across different interaction strengths, with the comparison revealing a crossover point where the long-lived excited state ceases to be the one with the highest lifetime. This crossover is accompanied by a corresponding change in the decay rate of the second excited state. Collectively, these results suggest the existence of a critical interaction strength beyond which a polaron molecule becomes the lowest-energy two-particle bound state. This finding offers a new perspective on the stability of the two-dimensional polaron molecule. We establish links between the spectra of powers of a specific symmetric matrix and a series of polynomials defined by a nonlinear recurrence relation. The matrix originates from an infinite directed regular wigwam graph, which models a symmetric random walk. Although the underlying random process is "self-similar," its associated class of "Wigwam groups" is relatively rare within the broader category of self-similar groups. The matrix exhibits relative simplicity due to being derived from a polynomial of low degree. Conversely, polynomials generated by an infinite family of graph traits—properties invariant under minor modifications—form a more complex series, characterized by an explicit two-term nonlinear recurrence relation and a high degree. The study concludes with an outline of the computational methods employed to identify the relationship between the spectrum and the recurrence relation for this series. These techniques are also applicable to other nonlinear recurrence relations, such as those arising in Hecke algebras. Furthermore, the approach can be adapted to other regular wigwam groups, including those based on specific finite groups of Lie type. However, adapting the method to general finite groups appears highly challenging. The resulting relationship between spectral properties and recursive polynomial series is highly nontrivial, particularly in its inverse form: reconstructing the matrix's spectrum from the associated polynomial series. Consequently, this relationship offers a novel approach to investigating spectral properties within this class of groups. Additionally, the methodology provides a means to calculate matrix entries directly from the associated polynomial series. This capability has potential applications in quantum physics, specifically within the context of quantum Ising models. Finally, the paper includes several examples to illustrate the relationships discussed. One of these examples involves the Petersen graph, which is based on a finite group; however, the construction here relies on the properties of a finite wigwam graph rather than the automorphism group of the graph. This distinction demonstrates that our approach is applicable to wigwam graphs that are not necessarily vertex-transitive. This connection is significant for understanding the relationship between our specific Wigwam groups and the affine Weyl groups that are central to the work of van Diejen and his team. This relationship is highly nontrivial, as the Wigwam groups are not contained within the affine Weyl groups. Over recent years, organizations have increasingly adopted distributed structures, leading many Scrum teams to operate in remote or hybrid environments. However, research indicates that these settings often face challenges, including reduced efficiency, lower product quality, and diminished team satisfaction. This study investigates how distributed modes impact project success within Scrum frameworks. Utilizing a multi-method approach, the research first analyzes data from three sources—literature, surveys, and interviews—before examining project success through the lens of three specific team dynamics: cohesiveness, communication, and collaboration. These dynamics were selected based on their established significance in distributed Scrum contexts. The findings reveal a clear trade-off: while distributed Scrum teams experience less successful projects, they report more satisfactory team experiences. These results are attributed to variations in the influence of the three dynamics across different experience types. Specifically, in successful teams, cohesion is the most critical factor for communication, whereas in satisfied teams, collaboration holds this role. The study concludes that distributed Scrum projects can be enhanced by implementing various strategies to foster team cohesiveness. These strategies include facilitating face-to-face interactions, developing effective onboarding processes, and providing comprehensive training on Scrum in distributed settings. This research is significant as it is the first to quantitatively link team dynamics with project success in a remote Scrum context. Furthermore, it offers the most extensive literature review on the topic to date, providing a robust foundation for future research in this field. Finally, the study demonstrates the value of the multi-method approach in generating new insights regarding the interplay between the examined variables. By integrating these elements, this research aims to guide practitioners in successfully managing Scrum teams in remote settings. Specifically, it offers a new perspective on how to improve Scrum team operations in remote environments. The study also provides practical advice on fostering team cohesiveness, addressing a topic that has received limited attention in both practice and academia. Ultimately, this work seeks to assist Scrum practitioners in achieving greater project success in distributed settings. Additionally, the work is the first to establish a foundation for research on the relationship between team dynamics and project success in a remote Scrum context, a topic that has previously been overlooked in both domains. Finally, the research employs the most comprehensive literature review on this subject to date, ensuring that the insights generated will serve as a valuable starting point for future studies in this area. The study is the first to investigate the relationship between team dynamics and project success in a remote Scrum context, a topic that has previously been neglected in both research and practice.
