This paper investigates high-peak-power Kerr-lens mode-locked oscillators by applying resonator stability diagrams to analyze how cavity perturbation influences fundamental stability. It is demonstrated that when peak power surpasses a critical threshold, the resonator geometry shifts from elliptical to circular. Additionally, using the ABCD matrix method, we examine how specific Kerr lens disturbances affect both the resonator and beam stability, as well as how combined perturbations impact resonator geometry. Finally, we apply these stability diagrams to two Kerr-lens oscillators operating at 105 fs and 2.7 ps, showing that the methodology is applicable to both femtosecond and nanosecond oscillators. Additionally, we present a technique for measuring pulse peak power by examining the transition between circular and elliptical resonator geometries. This simple approach avoids the need for pulse characterization tools like autocorrelators or optical sampling, which are often essential for other cavity perturbations. We illustrate that the Kerr-lens oscillator in this study undergoes this geometry change when the intracavity peak power exceeds 1.5 GW. Furthermore, we show that measuring the angular separation of degenerate modes provides a straightforward method for determining pulse peak power. This technique is advantageous because it eliminates the necessity for an optical switch required in other perturbative methods. We demonstrate that the angular separation between degenerate modes correlates with peak power, enabling the Kerr-lens oscillator to function as a cavity-perturbation-based pulsed laser power meter. This establishes a straightforward path to developing an affordable, user-friendly Kerr-lens oscillator-based power meter. This paper introduces a method for computing the tetration function $z \mapsto z \upuparrow^z 1$ along horizontal lines, and derives a formula with comparable accuracy for vertical slices. Additionally, we develop a complementary formula applicable to tetration along the third dimension. Together, these three formulas constitute a complete asymptotic answer regarding the local behavior of tetration for large hypercomplex arguments. Furthermore, we demonstrate how the third formula can be refined through successive approximations of a corresponding iterated exponential function. In this concluding section, we also outline the asymptotic behavior of these hyperfunctional approximations as the iteration count tends to infinity.

The study investigates the magnetic properties of a new, previously unidentified centered honeycomb antiferromagnet, GdInO$_3$, a material notable for its exceptional structural stability. Through a combination of DC magnetization, AC susceptibility, and neutron diffraction experiments, we establish that the site-isolated Gd$^{3+}$ ions form a two-dimensional (2D) centered honeycomb lattice. This lattice exhibits weak interlayer interactions and orders into a ferromagnetic honeycomb structure within the $ac$ plane. We further determine the magnetic phase diagram, which includes ferromagnetic honeycomb (FMH) and antiferromagnetic distorted honeycomb (DHH) phases. Additionally, we calculate the exchange interactions and single-ion anisotropy, finding that the exchange interaction $J_{12}$ along the $a$ axis is approximately three times stronger than $J_{11}$ along the $b$ axis. These findings suggest that GdInO$_3$ is a promising candidate for the study of frustrated magnetism in quasi-2D ferromagnetic honeycomb lattices. Finally, we provide a detailed discussion of the low-temperature magnetic behavior, highlighting the potential for emergent quantum phases in this system. Ultimately, we conclude that GdInO$_3$ serves as a significant model system for investigating low-dimensional magnetism. By employing a combination of experimental and theoretical approaches, we aim to advance the understanding of quantum magnetism in complex magnetic systems. This research contributes to the broader goal of developing new materials with unique magnetic properties for applications in spintronics and quantum information processing. Additionally, the detailed characterization of the magnetic phases and exchange interactions in GdInO$_3$ provides valuable insights into the fundamental principles governing magnetism in low-dimensional systems. Overall, this work represents a significant contribution to the field of magnetism and paves the way for future investigations into the fundamental principles of magnetism in low-dimensional systems. Furthermore, the findings of this study may have potential applications in the development of new magnetic materials with unique properties for use in next-generation magnetic devices. In conclusion, this work is a significant contribution to the field of magnetism and provides a foundation for future research into the fundamental principles of magnetism in low-dimensional systems. The detailed characterization of the magnetic phases and exchange interactions in GdInO$_3$ not only advances our understanding of magnetism in low-dimensional systems but also has the potential to impact the development of new magnetic materials for various applications. This study introduces a node embedding technique designed for link prediction within sparse networks, utilizing non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) to generate low-dimensional representations of nodes and edges. By reformulating the traditional NMF objective function to include an additional term that specifically targets the reconstruction of the sparse portion of the network, we enable the algorithm to concentrate its learning efforts on predicting missing links rather than fitting the already existing edges. Numerical experiments across various real-world datasets demonstrate that this approach not only significantly enhances the algorithm's capacity to capture the network's underlying structure but also leads to superior performance in link forecasting compared to current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, the proposed method ensures a linear computational complexity relative to the number of nodes. Finally, biological case studies highlight its effectiveness, showing that it can identify a broader spectrum of novel gene connections essential for cellular processes during differentiation. Silicon microchambers serve as essential components in the optical and sensor sections of quantum information experiments utilizing trapped atoms. We present a technique for creating micro-fabricated, deep silicon atomic vapor chambers tailored for these applications. This method involves anisotropic silicon etching, followed by anisotropic oxidation and removal, and finally, dry-film photolithography. The resulting chambers feature a two-dimensional micro-fabricated structure with an integrated, planar silicon surface measuring 1.5 cm², suitable for trapping and optically manipulating atoms alongside an enclosed alkali metal vapor. This design is especially beneficial for experiments requiring laser cooling within chamber enclosures, such as those studying optical dipole traps and scattering-mediated entanglement generation. Furthermore, the proposed structure can be adapted for other applications like quantum key distribution and radiation detection. We present a model describing nonlinear distortion in dual-polarization wavelength division multiplexed (DP-WDM) fiber links, accounting for the impact of dual-channel cross-phase modulation (DC-XPM). This model demonstrates that significant three-dimensional effects from DC-XPM can be captured using a reduced-order nonlinear perturbation approach, thereby eliminating the need for detailed channel-specific data. By applying the model to a dense dual-polarization four-dimensional (DP4D) system, we quantify how DC-XPM influences accumulated nonlinear distortion. Furthermore, we utilize the model to establish a lower bound on the power scaling exponent for dual-polarization four-dimensional Nyquist WSM (DP4D-NWSM) power efficiency. Additionally, we offer an analysis of the model's validity across various fiber types. Finally, we determine an upper bound for the power scaling exponent of DP4D-NWSM power capacity within a dual-polarization four-dimensional orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (DP4D-OFDM) system. In this context, we account for the substantial contribution of intra-symbol DC-XPM, which arises from the statistical characteristics of dual-polarization four-dimensional formats. This intra-symbol DC-XPM effect is significant enough to hinder the achievement of a power scaling exponent of 1/3. However, we also demonstrate that this limitation can be overcome by employing optimized subcarrier spacing in DP4D-OFDM. We conclude by discussing the model's application to other modulation formats and systems. This study investigates the influence of coupling between isoscalar dipole ($J^\lambda=1^-$) and monopole ($J^\lambda=0^-$) components, as well as quadrupole ($J^\lambda=2^-$) components, on the characteristics of isoscalar monopole (ISGMR) strength in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si. Utilizing the relativistic RPA framework, we calculate energy and strength distributions for ISGMR in these nuclei. The computed ISGMR energies align with experimental data, while the calculated strength distributions mirror experimental findings. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of quadrupole and isoscalar monopole-quadrupole couplings on ISGMR energy and strength. Our results indicate that monopole and quadrupole couplings significantly affect ISGMR strength, whereas the effect of $J^\lambda=1^-$ isoscalar components is negligible. Additionally, we observe that the monopole-quadrupole coupling strength is more pronounced in $^{28}$Si compared to $^{24}$Mg. Consequently, the ISGMR strength is notably reduced in $^{28}$Si relative to $^{24}$Mg. This finding is corroborated by a non-relativistic calculation that includes the same couplings. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the energy and strength of the ISGMR. These findings suggest that the ISGMR in $^{28}$Si is weaker than in $^{24}$Mg, a conclusion supported by existing experimental evidence. We also explore the potential for future experiments to measure the ISGMR in $^{28}$Si. Additionally, we examine the impact of the monopole-quadrupole coupling constant on ISGMR energy and strength, demonstrating that a larger constant leads to lower energy and strength values. This work examines stick-slip phenomena and trajectory convergence within feedback-controlled motion systems encountering Coulomb resistance. Such friction models are prevalent in various engineering contexts, including manufacturing, material handling, and other mechanical designs. The primary objective is to demonstrate that, under a sufficiently smooth control input, the system trajectories converge to a sliding surface ensuring uniform convergence to the desired output, thereby eliminating limit cycles. This approach is applicable to any control-affine system where the control coefficient matches the friction term. A key advantage is that the required control input can be derived from a system free of Coulomb friction, requiring only the superposition of an auxiliary term. In this study, that auxiliary component is an integrator with a negative feedback gain designed to ensure the smoothness of the total control signal. We analyze the resulting closed-loop system and prove the absence of limit cycles, confirming convergence to the sliding surface. Furthermore, we illustrate the methodology's applicability by regulating the output of a two-dimensional system to a step reference signal in the presence Coulomb friction. The paper includes simulations of the proposed control law and compares the results against an alternative sliding mode controller. Finally, experimental data from a motor setup are presented to validate the approach in a real-world context. The proposed solution offers several benefits, such as simplifying the design process, reducing the number of parameters, and mitigating chattering effects. Additionally, it avoids the complexity of specialized limit cycle analysis techniques required for sliding mode control methods. However, the method is not universally applicable to all systems. To address this, we introduce a sufficient condition for reachability to the sliding surface, which depends on the Lie bracket bracketing of the control vector fields and the system drift. We introduce a symmetry unfolding for the inhomogeneous double confluent Heun equation, where the source function transforms under the equation's symmetry group. This symmetry is broad enough to accommodate essentially arbitrary solutions to a transformed version of the equation. We demonstrate that this transformable unfolding is compatible with two previously established methods: one producing a symmetric homogeneous version and another generating a higher-order inhomogeneous equation. Additionally, we outline a general approach for identifying equivalent transformable unfoldlings and illustrate this with a specific case involving Heun's equation, which yields three distinct transformable unfoldlings, two of which are related through our proposed symmetric unfolding. Furthermore, we show a second method for achieving symmetric unfolding by utilizing the correspondence between solutions of inhomogeneous and homogeneous double confluent Heun equations, a technique also applicable to other Heun equations. In these homogeneous unfoldlings, the source function resides within a specific subspace of solutions, allowing source transformations to be viewed as restrictions of the broader Heun symmetry. We also address an apparent contradiction between this correspondence approach and the transformable unfolding when applied to Heun's equation. Finally, we examine a double confluent Heun equation that admits two transformable unfoldlings connected by a symmetric unfolding, highlighting a significant difference between these cases: one equation possesses a solution invariant under all symmetries, while the other does not. This distinction proves crucial for understanding the relationship between the symmetric and transformable unfolding procedures. These findings deepen our current understanding of special forms of the Heun equation and may offer new perspectives on its general form. Specifically, they underscore the importance of examining transformations that leave a particular solution invariant, a concept we extend to a broader context. Such an approach may facilitate uncovering new special cases and potentially lead to a global unfolding of the inhomogeneous double confluent Heun equation. To achieve this, it may be necessary to employ transformations that map solutions to functions that are not necessarily solutions. We conclude by exploring the consequences of such an extension. To facilitate this understanding, we provide a comprehensive summary of all existing symmetry-preserving transformations for the double confluent Heun equation. This work serves as a foundation for a broader investigation into the symmetries of Heun's equation, with a future publication dedicated to this topic. In that context, we will examine solutions invariant under transformations linked to Heun's original 1913 investigation and Heun himself, as well as those related to the connection problem. This letter investigates the inherent topology of a driven-dissipative classical spin model that lacks spatial- and point-group-symmetry. Our analysis demonstrates that this system possesses a non-trivial K-theory $K = U(1) \oplus KU(1)$, which is significantly larger than the K-group of any crystal class. Furthermore, we identify that this rich topological structure remains robust against both the restoration of symmetry and disordered driving. We also explore the potential for constructing a classical Ginzburg-Landau framework to describe the same system. Notably, this model is experimentally accessible in driven colloidal crystals. We anticipate that our findings will stimulate further investigation into the inherent topological properties of non-equilibrium driven-dissipative systems. Finally, our framework is applicable to both classical and quantum systems where the Hamiltonian does not depend on spin operators. In such cases, the inherent topology is determined by the tensor product of the individual K-groups of the spin and orbital degrees of freedom. This approach reveals that a generic system with $O(N)$ symmetry exhibits a rich inherent topology, a feature that may prove significant for understanding non-equilibrium phenomena in driven-dissipative systems. Furthermore, it suggests that existing topological models may be extended to achieve higher symmetry classes. Specifically, a generic system displaying $O(N)$-symmetry symmetry-protected topological (SPT) orders can be interpreted as an $O(N-1)$-SPT system. This insight may facilitate the discovery of novel topological phases in non-equilibrium settings. Self-supervised learning (SSL) has emerged as a highly effective approach for automatic speech recognition (ASR), yet the impact of hostile conditions, such as speech enhancement, remains uncertain. This study investigates how speech enhancement influences the performance of speech self-supervised learning (SSL). Specifically, we examine various deep learning-based enhancement techniques applied to both training and inference stages across multiple ASR tasks. Our findings indicate that speech enhancement is more effective for conventional ASR than for speech self-supervised learning (SSL). Furthermore, while a standard 3-sentence test set is generally adequate for evaluating speech enhancement performance, it may be misleading when used with speech self-supervised learning. Consequently, a larger test set is necessary to accurately characterize system behavior. Finally, we analyze the underlying reasons for these observations and propose a speech enhancement pipeline designed to optimize speech SSL performance. To our knowledge, this represents the first systematic investigation into the effects of speech enhancement on speech self-supervised learning. We propose an empirical Bayesian framework to calculate marginal posterior distributions of the E-value, which integrates model assumptions about unmeasured confounders. This approach is demonstrated using data from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth. Additionally, we identify several novel properties of Laurent extensions, including their realization as generalized induced representations and the presence of additional second-order quantum spaces within $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$. Finally, we demonstrate that our classification results extend naturally to the second-order Laurent extensions of the quantum groups $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_3)$ and $U_q(\mathfrak{sp}_4)$. Results for non-prompt and prompt production were derived across central rapidity regions, covering transverse momenta ($p_{\mathrm{T}}$) from 20 to 100 GeV and central rapidities ($p_{\mathrm{T}}$) from 0 to 5. The rapidity integrated ratios of beauty to charm ($b/c$) production were also determined. These findings align with predictions from leading-order perturbative QCD. Additionally, the rapidity-integrated $b/c$ cross-section ratio was compared against ALICE measurements at $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV and 13 TeV, revealing an increasing trend with collision energy. The rapidity-integrated $b/c$ ratio at $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV is compared with CMS data at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV, showing excellent agreement between the two experiments. Furthermore, the study examined the rapidity-integrated cross-section ratios for beauty production relative to inelastic proton-proton cross-sections, comparing them with theoretical predictions and those from the LHCb collaboration at $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV and 8 TeV. Both the current and LHCb measurements exhibit an energy-dependent rise in the $b/c$ ratio, which the authors attribute to different rapidity selections. The paper concludes with a discussion on the energy dependence of these measurements and their implications for understanding beauty and charm production. Additionally, the study reports on the longitudinal momentum distributions of prompt beauty and charm production, comparing them with energy-predictions from PYTHIA 8.2 and POWHEG-BOX-4FLO. Finally, the study examines the transverse momentum distributions of prompt beauty and charm production, comparing them with predictions from PYTHIA 6.4, PYTHIA 8.1, and POWHEG-BOX-4FLO. The study concludes with a discussion on energy-dependent features of these measurements and their implications for understanding beauty and charm production. The paper also discusses the implications of these measurements for understanding beauty and charm production.

This study examines the application of Python crypto libraries in 1,300 real-world projects. Our findings indicate that, despite Python's extensive selection of robust and secure crypto libraries, developers frequently employ them incorrectly. Through an analysis of 1,300 repositories, we identified 1,077 instances where crypto libraries were utilized in a flawed manner. Our investigation reveals that 50% of these errors stem from developer misunderstandings of how Python crypto libraries operate. Furthermore, we observed that many projects employ deprecated libraries or those lacking security patches. To address these issues, we have developed a novel static analysis tool designed to detect common crypto programming errors, offering developers in Python projects guidance on the correct usage of crypto libraries. The complete code and documentation for this tool can be accessed at https://github.com/SeoulTech/PyCryptoCheck. We anticipate that this tool will assist Python developers in creating more secure applications. The research paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1145/3421531.3444989. Additionally, the study includes interviews with 10 experts from academia and industry, which provide insights into the challenges and barriers associated with adopting Python crypto libraries. Our work offers valuable insights to the Python developer community, helping to foster more secure Python applications. We have made our tool publicly available to assist developers in identifying and rectifying crypto-related errors in their projects. We anticipate that community feedback will facilitate the tool's evolution and enhancement. We welcome any contributions from the community to improve the tool and look forward to collaborating with researchers to advance the field of Python security. This paper introduces a novel automatic annotation framework called VALUE (Voting-based Urban Labeling Extensive for all), designed to generate high-quality labeled datasets for training autonomous driving models. While current automatic annotation methods often suffer from low recall, VALUE addresses this by leveraging ensembles of off-the-shelf models to perform prediction voting. We further enhance the quality of both bounding boxes and semantic segments by implementing a new approach for label correction. Extensive experiments across three real-world cities demonstrate that VALUE can produce annotation volumes comparable to human-created datasets while achieving superior accuracy. Additionally, retraining models on VALUE's automatic annotations yields better performance than when human-labeled data is augmented with the method's outputs. Ultimately, VALUE offers a robust, cost-effective, and high-quality solution for large-scale automatic annotation in urban settings. For further details, visit https://github.com/wayve-ai/VALUE. This study introduces a new class of proximal means tailored for application to near-sparse frameworks. The proposed methods are provably non-convex and utilize a non-uniform weight function to assign higher weights to sparse points, thereby enhancing the representation of seismic reflectivity. By integrating these techniques into a deep network architecture, we develop the proximal sparse network (NuSPAN), the first model-driven proximal mean for near-sparse frameworks. Numerical experiments demonstrate that NuSPAN effectively and rapidly reconstructs seismic profiles, yielding superior results compared to current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, the implementation code and a pretrained model are publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhongyong/NuSPAN. This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces by analyzing their associated invariant maximal operator semigroups. Initially, we establish sufficient conditions guaranteeing that the semigroup remains invariant in a specific weighted Dirichlet space. Subsequently, by adapting these findings to a broader context, we examine semigroups of composition operators within BMOA-type spaces. Our results demonstrate that, under particular conditions, the orbits of initial functions consist entirely of analytic functions that vanish at a designated point. Furthermore, we link this inquiry to the study of continuous linear functionals on BMOA-type spaces, revealing that semigroups invariant under all composition operators are precisely those whose functionals are invariant under all composition operators. We provide explicit descriptions of such invariant functionals and identify the corresponding invariant subspaces. Additionally, we present a criterion for identifying hyper invariant subspaces based on the properties of their functionals. Finally, we construct examples of hyper invariant subspaces of BMOA-type spaces and explore the structural characteristics of their functionals. Notably, our methodology extends to the broader class of weighted Bergman-type spaces, yielding several significant findings. Throughout the study, the concepts of composition invariant subspaces and composition hyper invariant subspaces are also addressed. Specifically, we characterize composition invariant subspaces of BMOA-type spaces and investigate various types of composition hyper invariant subspaces within these spaces. In the process of examining hyper invariant subspaces, we derive several novel and significant results regarding analytic functions vanishing at a given point. The paper also includes illustrative examples of hyper invariant subspaces for BMOA-type spaces, alongside invariant subspaces generated by reproducing kernels and subspaces defined by zero sets. Finally, we explore additional hyper invariant subspaces of BMOA-type spaces by analyzing the properties of their functionals. As an application of these findings, we explore hyper invariant subspaces within Bergman-type spaces. The study also features examples of composition invariant subspaces of BMOA-type spaces, as well as composition hyper invariant subspaces of Bergman-type spaces. Throughout the work, we emphasize the importance of hyper invariant subspaces within Bergman-type spaces. The methodology employed here also facilitates the examination of weak hyper invariant subspaces of BMOA-type spaces. The article is structured into two sections. The first presents hyper invariant subspaces of BMOA-type spaces, while the second focuses on hyper invariant subspaces of Bergman-type spaces. We introduce a method for calculating operator expansions in integrable models by combining two independent exact wavefunction overlap methods. This approach utilizes the first two non-trivial terms in the finite-size expansion to determine the leading operator in the expansion. Applying our technique to the exact ground state of the generalized Ferrymans model, we successfully identify all essential properties of the corresponding spin operator. Our findings reveal that the second term of the finite-size correction is universally proportional to the second eigenvalue of the target operator, with a proportionality constant that is universally equal to 2pi/v. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the spectrum of the Ferrymans model exhibits a unique form of operator merging, where an operator with scaling dimension 1/2 merges into the identity as the model approaches its critical point. This phenomenon is also observed in the critical Ising model. These universal properties are anticipated to hold for all second-order phase transitions. Our results are also applicable to non-integrable models possessing a nearly exact low-lying spectrum. As a demonstration, we analyze a perturbed Haagerup model, which displays an anomalously slow convergence to its critical point. Our analysis confirms that the perturbation corresponds to the second non-trivial operator of the critical model. Additionally, we observe that the perturbed spectrum displays a distinct form of operator merging, where a pair of operators merge into the identity. This behavior is also present in the perturbed Ising model. Finally, our study suggests that the operator merging phenomenon is more prevalent than previously believed. Specifically, the third operator of the critical Haagerup model does not merge into the identity, whereas the third operator of the critical Ising model does. This distinction highlights a qualitative difference between the perturbed models. We further demonstrate that the perturbed Ising model exhibits a unique form of operator merging, where a pair of operators merge into the second non-trivial operator of the critical model. This behavior is also observed in the perturbed XXZ model. These findings suggest that the operator merging phenomenon is more complex than previously thought. Specifically, the third operator of the critical Ising model merges into the second operator of the critical model, while the third operator of the perturbed Haagerup model does not. This distinction underscores the qualitative differences between the perturbed models. Our results also suggest that the operator merging phenomenon is more complex than previously believed. This study develops a unified framework for analyzing when families of real integrable functions are non-uniformly integrable. By introducing a novel concept of order for such families based on their simple infusions, we establish sufficient conditions for non-uniform integrability within an expansive class of families that encompasses those examined in existing literature. The paper also addresses the reverse scenario, detailing sufficient conditions for uniform integrability. This approach relies exclusively on Riemann integration and avoids the extensive technical requirements typically associated with measure theory. Consequently, the results are Tychonoff spaces, although the derived conditions can be extended to more general topological settings. All order comparisons between families of functions can be visualized using Hasse diagrams, which are provided for the specific families considered in this work. Furthermore, the study presents a non-constructive algorithm for constructing simple infusions of real integrable functions, accompanied by examples and illustrations. The utility of these methods is demonstrated through their application to issues concerning the uniform integrability of sequences and series, as well as the uniform integrability of function sequences and series. Additionally, the concept of order is applied to the uniform convergence of sequences and series of integrable real functions. Finally, the authors suggest several open questions and potential lines of future research. Keywords: non-uniform integrability, uniform convergence, order, Hasse diagram. This study introduces a new approach to automatically transform urban development requirements into a formal specification language using the SmARcY system. SmARcY stands for an Intelligent Assistant for Translating Urban Requirements, where the 'Y' signifies its function as another formal specification language. The process involves three core components: an ontology library, a user interface, and a requirement transformation engine. The interface enables non-technical stakeholders to input urban requirements in a semi-formal format, while the engine converts these inputs into formal specifications. To facilitate this conversion, a domain-specific ontology library provides knowledge that supplements the provided requirements. Drawing on the foundational work of Dastani et al., this ontology library is designed to support various transformation tasks, including ambiguity detection, feature extraction, entailment reasoning, and feature enrichment. Furthermore, the system addresses ambiguity by leveraging the ontology library to introduce missing elements, thereby enhancing both the formalized requirements and the original natural language input. The system successfully operates across multiple domains, such as traffic management, waste management, and water distribution. A pilot study was conducted to evaluate SmARCY's performance in transforming requirements from different urban domains. The results indicate that SmARCY is effective in producing formal specifications free of redundancy and inconsistency. Additionally, user feedback demonstrates that SmARCY is user-friendly and intuitive for domain experts. This paper serves as a tutorial for developing a requirement transformation system and reports on the application of formal methods to transform urban development requirements. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhaleem99/Smart-Assistant-for-transforming-requirements. Future work will focus on refining the system's performance and usability. To achieve this, we plan to conduct more comprehensive case studies involving diverse users, such as urban developers and city managers, to gather broader feedback. In the realm of superconducting quantum computing, operational errors are typically reversible, yet the conventional method of applying inverse operations for error correction is hindered by noise accumulation during gate operations and the finite success probability of syndrome measurements. To address these limitations, this study introduces a quantum error correction framework utilizing concealed inverses, specifically tailored for superconducting quantum devices. The core strategy involves reversing errors by concealing inverse operations within logical qubits; subsequently, random logical operations are applied to "reveal" these inverses and facilitate error recovery through syndrome measurement and decoding. This approach effectively functions as a complete quantum error correction scheme and can be seamlessly integrated into standard quantum error correction circuits. Notably, by eliminating inverses, the protocol mitigates noise accumulation and enhances fault tolerance. A proof-of-concept experiment conducted on the 64-qubit SQUARD hardware demonstrates an experimental quantum error correction circuit on a 4-qubit colorless graph state that surpasses a threshold. Furthermore, the results indicate a substantial improvement in the fidelity of multi-qubit gate operations. These findings hold significant promise for the practical implementation of quantum error correction in near-term superconducting quantum hardware. Furthermore, this work serves as a foundation for developing fault-tolerant quantum error correction protocols in subsequent research. **Keywords:** quantum error correction; colorless graph state; superconducting quantum; concealed inverse operation.

This paper investigates the cocartesian representation of equivalence relations and preorders within regular categories, with a specific focus on the cocartesian functor $Q: \operatorname{Rel} \to \mathbf{Set}$, commonly referred to as the quantale of an equivalence system. We demonstrate that every preorder in a regular category admits a cocartesian depiction, whereas the existence of such a depiction for $Q$ is not guaranteed. To address this, we introduce the concept of a strongly effective equivalence system, proving that a categorical equivalence exists between regular categories featuring this structure and those where $Q$ admits a cocartesian depiction. A key example of a strongly effective equivalence system is an extensible one, as defined by J. M. Roy. Furthermore, we examine the implications of this result for the cocartesian depiction of complete lattices, utilizing the extensive lattice functor as a specific instance of $Q$. This functor was pivotal in J. M. Roy's development of the theory of extensible lattices, a framework that has significantly influenced the theory of modular lattices. We establish that a regular category possesses an equivalent formulation to an extensible lattice category precisely when the categorical equivalence mentioned above restricts correctly to modular equivalence systems and modularity is incorporated into the definition of a strongly effective modular equivalence system. Additionally, we characterize strongly effective equivalence systems through the existence of a left adjoint to $Q$, thereby providing an alternative characterization of modularity. Finally, the paper concludes with an algebraic analysis of strongly effective equivalence systems. This analysis includes a straightforward algebraic proof that any equivalence relation $R$ on a set $X$ is strongly effective if, for every subset $A \subseteq X$, there exists an element $a \in A$ such that the equivalence class $[a]_R$ intersects $A$ exclusively at $a$. This result stands in contrast to the analogous property for lattices, where the existence of such an atom-like element cannot be derived from the lattice's axioms alone. Consequently, we define this type of lattice as atomic, showing that the atomic nature of such lattices offers a more natural explanation for the existence of the functor $Q$ compared to the current theoretical framework. Specifically, we provide an algebraic proof that any atomic lattice is extensible. The forecasted rise in the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, including hurricanes and typhoons, has significantly increased the demand for precise and actionable flood warnings. To enhance spatial alerting, we introduce a new multivariate spatial model for multivariate conditional peak over threshold (PePT) exceedances, specifically designed for multivariate spatial processes. This method relies on a multivariate linear model and multivariate spatial covariance structures, with parameter estimation achieved through a two-stage procedure. The first stage involves fitting the models and estimating their parameters using a two-stage restricted maximum likelihood approach, while the second stage calculates multivariate PePT exceedance probabilities via simulation. We demonstrate this multivariate PePT exceedance estimation technique using a dataset of significant wave heights from the North Sea. Furthermore, the study presents spatial forecasts for conditional peak wave heights and potential multivariate extreme sea level exceedance probabilities for the English Channel. Finally, we suggest extensions to improve the model's performance. This framework offers a versatile solution for multivariate spatial PePT exceedance estimation across various disciplines. The R package `sp5dcPePT` is available to facilitate these analyses. The source code can be found at: https://github.com/JoaoGoncalves10/sp5dcPePT. This study addresses the challenge of \emph{operator transitioning} (OT), a process that transforms a noisy operator on a Hilbert space into a target operator possessing specific desirable properties. This framework encompasses various established problems, such as the low-rank matrix completion under RIP constraints and phase retrieval from magnitude-squared measurements. We introduce a unified framework that accommodates a broader category of target operators defined by convex constraints and more general noise models. To solve this, we propose the Operator Transitioning (OT) framework and a corresponding algorithm, \textit{OT-PCA}, which extends the previously known \text{OPCA} (Truncated Power Method for Noisy Matrix Transitioning) algorithm. We establish rigorous convergence guarantees for \text{OT-PCA}, demonstrating that it reliably recovers target operators even when noise is color-dependent on the input, a significant improvement over prior convergence results for \text{OPCA}. Furthermore, numerical experiments validate the efficacy of \text{OT-PCA} in solving matrix completion and phase retrieval tasks. This research examines the Hilbert polynomial and $F$-invariant rings via the resolution of singularities proposed by William Liu. We establish a tight link between the coefficients of the Hilbert polynomial and the Hodge numbers, thereby demonstrating that the tightness of the Hilbert polynomial serves as a criterion for the existence of specific topological structures within the graded mixed $t$-structure. Furthermore, we derive a criterion for the existence of $F$-pure singularities based on the Hilbert polynomial. Additionally, by expressing the Hilbert polynomial as a sum of polynomials, we provide a criterion for when a local ring is $F$-pure by analyzing the tightness of each individual component polynomial. Finally, we outline an algorithm to construct a sequence of ideals that yields an $F$-pure local ring. This method is inspired by the strategy in [Yongnam Lee, Eun-Sang Kim, JSC 2021] for identifying Cohen-Macaulay rings through the Hilbert function of a quotient ring, representing a novel approach to building such rings. Finally, we conclude by investigating the tightness of both polynomials and local rings. Specifically, we demonstrate that an $F$-pure graded local ring is tight if it is Cohen-Macaulay, whereas an $F$-pure ring need not be tight in general, even within the Cohen-Macaulay category. Consequently, we propose the concept of an $F$-pure and tight ring, which is tight whenever it is Cohen-Macaulay. We then explore the relationship between these two types of rings by defining a class of rings that are both tight and $F$-pure, and we investigate the properties of these rings. Finally, we examine the relationship between the Hilbert function and the Cohen-Macaulay type through the lens of the Hilbert polynomial. In this context, we identify a class of rings that are tight, Cohen-Macaulay, and possess a Hilbert polynomial of degree $d-1$ with a coefficient of 1 for every $d \geq 2$. This class includes both tight Cohen-Macaulay rings and rings that are both tight and $F$-pure. We also analyze the properties of these rings and present examples that are tight, Cohen-Macaulay, and $F$-pure. Notably, we construct an infinite family of such rings, thereby resolving an open question posed in this study. Additionally, we identify a class of rings

We introduce highdicom, a lightweight Python framework designed for the creation of image-related remarks and machine learning (ML) outputs, developed in direct response to the growing demand for the rapid and accessible application of AI in clinical environments. Our approach diverges from the conventional workflow where researchers first train models and then build software for deployment; instead, we develop tools for generating these AI outputs first, subsequently integrating them into end-to-end pipelines. These tools are based on DICOM, the international standard for handling image data in radiology and pathology. Specifically, the highdicom package offers high-level abstractions for creating suggestive AI results, such as segmentation contours and cancer markers, while providing access to low-level DICOM encoding and validation through the pydicom package. To facilitate collaboration between AI researchers and software engineers, we provide a robust library of image remarks that can be easily customized. Furthermore, highdicom enables the generation of both image and patient tags in compliance with DICOM standards, ensuring that AI outputs are readily accepted by hospital DICOM viewers and information systems. We demonstrate that highdicom significantly streamlines the development of AI tools that are easily integrated into standard clinical workflows. The package is released under the permissive Apache 2.0 license and can be accessed at https://github.com/highdicom/highdicom. Additional details are available at https://highdicom.org. Our roadmap outlines a future focus on supporting further AI applications, including nodule detection in radiology and cell classification in pathology, alongside a comprehensive suite of remarks to maximize interoperability with various DICOM systems. We demonstrate this with examples of contour segmentation and cell classification, illustrating how to create appropriate remarks for use cases such as "suggestive of tumor," "suggestive of benign," and "uncertain." We aim for highdicom to serve as a versatile tool for the broad community of AI researchers and software engineers who develop image-guided diagnostic tools. By streamlining the development and deployment of these tools, we enable them to be integrated into standard clinical workflows, thereby facilitating the widespread adoption of AI in clinical practice. Ultimately, we anticipate that highdicom will contribute to the broader goal of making the widespread and safe use of AI in clinical settings a reality. This paper was submitted to Radiology in July 2020 and is scheduled for publication in December 2020. The source code is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/highdicom/highdicom. The highdicom package is available on PyPI at https://pypi

Deep learning has recently become a leading approach for DNA pattern analysis, yet most existing frameworks rely heavily on human guidance, including the careful selection of learning targets, the definition of input features, and extensive hyperparameter learning. This study proposes an innovative framework that automatically learns representations to address DNA pattern analysis, thereby eliminating the need for human intervention in feature selection or learning target definition. Specifically, we introduce an attention-based autoencoder that learns unsupervised, high-level DNA patterns from raw sequences, subsequently applying a deep classifier for supervised pattern analysis. The attention mechanism facilitates attentional contrastive learning, which effectively filters out irrelevant information. Furthermore, we develop a general framework for autoencoder-based representation learning in DNA pattern analysis and demonstrate its robustness in DNA motif analysis. Finally, we illustrate the framework's utility in identifying potential transcription factor binding sites within the human genome. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/taehyounlee/Attention-AE. Given its broad generality, this approach is expected to be applicable to various DNA pattern analysis tasks. We anticipate that our study will inspire further research into representation learning, thereby enhancing the performance of deep learning methods in DNA pattern analysis. Additionally, our work seeks to promote the adoption of unsupervised learning techniques in this field. Finally, this research represents a significant step toward fully automating DNA pattern analysis. Specifically, our method enables the automatic learning of DNA patterns, facilitating the discovery of novel patterns without requiring prior knowledge of those patterns beforehand. For instance, this capability is highly relevant for applications such as annotating transcription factor binding sites in the human genome. By employing our attentional contrastive learning framework, researchers can identify novel DNA patterns that have not yet been discovered. We believe that our work will encourage the representation learning community to explore the application of autoencoders in DNA pattern analysis. In summary, this work marks a significant step toward automating DNA pattern analysis. Our attentional contrastive learning framework allows researchers to discover new DNA patterns by learning their high-level features from raw sequences. This enables the annotation of previously unidentified DNA patterns, such as new transcription factor binding sites, thereby reducing the time and effort required for annotation. Additionally, our work will inspire researchers to pursue more automated and unsupervised approaches for DNA pattern analysis. Specifically, our attentional contrastive learning framework enables the discovery of new DNA patterns by learning their high-level features from raw sequences, which facilitates the annotation of previously unidentified DNA patterns, such as new transcription factor binding sites. This reduces the time and effort required for annotation

The metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ has been extensively researched, with recent focus on how reduced dimensionality influences this phenomenon. This study examines V$_2$O$_3$ films of varying thicknesses grown on the C(111) surface of 6H-SiC. In very thin films, the metal-insulator transition shifts to higher temperatures, a shift that diminishes as film thickness increases. X-ray photoemission spectroscopy and low-energy electron diffraction confirm that these films have silicon-terminated surfaces, while x-ray photoemission spectroscopy and electron energy loss spectroscopy indicate that oxygen-termination is absent. To account for these transition characteristics, we employ a model utilizing the surface-terminated, metal-terminated bulk structure of V$_2$O$_3$ as a baseline. By applying this model to an ultrathin film with a metal-terminated surface, we observe a transition shift of nearly 100 K toward lower temperatures. These findings suggest that the metal-insulator shift in surface-terminated V$_2$O$_3$ films is primarily driven by surface effects, with the specific termination type playing a critical role. Furthermore, we propose that oxygen-termination could be responsible for the observed shifts in surface-terminated films. This research offers valuable insights for understanding the metal-insulator transition in ultrathin films and thin films. Additionally, it may aid in the design of new transition metal oxides with tailored surface termination and desired surface properties. Ultimately, this could lead to the development of advanced surface devices capable of functioning at room temperature. Finally, the results may contribute to the design of transition metal oxide heterostructures with unique surface properties. Such heterostructures could be fabricated using the growth technique employed here, which has already yielded fascinating results. Ultimately, this could unlock a new class of transition metal oxides with surface properties distinct from their bulk counterparts. This could pave the way for the creation of advanced transition metal oxide devices with a broad range of functionalities. The potential for such devices to achieve room-temperature operation would be highly significant. The unique surface properties of these materials could also enable the design of transition metal oxide heterostructures with surface characteristics different from those of their bulk components. Such heterostructures could be produced using the growth method used in this study, which has yielded intriguing results. The potential for surface effects to drive the metal-insulator transition in these films could also be responsible for the observed shifts in transition temperature. Notably, this generalized construction recovers Ratiu and Schaposnik's authorization method for co-adjoint orbits in $\mathfrak{so}(n)^*$. The paper concludes by presenting an authorization result for a Hamiltonian system on a co-adjoint orbit of $\mathfrak{u}(3)^*$, where the orbit is parameterized using the technique developed in this work. This specific case highlights the utility of the findings for exploring non-integrable Hamiltonian systems. Additionally, the technical section details the construction of a maximal Cartan subset and parametrizes its co-adjoint orbits based on the eigenvalues of a normal matrix. Finally, the final section examines the Hamiltonian dynamics associated with the parameterized Hamiltonian function. This process yields a system of ordinary differential equations featuring a non-Lipschitz right-hand side, which exhibits finite-time blow-up behavior along a specific trajectory. Overall, this research demonstrates the applicability of generalized Dubois-Clebsch authorization to certain Hamiltonian systems on co-adjoint orbits of simple Lie algebras, a domain that has seen limited exploration. This alternative yields a Lipschitz continuous right-hand side, resulting in well-posed trajectory behavior and motivating further investigation. We introduce the conclusion of the systematic KMTNet planetary irregularity search conducted for the 2018 sub-prime-field planets. This study focuses on planetary light curves that deviate from the standard transit shape, exhibiting either a concave or convex morphology. We present findings for 11 new planets identified via the KMTNet network, alongside a re-analysis of 15 previously reported cases. The combined dataset comprises 26 planets, with 11 featuring convex light curves and 15 showing concave ones. Notably, the convex planets are predominantly located in the Magellanic Clouds, whereas concave planets are mostly found in the background field. We demonstrate that a correlation between the fractional stellar flux and the impact parameter accounts for several convex cases, whereas a wavelength-dependent background effect explains most of the concave cases. Additionally, we discuss the potential for these phenomena to represent a new class of microlensing events. Finally, we outline the methodology for the subsequent systematic search involving the inclusion of 2018 sub-prime-field microlensing planets with convex light curves. This study evaluates the performance of 21 machine learning algorithms using 11 performance metrics across 120 distinct data configurations to evaluate their predictive accuracy in distinguishing a specific patient group from a control group. These configurations vary by 18 features, including 17 clinical variables and one non-invasive cardiac imaging feature. The results indicate that Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM yield the most accurate predictions, while also demonstrating the greatest stability and robustness against overfitting. Furthermore, Random Forest and LIME were employed to perform feature significance analysis on the best-performing single algorithm (Random Forest). The most significant features identified align with existing literature, comprising both continuous clinical variables and categorical diagnoses. Overall, this research provides critical insights into selecting the optimal machine learning algorithm for this specific dataset and highlights the value of these techniques for feature analysis. The source code and data are accessible at: https://github.com/ahmedhassan123/MachineLearningAssessment. Additionally, the analysis is being utilized to investigate potential differences between two distinct patient groups. The dataset is available on the MIMIC-III public database.

Dyck paths form a significant subclass of general graphs that has garnered growing interest due to their well-known chromatic properties. Specifically, counting the ways to color a Dyck path with $k$ colors can be expressed via the $q$-factorial, where $q$ represents the path's area. This article presents a combinatorial proof of this result by developing a $q$-weighting scheme based on derangements and fixed points. To achieve this, the path's triangulation is employed, linking the problem to $q$-rook theory. Furthermore, the study extends this weighting scheme to chromatic symmetric polynomials, expressing them in terms of Dyck paths and their triangulations. The work begins with a review of the chromatic symmetric polynomial's definition and its current state of research. It then defines triangulation and chromatic symmetric polynomials for Dyck paths, demonstrating how their structure influences coloring. The paper also examines "mountain" coloring, a specific technique applicable to these paths. Subsequently, triangulations are utilized to define "mountain" components, which are analyzed through $q$-rook theory. The article presents two theorems that establish the connection between triangulations and chromatic symmetric polynomials, followed by an exploration of how these relationships influence the overall coloring of Dyck paths. Finally, the work concludes with an examination of the triangulation structure, offering additional insights into the coloring properties of Dyck paths. This approach yields a combinatorial proof for the $q$-factorial expression, providing deeper insight into the coloring behavior of these paths. Additionally, the article offers a combinatorial interpretation of the chromatic symmetric polynomial for Dyck paths, expressing it as a sum over paths weighted by their triangulations. The research culminates in a comprehensive proof of this conclusion, encompassing triangulations, mountain coloring, and Dyck path coloring. The article concludes with a discussion of future research directions, including generalizations to other graph subclasses, extensions to higher dimensions, and applications to network flow problems. These proposals aim to inspire further inquiry and contribute to the ongoing advancements in graph theory. Overall, this work provides a detailed exploration of the chromatic symmetric polynomial for Dyck paths, deepening our understanding of their chromatic properties and contributing valuable insights to the field of graph theory. By addressing the topic from multiple angles, the article offers a thorough examination that will prove beneficial to researchers and students in the discipline. This paper introduces a novel convolutional network architecture designed to enhance image classification performance. We posit that standard convolutional layers fail to fully leverage orientation information within feature maps. To address this, we propose incorporating convolution operations between feature maps at different levels, utilizing a new layer type termed the "orientation conv layer." This specific operation convolves channel $i$ with channel $j$ by restricting the kernel to a sector-shaped region spanning an angle of $2\pi i/j$. This design effectively communicates orientation data across scales in a localized manner. We have integrated this observation into network architectures for the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets, resulting in significant performance gains. Furthermore, our approach is non-intrusive, allowing for the implementation of a dedicated network for any specific classification task without necessitating architectural modifications during training. Experimental results demonstrate substantial performance improvements across various configurations. This paper introduces a precision calculation of the top quark mass within Standard Model perturbation theory, specifically accounting for substantial flavor dependence. This approach addresses the issue of mass matching between the full Standard Model and its effective field theory (EFTE6), which is constructed by integrating out every quark flavor with a mass below the scale $\Lambda_{EFTe6}$. The top quark mass derived from the EFTE6 of a specific benchmark point can therefore be precisely extracted from experimental measurements of that benchmark. This methodology is particularly relevant for analyzing $t\bar{t}$ production at hadron colliders and electron-positron colliders, facilitating a rigorous interpretation of future high-precision $t\bar{t}$ data for fitting purposes. We demonstrate that incorporating substantial flavor dependence into top quark mass calculations yields a more accurate fit to future $t\bar{t}$ measurement data at hadron colliders, resulting in a more precise determination of the relevant benchmark point. Additionally, we outline the necessary modifications to existing top mass extraction methods to ensure they incorporate substantial flavor dependence. Our primary conclusion is that future measurements of the $t\bar{t}$ production cross section at hadron colliders will not suffice to precisely determine the Standard Model running top quark mass at the scale $\mu_t$; such an extraction would introduce uncontrolled theoretical uncertainties. Instead, a comprehensive global fit at a multi-TeV hadron collider encompassing all available precision observables is required to determine the top quark mass at the EFTE6 benchmark scale. Furthermore, we demonstrate that upcoming $t\bar{t}$ production data from the ILC and CLIC electron-positron colliders can significantly constrain the light Higgs coupling to top quarks, thereby enabling a precise determination of the specific benchmark point. This precision is essential for a thorough understanding of the Standard Model and its potential extension to a multi-Higgs framework. In this context, we illustrate how to precisely determine the top quark mass in the EFTE6 effective theory using CLIC $t\bar{t}$ data. We demonstrate that for any $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists a threshold $k$ such that nodes with degree at least $k$ in graphs where every node possesses a degree of at least $(1-\varepsilon)n$ can be re-colored using $\Delta$ colors. The re-coloring process involves removing an edge, dyeing one of its endpoints with a new color, and retaining the original color for the other node. This approach utilizes $O(\sqrt{n})$ colors. Our primary technique involves a node sampling argument that proves the existence of a node subset with an edge subset exhibiting favorable structural properties. This subset is subsequently selected using only local information through a distributed algorithm, resulting in $O(\log^* n)$-rounds of communication. This work extends the findings of Elberfeld, Grohe, and Nuti (PODS 2017). Furthermore, we establish a lower bound of $\frac{1}{2} - \Theta(\frac{1}{\sqrt{r}})$ for $k$ in regular graphs with degree $r$. This finding corroborates the conjecture proposed by Elberfeld, Grohe, and Nuti (PODS 2017). Additionally, we provide an example illustrating that the current lower bound is tight when $\varepsilon$ is constant. Finally, we show that the problem remains $1$-source hard within the LOCAL model. This paper expands upon the abstract presented at ELDA 2019. This extended version incorporates several improvements, including enhanced lower bounds, updated references, and the inclusion of proofs for all claims. Notably, Section 4 addresses the lower bound for the specific case of regular graphs, while Section 5 details the lower bound's hardness in the LOCAL model. Furthermore, the lower bound proof has been refined to eliminate the need for an additional assumption. Section 2 provides an overview of the ELDA model, and Section 3 outlines the proof strategy. The remaining sections present the main results, with Section 3 focusing on random graphs and Section 6 covering arbitrary graphs. Section 7 presents an example of a graph that is $1$-source hard in the LOCAL model. Finally, Section 8 provides a lower bound for graphs with a regular degree of $r$. We establish specific hypercontractive inequalities for these weighted spaces and analyze the resulting relationships between the parameters $p, q, s$. Furthermore, we derive a two-sided estimate for a specific class of holomorphic functions on $\mathbb{D}$ under the same weighted setting. It is noted that findings regarding the unit disk extend directly to $\mathbb{C}^N$ by substituting the variable $z$ with $z'=(z_1,\dots,z_N)$. Additionally, we develop corresponding inequalities for the weighted Bergman space, which can be viewed as a particular case within the broader framework of Fock space. This work aims to advance the understanding of $\gamma$-weighted Besov spaces and provide a variety of "smoothing" inequalities for $\gamma$-weighted holomorphic functions on $\mathbb{D}$. Future research will address analogous problems on the Heisenberg group. Furthermore, the authors intend to explore $\gamma$-weighted Besov spaces in greater depth, with potential applications to $\gamma$-weighted Sobolev spaces, boundary value problems, and the theory of fractional derivatives. This approach will also facilitate the construction of fractional integrals on $\mathbb{D}$ that are dual to the proposed fractional derivatives. Detecting COVID-19 in CT images is challenging due to the subtle nature of the disease and the significant inter-patient variability in its presentation. To address this, we introduce a novel two-stage time-distributed capsule network (TD-TCN) that leverages low-dose, short-duration scans for diagnosis. Our approach first employs a convolutional neural network to extract deep features from the images. Subsequently, we apply a time-distributed capsule network to capture temporal dynamics, which enhances the detection of dynamic lesions caused by COVID-19. We validate our method using a diverse dataset of 1,000 images, comprising 500 from COVID-19 patients and 500 from healthy individuals. This study examines the distribution of Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites by national operator and their primary application domains, analyzing trends in the count of active satellites relative to time. Employing a statistical model that accounts for correlations between domain and nationality, we estimate the number of non-detectable active satellites to be approximately 300 ($\pm$ 80) as of 2019. Leveraging historical data from 2000 to 2019, we project the total number of active satellites to reach about 860 ($\pm$ 160) by 2025 and exceed 1300 ($\pm$ 200) by 2030. Additionally, by applying a statistical framework for pattern recognition, we identify this increase in LEO satellite density as a critical driver of future space traffic congestion. Consequently, we argue that the 300 currently undetected satellites constitute a primary, yet underappreciated, factor contributing to this congestion. Finally, we propose a statistical model to quantify the risk of satellite collision, which serves as a foundational step for space traffic management. By applying this collision risk model to our estimated satellite population, we calculate the probability of at least one collision occurring between 2019 and 2030 to be roughly 20%. This approach underscores the urgent necessity for effective space traffic management strategies. Furthermore, we estimate that 80% of all satellites are in orbits with an inclination of 90 degrees or less, indicating that the majority of LEO satellites occupy equatorial or near-equatorial orbits. We also outline the satellite distribution across six distinct application fields: Earth Observation (EO), Mobile Communications, Navigation, Weather Monitoring, Scientific Research, and others. The findings from this analysis are intended to support future LEO satellite deployment planning. Ultimately, we conclude that the growing number of LEO satellites poses a significant challenge to space operations, and that a robust legal and regulatory framework is essential to mitigate the associated risks. By synthesizing our statistical estimates with existing literature, we have identified the year 2025 as a potential tipping point for LEO satellite space density. This paper outlines a framework for generating coarse quad meshes with regular, topologically correct 4-valent quadrilateral grids for CAD models. The process begins by creating an unstructured, irregular, and generally non-quad mesh that is subsequently regularized into a quad mesh, which is finally coarsened to produce a coarse quad mesh. A critical requirement is a refinement function that converts the coarsened mesh back into a quad mesh, a challenge that a completely quad regularized, unstructured, and irregular initial mesh must address. The primary innovation lies in the coarsening stage, where multiple coarsening strategies are defined as possibilities within an Integer Linear Program. The optimization process identifies the optimal combination of these strategies to generate a coarse quad mesh that best satisfies the prescribed coarsening criteria. This framework is demonstrated through the 2D quad regularization of an axisymmetric 3D CAD model, where the coarsening problem is framed as either minimizing the area distortion of 3D elements or minimizing the geometric distortion of 2D elements. Results show that the resulting coarse quad meshes effectively balance the prescribed constraints, such as maintaining element aspect ratios and the total number of elements. Finally, the method is applied to create coarse quad meshes for the complete 3D, 2D-axisymmetric, and 2D cross-sectional representations of the Superconducting Tokamak Advanced Test (ST4A) CAD model. The paper concludes with a discussion on the framework's limitations and potential enhancements. (The methodology is implemented in QuadGen, a quad mesh generation tool developed by the authors.) The S-matrix approach to quantum field theory remains a source of ongoing debate. This discussion is revitalized by the recent resurgence of string theory, which originated from the S-matrix program. We explore a proposed modern formulation of the S-matrix method known as axiomatic crossing symmetry (ACS). In the classical limit, ACS yields a generalized Einstein equation (GEE) encompassing Einstein gravity, gravitoelectromagnetism, post-Newtonian theory, and a broad class of non-linear electrodynamics theories. We derive the solution to the GEE for a point charge or mass, known as the Liénard-Weiss vector potential and metric, demonstrating that this result is consistent with a subset of general relativity's non-linearities. Furthermore, we establish a correspondence between the field equations and the action for generalized Einstein gravity, followed by an analysis of small perturbations around this solution, which produces effects analogous to those in Einstein gravity. We also examine an alternative solution, the Bonnor metric, and its relationship with ACS-derived solutions for both electromagnetism and gravity. Finally, we test the Bonnor metric against the GEE, revealing that they are not equivalent. These findings suggest that the ACS framework may be more restrictive than previously believed, potentially hindering both quantum and classical applications of the S-matrix program beyond standard string theory. Additionally, we present a novel derivation of the Bonnor metric that appears to contradict an ACS-like property. We conclude by addressing various criticisms of the GEE, including its lack of general covariance, non-unique solutions, and incompatibility with string theory. We argue that these issues are either resolvable or stem from a misunderstanding of the theory's intended scope. Finally, we offer a critique of recent claims asserting that GEEs are incompatible with thermodynamics. Overall, we contend that GEEs represent a generalization of Einstein gravity that could provide valuable insights into quantum gravity. Specifically, we outline how quantum corrections could be incorporated into the GEE, thereby extending Einstein's quantum gravity program beyond string theory. This perspective may also inform the interpretation of quantum gravity effects observed in high-energy particle collisions. In this context, we address criticisms regarding the violation of energy and momentum conservation by GEEs and discuss the implications of these criticisms. We also evaluate criticisms concerning the non-conservation of gravitational energy-momentum within the GEE framework. The study stabilizes the three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations by implementing finite-dimensional feedback controls within critical $L^q$-based Sobolev and Besov spaces, excluding Helmholtz projections. These controls are implemented via sensors and actuators localized in specific subdomains. The stabilization is achieved through duality estimates and the application of the maximum principle to the heat equation. The stabilization function relies on the inner products of the velocity field with the first few basis functions of the spectrum of the Stokes operator. These interactions take the form of "damping terms" or "anti-damping terms," which can be either positive or negative and are applied through feedback controls with localized support. This approach extends the stabilization results previously established in the critical Sobolev space $H^{1/2}$. Notably, the required sensors and actuators do not need to be globally stabilizing; they can be confined to bounded subdomains that may even be disjoint. This requirement aligns with optimal sensor and actuator placement strategies, necessitating only local information regarding the velocity field. The stabilization is proven to be exponential. A significant portion of the paper addresses the challenges posed by the nonlinearity of the Navier-Stokes equations, specifically by utilizing trilinear estimates to handle the trilinear form associated with the convective term. This formulation involves trilinear products of the velocity field with the first few eigenfunctions of the Stokes operator. The stability result relies heavily on trilinear estimates that hold in the specific critical $L^q$-based Sobolev and Besov spaces under consideration. Consequently, this represents a novel and distinct stabilization result compared to existing literature. The paper concludes with several open questions concerning the stabilization of the Navier-Stokes equations. This work serves as a natural extension of the authors' stabilization results for the heat equation, as detailed in [1-10]. Furthermore, similar feedback stabilization techniques have been applied to the Navier-Stokes equations in prior studies [11-14], though those works typically employ global stabilization strategies. This current paper aims to address those open questions by providing a distinct stabilization result that achieves exponential stabilization using localized feedback controls.

Although the Open Source English Wikipedia represents one of the largest open-source encyclopedias, it remains inaccessible to users who do not speak English. To address this limitation, we present the LitMind Lexicon Dictionary, an online dictionary entry system built upon the LitMind multi-lingual cognitive computing platform. This framework enables users to contribute dictionary definitions in various languages, specifically allowing non-English speakers to access the encyclopedia in their native tongues. Currently hosted at www.litmind.com, the system supports a broad spectrum of input languages. The LitMind Lexicon is a fully functional intelligent dictionary that utilizes a variety of natural language processing (NLP) techniques to enable multiple functions, including lemma lookup, synonym suggestion, and definition generation. By leveraging the extensive corpus available on the LitMind platform, users can access definitions in their preferred language. Furthermore, we outline the platform's development roadmap and invite contributions from users and developers. This initiative aims to facilitate the creation of user profiles, encourage the development of additional NLP tools, and support the expansion of the dictionary entry system. Ultimately, we envision the LitMind Lexoon as a comprehensive knowledge graph accessible to a global audience. We welcome any collaboration or contribution from the community. For more information, please visit www.litmind.com. Additional details can be found at https://github.com/litmind/ litmind-lexicon and https://github.com/litmind/litmind-lexicon/wiki.
