Existing research on recommendation explanation methods has largely focused on generating local justifications, often neglecting the stability of these explanations across varying user-item pairs. This paper introduces a novel commitment-and-stability metric to evaluate the consistency of explanations for the global model. We also present a new framework called LIME-Transformer, which leverages transformer-based deep neural networks for black-box recommenders and employs attention maps to illustrate system behavior. Commitment-and-stability assessments were conducted on two datasets using sequence of length-biased, item-embedding, and transformer-based deep neural network recommenders. The findings indicate that LIME-Transformer significantly enhances the stability of explanations for black-box recommenders, surpassing the performance of state-of-the-art approaches. Furthermore, our LIME-Transformer explanations demonstrate strong correlation with both user perceptions and human expert interpretations. Additionally, we highlight that commitment and stability are more closely related to model interpretability than traditional fidelity. Finally, we make our code and data accessible at https://github.com/ashokkumar1992/LIME-Transformer.

The effectiveness of InAs quantum wells situated near the surface in serving as quality-gap materials for p-i-n photodiodes hinges on their ability to control Fermi level anchoring. This study examines, both theoretically and experimentally, how the thickness of undoped InAs quantum wells influences this phenomenon. Theoretical analysis indicates that the density of surface states declines as the quantum well thickness increases. This prediction is supported by experimental data showing that increasing the thickness of undoped wells shifts the Fermi level away from the valence band edge. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that a 10 nm thick undoped well is adequate to decouple the surface states from the empty-band region. These findings offer a robust design framework for developing high-performance wide-bandgap photodiode structures. Additionally, the paper explores the potential of InAs quantum wells near the surface as a general platform for engineering Fermi level positioning in p-i-n photodiodes. It outlines the necessary well structures to achieve the empty-band and absorption regions, while acknowledging that the surface region's impact on Fermi level anchoring in typical devices may be minimal. Finally, the study discusses the viability of implementing the proposed design using molecular beam epitaxy. This approach could enable the development of p-i-n photodiodes with extended spectral response and superior quantum efficiency. Specifically, such devices could be utilized in LiDAR systems to detect near-infrared laser pulses. The analysis reveals that undoped quantum wells with thicknesses between 2 and 4 nm are optimal for these applications. This design yields a significant bandgap increase, resulting in a substantial reduction in the photodiode's cut-off wavelength. Consequently, the resulting spectral response is well-suited for LiDAR applications. Ultimately, the proposed quantum well structure is expected to enhance the performance of Fermi-level-anchored p-i-n photodiodes. This improvement is achieved by expanding the spectral response range and boosting quantum efficiency. These gains are particularly relevant for near-infrared LiDAR systems, where the empty-band region is essential for effective target detection. The study concludes by detailing the specific surface structures that maximize quantum efficiency for p-i-n photodiodes. These structures are characterized by a minimal bandgap near the surface, thereby extending the spectral response range. The analysis confirms that the proposed quantum well design is compatible with existing fabrication techniques, such as molecular beam epitaxy. This compatibility ensures that the design can be readily implemented in practical devices. The paper also addresses the challenges associated with growing the required quantum well structures and offers potential solutions

Regional Correspondence Network (RCN) introduces a regional query mechanism that aggregates features from the same location across multiple instances to enhance robustness against perturbations. However, this study investigates when such mechanisms are beneficial versus when they may hinder adversarial robustness. We demonstrate that RCN can degrade resilience by over-relying on localized context, even against minimal perturbations. Consequently, we propose Local2Global (L2G), an alternative approach designed to mitigate these issues. Experimental results confirm that L2G achieves superior performance compared to RCN on both perturbed and clean data. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that perturbations often exploit the region's sensitivity to minute changes, a flaw that L2G effectively addresses. Finally, we apply the proposed method to the Urban Planet dataset, showing significant improvements in both accuracy and robustness. Building on the previous arXiv posting of our work, which introduced a Quick-Sinkhorn algorithm utilizing an adaptive triangular matrix to achieve an $O(N)$ average runtime for $N$-sized grids, this time, we present Quick-Sinkhorn II. This iteration employs a "collinear" matrix, which is more general than the "triangular" matrix used in the previous version. We demonstrate that this approach maintains the same $O(N)$ average runtime for the precise solution of Optimal Transport problems. Notably, the collinear matrix is significantly sparser than the adaptive triangular matrix, allowing for superior cache locality and memory efficiency. This makes it particularly advantageous for parallel computing on Graphics Processing Units (GPUs). Experimental results indicate that the algorithm is precise, delivering the exact solution at the same transport cost for both synthetic and real images, while running approximately 10 times faster on GPUs compared to current state-of-the-art methods. AU Microscopii serves as a critical benchmark for understanding the interaction between stellar winds and planetary atmospheres. This study examines the star's far-ultraviolet (FUV) variability across three epochs: one during quiescence and two coinciding with eruptive events. We analyzed 10 hours of FUV photometry from the Hubble Space Telescope's Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS) and obtained simultaneous far-UV and near-infrared (NIR) photometry using the ground-based MOST telescope. Our FUV data reveal a significant decline in FUV flux and FUV color index by a factor of 2.5 to 3.5 relative to baseline levels, a trend mirrored in the data. We identify a correlation between these FUV variations and H$\alpha$ activity, suggesting that the star's FUV output is intrinsically variable and likely modulated by the magnetic cycle. Additionally, we observed a substantial change in the most recent epoch that lacks a corresponding NIR signal, indicating that FUV flux variations are not solely driven by H$\alpha$ activity. We also detected a 0.01 mag change in the FUV color index between the most recent epoch and the baseline, implying that magnetic field configurations and/or chromospheric temperatures have altered. These findings support the conclusion that the FUV photosphere is highly dynamic. Furthermore, we observed a substantial increase in FUV flux during two eruptive events, with the most recent one showing a 100-fold increase. These FUV fluctuations are comparable in magnitude to those seen in other M stars. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the habitability of AU Mic b and c. We propose that frequent, large-scale FUV flux variations could sterilize or impede the development of life on these planets. Additionally, the high-activity levels observed in the most recent epoch suggest that both planets may have experienced significant biological impacts. These conclusions are reinforced by the fact that the FUV flux during the most recent epoch exceeds the maximum values recorded for the exoplanet host GJ 357. Consequently, AU Mic presents a unique opportunity to investigate the connection between stellar activity and planetary habitability. Future research should prioritize high-resolution FUV spectroscopy of AU Mic to investigate the link between stellar activity and planetary habitability. A particle's motion through a uniform, electrically conducting substance is governed by three primary forces: gravity, resistance (proportional to the square of velocity), and the interaction with the electric field generated by the medium. The particle's trajectory depends on its charge-to-mass ratio. When this ratio is sufficiently small, the particle follows a curved path driven by "radiation response drag," where the particle's own dipole radiation reaction force interacts with the medium's electric field. This phenomenon represents a novel form of radiation reaction; it causes the particle's trajectory to bend and ultimately settle into a steady state. The direction of the resulting drift is perpendicular to both the medium's current density and the gravitational force, distinguishing it from the magnetrophoretic effect, which occurs at large charge-to-mass ratios. Furthermore, the particle experiences energy dissipation via both the medium and radiation reaction, leading to a reduction in its kinetic energy. This reduction is not solely due to substance resistance drag but is significantly amplified by the radiation response drag, which is many orders of magnitude stronger than standard radiation reaction drag in vacuum. Consequently, this mechanism is particularly relevant for microscopic, highly charged particles (such as aerosols) traversing conducting fluids or plasma, though it may also apply to larger bodies under specific conditions. Additionally, the phenomenon has potential applications in particle separation and purification technologies. Finally, the paper explores the feasibility of detecting this effect through radiation emitted by the drifting particle. A key experimental signature is that the emitted radiation is linearly polarized, with an intensity that far exceeds that produced by standard radiation reaction drag. This robust experimental signature suggests that radiation response drag is a real physical effect. To detect it, an optical system with a narrow field of view, positioned to observe drifting particles, is required. The system must be sensitive to the specific radiation wavelength and capable of measuring its polarization. The paper outlines the design parameters for such an optical system. The study concludes that the existence of radiation response drag could have profound implications for astrophysics, including the evolution of charged aerosols, rain formation, and the charging of cosmic dust. It may also influence our understanding of charged particles and dust grains within planetary atmospheres and interplanetary space. Finally, the paper addresses the existence of radiation reaction drag relative to other model parameters. Specifically, within a gravitating, conducting, viscous, and radiating substance, there exists a critical charge-to-mass ratio; below this threshold, radiation response drag dominates, whereas above it, standard radiation reaction drag prevails.

The paper presents a novel approach to subset selection utilizing random feature mapping, which projects both training and testing data into a higher-dimensional space. This study presents the second data release of our ongoing survey to identify the brightest quasars at redshifts $z>2.5$ using SkyMapper Data Release 8 (SDR8). The survey targets a declination range of $-30^{\circ} < \delta < -10^{\circ}$ and a right ascension span of $18^{\mathrm{h}}$ to $21^{\mathrm{h}}$, covering approximately $1000\,\mathrm{deg}^2$. By applying photometric color criteria to SDR8, we discovered 11 new high-redshift quasars with photometric redshift estimates ranging from $z=2.6$ to $z>6.0$. These findings are complemented by a re-analysis of previously identified objects, yielding two additional bright quasars with spectroscopically confirmed redshifts of $z=3.0$ and $z=3.4$. Photometric analysis reveals that these ultra-bright quasars are luminous, with $L_{4500\,\mathrm{\AA}} > 10^{46}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$, and exhibit low dust extinction ($A_V < 1$). Furthermore, we estimate the bright-end slope of the bright quasar brightness function at $z=3$ to be $\alpha = -2.1 \pm 0.2$, indicating that the most luminous quasars are significantly more common than predicted by standard models. This result suggests that either the bright quasar population is heavily skewed toward extremely massive black holes, or that bright quasars at $z\sim3$ are exceptionally rare. Consequently, we propose that a significant fraction of these luminous objects may have been missed by current surveys. This study is the second in a series; the first will be published in a companion paper. The updated SkyMapper quasar catalog is accessible via the SkyMapper Data Portal. This study presents an experimental investigation into the exchange of electric charges between a quantum dot and a superconducting reservoir via the proximity effect. The dot was situated at the interface of two high-quality superconductors, one acting as a reservoir and the other as a terminal. By employing gate sensing, we measured the transferred charge as a function of d-wave pairing potential, bias voltage, temperature, and dot size. Our results show a clear dependence on all these factors, which we compare against both theoretical predictions and simulation outcomes. Our findings align closely with the mechanism of charge-tunneling from the superconducting reservoir into the dot, supported by theoretical and simulation data. Furthermore, the sensitivity of this charge-tunneling process to the superconducting pairing potential suggests its potential utility in investigating unconventional superconductivity. Additionally, this research holds promise for advancing fundamental studies of charge dynamics in hybrid quantum systems, which is a critical component for developing hybrid quantum devices. Finally, the observed effects may facilitate the investigation of proximity-induced superconductivity in quantum dots through radio-frequency gate sensing. These experiments were conducted using a high-impedance quantum dot, fabricated via an in-situ shadow evaporation technique, alongside a state-of-the-art radio-frequency gate-sensing setup. This comprehensive approach to studying quantum phenomena in hybrid quantum systems is expected to be valuable for future research. Finally, the experiments utilized a state-of-the-art dilution refrigerator operating at temperatures below 10 mK. Perpetual view generation aims to create novel views of a scene from a single input image, with recent approaches leveraging pre-trained 3D representations to synthesize these scenes and generate infinite new perspectives. However, a primary challenge remains the inconsistent quality of generated results, primarily caused by noise inherent in the 3D representations. To address this, we introduce DiffDreamer, a reliable framework that leverages conditional diffusion models to generate high-fidelity images. Unlike traditional methods, our approach does not rely on 3D volume constraints. Furthermore, we propose a conditional guidance strategy that integrates multi-view information and 3D volumes as conditions for the diffusion model, thereby enhancing both the fidelity and diversity of the output images. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, with quantitative metrics on the Plausible Scene dataset showing an improvement of over 0.03 in FID scores compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Additionally, we present a comprehensive ablation study to validate the contributions of each component within our framework. Finally, we demonstrate the method's effectiveness in generating high-quality images for virtual-to-real applications. Project resources can be found at: https://github.com/MyungJin/PerpetualViewGeneration. This work presents a prediction, power control, and data enhancement framework grounded solely in a linear state-space model. Unlike existing approaches that depend on system inputs and outputs, this method operates exclusively on data, utilizing a data kernel derived from the observability gramian of the networked process. The spectrum of this kernel offers insights into the process dynamics and the effectiveness of the prediction, power control, and data enhancement methods proposed herein. Specifically, regarding process control, the approach is applied to the SIS network epidemic model where the "power" of network nodes is regulated to suppress the disease. By solving a convex optimization problem based on second-order moments, the SIS model's data kernel can be optimized to eliminate infections. Furthermore, optimization is refined by incorporating network structural information to reduce costs and by addressing constraints on second-order moments to ensure problem feasibility. Numerical simulations confirm that, even with substantial initial infection levels, the SIS model can be cleared within a short timeframe. Additionally, the network structure reveals that a control cost of 1 is sufficient to eradicate the epidemic. Finally, the framework is applied to a small synthetic network to assess its performance in a model-free setting. Results indicate that while control costs are slightly higher, they remain within a reasonable range, and the disease is eliminated in a significantly shorter time compared to the SIS model. Consequently, this demonstrates that the proposed approach is viable for processes that are difficult to model. Simulations also reveal that the network structure influences the disease-free equilibrium state. Overall, the findings suggest that this methodology is effective for a broad class of networked processes. Furthermore, the predictions generated by the associated estimator are highly accurate for network processes. Most notably, this represents the first instance of a model-based estimator being analyzed purely from a data perspective. Additionally, a data kernel-based predictor for network processes has not previously been studied. Finally, the prediction capabilities of this framework are demonstrated through a case study of the US power grid. The associated predictor achieves a 99.9% accuracy rate in reconstructing power consumption for a region. Moreover, the predictor requires only a single region's data to function, eliminating the need for a process model. This underscores the potential of a data-driven approach for network process prediction. The associated source code is accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1992/DKPC. A thin, immiscible liquid film coats an elastic fibre within an immiscible bath. As the fibre rotates, the relative motion between the fibre and the liquid induces slip along the interface, significantly accelerating the slip-augmented Rayleigh-Plateau instability (SARPI) of the liquid film. This slip enhancement of Rayleigh-Plateau instability (RPI) is modeled using the lubrication approximation alongside slip-augmented Poiseuille flow. The slip component of the liquid's stress balance equation incorporates both lubrication and Poiseuille contributions, proportional to the slip length and shear stress, respectively. The primary slip effect is to amplify interfacial curvature, thereby accelerating SARPI. Notably, the most rapid growth mode is unaffected by the Poiseuille flow component of the stress balance, though this component does influence the optimal wavelength. These findings are benchmarked against experimental data. The study concludes that SARPI is a potent mechanism for shaping liquid droplets on rotating fibres. These insights may extend to other slip-augmented systems involving liquid films, such as capillary waves on a rotating soap bubble or droplets suspended from a rotating thread. The current model offers a framework for characterizing SARPI across a broader range of parameter values. Furthermore, the slip-enhanced growth rate of the fastest growing mode scales with the slip length as $\sqrt{\mu_{f}/\mu_{f}+\mu_{b}}$, where $\mu_{f}$ and $\mu_{b}$ represent the viscosities of the inner and outer liquids, respectively. This represents a substantial increase compared to the no-slip scenario, where the growth rate scales as $1/\sqrt{\mu_{f}+\mu_{b}}$. Consequently, a more permeable bath liquid can further accelerate SARPI. Finally, the slip-enhanced growth rate scales as $\sqrt{\Omega}$, where $\Omega$ denotes the fibre's angular velocity. This contrasts with the $\Omega$ scaling observed in purely hydrodynamic RPI, highlighting the distinct nature of SARPI. These findings are supported by both theoretical analysis and experimental validation. The slip effect is demonstrated to be more pronounced in SARPI than in pure hydrodynamic RPI. Overall, the slip effect is shown to be more significant in SARPI than in pure hydrodynamic RPI. These results suggest that SARPI is a more potent mechanism for droplet formation on rotating fibres than pure hydrodynamic RPI. This work investigates the stability of the Hunter-Saxton equation formulated as a flow on the projective Hilbert sphere. We establish Lipschitz stability for nearly sub-Riemannian geodesics, demonstrating that the Hopf-Laplace curvature of this sphere is singular, which precludes the existence of a sub-Riemannian geodesic spray. Furthermore, we prove stability within the projective special positive cone. Finally, we examine the influence of perturbations on the support of unit vectors. As an application, we demonstrates the stability of the Hunter-Saxton solution associated with a sequence of Fejer kernels. Additionally, we show that these specific solutions are uniquely determined up to isometries of the sphere and possess a Lipschitz continuity metric with respect to the initial data. These findings stand in contrast to recent results by Burbea regarding the non-uniqueness of geodesics starting from a fixed point $N$. However, this discrepancy does not contradict the existence and uniqueness theorem for sub-Riemannian geometry, as $N$ constitutes an abnormal initial condition. For such conditions, only abnormal extremals may arise, and they do not necessarily adhere to the Euler-Lagrange equations of the geodesic Lagrangian. In this specific scenario, the only abnormal extremals are constant curves. Consequently, the only critical curves for the geodesic Lagrangian at the point $N$ are constant curves, implying that no actual geodesics can originate from $N$. This conclusion aligns with our demonstrated instability in the positive cone, as no curve can maintain a constant direction in $\mathbb{R}^2$ while remaining confined to the positive cone. To address these findings, we propose an alternative initial data metric that exhibits Lipschitz stability for the associated solutions. We also present an explicit example illustrating the instability of perturbations on the support of unit vectors, thereby highlighting the necessity of the additional regularity condition imposed on the initial data in the original Hunter-Saxton paper. This condition mandates that the support of the initial data forms a closed set, thereby precluding oscillatory solutions. We demonstrate that oscillatory solutions demonstrate instability when subjected to perturbations. Additionally, we explore various applications of abnormal extremals in the context of the Hunter-Saxton problem. Finally, our methodology enables the extension of abnormal extremals to actual geodesics by utilizing a modified metric. The primary challenge in scoliosis assessment via robotic ultrasound (US) remains the difficulty patients face during manual scanning. This study aimed to evaluate the reliability of scoliosis measurements obtained through both manual and automated (robo) ultrasound techniques. Ultrasound images of the right thoracic region were collected from 20 healthy volunteers, and scoliosis metrics—including total angulation, upper and lower truncal rotations, and horizontal displacement—were calculated for each participant. The mean absolute error (MAE) and inter-rater coefficient of variation (CV) were determined for both methods. Results indicated that robo-scanning yielded scoliosis measurements with reliability comparable to manual scanning (MAE: 0.9°–1.5°; CV: 1.8%–11.1%). Consequently, robotic ultrasound emerges as a promising adjunct to conventional physical examinations and radiography in the clinical management of scoliosis. Key words: scoliosis, robotic ultrasound, reliability.

This study addresses the median-driven manipulation of speech duration across various clips. We assess the effectiveness of this approach by comparing the average perceived naturalness of evenly shortened median clips against those produced through traditional statistical methods. Our findings indicate that the median technique is effective for reducing clip lengths, resulting in a natural-sounding average with only a 1.5% increase in the mean number of dispreferred responses relative to statistical methods. Furthermore, applying the same principle to the non-statistical mean-blaster method yields the natural-sounding mag-blaster. By evaluating naturalness, semantic transparency, and the distribution of dispreferred responses, we conclude that both median-derived methods outperform their statistical equivalents in English, German, and Dutch. Additionally, when compared to statistical methods, the non-statistical approaches demonstrate superior performance across all three languages. Finally, we outline potential applications of these non-statistical methods in speech technology. Supplementary materials are available at https://osf.io/45q2b/. The code used to generate all figures and tables can be found at https://github.com/robertkoster/median-methods. With the rise of social media, online platforms have become increasingly susceptible to hate speech. This study introduces a novel approach utilizing Natural Language Inference (NLI) to detect hate speech. The proposed method focuses on identifying the target of the offensive language and extracting key features such as the target, sentiment, strength, and orientation from the text. These characteristics are then converted into a tensor and fed into a Siamese Network for hate speech classification. This technique, designated as NLI-Hate, is evaluated on the Target Detection (TD) task, representing a new perspective in social media analysis. The results demonstrate that the approach effectively identifies target information and achieves state-of-the-art performance on both the TD and the original NLI datasets. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar2001/NLI-Hate. Furthermore, the experimental outcomes indicate that the target detection component successfully identifies the target in 92.1% of cases. The author can be contacted at ashishkumar2001@iitkgp.ac.in. Keywords: NLI, Target Detection, Social Media, Deep Learning.

This paper introduces a novel, efficient feature sharing strategy designed to minimize parameter counts in end-to-end MIMO communication systems. The proposed approach employs an intermediate sharing mechanism at the encoder and decoder, where features are transmitted between sequential network layers. By reducing the depth of individual component networks, the method lowers optimization complexity and enhances performance. Experimental results demonstrate a significant parameter reduction of 51% alongside a 4.2% gain in Bit Error Rate performance compared to current state-of-the-art systems. Furthermore, the approach achieves a 2% improvement in Bit Error Rate relative to system-level quantization. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ehsan-nejati/MIMO-Share.

Historical research depends on digitized primary sources, including maps, manuscripts, newspaper archives, census records, and census maps. Access to these sources enables historians to investigate topics and scholars to verify citations. However, the vast volume of these documents often overwhelms researchers, making it difficult to locate specific information. Knowledge Graph-based Search offers a solution by allowing researchers to query historical data through semantic concepts. To facilitate the development of such systems, this paper introduces a comprehensive survey of public image datasets containing historical records. Our analysis covers datasets across seven categories: maps, manuscripts, birth and death records, newspaper articles, family trees, land records, and land surveys. We have compiled a survey of 60 datasets and identified key challenges in dataset preparation, such as annotation quality, class imbalance, and image degradation, as well as critical gaps in current research. We hope this survey will encourage further work on historical record datasets and support the advancement of historical research. The primary objective is to enhance system performance by increasing the sampling rate for derivative estimation. By utilizing auxiliary encoders, the proposed SBC method improves tracking performance. Formulated within a feedback linearization framework, the method compensates for nonlinear effects. To ensure robustness against model uncertainties and external disturbances, a robust control strategy is integrated with SBC. The validity of this approach was verified through experiments on a real DD robot joint, with results benchmarked against a conventional proportional-integral (PI) controller. Results indicate that the SBC method outperforms the PI controller in terms of both tracking accuracy and power consumption. Furthermore, the method demonstrates its effectiveness in achieving high-performance control, as evidenced by improved tracking precision. This confirms the efficacy of the proposed SBC approach for controlling DD robot joints. The study underscores the importance of the designed robust control strategy for handling model uncertainties and external disturbances. This study outlines the Multiple State Examination (MSE) framework, applied to real-world data, as a solution for analyzing multiple time-to-event datasets. In the absence of sophisticated alternatives, a complex correlation structure often results in significant Type I errors. By providing a novel analytical approach, the study aims to enhance the validity of statistical inferences regarding treatment effects in time-to-event analyses. The methodology was demonstrated using a dataset comprising patients who experienced myocardial infarction. The analysis examined the impact of a specific treatment on a subgroup of these patients, defined by a second event that could occur during any treatment period. This example illustrates a new capability to evaluate time-to-event data subject to an additional selection criterion, thereby generating a "time-varying" treatment effect. The study examines the mathematical foundations of the model, the correlation between time-to-event variables, and the associated estimation and inference challenges. The discussion focuses on the statistical and computational issues inherent in a complex model, the development of a multi-level analysis strategy, and the interpretation of the treatment effect. The primary statistical contribution lies in the multidimensional approach to time-to-event data, while the computational aspect involves a multi-level analysis strategy. From a practical standpoint, the study demonstrates how to analyze time-to-event data with a time-varying treatment effect and how to incorporate time-varying covariates into such analyses. Furthermore, the study explores the concept of "multiple state examination," offering a novel perspective on time-to-event analysis. This allows for the consideration of a patient's entire history rather than just a single point in time, facilitating a more comprehensive assessment of patient status. The MSA framework is also applied to a related dataset to examine how a patient's health trajectory evolves over time. This demonstrates how time-to-event data can be utilized to investigate how early-life factors influence later health outcomes. The study begins by detailing the data collection methodology and its implications for time-to-event analysis. Subsequently, the MSE model is presented, followed by a discussion of model fit and the interpretation of time-varying treatment effects. Finally, the study concludes with a discussion of the selection criteria applied to the patient subgroup and the broader implications of the MSA framework. The multiple state examination serves as a valuable tool for time-to-event analysis, offering a more nuanced understanding of how various factors influence a patient's health trajectory. This capability is particularly relevant in medical research, where such data is frequently available. This paper introduces a quadrature approach to solve the one-dimensional integro-differential equations governing the continuum spectrum of molecules. The technique is built upon a multi-site representation of the molecular Hamiltonian within a localized basis framework, which facilitates the efficient resolution of the continuum spectrum. The resulting quadrature functions accurately model the long-range behavior of wavefunctions and potential energy surfaces. Ultimately, this quadrature method achieves high accuracy with minimal computational cost. We successfully apply this approach to determine the continuum spectrum for various polyatomic molecules, including HF, H$_2$O, NH$_3$, and C$_2$H$_2$. Furthermore, the method demonstrates the ability to predict photoionization cross-sections. Specifically, for the C$_2$H$_2$ molecule, the computed photoionization cross-sections align well with experimental data. Additionally, the proposed approach offers a pathway to calculate two-electron wavefunctions for polyatomic molecules. These capabilities enable the derivation of electron-impact ionization and excitation cross-sections, as well as the inelastic and elastic scattering differential cross-sections. These outcomes are essential for validating the accuracy of the multi-electron multi-site method. Finally, the paper includes a description of a Fortran-90 code implementing the method, along with an analysis of its computational efficiency. All code and input files required to reproduce the presented results are available for download from the corresponding author's website. This methodology forms a key component of the QMulti framework, a general-purpose electronic structure program designed for both bound and continuum states. Details about QMulti can be found in reference [1]. Furthermore, the method is also integral to the MMS program, a general-purpose electronic structure code for bound states. Information on MMS is available in references [2–4].

We analyze parameterization via feedback vertex set, vertex cover, and similar structures. Our findings indicate that the problem is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by feedback vertex set, vertex cover, and treewidth. In contrast, we demonstrate that for a fixed integer $k$, it is NP-hard to decide if the metric dimension of an $n$-vertex graph is at most $k\log(n)$, implying that feedback vertex set, vertex cover, and treewidth are insufficient to establish fixed-parameter tractability. Furthermore, we show that parameterization by pathwidth does not yield fixed-parameter tractability, though it does admit a conditionally fixed-parameter linear-time algorithm. Finally, we prove that parameterizing by tree-depth results in fixed-parameter linear-time computability, contingent upon the ability to enumerate cliques in graph algebras—such as monoids or circuits—in fixed-parameter linear time. We introduce the concept of an authority framework, which endows a directed space with a hierarchy of subspaces characterized by specific directional properties, thereby modeling various forms of information flow within that space. We examine key categorical properties concerning these frameworks and their relationship with directed spaces, demonstrating that the hierarchy emerges naturally under a reindexing functor. Furthermore, we highlight a significant analogy with the hierarchy of algebras found in multidimensional directed spaces. Finally, we analyze the special case of a two-step authority framework, which models a bisource of information flow, noting its strong analogy with a statistical experiment composed of two interconnected information sources. This statistical framework is integrated into a larger analogy connecting our theory with statistical relevance logic. Additionally, we provide a sketch of a theory of categories equipped with authority frameworks, which serves as a many-sorted variant of the theory of framed categories. This latter concept is part of an analogy linking our work to a hierarchy of categories featuring dual frames, a hierarchy that arises under a functor similar to the one connecting directed spaces with authority frameworks to directed spaces without them. The paper concludes with a discussion of this analogy and its potential applications. This work serves as a foundational step toward developing a theory of relevant directed spaces, which are intended to function as the counterpart to multidimensional directed spaces within the realm of relevance logic. This parallel mirrors the analogy between directed spaces and pretopological spaces, as well as multi-dimensional directed spaces. The theory of relevant directed spaces is to serve as the multi-dimensional directed space analogue for relevance logic, in the same manner that directed spaces serve as the pretopology analogue. The analogy with pretopology stems from the functor that maps directed spaces to them by disregarding directionality. Similarly, the analogy with multi-dimensional directed spaces arises from a functor that eliminates dimensionality. Consequently, relevance logic is anticipated to be analogous to both pretopological spaces and multi-dimensional directed spaces. This analogy is also consistent with the approach of viewing relevance logic as a logic featuring two distinct types of conjunction. The first type of conjunction, which is commutative and associative, corresponds to standard conjunction in both directed spaces and pretopological spaces. The second type of conjunction is non-commutative and non-associative; it shares an analogy with multi-dimensional directed spaces as well as with directed spaces, since it is analogous to directionality in both pretopological spaces and directed spaces. Utilizing a coupled atmosphere-ocean model, we investigated climate dynamics within a 1.5-bar carbon dioxide atmosphere on an Earth-like planet. Recurrent, rapid exchanges of heat between the poles and equator drive episodic floods that temporarily reshape the landscape. These reconfiguration events are preceded by a significant lag in the planetary greenhouse effect, a phenomenon attributed to a delayed atmospheric response. This critical delay arises from the interaction between the thermal inertia of the oceans and the nonlinearity of the infrared opacity of carbon dioxide. Consequently, this mechanism facilitates a climate regime where liquid water can persist on the planetary surface despite high atmospheric temperatures. Our findings indicate that such a transient greenhouse climate, featuring warm air but cooler surfaces, may have been a common occurrence during the early stages of terrestrial planet evolution. This has significant implications for the long-term habitability of exoplanets. Specifically, our results suggest that even planets receiving a low stellar flux, such as Proxima Centauri b, could theoretically sustain a surface temperature low enough for liquid water, provided they possess an ocean and a sufficiently high atmospheric pressure. Furthermore, our simulations demonstrate that even minor fluctuations in the host star's luminosity can trigger catastrophic floods, implying that floodplain deposits found in extreme greenhouse climates on terrestrial planets could serve as valuable tracers for understanding the evolution of the planetary atmosphere and orbit. Finally, our analysis of the climate system's response to perturbations reveals that, in the absence of an active atmosphere, even a slight increase in the planet's orbital distance would be sufficient to trigger a runaway freeze. This implies that the presence of extensive ice caps in the present-day climates of simulated terrestrial planets could indicate that the planet formed around a faint star or experienced a significant decrease in stellar luminosity. These insights highlight the complex interplay between a planet's formation history and its long-term climatic evolution. In summary, our research underscores the intricate nature of planetary climate dynamics and the critical role of atmospheric and orbital evolution in shaping the habitability of exoplanets. By advancing our understanding of these dynamics, we can better predict the likelihood of life emerging and persisting on other worlds. Ultimately, this study highlights the complex and dynamic nature of planetary climates and the significance of atmospheric and orbital evolution in determining a planet's habitability. This extension is founded on the small gauge transformations of the holomorphic curvature, which carry both color and spin charges. A corresponding higher-spin, both-dual Yang-Mills extension can be derived through a complex conjugation operation. The action exhibits color and higher-spin charges arising from both holomorphic and anti-holomorphic transformations, with the latter being small and interpreted as general self-dual higher-spin transformations. Quantum corrections are shown to vanish due to the curvature's self-dual nature, mirroring the behavior in self-dual Yang-Mills theory. Generalizing the finding from the original extension, the higher-spin both-dual symmetry reduces to a higher-spin little dual symmetry in the self-dual sector, which in turn reduces to the higher-spin charge as a consequence of the equations of motion. These reductions are interpreted as additional transformations with only small gauge charges, consistent with both self-dual and complex-dual higher-spin transformations. Consequently, the action's higher-spin both-dual symmetry can be comprehended through the lens of self-dual and complex-dual higher-spin transformations. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success across numerous image processing applications, yet this success is often constrained by the presence of label noise, which can severely hinder model performance. This study introduces a novel framework designed to enhance data quality within annotated medical image datasets. Our approach utilizes Bayesian statistics in conjunction with deep learning to probabilistically identify and correct noisy labels. By employing a Bayesian minimum risk data-dependent rule, we effectively mitigate label noise, thereby improving DNN classification accuracy. We benchmark our method against state-of-the-art data augmentation techniques using various datasets, including two publicly available medical image categorization sets. This paper introduces the "Transition Probability Matrix" for a related random walk on a graph. Defined specifically for undirected graphs with non-negative weights, this matrix is stochastic and unitary, ensuring that all its eigenvalues are real, unitary, and of the first kind. We present two alternative definitions utilizing functions $f$ and $g$, respectively, establishing their equivalence through a lemma. Furthermore, we introduce the "Polynomial of The Transition Probability Matrix," offering its conceptual definition alongside an alternative formulation. This new polynomial is demonstrated to be orthogonal, with its degree equal to the number of partitions of an integer. The study provides numerical examples for the complete graph $K_4$ and the Petersen graph, illustrating the behavior of these matrices and their associated polynomials. Finally, the paper concludes with several open problems. This research was conducted in 2021. Timed definitions offer an alternative to traditional holdef, allowing holdef to be interpreted as a definition valid from 0 seconds onward. Alternatively, one can adopt a granular time-based approach, where each definition has a specific start time, effectively functioning as database views that reveal different aspects of a theory based on how long the researcher has spent deriving results. Although this concept may initially seem whimsical, it has significant practical applications, particularly within the Isabelle/TBT project, which aims to model the BT model checkers developed at Cambridge University. In that context, a theory is partitioned into subsets that become accessible only after a proof term is available, with each segment becoming available at a distinct time. This paper explores the challenges of implementing timed definitions within HOL and outlines our strategy for addressing them. The proposed solution is being developed using a definitional type theory framework, with the timedef tool currently under construction. We demonstrate the timedef tool's functionality using the BT theory as a case study. Finally, we address the theoretical implications of timed definitions on foundational issues, specifically the anti-foundational character of the BT theory. This study presents numerical simulations of turbulent incompressible channel flow at friction Reynolds numbers ranging from 3050 to 7200, utilizing the spectral element method. Leveraging existing numerical frameworks, we generated three-dimensional velocity fields to investigate how key structures within the inner layer influence coherent structure-based (CSB) models. Our approach incorporates three distinct enhancements to standard NSR08-type models: (i) a Fourier spectral representation of the mean velocity profile alongside the original parabolic-inharmonic form; (ii) inclusion of the three-dimensional component of the mean velocity profile; and (iii) a novel model integrating all three structures. We evaluated the turbulent skin-friction coefficient ($C_\tau$) and mean velocity profiles against experimental data. Results indicate that the third enhancement, which utilizes all three structures, yields the most accurate predictions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Fourier spectral representation of mean velocity provides superior modeling for various wall turbulence scenarios. Finally, we show that the proposed CSB models remain valid across a broad spectrum of wall turbulence conditions. These findings collectively suggest that the developed models hold significant potential for large-scale wall turbulence simulations. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive comparison of the computational costs associated with each model variant. This research supports the EP/H016105/1 (EPSRC) and EP/S000252/1 (EPSRC) grants. Magnetic flux applied to a two-dimensional lattice distorts the band structure, giving rise to the Hofstadler spectrum. This Hofstadler regime, characterized by a flux per unit cell that is a rational fraction of the flux quantum, generates a gapped bulk with a spectrum of Landau levels situated at the Brillouin zone boundaries. We demonstrate that applying a time-reversal-violating perturbation to this two-dimensional lattice semimetal transforms the bulk Landau levels into Weyl semimetal states, with the corresponding Weyl points positioned at the Landau levels. Furthermore, a novel Hofstadler Weyl semimetal emerges when a second, distinct type of perturbation is applied. Finally, we examine the Hofstadler Hofstadler regime, where the system operates within the Hofstadler regime while simultaneously experiencing a Hofstadler lattice deformation. In this configuration, the system exhibits a double-periodic spectrum, displaying characteristics akin to a two-dimensional photonics crystal. This spectrum features "Weyl lines" formed by the bulk Landau levels, alongside "edge Weyl points" situated at the boundaries. This system may be realized through a two-dimensional material embedded within a photonic crystal. Additionally, we explore the connections between this Hofstadler Hofstadler regime and recent findings regarding Hofstadler states within a photonic crystal. This study extends the definitions of the Hofstadler and Hofstadler domains into three dimensions, revealing a Weyl semimetal state populated by Weyl points, complemented by Weyl lines and surface states manifesting as Majorana fermions. These concepts extend to both electromagnetic and acoustic perturbations, suggesting the existence of Hofstadler domains within three-dimensional photonic and phononic crystals. Consequently, the Hofstadler domain is poised to become a significant area of research in these specialized materials. We present a hybrid dielectric-plasmonic nanoantenna system designed to enable effective photon sources. This setup, comprising a dielectric block and a metal nanoparticle, directs the non-radiative photonic and plasmonic polariton states to emit light in a specific direction. The dielectric material is doped with quantum dots (QDs) to act as the photon source, operating at a resonance frequency aligned with the metal nanoparticle's plasmon. This configuration creates a hybrid source that is both external and accessible. We demonstrate that this device functions as a unidirectional and luminous photonic-plasmonic polariton source, with the output intensity tunable via the optical properties of the QDs. This system is anticipated to find diverse applications in nanophotonics and quantum information processing. Furthermore, we illustrate the potential of this hybrid source in enhancing the nonlinearity of a third-degree nonlinear material, such as gold. This capability is crucial for the successful implementation of a Kerr nonlinear splitter based on a four-wave mixing mechanism within a waveguide integrated with the nanoantenna. Anomalous screening, a phenomenon where smaller particles preferentially fall from the gaps between larger ones rather than from beneath them, has been observed in both laboratory and industrial settings. This study investigates the mechanical dynamics of screening, focusing on the impact of particle size distribution. Our findings indicate that screening efficiency increases as the system moves from uniform to slightly polydiscrete states, after which it plateaus. To explain this behavior, we employ the Discrete Element Method (DEM) and introduce Anomalous Screening Theory (AST), a statistical model that predicts the long-term screening efficiency of both continuous and discrete size distributions. The agreement between AST and DEM simulations is excellent, with predicted and simulated screening rates differing by no more than 10%. Furthermore, AST successfully explains the initial segregation mechanisms in both dry and wet screening processes. By integrating AST with the wet screening literature, we demonstrate that anomalous screening offers a unifying principle that explains the fundamental mechanics of screening efficiency across various methods. Finally, we show that AST can forecast the effects of size distribution modifications on industrial screening applications. Overall, AST and the associated experimental data provide a comprehensive framework for quantitatively predicting and enhancing screening efficiency. The source code for AST is publicly accessible at https://github.com/JamesBuckingham1999/Anomalous-Screening-Theory. This study investigates the electronic properties of silicene supported on hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) with individual manganese (Mn) atoms adsorbed at various sites. First-principles calculations reveal that while pristine systems exhibit type-II electronic characteristics, Mn adsorption induces magnetic moments and transforms the band structure into that of a local magnet. Notably, the Mn atom favors the top Si-hBN interface, where it forms strong bonds with two bottom Si atoms. This interaction lifts the degeneracy of the silicon valence and conduction bands, creating a type-II electronic band structure with a reduced band gap. Furthermore, Mn adsorption induces an in-plane magnetic moment of approximately 4.95 $\mu_B$, of which roughly 3.5 $\mu_B$ is attributed to the Mn atom itself. The resulting magnetic moment is perpendicular to the system, and out-of-plane magnetization is anticipated to be lower than in-plane magnetization. These findings suggest that Mn-adorned silicene-sheets could serve as a foundation for developing spintronic devices. Additionally, the research examines the magnetic and electronic behaviors of the system across various Mn configurations, including bilayer setups. Finally, the study explores the potential for achieving spin-polarized electron injection into pristine silicene sheets via double Mn adsorption. These results highlight the electronic and magnetic tunability of silicene through Mn adsorption, offering promising prospects for future spintronic applications. Sgr A East, a radio source situated near the Galactic center, is believed to be the remnant of a supernova that occurred a few thousand years ago. The recent detection of a radio flare at the Galactic center's core, attributed to Sgr A*, has sparked speculation that it might be the source of the supernova responsible for Sgr A East. To evaluate this hypothesis, we analyzed the Sgr A East cloud using 12CO and 13CO J = 1-0 data from the Mopra telescope, alongside 13CO and 12C18O data from the Nobeyama Radio Observatory 45 m telescope. Our findings reveal a complex structure within the cloud, characterized by a prominent ridge of high 12CO/13CO intensity ratio running along the Sgr A East-Sgr A West axis, alongside a newly identified compact source of high 12CO/13CO ratio. This latter source is located approximately 0.5 pc from Sgr A*. We propose that a supernova explosion occurred roughly 2.5 ka ago at the position of this compact source, which lies at the boundary between the molecular clouds of Sgr A East and Sgr A West. The Sgr A East-Sgr A West axis represents a shock front generated by the supernova, with the Sgr A* region positioned near the edge of the Sgr A East-Sgr A West ridge. This research outcome provides a valuable framework for future investigations into the supernova event that formed the Sgr A East-Sgr A West cloud. The preservation of physical quantities serves as a rigorous benchmark for assessing the accuracy of numerical simulations. In the rapid multipole method, the conservation of angular momentum is maintained exclusively through exact arithmetic; consequently, when applied to floating-point arithmetic, this conservation law is not guaranteed. This work examines the failure to conserve angular momentum in such algorithms and demonstrates how to enhance accuracy by introducing specific correction terms. These corrections are derived using failure analysis based on the backward error analysis framework, which is the most prevalent form of error analysis in floating-point arithmetic. Furthermore, the study analyzes how these corrections improve accuracy across both near and far field regions, supported by error assessments through case studies. Additionally, the paper outlines several strategies for determining an optimal number of corrections to balance accuracy with computational cost. Finally, the angular momentum preservation property of the rapid multipole method, augmented with these failure-based correction terms, is validated within a simulation modeling the three-dimensional motion of charged particles under electromagnetic fields. This methodology offers a viable approach for accelerating the interaction evaluation between charged particles in electromagnetic simulations. Finally, the relationship between the number of corrections and computational cost is evaluated in the context of the rapid multipole method combined with particle-mesh E-field algorithms for charged particle simulations in electromagnetic fields. This relationship is quantified by several metrics, including computational cost, simulation duration, and error analysis regarding angular momentum conservation. Ultimately, these metrics provide a means to identify the optimal number of corrections that minimizes both computational expense and angular momentum loss. To the authors' knowledge, this represents the first investigation into the number of failure-based correction terms required to ensure the conservation of physical quantities when using the rapid multipole method within charged particle simulations in electromagnetic environments. Furthermore, the study addresses a broader issue: how to determine the optimal number of failure-based correction terms to mitigate the loss of physical quantities in any computational algorithm. This algorithmic approach is highly effective for correcting loss caused by finite-precision floating-point arithmetic, thereby enabling the design of more accurate computational algorithms. Specifically, it provides a means to identify the minimum number of correction terms necessary to eliminate loss entirely, thereby preventing unnecessary computational costs. Additionally, it offers a framework for selecting the optimal number of correction terms that achieves the highest level of accuracy for a given computational expense. Finally, the work provides a means to identify the minimum number of failure-based correction terms required to achieve the highest accuracy in any computational algorithm. By minimizing the number of correction terms, this approach reduces computational costs, offering a highly effective strategy for developing efficient computational algorithms. This paper introduces a new framework designed to assess the impact of data volume on the influence of features within supervised learning models that rely on external knowledge sources, or "authorities." The study demonstrates that when an authority functions as an efficient learner, the signs of feature correlations can be recovered from $O(N/\text{polylog}(N))$ examples, where $N$ represents the total number of features. Conversely, if the authority learns using the majority rule, recovering signs requires $O(N)$ examples. Extending prior work by Braverman, Kalai, and Leung (2013), we show that under weak assumptions, the algorithm can recover not only the signs of features interacting with a single bit but also those involving two bits. This note examines K3 surfaces featuring Siegel disks and investigates the arithmetic properties of their associated Picard groups. We derive effective upper limits for the algebraic multiplicity and the largest possible cardinality of these Picard groups. Furthermore, we demonstrate that infinite families exist with arbitrarily large dimensions, situated near families linked to Godeaux surfaces and Del Pezzo surfaces. Additionally, we explore how the moduli of these K3 surfaces can be represented within Shimura varieties and examine the rationality of points found inside them. Finally, we provide an overview of techniques for estimating the rationality of points in both moduli spaces and broader contexts. This work expands upon the final chapter of the speaker's PhD thesis, for which it serves as an inspiration. Several results presented here are based on the thesis, while others were developed in response to questions raised during the presentation. These findings are detailed in Sections 1, 2, and 3, with the final section providing an overview of methods for estimating the rationality of points in moduli spaces (Section 4). This paper introduces and analyzes the Randomized Newton Method (RNM) for stochastic convex optimization, a scenario where only unbiased stochastic gradient information is accessible. We then extend RNM to a distributed setting, yielding a novel algorithm called Distributed Randomized Newton (DRNM). We establish convergence rates for DRNM under diverse assumptions regarding the objective function and coordinate sparsity. Specifically, we demonstrate that DRNM achieves a linear convergence rate when applied to block-separable strongly convex functions with a condition number $\kappa$. By leveraging structural sparsity, we reduce communication overhead, allowing DRNM to reach a $\epsilon$-accurate solution using $O(\sqrt{\kappa\log_2(\epsilon)})$ communication rounds. We also present results for smooth non-convex functions with $\lambda$-strongly convex components and coordinate-wise $\mu$-strong convexity. Finally, numerical experiments on image processing tasks validate the superior performance of DRNM compared to other state-of-the-art distributed algorithms. Additionally, we explore a scenario involving variable communication rounds and prove the convergence of a proposed algorithm, highlighting the robustness of DRNM across various practical communication constraints. Furthermore, we address network failures in distributed optimization by proposing a novel algorithm that maintains robustness despite such issues. We provide convergence guarantees for this proposed algorithm under different failure conditions and establish its convergence under both successful and failed communication assumptions. Our numerical experiments confirm the efficacy of this approach, showing that DRNM outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. In summary, this work offers a comprehensive analysis of DRNM, establishing convergence rates under various functional assumptions and coordinate sparsity, while also considering practical communication constraints and network failures. These contributions pave the way for future research in distributed optimization. This research examines the task of identifying hate speech in Hindi and Bengali, focusing on the challenges associated with training deep neural networks on these languages. Additionally, we explore how pre-training on larger English corpora can mitigate these issues through the application of transfer learning. To support this effort, we have gathered and annotated a comprehensive dataset containing 1,00,000 examples of Hindi and Bengali text for both hate speech and non-hate speech categories. This open-source dataset is freely accessible to facilitate comparative analysis of various deep neural network architectures and their ability to generalize on limited training data. Our findings indicate that a Bidirectional LSTM model enhanced with a Contextual Word Embedding Layer (CWEL) achieves the highest accuracy, reaching 99.1% F1-score on Hindi and 98.1% F1-score on Bengali. Furthermore, we demonstrate that transfer learning from English significantly boosts performance on both languages. Specifically, models pre-trained on the larger Multilingual COWEL 1.0 corpus outperform those trained on smaller datasets by 1.5% on Hindi and 2.1% on Bengali. When fine-tuned on an expanded English corpus containing 100,000 examples of both hate and non-hate speech, the model reaches an impressive 99.6% F1-score on Hindi and 98.6% F1-score on Bengali. Our results also highlight that larger training datasets yield superior outcomes, and that the proposed model exhibits strong generalization capabilities across the three languages. We anticipate that the gathered data will enable researchers to develop even more robust models for multilingual hate speech identification. Gas time projection chambers (TPCs) function as detectors by recording the ionization produced when a target particle collides with a recoil nucleus. However, background signals from gamma rays and strays often mimic these ionization deposits, posing a challenge for tenuous targets. This study examines the feasibility of using tenuous gas TPCs as recoil detectors for dark matter, neutron, and other fixed-target experiments. We demonstrate that tenuous gas TPCs can distinguish ionization from recoil electrons by leveraging their three-dimensional spatial and temporal resolution. Specifically, we illustrate a discrimination technique that utilizes the drift time of ionization to separate signals from recoil electrons, gamma rays, and dark matter candidates. Our findings indicate that this method can substantially lower the recoil energy threshold for such detectors. We emphasize that the efficacy of this discrimination approach depends on the specific TPC design, particularly the tenuous gas pressure, detector volume, and drift time. Furthermore, we show that three-dimensional TPCs equipped with millimeter-scale pixel readout can achieve recoil energy thresholds an order of magnitude lower than those achievable using a single layer of ionization deposition. Additionally, we explore the potential for employing this capability to analyze the spin structure of dark matter candidates. Ultimately, we conclude that three-dimensional gas TPCs represent a promising technology for the next generation of recoil detectors. These systems could probe dark matter WIMP-nucleon cross sections down to $10^{-40}$ cm$^2$ (for a 10 GeV/c$^2$ particle) and serve as background suppression tools for neutron detectors in proton accelerator facilities. Commercial driving serves as a vital sector of daily life, encompassing roles such as trucking, delivery, and public transportation. Given the high stakes and safety implications, automated systems must handle driving tasks with precision. However, relying solely on commercial sensors to evaluate performance is insufficient; instead, the efficacy of these systems demands the integration of expert supervision. This study introduces a framework for supervised learning that manages uncertainty by combining machine predictions with human expert oversight. We demonstrate that this approach yields effective and fair performance assessments, utilizing uncertainty metrics to guide when experts should intervene in decision-making. Our findings indicate that incorporating expert supervision enhances fairness, improves overall performance, and reduces the frequency of human intervention compared to traditional supervised learning methods. These results hold significance for broader applications in high-stakes commercial environments. Furthermore, our proposed framework for intelligent systems with expert supervision is directly applicable to other domains, including medical diagnostics and legal proceedings. Finally, we demonstrate the framework's utility in commercial driving by applying it to two real-world datasets. The first dataset comprises simulated scenarios from a simulated semi-autonomous delivery robot, while the second consists of real-world data from a public transportation system. Both datasets illustrate the framework's practical implementation and its benefits in ensuring fairness and reliability within automated decision-support systems. Our work advances existing research by offering a more reliable method for supporting expert judgment and by providing a more nuanced understanding of how and when human-machine collaboration should occur. This study investigates spin transport through a narrow armchair graphene nanoribbon by analyzing the impact of on-site spin-orbit coupling (SOC) and exchange fields. The findings indicate that both the transmission probability and the spin polarization exhibit oscillatory patterns as a function of energy. Notably, the spin polarization can be smoothly tuned from 0 to 100% by adjusting the on-site SOC strength. This controllable spin polarization stems from the energy-dependent shift in the real part of the self-energy. Furthermore, the exchange field influences the spin polarization without altering the transmission probability. These results suggest that the proposed model holds promise for developing spin-related devices. Additionally, the study offers a viable alternative to the commonly used zigzag graphene nanostructures, which are typically associated with a robust, stable spin polarization. Finally, the effect of electron-electron interactions is examined, revealing that the spin polarization remains robust even under strong interaction conditions. These outcomes demonstrate that the on-site SOC-strength-tunable spin polarization is highly resistant to various forms of disorder. Consequently, this model is expected to find applications in spintronics. To facilitate experimental realization, we have designed a feasible setup for a realistic three-terminal setup. This configuration involves attaching leads to the side of the graphene nanostructure and applying perpendicular electric fields via back gates and an atomic force microscope. Such a design is practical for fabrication and could enable the observation of the predicted spin-related phenomena. We anticipate that these findings will contribute to the advancement of nanoscale spintronic technologies. To support these conclusions, we have included supplementary materials with additional details. We hope this work inspires further research in the field of nanoscale spintronics. A graph $G$ is defined as pancyclic if it contains cycles of every length from $3$ to $n$, where $n$ represents the order of $G$. The autonomy number $\alpha(G)$ is determined by the smallest integer $k$ such that $G$ remains pancyclic after the removal of any $k$ edges. This paper investigates the conditions under which a graph is pancyclic based on the Hamiltonicity of specific spanning subgraphs formed by deleting a small set of edges. Furthermore, we establish that the graph $K_{1, n-1} + e$ possesses the maximum autonomy number among all $n$-vertex graphs, and we derive an upper bound for $\alpha(G)$ using the minimum degree of $G$. The outward time-dependent Schrödinger equation incorporates a DC field within a complex scaling framework. This approach proves highly effective for investigating atoms and molecules subjected to intense constant electric fields. By utilizing a carefully selected complex scaling angle, the outward scheme successfully captures the correct tunneling probability across a broad spectrum of DC field strengths and initial states, all at a minimal computational expense. Furthermore, by steering clear of the self-adjoint extension issue common in inward schemes, the outward method offers greater simplicity and robustness. These advantages establish outward complex scaling as the preferred algorithm for constant DC field problems in atoms and molecules. Additionally, the work examines the influence of the initial wave function on tunneling ionization rates, employing Gaussian wave packets centered on various atomic orbitals to model the initial states. Finally, the outcome demonstrates that Gaussian wave packets positioned away from the nucleus yield higher tunneling rates than those centered on the nucleus itself. This finding contrasts with recent reports regarding Dirac wave packets and aligns with earlier research indicating that the position of the wave function packet significantly impacts tunneling probability. These results offer valuable insights for future tunneling ionization studies. Furthermore, the study investigates tunneling rates for molecules under DC fields, revealing that molecular tunneling rates are highly sensitive to the orientation of the molecular axis relative to the DC field. Finally, the paper concludes by outlining the potential of this framework for analyzing more complex systems. Specifically, it suggests that extending the technique to moving frames could facilitate the study of tunneling ionization induced by ultra-short laser pulses. Additionally, the method is anticipated to enable the study of tunneling ionization dynamics in molecules within time-dependent fields, thereby providing a more comprehensive understanding of tunneling ionization. Finally, the tunneling ionization of molecules is expected to serve as a critical test for theoretical models of tunneling ionization. The future applicability of this approach to molecules will be essential for developing new theoretical models of tunneling ionization and for testing these models against experimental data. The Sinkhorn algorithm is a prominent iterative technique for solving the Schrödinger problem, yielding the unique optimal pair of plans $(\pi_1, \pi_2)$ when a solution exists; however, such a solution does not always exist, particularly when the support of $\mu \otimes \nu$ excludes pairs $(x, y)$ with a finite cost $c(x, y)$. This study demonstrates that, given any coupling $(\bar{\pi}_1, \bar{\pi}_2)$ that maximizes entropy among all marginal couplings for $\mu$ and $\nu$, the Sinkhorn iterates $(\pi_{(n)}, \pi_{(n)})$ converge weakly to $(\bar{\pi}_1, \bar{\pi}_2)$, thereby generalizing prior findings. This result relies on a novel characterization of the set of marginal couplings with maximum entropy, derived through an auxiliary relaxed Schrödinger problem. Furthermore, an explicit formula is provided to express $\bar{\pi}_1$ and $\bar{\pi}_2$ in terms of the unnormalized densities $f_{(n)}$ and $g_{(n)}$ generated by the iterates. Finally, examples illustrating the failure of prior results are presented, alongside numerical evidence confirming the convergence of the Sinkhorn method even when these previous approaches are inapplicable. Additionally, the article concludes with an analysis of the failure mode, specifically regarding the behavior of the entropies of $\pi_{(n)}$ as $n$ increases. This study details an analysis of top quark pair production at a center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV using the ATLAS detector at the LHC, based on an integrated luminosity of 2 fb$^{-1}$ collected during the LHC Run 2. This study examines the localization dynamics of a quantum two-mass model featuring unequal masses and a centrally positioned $\delta$-barrier that couples the masses, which otherwise move and couple locally in isolation. We demonstrate that within the energy interval $[0, V_{0}]$, bound states transition from being delocalized to localized as the coupling constant $V_{0}$ increases, with the localization exponent rising monotonically. Furthermore, we establish the existence of a critical constant $V_{c}$ such that states are fully localized for $V_{0}>V_{c}$ and fully delocalized for $0<V_{0}\leq V_{c}$. Numerical simulations confirm these analytical findings, illustrating the evolution of quantum states from partially localized to fully localized configurations as $V_{0}$ grows. Additionally, we analyze the impact of two key parameters: the mass disparity and the potential strength. Our results indicate that increasing the ratio of the lighter mass to the heavier mass accelerates localization, whereas a stronger potential $V_{0}$ within the two-cavity system impedes this process. Finally, we examine the localization dynamics by monitoring the time-dependent probability distribution function. These findings offer valuable insights into controlling quantum state localization and may have applications in quantum information science. Additionally, we outline potential extensions of this research. Finally, we provide detailed implementation details for conducting these experiments, including the necessary equipment and step-by-step procedures. Urban interaction patterns serve as the foundation for analyzing city dynamics, making their study essential for urban planning. However, these patterns can be disrupted by factors such as the pandemic and lockdowns. This research examines how the pandemic altered interaction patterns in New York City across various income levels, with a specific focus on the resulting disparities. The study reveals that while the pandemic initially narrowed the gap in interaction frequencies between these groups, it subsequently widened the gap in interaction types and sizes. Furthermore, distinct disparities in temporal behavior were observed between the pre- and post-pandemic periods. Finally, specific characteristics of New York City's pandemic trajectory were identified as key drivers of these shifts in temporal, spatial, and typological disparities. These findings provide new insights into the socio-spatial consequences of the pandemic, underscoring the necessity of targeted urban policies to ensure equitable access to the benefits of a liveable city. Additionally, the study offers a comprehensive framework for analyzing the disparities of urban behaviors during the pandemic, which can be applied to other cities with different pandemic experiences. Residual-based variational multiscale methods (RBVMS) have demonstrated a superior convergence rate compared to standard finite element techniques when applied to challenging porous media flow problems. This study extends the previously developed field-split RBVMS framework to handle porous media with varying permeability by evaluating several nonlinear field-split variational multiscale preconditions. The work begins with a review of the nonlinear field-split RBVMS framework, followed by a detailed presentation and analysis of four preconditioning strategies. Finally, numerical experiments on a two-dimensional heterogeneous J-curve test case assess the influence of permeability contrast and anisotropy, as well as capillary dominance, to determine the optimal preconditioner for such scenarios. These tests involve solving the multiphase flow system using the black-oil formulation. The results indicate that, for the examined permeability contrast, the cross-flow pressure-based preconditioner performs best in heterogeneous media, while the cross-flow velocity-based preconditioner yields the most accurate and rapid convergence in anisotropic media. Furthermore, for highly heterogeneous cases, a preconditioner combining pressure and velocity components achieves the most efficient convergence. In all configurations, the RBVMS framework significantly enhances convergence relative to the baseline mixed finite element method. However, convergence remains sensitive to the numerical grid; specifically, the method performs best on meshes with a regular structure and a coarse-to-fine transition near the transition zone. Consequently, applying this approach to realistic heterogeneous reservoir models requires an unstructured mesh with a carefully selected transition region. Additionally, the study demonstrates that the black-oil formulation is susceptible to phase segregation issues, which can be mitigated by adjusting the time step. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive examination of the applicability and efficiency of various nonlinear field-split RBVMS preconditioners for two-phase flow in heterogeneous porous media. Finally, the high performance of these preconditioners in resolving the two-phase heterogeneous J-curve problem suggests their potential effectiveness for other complex flow scenarios, such as miscible flow.
