This paper derives the strong orthogonality relation, Beersma's relation, and the asymptotic behavior for polynomials $P_n(x)$ that are orthogonal against a logarithmic weight function $\omega_n(x) = \prod_{j=1}^n (x-\xi_j)$. The analysis covers the general scenario where $\xi_1, \ldots, \xi_n$ form arbitrary perturbations of the roots of $z^n - 1$, alongside the limiting case where these roots coincide at zero. The findings rely on a newly established asymptotic relation between the corresponding Jacobi matrix entries and the separation distance among the roots of $\omega_n(x)$. Furthermore, the asymptotic behavior of the Christoffel-Darboux kernel is derived. We demonstrate that, provided the separation distance remains bounded away from zero, the asymptotic behavior of $P_n(x)$ mirrors that of the Hermite polynomials. In contrast, when the separation distance approaches zero, the limiting behavior aligns with that observed for the polynomials orthogonal with respect to the weight $e^{-x^2/2}$. Additionally, we present the first instance of the strong orthogonality relation, which extends the well-known Beersma relation applicable when $\xi_1, \ldots, \xi_n$ are roots of $z^n - 1$. This relation expresses the product $\prod_{j=1}^n P_n(\xi_j)$ as a linear combination of principal minors of the Jacobi matrix, with coefficients that are polynomials in $n$. Finally, we outline the application of these results in the context of the inverse spectral problem. Specifically, we derive an explicit formula for the distance between the roots of $\omega_n(x)$ given the asymptotic behavior of the diagonal entries of the Jacobi matrix, thereby recovering a result by J. Van Iseghem.

Human evaluation remains a critical component of research, yet recruiting crowdsourced workers for such tasks presents difficulties. This study investigates the challenge of identifying suitable workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) for summarization evaluation, specifically examining the impact of instructions and prior experience. Results indicate that crafting precise instructions can significantly boost the proportion of high-quality responses, while also revealing that the majority of workers possess general writing skills rather than domain-specific expertise. Although targeting workers with relevant background is ideal, sufficient qualified workers can typically be found by providing clear instructions. To assist future researchers, we release a resource comprising 1,442 worker profiles, including their written outputs, instructions, and in-session writing metrics, which are available at https://github.com/joshuagentry/nturk. We hope this tool will facilitate improved targeting of crowdsourced annotators in summarization and related fields. Finally, we apply this resource to evaluate the reliability of crowd-sourced labels in summarization, demonstrating that with carefully crafted instructions, the performance of crowd-sourced labels approaches that of native speakers. This offers a cost-effective alternative to the time-intensive process of gathering native speaker labels. Our code and instructions for recruiting are available at https://github.com/joshuagentry/nturk. Additionally, the paper details the recruitment of workers for summarization, outlines the recruitment process, and provides a guide for creating reliable crowd-sourced instructions. The code used to analyze the data is also included. We hope this resource will enable other researchers to replicate our findings and explore the recruitment of workers for other NLP tasks. Text-video retrieval (TVMR) is a critical yet difficult task that demands a robust grasp of video content and a robust index to manage the massive scale of potential video candidates. To address these challenges, we introduce the Token Shift and Choice Transformer (TS2-Net), a novel architecture designed to extract kernel clips and aggregate token representations. We observe that relative shifts between adjacent tokens effectively capture kernel clips, while the choice transformer facilitates the video aggregation process. This network structure is lightweight, enabling efficient training and rapid inference. Extensive experiments across two public datasets, LSV2 and LSV2C, demonstrate that TS2-Net achieves state-of-the-art performance. Furthermore, an ablation study on the mLV0 dataset confirms the model's effectiveness. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/Chenchen2020/TS2-Net. Finally, the model is deployed on the open-source server at https://demo.mlv2.org/ts2-net. We hope this resource will be valuable to the community. Although no beyond-Standard-Model effects have been detected to date, the abundant data available from current and upcoming LHC runs could reveal such phenomena. We investigate the structural characteristics of directed hybrid random networks formed by combining two growth mechanisms: preferential attachment and uniform attachment. In this model, new nodes are introduced into an existing network of $n$ nodes, where the probability of connection to node $i$ is proportional to $d_{i}^{in}+2d_{i}^{out}+3$. Conversely, the uniform attachment mechanism dictates that new nodes connect to existing nodes with a probability proportional to $1$. This study analyzes the structural properties of this hybrid network, demonstrating that it behaves similarly to a pure preferential attachment network. Specifically, we establish that the degree distribution follows a power law, the diameter scales logarithmically, and the diameter is approximately $\frac{\log n}{\log \log n}$. Furthermore, these structural traits remain consistent regardless of the initial network configuration. Finally, we extend the analysis to a more complex network where connection probabilities are proportional to $x d_{j}^{in}+(1-x)d_{j}^{out}+y$, with $x$ and $y$ representing constants. For this scenario, we determine the conditions under which the degree distribution adheres to a power law and derive the resulting degree distribution along with the logarithmic scaling of the diameter. Additionally, we derive the Hausdorff dimension for this extension using random walks. To support our findings, we include simulations. The results indicate that while the degree distribution remains a power law, the diameter is no longer guaranteed to be logarithmic, and the degree distribution exhibits asymmetry. We attribute this asymmetry to the extension's increased complexity. We conclude that the directed hybrid network is an appropriate model for systems exhibiting the "rich get richer" phenomenon. Furthermore, the extension of this network is well-suited for systems where one direction of communication is more critical than the other. This conclusion is backed by an example of a communication network, where the proposed model can be applied to determine the most effective route for message delivery. Finally, we propose that the combination of preferential and uniform attachment mechanisms serves as a viable approach for constructing random networks. This combination offers a straightforward method for generating networks with the desired properties, such as a power-law degree distribution. We also discuss potential future research directions. The study confirms that small-world characteristics are preserved in both the preferential attachment case and, more significantly, in the more complex scenario. Multimedia content, including video and audio, is increasingly being consumed across various digital platforms. However, this material can be interfered with by a diverse range of wireless devices operating in the air. These digital disturbances are unavoidable and are typically categorized into two types: analog, such as static and digital noise; and digital, such as short packets and bitstreams. To mitigate the impact of such analog and digital interference on digital transmission, researchers have developed several mitigation techniques. These methods are critical for ensuring the quality of service in emerging applications like 5G, the Internet of Things (IoT), and autonomous driving. This paper introduces a deep learning-based machine learning approach utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to detect simultaneous interference in the 2.4 GHz band. The proposed system is designed to identify a variety of disturbances, encompassing both analog and digital modes. Experimental results indicate that the method achieves a precision of 98.2% and a recall of 97.3%. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the CNN architecture is capable of learning and distinguishing between different types of simultaneous wireless disturbances. This technique is applicable to software-defined radio (SDR) platforms and can be deployed on edge computing devices to monitor and mitigate interference in real-time. Additionally, the approach is scalable for use across diverse wireless technologies, such as Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and ZigBee. The proposed solution is expected to significantly enhance Quality of Service (QoS) in next-generation communication systems. Additionally, it is anticipated to assist wireless engineers in diagnosing and troubleshooting complex interference issues in wireless networks. A Python implementation of the proposed method is available at: https://github.com/abdullahkaya1999/wireless_interference_detection. The corresponding source code can be found at: https://github.com/abdullahkaya1999/wireless_interference_detection/tree/master/MLCNN. The vorticities $\xi$ of a Klein-Gordon field are examined within the Som-Raychaudhuri spacetime, representing a cosmic spacetime characterized by non-zero twist and charge. This metric, representing a specific class of spacetimes, describes a static, cylindrically symmetric gravitational field generated by a moving line of dust, featuring a finite self-twist. We establish that the relationships between vorticity, charge, energy, and angular momentum mirror those found in classical particles. Specifically, we derive a classical-like correlation between a Klein-Gordon particle's charge and its twist. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Klein-Gordon space-time twist corresponds to a vortex line density in the charged particle's wave function. Consequently, we conclude that the twist of a Som-Raychaudhuri cosmic string manifests as a field vortex. These findings hold significant implications for understanding the physical nature of Klein-Gordon particles, including their internal angular momentum, and for modeling vortex-like structures in superfluids and superconductors. Finally, the associated correlations are used to suggest a method for generating vortices. These results are expected to facilitate the investigation of similar correlations for other field twists in various cosmic spacetimes. Additionally, the corresponding correlations for a Dirac field have been identified. The study begins with the identification of the Som-Raychaudhuri metric and its associated geodesic equations, followed by the identification of the Klein-Gordon field's twist and its relationship to the field's vortex line density. Finally, the correlations between twist, charge, energy, and angular momentum are derived. Given the established analogy between classical particles and their field counterparts, these results are also applicable to classical particles. Finally, the resulting vortex generation method is applied to a classical particle. A Boolean algebra $\mathcal{B}$ is defined as locally $\sigma$-complete if every $\sigma$-closed filter intersects, and as locally normal if its conditionally convergent filters are normal. The primary objective of this brief note is to demonstrate that $\mathcal{B}$ is locally $\sigma$-complete precisely when it is locally normal. This result holds general interest within lattice theory and lattice theory grounded in measure. Consequently, for any locally convex Hausdorff space $E$, the collection $\mathcal{B}_E$ of Borel $\mathcal{B}$-ideals defined on $E$ constitutes a locally normal Boolean algebra. Since $\mathcal{B}_E$ lacks a countable generating $\sigma$-closed filter base, it follows that $\mathcal{B}_E$ is not $\sigma$-complete nor $\sigma$-finite. Furthermore, the algebra of Borel $\sigma$-algebras is inherently $\sigma$-finite. We present a theoretical framework for experimentally observing a shift in the thermal modification of superfluidity within a lattice system of ultracold bosons featuring spin-orbit coupling. This modulated shift in the transition temperature arises from the competition between superexchange interactions driven by tunneling and those generated by long-range Coulomb forces. This phenomenon may be observable using current experimental techniques. Specifically, we outline a protocol to detect this effect in optical lattice systems involving spin-orbit coupled $^{41}$K atoms, suggesting that such transitions could be verified with near-future technology. Furthermore, this approach may hold significant relevance for understanding the physics of correlated bosons. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of these findings. Structure and graph embeddings of Cayley graphs associated with finite abelian groups. Let $G$ denote a finite abelian group and $\mathcal{C}(G)$ represent the collection of all generating sets for $G$. The embedding number of $G$, denoted by $\text{emb}(G)$, is defined as the count of non-isomorphic Cayley graphs formed by all elements in $\mathcal{C}(G)$. This paper investigates the embeddings of finite abelian groups within various graphs, with a specific focus on cycles, paths, and trees. We demonstrate that $e(\mathbb{Z}_p) = 1$ for any prime $p$, establishing that every Cayley graph of a prime group is both degradable and planar. Furthermore, for an arbitrary finite abelian group $G$, if $G^\circ$ signifies the subgroup comprising all elements of order 2 in $G$, then $\textemb(G) = \textemb(G/G^\circ)$. We provide a complete classification of Cayley graphs for the group $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$ that admit an embedding in the projective plane. Additionally, we establish that the degenerations of these Cayley graphs are limited to the projective plane, the Euclidean plane, or the sphere. Finally, we outline an algorithm for constructing embeddings of Cayley graphs derived from finite abelian groups.

However, this design faces significant challenges, particularly from beam-induced noise generated by backscattered muons striking the beam pipe and striking the beam itself. Consequently, strategies to mitigate these effects are crucial for achieving the performance needed to uncover new physics. This paper outlines various mitigation tactics, including reducing the beam pipe's inner radius, lowering background levels via advanced detector design, implementing event selection methods, and minimizing systematic uncertainties through event-by-event measurements. Additionally, the study provides a detailed analysis of the most promising mitigation approaches for the Vertex Etalon 3.5 TeV (VE3.5V) detector concept. These tactics could serve as a foundation for evaluating other mitigation strategies and may be applicable to other hadron-induced collider environments. Ultimately, this work aims to facilitate a comprehensive comparison of vertexing capabilities among various proposed detector concepts. We introduce Spartan, a framework designed to learn sparse models by applying a mass regularization term that penalizes the count of non-zero weights. This approach achieves regularized learning differentiability through a "conveyance" function, which maps model capacity to the average wavefunction curvature of individual weights. Spartan models can be trained via gradient descent to maintain a predefined sparsity level throughout the training process. When applied to ResNet models trained on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets, Spartan successfully learns compression strategies without sacrificing accuracy, often surpassing the performance of standard models. Furthermore, Spartan significantly outperforms existing sparse models in inference speed while retaining comparable accuracy. Additionally, we demonstrate that Spartan can discover structured sparsity, such as channel sparsity in CNNs and input sparsity in MLPs, by incorporating a minor network reconfiguration step between training iterations. Finally, we illustrate that Spartan can identify interpretable sparsity patterns in fully connected networks trained on MNIST and EMNIST datasets. A comprehensive codebase for Spartan, including various sparsity configurations, is available at https://github.com/StanfordVL/Spartan. The Pauli principle is a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, dictating that fermions cannot occupy the same state, a constraint that generates unique many-body behaviors. In contrast, bosons can freely share quantum states. This study demonstrates that an effective Pauli obstruction arises in weakly interacting Bose fluids when their de Broglie wavelengths interact strongly with the system's Pauli length. The obstruction manifests as a finite momentum gap in excitation spectra and suppressed de Broglie condensation. We establish that this phenomenon results from a quantum geometric contribution to enthalpy that becomes significant under these conditions. By employing both static Debye screening and dynamic deconfined quantum chromodynamics, we show that this Pauli-effectiveness in Bose fluids can be significant. Specifically, we predict that Bose-Einstein condensates may form within the interior of neutron stars, driven by the pairing of polarized deconfined quark-like degrees of freedom. Consequently, these findings may enable the observation of the Pauli obstruction in Bose fluids, offering a potential pathway to uncover a quark-like phase inside neutron stars. Finally, our results provide a comprehensive framework for investigating an effective Pauli principle across diverse physical systems. Notably, we identify that a Pauli obstruction exists in the interior of neutron stars, alongside a deconfined quark-like phase, with many of these features being experimentally accessible. This represents a significant advancement in the investigation of many-body quantum effects. Furthermore, our findings offer a unified framework for understanding Pauli obstructions in Bose fluids, which may help explain the enigmatic presence of protons inside neutron stars. Overall, our findings offer a unified framework for understanding the enigmatic presence of protons within neutron stars. Test odors are undesirable practices that hinder the testability of software systems. This study investigates the severity of test odors from a developer's perspective. Through an online survey, we gathered responses from 100 software engineers with a mean experience level of 11.5 years. Our findings indicate that developers perceive code containing test odors as more difficult to comprehend and maintain, and they anticipate that these odors will lead to an increased frequency of code changes. Additionally, developers expect that adhering to refactoring guidelines for test odors will enhance the modularity of test code. We also examined the relationship between the perception of the severity of test odors and the adoption of tool support for detecting them. The resulting model demonstrates that developers who view test odors as severe are more likely to utilize tool support for their detection. This evidence suggests that developers recognize the benefits of managing test odors and are motivated to eliminate them. The study's limitations and avenues for future research are also discussed. The paper concludes that test odors represent a significant issue that should be prioritized for further investigation. Finally, we suggest that the Software Engineering community should prioritize research on the actual impact of test odors on software products and their development processes. Additionally, we advocate for a shift in focus from the practicality of test refactoring to the creation of effective tool support for test refactoring. We contend that tool support for test refactoring is more critical than it currently is, as this area remains significantly under-researched. Furthermore, we argue that the practicality of test refactoring is less important than previously thought, as developers are already actively working to eliminate test odors. We contend that the importance of tool support for test refactoring is greater than many researchers believe, and that the importance of test refactoring itself should be reconsidered. Finally, we recommend that the importance of tool support for test refactoring be elevated, as this remains an area that requires much more attention. The online survey is titled: "Developers' perception of the seriousness of test odors." Its subtitle reads: "An empirical study."

We introduce {\tt KKMCee}, a flexible Monte Carlo event generator designed for electron-positron annihilation, specifically tailored for precise studies of Higgs boson formation at future lepton colliders. The tool covers the creation of lepton and quark pairs through various channels, including tree-level processes, Z and $\gamma$-boson fusion, as well as WW and ZZ-boson fusion. Implementations are provided for Higgs boson production alongside final-state photons, as well as final-state top quark pairs. Beyond these, we have incorporated the production of bottom quark pairs via photon-photon fusion, utilizing both light and heavy photon components. These features facilitate the analysis of Higgs boson production mechanisms and the associated production of a second, distinct scalar particle, such as a heavy CP-odd state, occurring through photon-photon or WW-boson-associated production. The output quality is assessed against experimental data and measurements from prior simulations. Our findings indicate that the inclusive cross section for photon-photon induced $b\bar{b}$ production, incorporating both real and effective light and heavy photon contributions, aligns well with results from the PHOTOS and PPHEGS software packages. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the inclusive cross section for top quark pair production at the ILC can be normalized to experimental data with an accuracy of approximately 1\%. Finally, we illustrate how the relative rates for different production channels can be determined by normalizing to data, and how branching ratios and coupling constants can be extracted from the resulting cross sections. These capabilities are particularly relevant for investigating final-state particles resulting from the decay of a single, yet undiscovered, scalar particle at future lepton colliders. Additionally, we examine the significance of photon-photon induced production for $b\bar{b}$ and $t\bar{t}$ production, as well as WW-boson-associated production of a heavy CP-odd state, in the context of searching for a new scalar particle at the International Linear Collider (ILC). To facilitate this, we have also included an option to vary the transverse momentum cut for final-state vector bosons. The source code for {\tt KKMCee} can be accessed at \url{https://github.com/ChengFengDing/KKMCee}, and user documentation is available at \url{https://chengfengding.github.io/KKMCee-doc/}. Future updates will incorporate additional production channels and final-state particles, alongside various radiative corrections.

We investigate methods for modeling the temporal evolution of undirected and undweighted social networks. In these communities, new members join over time, existing connections form, and the participant set can also shrink. We introduce and examine various techniques for creating low-dimensional, time-specific, dense, and accurate network representations. Our study covers both supervised and unsupervised approaches. Specifically, for prediction tasks, we demonstrate that even with a sparse input graph, simple models can achieve strong results if they effectively leverage data from the dense preceding time step. Additionally, we present several projection-based techniques that model the temporal process by treating it as a sequence of time-specific sparse graphs, which are then embedded into a low-dimensional dense space. These are contrasted with methods that directly embed a single, unified temporal graph. Our experimental results indicate that low-level projection-based models often outperform direct models in accuracy. Finally, we introduce our novel Graph Evolution Embedding (GEE) model, which outperforms all other methods in prediction and achieves competitive performance for downstream tasks. GEE models the evolving participant set as a sequence of independent single-time-step graphs and projects them into a shared latent space using a single, unified projection model. We also explore extensions of GEE that incorporate spatio-geographic information and temporal dependencies among time steps. Finally, we provide Python code for all comparison models, which are part of a new open-source library called Pyevolve. Investigating the structure of very neutron-rich nuclei presents a significant challenge, necessitating measurements of life-time, half-life, and reaction cross sections alongside theoretical analysis. This study examines the $^7$H resonance generated via the $^6$H(n,$p$)$^7$H reaction. The resonance was identified by measuring the excitation function of the reaction, analyzing neutron spectra from a $^{12}$C target using the LEPSI spectrometer at the LNL-TRISTAN accelerator, and studying the $^7$H energy loss in a plastic scintillator. The resulting $^7$H width is determined to be $\Gamma = 1.1 \pm 0.4$ MeV, aligning with prior experimental data. The measurement of the total momentum of the $^7$H in the target frame allowed for the determination of its life time as $\tau = 1.05 \pm 0.15$ fm/c. These findings are compared with theoretical predictions derived from both no-core shell model and three-body cluster model calculations. The results confirm the existence of a narrow, low-lying state situated 0.7–1.4 MeV above the $^3$H+$4n$ threshold, which exhibits a highly excited configuration. Furthermore, the derived life time and width suggest that this state possesses a cluster structure composed of a $^3$H core surrounded by four neutrons. Consequently, this research demonstrates that neutron emission can occur from a nucleus without passing through the ground state. The findings are also discussed in relation to other similar narrow resonances, such as the $^5$He ground state and the $^9$H narrow low-lying state. The success of Deep Learning hinges on the quality of feature representations, which are essential for both algorithmic interpretability and human understanding. This paper introduces a representation learning framework grounded in supervised manifold learning. By utilizing an embedding function, we map data points onto a manifold. The quality of this embedding is evaluated through Sinkhorn distances calculated between manmifolds and both training and testing datasets. Consequently, representing learning is formulated as an optimization task designed to minimize the Sinkhorn distances for training data pairs while simultaneously maximizing the minimization for training-testing data pair pairs. The framework's effectiveness is validated using the CIFAR-10 and MNIST datasets. The resulting optimized representations are subsequently employed as inputs for a classifier. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on CIFAR-10, outperforming all baseline methods. Furthermore, our method matches the accuracy of the MNIST AlexNet architecture. On average, we secure the top rank across four out of six datasets when compared to existing supervised manifold learning techniques. This study employs a stochastic SIR model to simulate the impact of contact tracing on COVID-19 transmission within a population in England, where individuals can belong to multiple tracing collaborations. We demonstrate that when participation in these collaborations is random, transmission is reduced by up to 50% compared to no tracing, with the specific outcome depending on collaboration size, membership distribution, and the proportion of collaborations exceeding the critical reproduction number. Furthermore, transmission is significantly lower than in the random tracing scenario across a broad spectrum of collaboration size and membership parameters, provided that approximately 10% of collaborations have a size exceeding the critical threshold. This result holds true even when the basic reproduction number for COVID-19 is 2.5 and is independent of infection duration. Finally, our findings indicate that interventions aimed at creating larger collaborations can substantially enhance the efficacy of contact tracing programs. These insights are derived from an analytical approximation of the distribution of individuals across collaborations of varying sizes, which remains valid for scenarios with at least two collaborations. Additionally, we discuss how these results can inform the design of effective contact tracing initiatives. The model simulations were conducted using Python and PySBench. We establish a bound for the expected Betti numbers of a random level set of a Gaussian polynomial, conditioned on the event that the zero level set is exceptionally sparse. This estimate is expressed through Gaussian correlations and remains valid for polynomials of varying degrees up to approximately $n^{1/3}$, where $n$ represents the dimension. Given that the sparse regime lies well beyond the critical threshold, we anticipate that the Betti number bounds can be further refined in lower regimes. Additionally, we demonstrate that for sufficiently sparse zero level sets, the expected Betti numbers are governed by the number of sign changes. Finally, we examine a scenario with vastly different characteristics: we analyze the behavior of Betti numbers in random polynomial zero level sets when restricted to the fewest possible number of sign changes. In this context, we show that the expected Betti numbers are generally small, although we observe a notable exception in the case of Gaussian polynomials with quadratic degrees. This exception stems from the presence of caustics, which are highly concentrated structures inherent to quadratic maps. We illustrate how this phenomenon occurs in quadratic maps and elucidate its underlying causes. Furthermore, we explore the implications of this phenomenon for the case where quadratic maps are defined over projective space. Our findings are supported by numerical computations. Eyebots are emerging robotic systems designed to provide first-person visual monitoring for humans, making the calibration of their extrinsic parameters crucial for downstream applications. However, traditional calibration techniques struggle with eye-in-hand robots due to challenges in accessing the robot's joints and designing appropriate calibration objects. This study introduces a novel approach to estimating the extrinsic parameters of eye-in-hand robots using a single RGB image. By leveraging the geometric consistency between a real-world capture and a synthetic counterpart, our method enables back-projection of 2D keypoints to estimate the transformation matrix between the camera and the robot. We validated this approach in an indoor setting, achieving an average error of 0.01 meters in position estimation and 0.03 radians in rotation estimation against ground truth values. Furthermore, we demonstrated that these parameters can facilitate object detection by validating the method's efficacy using OpenCV's SIFT keypoint extraction and YOLOv3 network. The corresponding source code is accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan123/Eye-in-Hand-Calibration. In summary, this paper presents a new technique for estimating extrinsic parameters of eye-in-hand robots from a single image, validating the approach's effectiveness through both robot calibration and object detection. The method's simplicity and efficacy suggest it could enable the development of new robotic systems. We hope this research encourages further investigation into single-view calibration for eye-in-hand robots. We introduce Reverse Constrained Reinforcement Training (RCRT), a framework designed to reverse engineering learning rules from observed behaviors. Our primary objective is to derive a constrained optimization framework that is consistent with a specified training dataset. Consistency is defined as the capacity of the learned model to reconstruct the entire training dataset. To achieve this, we develop an efficient and systematic approach for learning the reverse constrained optimization framework using a proposed reverse inference algorithm. Furthermore, we demonstrate that RCRT can effectively reconstruct both training and testing rulesets in Concept Learning and can also recover structural elements from neural networks. This makes our work the first instance where a comprehensive learning rule can be successfully reverse-engineered. Additionally, empirical results show that models trained via RCRT achieve performance comparable to that of forward learning rules. GAIA, a mission by the European Space Agency's Science Programme, is designed to survey the entire sky, cataloging up to one billion stars with high precision. The mission will generate comprehensive 3D maps of Galactic stars and the local interstellar medium, detailing their positions, distances, and parallaxes with an accuracy of 10%. Additionally, it will significantly enhance measurements of proper motions and helioseismic radial velocities. By analyzing the colors and brightness of stars across 46 bands, GAIA will determine absolute magnitudes and interstellar extinction. The survey will also report relative transverse motions within the Galactic disk, offering unprecedented insights into the kinematics of individual stars and the collective motion of stellar groups. The interstellar medium will be mapped through relative radial motions. Furthermore, GAIA will generate high-resolution images of bright stars and astrometric images of faint stars. This paper outlines the scientific objectives of GAIA and the data products it will deliver. It also addresses the challenges posed by the mission's extreme data volume and the novel data analysis techniques required to process it. Finally, the paper highlights the synergies between GAIA and other major astrometric and Galactic surveys. This work introduces a novel vertex divider that, when applied to a graph together with an optimal branch decomposition, partitions the graph into two sections whose combined treewidth exceeds the original treewidth by a constant factor. Assuming the Exponential Time Hypothesis, the existence of such a divider implies that the $P$3-SET-COVER problem is NP-hard on graph classes defined by treewidth-bounded branch decompositions. The concept of employing dividers to establish lower bounds for algorithmic problems was first proposed by Bodlaender et al. in 2015; this paper presents the first application of that technique to a problem other than vertex cover. Additionally, the study investigates how to minimize the increase in treewidth caused by the divider, demonstrating that the optimal branch decomposition does not always indicate the best divider. The research concludes by identifying graph classes for which no divider exists that increases treewidth by a constant factor. Finally, the paper presents a new exponential-time algorithm for the feedback vertex set problem, which, when combined with a specific divider, achieves a worst-case running time that improves upon the best known polynomial-time approximation algorithm for feedback vertex set, assuming the Exponential Time Hypothesis. This outcome is part of a broader trend where the divider enables the design of more efficient algorithms on general graphs by adapting solutions created for graphs with excluded minors. The article also examines the trade-off between the running time of algorithms and the treewidth inflation introduced by a divider. Furthermore, the authors present an algorithm that, given any graph and a tree decomposition, constructs a divider that achieves minimal treewidth inflation. This construction runs in linear time relative to both the input size and the square of the treewidth of the provided decomposition. Finally, the study explores the relationship between vertex dividers and separators, presenting an algorithm that, for any graph with a known separator system, produces a vertex divider that can be converted into a separator with comparable size. The paper concludes by investigating the problem of identifying a small vertex divider for a given graph. The authors establish that this problem is fixed-parameter intractable with respect to the treewidth, and, under the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis, it lacks a polynomial-time $(|V|^{1-\epsilon})$-approximation algorithm for any $\epsilon > 0$. However, they also present a fixed-parameter linear-time algorithm for this problem when the graph class is restricted by a treewidth-bound. The study ends with an analysis of the relationship between separators and vertex dividers.

Recent years have seen a surge in the adoption of network and graph theory to model complex systems across diverse fields. These networks, characterized by nodes and edges, serve as the foundational framework for analyzing interactions among physical or conceptual entities. However, network models vary significantly in the types of systems they can represent and the nature of the systems they describe. This study aims to elucidate the underlying assumptions and conceptual requirements necessary to derive meaningful insights from networks, with a specific focus on the attributes and characteristics of individual nodes and edges. We examine how the nature of a network's edges influences its interpretation and application, particularly in contexts where edge data is either directly observed or inferred. These considerations are especially pertinent to systems exhibiting heterogeneity in the properties of their constituent elements. By addressing these issues, we clarify the validity and limitations of various analytical methods. Furthermore, this work serves as a comprehensive introduction to networks, their analysis, and the challenges inherent in their construction. The proposed methodologies and examples are intended to assist researchers in developing and interpreting new network models. Our approach is grounded in the extensive experience of the authors in applying network theory to a wide array of biological and social systems. We advocate for a more critical evaluation of the data used to define nodes and edges, as well as the analytical techniques applied to them, thereby enhancing the reliability of the resulting conclusions. This paper provides foundational guidance for researchers aiming to construct networks from inferred or measured data, offering strategies to ensure the robustness of their analytical outcomes. Additionally, we outline key considerations for researchers in emerging disciplines seeking to formulate innovative and effective network models. Ultimately, this work seeks to facilitate a more profound understanding of the opportunities and limitations of network models, thereby advancing their application in both fundamental research and practical settings. This initiative is essential for ensuring that new analytical and modeling tools are appropriately utilized and that the valuable insights they provide are correctly interpreted. We illustrate these points through numerous examples, many of which are derived from our own recent studies.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) represent a method for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) by utilizing the solution's a priori knowledge to enhance model performance and reduce the reliance on extensive labeled datasets. However, the PINN framework is vulnerable to the hallucination of false data, which can compromise the integrity of the solution. To address this, we introduce a post-hoc error estimation technique that serves as a detection mechanism against hallucinations in PINN solutions. This approach is grounded in a novel concept of a posteriori authorization derived from a multiphysics perspective. We validate the effectiveness of this error estimation method through various benchmark PDEs, including those with incomplete training data, and by applying it to forecast sea surface temperatures using multiple PINN configurations. Our findings demonstrate that this method reliably identifies erroneous PINN solutions without altering the network architecture or introducing modification costs. Furthermore, the technique exhibits robustness across different PINN architectures and is capable of distinguishing between erroneous and correct solutions. Finally, we argue that this error estimation approach can be extended to other machine learning frameworks, offering the means to assess solution validity and reliability. While epidemiological studies have established the health risks of particulate matter (PM), the specific pathways linking exposure to disease remain unclear. This paper outlines current atmospheric contamination models used in such research, emphasizing their integration with geostatistics and machine learning. We examine both monitoring-based and satellite-based models, detailing their mechanisms and applications. Furthermore, we address the challenges in creating robust models that accurately estimate both spatially and temporally resolved exposure data and individual-level concentrations. Linear contextual bandits are a widely adopted framework for sequential decision-making, where agents select actions based on partial observations of underlying distributions. This study examines a generalized framework featuring action sets of varying sizes, demonstrating that standard regret analysis techniques fail in this context. We introduce a new framework that yields a logarithmic regret bound and reveal a critical limitation in this setting: it becomes impossible to recover the true linear model parameters even when all action sets are available. To address this challenge, we propose two novel heuristic methods for inferring unobserved parameter vectors. We evaluate these approaches using synthetic data and validate their efficacy on a real-world application involving product recommendation. Furthermore, we conduct comprehensive ablation studies to assess the performance of both heuristic methods. Finally, we suggest several promising avenues for future research regarding this problem. Our work aims to stimulate interest in linear bandits with diverse action sets and to promote a more rigorous understanding of the inference challenges inherent to this framework. Although the orbital Hall effect in time-reversal symmetric systems is generally considered non-local and difficult to detect, we demonstrate that in graphene quantum dots, it generates a measurable current. Specifically, in a time-reversal symmetric two-valley system, this effect can be detected via transport experiments without needing to break time-reversal symmetry. In this regime, chiral edge states cross the sample's center, and their motion is influenced by an orbital magnetic moment derived from an orbital magnetic field. This phenomenon, akin to the orbital Hall effect in bulk materials, serves as an alternative to valley Hall effect-based methods for exploring this field, which is a promising approach for valleytronics. The orbital magnetic field can be tuned by adjusting the shape of the graphene domain, making it a highly promising tool for investigating this previously elusive field. Additionally, we examine how this orbital magnetic field impacts the valley polarization of the current. This polarization is a fundamental characteristic of valley Hall devices, which are essential for developing valleytronic technologies. Furthermore, we show that valley polarization can be enhanced by introducing a symmetry-breaking perturbation, such as strain, that suppresses the orbital Hall effect. This finding is significant for designing optimal valley Hall devices, where maximizing the separation between valley Hall currents is crucial. Consequently, our study holds dual importance for both fundamental research and practical device applications. Notably, our work highlights the potential of graphene quantum dots as a platform for investigating orbital physics, a field that has been largely inaccessible in this system until now. This is particularly relevant for quantum dot spin qubits, where orbital degrees of freedom play a critical role in qubit operation. Our findings may aid in optimizing the performance of existing qubits and guide the design of future ones. Moreover, our results may pave the way for realizing the Kerr Kerr interaction in graphene quantum dots, a step toward achieving a quantum simulator for the Kuramoto model, a promising development for quantum information processing. Finally, our findings may contribute to the development of a new generation of graphene Hall bars, where valley polarization is maximized, thereby advancing the field of valleytronics. This could lead to the creation of highly efficient valley Hall devices capable of operating at higher temperatures. To achieve this, we propose a device geometry where valley polarization is significantly improved compared to conventional Hall bar designs. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are machine learning models specifically engineered for processing data on graphs, demonstrating strong performance in fields like chemistry and physics. However, their performance can be severely compromised when trained on maliciously altered graphs. This study investigates whether reinforcement learning can be utilized to introduce graph contamination to deceive GNNs. We formulate this graph contamination problem within a Markov Decision Process (MDP) framework and propose a novel algorithm called REINFORCE-GNN to solve it. This approach employs reinforcement learning to learn a policy that maximizes the decrease in a GNN classifier's accuracy. Experimental results on the OGBlbfg graph dataset demonstrate that the solutions generated by REINFORCE-GNN successfully deceive the GNN classifier. Additionally, we analyze the computational complexity of our proposed method. Finally, we highlight ethical considerations and potential applications of graph contamination using reinforcement learning, such as graph attacks and adversarial testing. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/rahul-agarwal19/REINFORCE-GNN.

Catalogue matching serves as a critical yet computationally demanding task in modern astrophysics, demanding high precision and recall. While a given catalogue may contain millions of sources, cross-matching algorithms can be restricted by specific user-defined constraints. Although a catalogue source ID is essential for research, such identification might not be possible for every object during initial discovery. Consequently, even with optimal user settings, certain identifiers may remain unidentified. This paper introduces a catalogue matching algorithm designed to enhance the recovery of previously matched catalogues by leveraging additional photometric data. By training a multi-class neural network on photometric information, the method achieves a 10% increase in recall for sources with IDs compared to traditional 2D cross-matching techniques. Furthermore, the study explores the potential for improving recall among sources without IDs by training the model on such cases. Ultimately, this approach aims to facilitate research on a broader range of astronomical sources. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1996/cataloguematching. This work is based on the author's undergraduate thesis completed at the University of Oxford, which utilized data from the ZTF Legacy Survey. Additionally, the research was supported by a Google Summer of Code grant from Google. The findings are currently under review by Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society. Keywords: methods: data analysis, methods: machine learning, methods: statistical, cosmology: multivariate analysis, cosmology: multivariate analysis.

This paper demonstrates that for any hypergraph $\mathcal{H}$ defined on a set $X$ where the union of all edges is exactly $X$ (i.e., $\bigcup \mathcal{H} = X$), every minimal base of $\mathcal{H}$ can be expressed as a union of disjoint minimal edge covers. Consequently, this implies that the property of having a base representable as the union of disjoint minimal edge covers is hereditary. Furthermore, the article provides an explicit method for constructing such a base. The results presented here serve as an extension and refinement of the classical inclusion-exclusion formula applied to the probability that the union of events is complete. Specifically, the inclusion-exclusion formula can be derived from the construction process used to determine the existence of a base. Ontologies serve as formal frameworks for knowledge, enabling machines to comprehend the relationships between various concepts. While traditional ontology visualization techniques are designed for browsing small to medium-sized collections (typically under 1,000 classes), they struggle with large-scale ontologies containing thousands of classes and hundreds of properties. This paper introduces OntoPlot, a new visualization system that employs a multi-level strategy to enable efficient navigation of large-scale ontologies. The results demonstrate that OntoPlot offers a superior user experience compared to other existing visualization approaches. Additionally, version 1.0 of the OntoPlot software is now publicly accessible at https://ontoplot.org. This tool is developed in collaboration with the University of Vienna, the Austrian Academy of Sciences, and the Austrian Research Centers. It supports multiple formats, including RDF6 and the proprietary OntoPlot format, and provides a browser interface for rendering OntoPlot graphs of large ontologies. Users can navigate these graphs using both mouse and keyboard controls. Furthermore, the interface allows for browsing and searching classes and properties across three dimensions: IRI, label, and URI. A three-pane layout facilitates side-by-side comparison, while a built-in data analysis feature allows users to identify the most frequent class and property types. A sample OntoPlot graph of the DBpedia ontology is available at https://ontoplot.org/demo, and a blank instance can be accessed at https://ontoplot.org/blank. The interface also supports loading and comparing versions of the same ontology from different sources. Users can switch between two graph views: the default circular view and a tree-like hierarchical representation. A sidebar allows for the selection and activation of different relationship types, enabling users to browse specific aspects of the ontology. A search function allows users to quickly locate and highlight classes, properties, or instances. Finally, a visualization settings panel allows users to customize their graph view, including options to display or hide specific relationship types. The tool further supports exporting graphs as images in various formats and includes a link to the original ontology for direct browsing. This interface is compatible with all major browsers, including Chrome, Firefox, and Safari. The authors welcome feedback and suggestions for future improvements. This study addresses cross-domain automatic speech recognition (ASR) through a semi-supervised, end-to-end approach utilizing both supervised unsupervised domain adaptation (SUADA) and unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) techniques. SUADA remains the preferred method for the speech community due to its lower complexity compared to state-of-the-art UADA approaches, despite recent efforts to enhance it. Our work focuses on enhancing semi-supervised ASR systems by integrating a recently proposed SUADA system with the latest state-of-the-art UADA framework for self-supervised domain penalization, yielding three key improvements:

1. We demonstrate that SUADA is viable for scenarios where UADA alone is insufficient to solve certain challenges.
2. We show that combining SUADA and UADA achieves superior performance compared to SUADA used in isolation.
3. We provide evidence that this hybrid approach can significantly reduce the data requirements for SUADA systems.

To validate our findings, we applied these methods to a challenging task involving two datasets with substantial domain divergence: LibriSpeech and VCTK. Our results indicate that SUADA and the combination of SUADA with UADA strategies can substantially lower the data needs for state-of-the-art ASR systems. Specifically, we utilized only 100 hours of supervised data for ASR and 100 hours for the model-free domain penalization task. Conversely, SUADA achieved these results using a larger supervised dataset, while the combination approach used a medium-sized one. This underscores the effectiveness of our proposed methods in scenarios where data availability is constrained. Additionally, we demonstrate that SUADA remains a viable solution for very low-resource environments, such as those with just 10 hours of supervised data. Our findings suggest that SUADA and the combination of SUADA with UADA are promising pathways for future research in low-data ASR scenarios. Finally, we evaluate the impact of various UADA loss functions on the performance of these methods. We introduce a novel self-supervised loss function that outperforms existing methods and offer insights into its application to enhance ASR system performance. Our proposed UADA loss functions are available on GitHub. This work was conducted as part of the EuCAP 2021 conference. This paper introduces a new method for robot navigation and control, termed "Profound Active Inference" (PAI). Unlike traditional approaches that depend on pre-defined reward functions, PAI generates its own rewards by internally representing the world and the robot's place within it. This capability eliminates the need for time-consuming reward engineering. We evaluated PAI against two established algorithms—Deep Q-Learning (DQN) and Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG)—across two problems: a simplified independent multi-robot navigation task and a complex, realistic simulation featuring a 1:1 scale mobile robot moving through a real university campus. The study aimed to determine if PAI could match the performance of trained robots while significantly reducing the development time required for reward function creation. Our results demonstrate that PAI outperforms both DDPDG and DQN on these problems. Specifically, compared to human-designed rewards, PAI achieves a 99.5% reduction in development time for simple navigation tasks and a 97.1% reduction for realistic campus environments. Consequently, PAI offers a more efficient alternative to active inference and other world-modeling-based control strategies. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/robertkelly1/ProfoundActiveInference. Through a combination of theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, we demonstrate that the internal mobility of flexible molecules significantly influences the Soret effect in binary liquid systems. Specifically, our findings indicate that the activation energy associated with internal conformational transitions is not a determining factor for the Soret coefficient; rather, the efficacy of this internal degree of freedom in enhancing the Soret effect relies instead on the ratio of internal to external activation energies and the average potential energy of internal states. These insights are derived from a simplified yet representative model of internally soft molecules and are expected to hold true for a broader range of systems. Consequently, our results provide a viable strategy for improving the photothermal radiometry (PTR) signal in polymer materials by selecting appropriate monomers, thereby increasing the sensitivity of nondestructive testing (NDT) methods that rely on PTR. Finally, we outline several promising avenues for future research in this field. [Note: This work was conducted prior to the publication of the comprehensive theory by J. Chem. Automated Composition Evaluation (ACE) assesses student essays by grading them according to a rubric based on responses to specific prompts. While deep neural networks (DNNs) have been employed to address this task, their performance lags significantly behind human graders. This study investigates whether pre-trained transformer-based language models (LMs) can enhance composition grading. Although these models excel at reading comprehension, they struggle to grade essays effectively because they fail to capture the non-linear relationship between prompts and responses. To address this, we introduce a novel method that leverages the strengths of transformer-based LMs for ACE. First, we develop a new data augmentation technique to generate more diverse (p, r) pairs from existing data. Second, we propose a new essay representation method that integrates information from both the prompt and the essay without overfitting. Experimental results on two datasets, CHINESE-SEED and CHINESE-CMEE, demonstrate that our approach yields state-of-the-art performance. False positives are a primary hurdle in domain adaptive pedestrian identification, where models trained on a source domain are tested on a target domain. Unlike false negatives, which are common in all machine learning tasks, false positives are distinct because they are unsuitable for automated pipelines, such as those involving re-ranking. This occurs because most systems cannot verify or retrieve the specific identities behind these detections. We demonstrate that these false positives can be mitigated by training a separate classifier on the target domain using only positive detections derived from the primary domain-adaptive model. To enable unsupervised propagation of this classifier, we introduce box-level re-ranking, a method that leverages the model's own predictions to enhance its classification capabilities. Our approach, Box-R, is domain-agnostic and can be applied to any detection and identification model. We evaluate its impact on domain shift using state-of-the-art pedestrian identification models, showing that it reduces false positives by 15.5% on average across three real-world datasets. Furthermore, we observe that domain adaptation is not required for most applications, as our method achieves results comparable to supervised baselines. These findings underscore the potential of our method for developing more robust and generalizable computer vision systems. The code is accessible at https://github.com/robertkoster/box-re-ranking. Finally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the method's failure cases to guide future improvements. By addressing false positives, Box-R represents a significant step toward safer and more reliable computer vision applications. Our failure analysis reveals that the method is highly robust, with the most common failure mode being the re-ranking of a small subset of false positives. Additionally, we show that the method is less effective in dense crowds, where the benefit is reduced due to increased competition among pedestrians. Overall, Box-R is a promising solution for enhancing the reliability of pedestrian identification systems in real-world settings. We hope this work will inspire further research into the generalization capabilities of machine learning models. The detailed failure analysis can be found in our supplementary material. In summary, our work advances the reliability of computer vision systems by effectively addressing false positives. The code for Box-R is available at https://github.com/robertkoster/box-re-ranking. This paper introduces a novel audio enhancement technique based a convolutional neural network that converts audio into a visual format, specifically a Mel spectrogram with neural darkening, before converting it back to audio. The primary advantage of this approach is its model-agnostic nature, allowing any existing audio enhancer to improve the fidelity of the resulting audio. We evaluate various neural audio enhancers and their corresponding visualizers using the test set of the open-source FFMPEG Audiophile Test (FFMAT). Our results indicate that a straightforward combination of the 32kHz Audiophile Enhancement (AEE) system and the Audiophile Visual Enhancement (AVEE) system yields the highest quality audio. Additionally, a secondary experimental model is proposed to convert audio directly to the Mel spectrogram, bypassing the initial audio enhancer step. Finally, we offer some concluding remarks and potential directions for future research. Overall, this research aims to facilitate the creation of the most high-fidelity audio possible. By focusing on audio quality rather than musical features, we advance the field of audio visualisation and contribute to the development of a new category of audio enhancers designed to produce the highest possible fidelity. Furthermore, this work may foster the emergence of a new field dedicated to the study of audio visualisation. Specifically, the proposed AVEE system could be utilized to create a custom visualizer for a visual listening neural enhancer. Additionally, AVEE-enhanced visualizers could serve as neural audio enhancers for the visual modality. Finally, we propose a new field of study centered on the perception of audio quality. However, we argue that a more accurate and comprehensive method for assessing audio quality enhancers involves a more objective and holistic approach to human perception. By incorporating a more complete understanding of human auditory perception, we can develop neural audio enhancers capable of producing the highest possible fidelity. This proposed field of audio quality perception represents a fundamental shift in how we evaluate and enhance audio fidelity. Ultimately, this research aims to facilitate the creation of the highest quality audio possible. Through this pursuit of audio fidelity, we aim to advance the field of audio visualisation and contribute to the development of the most high-fidelity audio experience achievable. Humans frequently make and learn from mistakes. In the context of throwing, a critical error involves releasing the object at an incorrect angle or distance, which dictates the final release parameters. This study examines the impact of such a specific error, known as "incorrect point of release" (IPR), by analyzing how the visual system manages the transition from reaching and releasing to actually releasing. We investigated whether IPR disrupts the planned release trajectory, alters the timing of the motor switch from reaching to releasing, or causes a reconfiguration of reaching parameters. Using a novel experimental approach, we recruited participants to throw while deliberately releasing at an IPR. Our results indicate that IPR does not significantly affect the switch from reaching to releasing, nor does it reconfigure reaching parameters. However, we observed that the deviation from the planned release trajectory increases. These findings suggest that the feedforward motor plan remains largely unaffected by IPR, yet the thrower must dynamically adjust the throw mid-flight to compensate for the unexpected release location. This raises the question of how such adjustments are executed. We demonstrate that IPR does not degrade online control, and the observed adjustments are made with the same precision as under normal conditions. Furthermore, we show that these corrections rely on a feedforward strategy, indicating that the thrower anticipates the necessary modifications. Finally, we demonstrate that IPR does not impact memory for reaching and releasing. Collectively, these results suggest that the effects of IPR are primarily confined to the throw's spatial accuracy, with the mechanisms responsible for correcting this error remaining unclear. This highlights a critical link between the reach-release-release sequence and the visual system's ability to manage the complexity of throwing. Future research should explore the mechanisms that allow the visual system to handle IPR without compromising other aspects of the throw. Our results also offer a novel perspective on the relationship between the reach-release-release sequence and visual processing during throwing. Specifically, IPR does not affect the transition from reaching to releasing, but it does influence the throw's spatial accuracy. This suggests that the visual system's role in throwing begins at the end of the reaching phase, initiating the release phase, and culminates in the throw corrections that ensure accurate targeting. These findings provide valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying throwing and the learning process involved in mastering this complex motor skill. Understanding how IPR affects throwing could help develop new training methods to improve throwing accuracy and efficiency. We introduce a straightforward yet effective method for performing simultaneous neural machine translation (MT) and parsing by integrating grammatical structure from a pre-trained parsing model into the decoding phase of an MT model. This approach, which leverages a tree-structured syntax-link mask to direct self-attention within the MT model and employs an enhanced beam search to respect grammatical constraints during decoding, LLM-based evaluations show that it substantially enhances joint parsing and translation performance with zero training. Furthermore, it significantly improves translation quality on low-resource languages without compromising the existing translation performance of the MT model. By facilitating the combination of the complementary strengths of both models, our technique offers a promising pathway for advancing the simultaneous execution of multiple NLP tasks. Code is available at: https://github.com/taehyunglee97/Syntactic-Link-Mask.

The binding energy (BE) of molecules onto icy grains is a critical parameter governing chemical reactions on dust particles in the interstellar medium (ISM) and circumstellar environments. This study introduces the Binding Energy Assessment Platform (BEAP), a newly developed database containing 1,000+ BE values derived from 10 distinct theoretical methods. These data were generated using 18,000 individual calculations involving 250 molecules (ranging from 2 to 10 atoms) adsorbed on amorphous water ice surfaces. BEAP is freely accessible online and is designed to enable researchers to evaluate the reliability of various BE calculation methods and ice surface models. The dataset covers a broad spectrum of chemical classes, including hydrocarbons, water-bearing species, and ions, with adsorption BEs spanning from 0.12 to 0.90 eV. Additionally, BEAP includes adsorption sites on ice surfaces and analyzes BE variations based on molecular size, polarity, and acid-base characteristics. This work represents a significant advancement in enhancing the accuracy and reliability of BE data for astrochemical and planetary science modeling. BEAP can be accessed at https://beap.astro.ubc.ca. Assessing expectation values is a fundamental task in quantum information processing. We introduce a variation termed "shallow shade," which computes the average of a target operator's expectation values over random quantum circuits. By adjusting circuit depth, users can tune the trade-off between bias and variance. This protocol leverages the isotropic moment expansion to evaluate bias and utilizes the central limit theorem for statistical analysis. Notably, the shallow shade problem is QMA-complete, even when considering only a single term in the isotropic expansion. Furthermore, we demonstrate that shallow shades can be simulated on a classical computer with a cost that scales polynomially with the target operator's size and the inverse of the bias, while remaining exponential in the circuit's depth. This work offers a systematic framework for designing shallow shade problems tailored to specific applications. As a practical application, we illustrate how shallow shades can assist in identifying phase transition points in many-body systems and in locating the ground state of Hamiltonians within gapped phases. Additionally, we show that shallow shades can facilitate the generation of entanglement between two subsystems separated by a qubit chain, utilizing a figure of merit that scales polynomially with $N$, the chain length. Finally, we present a variational algorithm capable of preparing the ground state of the ferromagnetic Heisenberg model using the shallow shade problem. Our findings suggest that shallow shades are well-suited for current and near-term quantum hardware. We have made the associated code accessible to the community. Ensuring robust text categorization is a critical challenge, particularly given the dynamic nature of language, which evolves through slang, new terms, and shifting connotations. These linguistic shifts can cause category labels to become outdated or ambiguous. To address this, we introduce a novel, general, and data-driven methodology utilizing synonym replacements to enhance model robustness. Our approach features a new, straightforward metric designed to quantify synonymy, an efficient and precise sampling strategy for generating hard examples, and a new objective function that optimally balances prediction accuracy and robustness. We validate this framework on a large-scale news categorization dataset, demonstrating that it yields more robust models without compromising overall performance. Furthermore, we show that the robustness mechanism inadvertently mitigates category label aging, resulting in higher F1 scores when evaluated against a vocabulary constructed from a later time period. Finally, we release a comprehensive collection of robust categorization benchmarks to facilitate future research in this domain. Our findings indicate that even without fine-tuning, pre-trained language models can be made robust through categorization training in under an hour, offering a highly cost-effective solution for both industry and academic applications. We introduce a novel category of visual illustration designed to support meta-learning with minimal data. In these illustrations, each class is represented by a distinct color applied to a consistent visual element (e.g., cat, dog, bird, frog), enabling the model to associate features with specific classes across various instances of this element. We present Learning Linear Illustrations (LLI), a new method capable of automatically determining the visual element for a given set of classes through an elegant linear dynamical system. Experiments across diverse datasets and configurations demonstrate that LLI achieves performance comparable to or better than state-of-the-art approaches requiring substantial amounts of data. Furthermore, we highlight the significant advantages of LLI for few-shot learning. The code and illustrations are publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashkanf/LLI.

Low-resource multilingual machine translation (LRMT) is essential for facilitating language services in regions lacking sufficient training data. A promising strategy involves training an extractor model to isolate language-specific segments from a many-to-many multilingual model, allowing these models to maintain a many-to-many architecture while achieving a mony-to-one output mapping. Our research investigates whether this technique is robust enough to function effectively when applied to freely available, pre-trained many-source hierarchical transformer models, which are then distilled. Specifically, we assess stability across different extractions, LR languages, multilingual architectures, and distillation configurations. By analyzing performance shifts between the full pre-trained many-source model and the distilled many-to-many intermediate, we identify patterns that explain the observed stability results. We conclude by proposing future directions for the method, such as exploring intermediate checkpoints during pre-training and utilizing stronger backbone models. The code and data required to replicate our findings are available at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/intermediate-extraction. Our repository includes a dataset of 13 many-source multilingual models sourced from the Quantization Extraction Repository. We hope these resources assist researchers in replicating our findings and fostering further investigation into LRMT. Our analysis indicates that the extraction technique is robust enough to support a functional LRMT solution. This paper focuses on the stability of the method, with our findings supporting the robustness of both the approach and the LRMT solution. Our results demonstrate that intermediate extraction yields superior performance, is more robust, and generalizes better across various LR languages. Additionally, we observed that many-to-many architectures tend to be more stable than many-to-many + 1-to-1 setups. We attribute this stability to the hierarchical nature of LRMT models, which prioritize cross-lingual mapping over target language generation. Finally, we note that the pre-trained many-source multilingual models utilized in this study are not representative of typical LRMT models, as they were trained on high-resource languages. We hope this work inspires researchers to investigate the stability of intermediate extraction in many-source multilingual models trained on low-resource languages. The density of the solitary doublegraph, interpreted as a two-quark particle named diquark, serves as an initial application of hyperphysics. The resulting action principle and its associated conservation laws are expressed in terms of surface functionals defined on the manifolds of space and time. A specific application to Newtonian mechanics demonstrates that the solitary doublegraph moves at a constant velocity within a flat spacetime described as a double atlas. The term "illogical" is applied to the Lagrangian density of the solitary doublegraph because, unlike the densities of other elementary particles (such as electrons), it cannot be expressed as a product of temporal and spatial components. This characteristic arises because the two surfaces constituting the doublegraph are interdependent, forming a unified manifold rather than existing as separate entities. We introduce a novel approach to reduce the dependency on labeled training data for pixel-level segmentation, a task that typically demands extensive expert annotation. Given the high cost of such labeling, especially for identifying pneumonia regions in chest X-rays, our method avoids direct data usage by employing image enhancements. These enhancements are chosen for their ability to improve segmentation performance while preserving the original image structure. We evaluate four specific transformations: histogram matching, contrast limited adaptive histogram equalization (CLAHE), autoencoder-based data augmentation (AD), and a newly proposed method called differential non-uniform contrast enhancement (DNUCE). For each transformed dataset, we train a U-Net segmentation network. Our findings demonstrate that applying DNUCE to transform training data can lower the required training set size from 1,000 to 200 images while maintaining segmentation performance. This paper investigates the concept of damage, arguing that it cannot be understood without a causal framework. We demonstrate that a widely used definition, which equates damage with an object's missing parts, necessitates an examination of how missingness should be interpreted to align with general causal principles. Drawing an analogy to the removal of confounders in causal diagrams, we propose that missingness must denote active removal rather than mere absence. Furthermore, we show that this revised definition of damage is sufficient to formally establish the principle of composability, which dictates that the damage resulting from the fusion of two systems arises from the intersection of their respective damaged subspaces. Finally, we explore the implications of this composability for defining both fused and hierarchical systems. Collectively, our findings indicate that damage possesses a rigorous mathematical structure rooted in causal structure, a perspective that may inform various applications involving system damage. Additionally, our framework for system fusion offers a versatile tool for addressing diverse challenges in quantum gravity research. Specifically, we extend our definitions of damage and fusion to the context of AdS/CFT, applying our definitions of damage and damageable regions to examples drawn from existing literature. Finally, we examine how our definition of damage informs the entanglement wedge reconstruction problem. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance where damage is employed to investigate reconstruction issues within holography. We conclude by discussing the broader implications of our definitions for field theory and their potential relevance to other areas of quantum gravity. Notably, we offer a new argument supporting the conjecture that black hole damage corresponds to entanglement. Overall, this work provides the first comprehensive formalization of damage and its associated properties.

Keywords: quantum information, quantum field theory, quantum gravity.

Conventional methods typically depend on paired data, where voice sentences in different languages are spoken by the same individual. Such data is often difficult to obtain, and even when available, it is not always publicly accessible. We introduce an unsupervised framework for voice translation that operates without requiring paired data. In this data-free environment, the only necessary inputs are unpaired monolingual speech datasets and text-based parallel corpora across the target language pairs. This data-free strategy significantly lowers the data requirements for voice translation tasks. Furthermore, this approach facilitates zero-shot voice translation, enabling voice generation between two languages for which no direct training examples exist. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance compared to supervised approaches on in-distribution tasks and exhibits promising capabilities for zero-shot voice translation.
